item.title: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS)
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon ECS, GPU sharing, NVIDIA MPS, tasks, infrastructure costs

Summary: Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing through NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), allowing multiple ECS tasks to run simultaneously on a single NVIDIA GPU. This feature optimizes GPU utilization and lowers infrastructure costs for workloads that require only a fraction of a GPU's capabilities, such as small-model inference and AV/ADAS simulations. With GPU sharing, users can deploy more workloads on each GPU instance without needing to alter application code. Users specify the required GPU memory for each container and can limit GPU compute allocation. Amazon ECS efficiently schedules tasks based on available GPU capacity as services scale. The GPU sharing feature is compatible with both Amazon ECS Managed Instances and ECS on EC2. Notably, Amazon ECS monitors the MPS control daemon on Managed Instances. If the daemon fails or becomes unhealthy, ECS automatically replaces the instance, ensuring uninterrupted GPU workload operations without manual intervention. To utilize this feature, users can set it up via the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or infrastructure-as-code tools by defining a capacity provider with NVIDIA GPU instances, determining GPU sharing strategies, and creating a service accordingly. The feature is accessible in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US).

Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS), enabling you to run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU. GPU sharing helps you increase GPU utilization and reduce infrastructure costs for workloads that use only part of a GPU's capacity, such as small-model inference, AV/ADAS simulations, embedding generation, and multi-model serving.

With GPU sharing, you can pack more workloads onto each GPU instance without changing your application code. You define the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally set a maximum share of GPU compute, and Amazon ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale and deploy. GPU sharing is supported on Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. On Amazon ECS Managed Instances, Amazon ECS also monitors the MPS control daemon that enables sharing on each instance. If the daemon stops or becomes unhealthy, Amazon ECS automatically replaces the instance and moves your tasks to healthy capacity, so your GPU workloads keep running without manual intervention.

To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, or other infrastructure-as-code tools to create a capacity provider with NVIDIA GPU instances, set the GPU sharing strategy and memory in the container definition of your task definition, and create a service on that capacity provider. This capability is available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS GPU sharing documentation.

item.title: SageMaker MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, MLflow 3.16, tracing experience, experiment tracking, generative AI

Summary: Amazon SageMaker has launched support for MLflow 3.16, enhancing the tracing experience and speeding up experiment tracking for generative AI and machine learning workflows. The new version focuses on improving debugging and analysis of generative AI applications and agents. Notably, the redesigned trace explorer is now the default interface, offering features such as adjustable row heights, reorderable columns, and the ability to add custom columns based on any trace tag or metadata field. Additionally, MLflow 3.16 significantly accelerates the performance of metric charts for experiments that involve large metric histories. New MLflow Apps will be created on this updated version by default, ensuring users have access to the latest features immediately. For those using existing MLflow Apps, an automatic upgrade to MLflow 3.16 will occur during an upcoming maintenance window, requiring no action from users. MLflow 3.16 is now available in all AWS Regions where MLflow Apps are offered. Users interested in learning more can visit the appropriate page for further details.

Amazon SageMaker AI MLflow Apps now support MLflow 3.16, bringing a redesigned tracing experience and faster experiment tracking to your generative AI and machine learning workflows.

MLflow 3.16 improves debugging and analysis of generative AI applications and agents. The redesigned trace explorer is now the default, with adjustable row height, reorderable columns, custom columns from any trace tag or metadata field. This release also accelerates metric charts for experiments with large metric histories.

New MLflow Apps are created on MLflow 3.16 by default. Existing MLflow Apps will be upgraded to MLflow 3.16 during an upcoming maintenance window, with no action required.

MLflow 3.16 is available in all AWS Regions where MLflow Apps are available. To learn more, visit the SageMaker AI MLflow developer guide.

item.title: Amazon Aurora serverless now supports up to 384 ACUs
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Aurora, serverless, PostgreSQL, ACUs, capacity

Summary: Amazon Aurora now supports up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for its PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, marking a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU offers approximately 2 GiB of memory, allowing a single Aurora serverless database to scale up to 768 GiB of memory. This feature is particularly advantageous for agentic AI applications, which often experience variable workloads with active bursts followed by idle periods. Aurora serverless automatically scales capacity based on usage, enabling users to pay only for the resources consumed, even scaling down to zero when not in use. With the introduction of 384 ACUs, customers can now manage more demanding workloads while still benefiting from the cost-effectiveness of serverless architecture. To take advantage of this new capacity, users can create new clusters with a supported Aurora PostgreSQL engine version or modify existing clusters on Platform Version 4 to update their maximum capacity. There’s no downtime for existing databases running on Platform Version 4 during this modification. Customers using older platform versions need to upgrade to Platform Version 4 via a pending maintenance action to access the expanded capacity. The supported Aurora PostgreSQL versions for 384 ACUs include versions 18.4, 17.10, 16.14, 15.18, and 14.23.

Amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use.

With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For new clusters, select a supported Aurora PostgreSQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to update the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora PostgreSQL versions 18.4, 17.10, 16.14, 15.18, and 14.23, running on Platform Version 4.

To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing.  To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.

item.title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now supports changing durability on existing clusters
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: ElastiCache, durability, synchronous writes, asynchronous writes, AWS Regions

Summary: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey has introduced a feature that allows users to enable or disable durability on existing node-based clusters without needing to create a new cluster. Previously, changing the durability configuration in place was not possible, complicating the transition from caching to persistent data storage as application needs evolved. Now, developers can adjust durability at any point in their application's lifecycle. The service offers two durability options: synchronous and asynchronous writes. Synchronous writes ensure data is persisted across at least two Availability Zones (AZs) before client acknowledgment, achieving zero data loss with low write latency. In contrast, asynchronous writes offer microsecond write latency after the client is responded to, with a potential loss of up to 10 seconds of uncommitted data during rare failures. Both options retain microsecond read latency. This enhancement broadens ElastiCache's applicability to use cases where data loss is unacceptable, such as AI agent long-term memory, payment tokenization, and real-time inventory management. The feature is available in all AWS Regions with ElastiCache for Valkey 9.0 and later, and it can be accessed via the AWS Management Console, SDK, or CLI.

Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now lets you enable or disable durability on your existing node-based clusters without creating a new cluster. Previously, you couldn't change the durability configuration of an existing cluster in place. This made it harder to move from caching to persistent data store use cases, or to adapt as your application requirements change. Now you can change durability at any point in your application's lifecycle.

You can choose between two durability options: synchronous and asynchronous writes. Synchronous writes persist data across at least two AZs before responding to the client, designed for zero data loss at single-digit millisecond write latency. Asynchronous writes persist data after responding to the client, maintaining microsecond write latency at no additional cost. However, up to 10 seconds of uncommitted data could be lost in the rare event of a failure. Both options maintain microsecond read latency. You can now use ElastiCache for a broader set of use cases beyond caching where data loss is unacceptable such as AI agent long-term memory, AI agent workflow state, knowledge bases for RAG applications, payment tokenization, and real-time inventory management.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where ElastiCache for Valkey 9.0 and later is available. To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS SDK, or AWS CLI. For pricing, see the  Amazon ElastiCache pricing page . To learn more, see  Durability  in the ElastiCache documentation.

item.title: Amazon Corretto October 2026 Patch Updates
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon, Corretto, OpenJDK, patch update, LTS

Summary: On October 26, 2026, Amazon announced a patch update for several versions of Amazon Corretto, which includes Long-Term Support (LTS) and Feature Release (FR) versions of OpenJDK. The updated versions are Corretto 27.0.1.0.11, 25.0.5.0.10, 21.0.13.0.11, 17.0.21.0.11, 11.0.33.0.10, and 8u512. Amazon Corretto is highlighted as a no-cost, production-ready distribution of OpenJDK that is available across multiple platforms. Users are encouraged to visit the Corretto website to download the new updates for Corretto 27, 25, 21, 17, 11, or 8. Additionally, users on Linux systems can obtain the updates by configuring their systems accordingly. This release aims to ensure that users have access to the latest security and performance improvements in their Java development environment. Amazon emphasizes its commitment to providing reliable, open-source tools for developers and organizations by making these updates readily accessible. Users are encouraged to provide feedback on the updates, contributing to the improvement of the Corretto distribution.

On October 26, 2026 Amazon announced a patch update for the following Amazon Corretto Long-Term Support (LTS) and Feature Release (FR) versions of OpenJDK. Corretto 27.0.1.0.11, 25.0.5.0.10, 21.0.13.0.11, 17.0.21.0.11, 11.0.33.0.10, and 8u512 are now available for download. Amazon Corretto is a no-cost, multi-platform, production-ready distribution of OpenJDK.

Visit the Corretto home page to download Corretto 27, Corretto 25, Corretto 21, Corretto 17, Corretto 11, or Corretto 8. You can also get the updates on your Linux system by configuring a Corretto Apt, Yum, or Apk repo.

Feedback is welcomed!

item.title: Amazon Neptune now supports online index rebuild to reclaim storage
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: online index rebuild, Amazon Neptune, fragmentation, performance tuning, database maintenance

Summary: Online index rebuild is a new feature available in Amazon Neptune engine release 1.5.0.0, allowing database administrators to defragment indexes without taking the database offline. Over time, data operations like inserts, updates, and deletes can create unused space, artificially inflating the VolumeBytesUsed metric and degrading query performance. This fragmentation adversely affects workload performance for Gremlin, openCypher, or SPARQL queries. With online index rebuild, both read and write queries remain uninterrupted during the rebuilding process, ensuring continuous access. Users can target all indexes, only quad indexes, or just dictionary indexes, making this feature ideal for post-deletion cleanup, regular maintenance, storage management, and performance tuning on fragmented databases. The feature includes tunable settings for concurrency and write buffer size, enabling a balance between rebuild speed and workload impact. Additionally, built-in safety mechanisms help protect against storage exhaustion during operations. Online index rebuild is supported in all regions where Amazon Neptune Database is available, enhancing the efficiency and performance of Neptune databases significantly. For configuration and execution guidance, users can refer to the official API documentation.

Amazon Neptune Database now supports online index rebuild, a new capability that helps database administrators and application teams defragment Neptune indexes and reclaim unused storage space without taking their database offline. Over time, insert, update, and delete operations create gaps of unused space within data pages, keeping the VolumeBytesUsed metric artificially elevated even after data is deleted. This fragmentation increases I/O costs and degrades query performance for teams running Gremlin, openCypher, or SPARQL workloads at scale.

With online index rebuild, read and write queries continue uninterrupted on both the writer instance and read replicas throughout the entire rebuild process. You can target all indexes, only quad indexes, or only dictionary indexes, making this feature well-suited for post-deletion cleanup, periodic maintenance, storage limit management, and performance tuning on heavily fragmented databases. Tunable concurrency and write buffer size settings let you balance rebuild speed against workload impact, while built-in storage safety mechanisms protect against storage exhaustion during the operation.

Online index rebuild is available starting with Amazon Neptune engine release 1.5.0.0 on provisioned writer instances, in all regions where Amazon Neptune Database is supported. To learn more about configuring and running online index rebuild, including API references and tuning guidance, visit the Amazon Neptune documentation.

item.title: Amazon ECR now supports replication backfill for existing container images
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon ECR, replication backfill, private registry, API call, AWS Regions

Summary: Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) has introduced replication backfill, allowing users to replicate existing images in their private registries to configured replication registry destinations. Previously, replication was limited to images pushed after the replication configuration was enabled, necessitating manual retagging of preexisting images for replication. Now, with replication backfill, customers can replicate their entire image catalog to new or existing destinations with a single API call. This feature is particularly beneficial for users expanding to new AWS Regions, validating disaster recovery processes, updating replication rules, or ensuring complete image catalogs across Regions for compliance. Users can execute up to ten backfill jobs concurrently, monitor the progress, and check per-image results through newly provided APIs. Additionally, they have the flexibility to stop a backfill job at any time without affecting images that have already been replicated. Replication backfill is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR operates. For further details, users are encouraged to refer to official documentation or resources.

Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replication backfill, enabling you to replicate existing images in your private registry to your configured replication registry destinations. Previously, replication only applied to images pushed after the replication configuration was enabled, requiring customers to manually retag images to trigger replication of preexisting images. With replication backfill, you can now replicate your full image catalog to new or existing destinations with a single API call.

Replication backfill is useful when expanding to a new AWS Region, validating disaster recovery readiness, updating replication rules, or ensuring complete image catalogs exist across Regions for compliance purposes. You can run up to ten backfill jobs concurrently, monitor progress and per-image results through new APIs, and stop a job at any time without deleting images that have already been replicated.

Replication backfill is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is available. To learn more, refer to the Amazon ECR user guide.

item.title: Amazon IVS Low-Latency Streaming now provides a failover slate
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon IVS, low-latency streaming, failover slate, audience retention, live playback

Summary: Amazon Interactive Video Service (Amazon IVS) has introduced a failover slate feature for low-latency streaming, which displays an animated image to viewers when a broadcaster's stream experiences unexpected interruptions. This solution replaces the buffering wheel or a frozen frame with a slate, ensuring that viewers see a continuous visual experience while waiting for reconnection. Once the broadcaster reconnects, live playback resumes automatically without requiring viewers to refresh their players. The failover slate is particularly beneficial for broadcasters using mobile devices or operating in areas with unstable connectivity, helping to retain audience engagement during brief disruptions. Users can enable this feature on both new and existing channels, enhancing the overall streaming experience. Additionally, the feature can be monitored through Amazon EventBridge events and Amazon CloudWatch metrics, providing valuable insights into slate activity. Amazon IVS serves as a managed live streaming solution designed to deliver low-latency or real-time video to a global audience. For more information, users can visit the Amazon IVS console to check the full list of AWS Regions where the service is available. Further details can also be accessed through related documentation.

Amazon Interactive Video Service (Amazon IVS) Low-Latency Streaming now provides a failover slate, an animated image that IVS displays to viewers when a broadcaster's stream is unexpectedly interrupted. Instead of a buffering wheel or frozen frame, viewers see the slate until the broadcaster reconnects. Live playback then resumes automatically, without viewers needing to refresh their player.

The failover slate helps you retain your audience during momentary disruptions and is ideal for broadcasters streaming from mobile devices or from locations with unreliable connectivity. You can enable the failover slate on new or existing channels and monitor slate activity with Amazon EventBridge events and Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

Amazon IVS is a managed live streaming solution designed to make low-latency or real-time video available to viewers around the world. Visit the AWS Region table for a full list of AWS Regions where the Amazon IVS console and APIs for control and creation of video streams are available.

To learn more, see the Amazon IVS Failover Slate documentation.

item.title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports endpoint connection management
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: endpoint registry, cross-account sharing, MediaConnect, AWS RAM, live video workflows

Summary: The new endpoint registry in AWS Elemental MediaConnect enables centralized management of external connections, including standard endpoints like cameras and software, as well as connections to other AWS accounts. This feature supports direct sharing of registered endpoints with other AWS accounts, which streamlines live video workflows across organizations. By facilitating cross-account endpoint sharing, it reduces costs by minimizing the number of required compute instances and decreases latency by lowering the number of network hops needed for live content sharing. The endpoint registry eliminates manual tasks such as chaining router inputs and outputs, coordinating IP addresses, and managing connection security. Users can leverage a single interface to manage all external connections to MediaConnect, benefiting from AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) for cross-account sharing, transparent verification of encryption and protocol controls, and built-in connection management through Connection Manager. Potential use cases include content distributors sharing live feeds with partners, broadcasters collaborating across different organizations, and secure media workflows needing cross-account video transport. The MediaConnect endpoint registry is accessible in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router operates, with no additional cost involved. For further details, refer to the AWS Elemental MediaConnect documentation.

AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports managing external connections through a new endpoint registry. The registry provides a centralized interface to register and manage both standard endpoints—devices or software outside the service, such as cameras, sources, monitors, and other destinations—and connections to other AWS accounts. You can share registered endpoints directly with other AWS accounts, streamlining cross-account live video workflows. 

Cross-account endpoint sharing lowers costs by reducing required compute instances and decreases latency through fewer network hops when sharing live content across AWS accounts.. It also eliminates the need to manually chain router inputs and outputs, coordinate IP addresses out of band, and manage connection security. The endpoint registry gives you a single interface to manage all external connections to MediaConnect for seamless integration with your existing infrastructure. You get cross-account sharing through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), transparent verification of encryption and protocol controls, and built-in connection management with Connection Manager. Use cases include content distributors sharing live feeds with downstream partners, broadcasters collaborating across organizational boundaries, and media workflows that require secure cross-account video transport.

MediaConnect endpoint registry is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router is available, at no additional cost. For more information, see the AWS Elemental MediaConnect User Guide.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to use flow modules in agentic CX designer
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, flow modules, customer experience, AWS Lambda, agentic AI

Summary: Amazon Connect Customer has introduced flow modules that allow for data requests within the agentic CX designer, enabling reusable logic across customer experience flows. These flow modules can be executed at specific steps via a Data request node or utilized as tools in a Generative journey. You can leverage these modules to update customer profiles and cases, create tasks, look up data tables, send SMS confirmations, or verify operational hours and staffing before escalating to a human agent. Additionally, they facilitate access to data within private networks, such as banking or claims information. For instance, a flow module can call an AWS Lambda function in a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to fetch an account balance or claim status during an interaction. The feature is currently available in several AWS Regions, including US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), and various locations in Asia Pacific and Europe. For further details, consult the Connect Customer documentation or visit the Amazon Connect Customer website to learn more about this agentic AI solution.

Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to use flow modules as data requests in agentic CX designer, so you can build and apply reusable logic across your customer experience flows. You can run a flow module at a fixed step in a conversation with a Data request node, or give it to a Generative journey as a tool to call when the conversation needs it.

With this launch, you can use flow modules to update customer profiles and cases, create tasks, look up data tables, send an SMS confirmation, or check hours of operation and staffing before escalating to a human agent. You can also retrieve data that sits inside a private network, such as core banking, policy, or claims systems. For example, a flow module can invoke an AWS Lambda function in your VPC to return an account balance or claim status in the middle of an interaction.

This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). To learn more, refer to Data requests and Flow modules in the Connect Customer documentation. To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Terra, Amazon Bedrock, enterprise

Summary: AWS has announced the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra on Amazon Bedrock, which enhances the GPT-6 family with improved capability, speed, and cost efficiency for everyday tasks. This model combines advanced visual reasoning, precise computer usage, and better factuality and writing compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra outperformed its predecessor by 15 percentage points, matched the performance of GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. It offers lower input and output token prices, at least 50% less than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra, and supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens, accepting both text and image inputs. Featuring an efficient inference engine, it is designed to meet the demands of enterprise workloads. Users can access GPT-6.1 Terra via Amazon Bedrock APIs or through ChatGPT Work and Codex integration. Applications range from drafting proposals to interpreting technical drawings. AWS provides controls for security, access governance, and auditing of model activity, making it easy to start via the Amazon Bedrock console or APIs.

Today, AWS announces the general availability of OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra on Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6.1 Terra expands the GPT-6 family with a balance of capability, speed, and cost efficiency for everyday workloads. 

As the newest model in the Terra line, GPT-6.1 Terra combines detailed visual reasoning, accurate computer use, and improved factuality and natural writing over GPT-5.6 Terra, for complex workflows. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. GPT-6.1 Terra offers balanced performance with input and output token prices at least 50% lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It supports a context window of up to 1 million input tokens and accepts both text and image inputs. The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and scale required for enterprise workloads. 

You can call GPT-6.1 Terra directly through Amazon Bedrock APIs or configure ChatGPT Work and Codex to use the model on Amazon Bedrock. Use it to draft proposals, interpret technical drawings, investigate codebases, and build agents that operate across business systems.  Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. 

You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

item.title: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports ModifyVolume API
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon WorkSpaces, ModifyVolume API, volume modification, managed instances, Amazon EBS

Summary: Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances has introduced the ModifyVolume API, enabling users to modify storage configurations without needing to detach volumes or restart instances. Previously, making changes to storage capacity or performance required rebuilding the instance, which was inconvenient. With this new API, users can increase volume sizes up to 16,384 GiB, switch between supported Amazon EBS volume types, and adjust IOPS for gp3, io1, and io2 volumes. Additionally, users can modify the throughput for gp3 volumes. The ModifyVolume API includes support for idempotency tokens, ensuring that duplicate changes are prevented. Users can also monitor the progress of their modifications using the Amazon EC2 DescribeVolumesModifications operation. This functionality is now available in all AWS Regions that support Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances. To utilize the ModifyVolume API, users can call it directly or integrate it through their WorkSpaces Core partner solutions when available. For more information, users are encouraged to check the WorkSpaces Instances API Reference and the Amazon EBS User Guide.

Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances now supports the ModifyVolume API, which lets you change volume size, volume type, IOPS, or throughput in place, without detaching the volume or restarting the instance. Previously, changing storage capacity or performance on a deployed managed instance required rebuilding it.

With ModifyVolume, you can increase volume size up to 16,384 GiB, switch between supported Amazon EBS volume types, adjust IOPS for gp3, io1, and io2 volumes, and modify throughput for gp3 volumes. The API supports idempotency tokens to prevent duplicate changes, and you can track progress with the Amazon EC2 DescribeVolumesModifications operation.

ModifyVolume is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces Core Managed Instances is available.

To get started, call ModifyVolume directly, or use it through your WorkSpaces Core partner solution once available. To learn more, see ModifyVolume in the WorkSpaces Instances API Reference and Limitations in the Amazon EBS User Guide, or visit WorkSpaces Core.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio adds light mode support for IDC-based domains
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, light mode, dark mode, visual appearance, accessibility

Summary: AWS has announced the introduction of light mode support in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio for Identity Center (IDC) based domains. Customers can now customize the visual interface to their preference by selecting between dark and light themes, applicable to both IAM-based and IDC-based domains. The addition of light mode enhances readability in bright environments and offers a familiar experience for users who favor lighter interfaces. Coupled with the existing dark mode, this update empowers customers with control over their development environment's appearance, which can enhance accessibility and reduce eye strain under various lighting conditions. Users can access the feature in SageMaker Unified Studio settings by selecting 'Customize appearance' under Profile settings, enabling them to choose between dark mode, light mode, and device settings that align with their operating system's preferences. Furthermore, these settings are designed to persist across different browsers and devices, ensuring a seamless experience. This feature is now available across all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is present, making it widely accessible to users. For more information, users are encouraged to consult the official AWS documentation.

Today, AWS announces light mode support in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio for Identity Center (IDC) based domains. Customers can now configure the visual interface mode to match their preference, choosing between dark and light themes. With this launch, customers can set this visual preference in both IAM-based and IDC-based domains. 

Light mode helps improve readability in bright environments and provides a familiar visual experience for customers who prefer lighter interfaces. Combined with the existing dark mode, this update gives you full control over the appearance of your development environment, improving accessibility and reducing eye strain across varying lighting conditions. In SageMaker Unified Studio settings, you can choose 'Customize appearance' under your Profile settings to select between visual modes including dark mode, light mode, and device setting, which matches your operating system's setting. The setting persists across browsers and devices.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio User Guide.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer expands testing and simulation to validate flow action outcomes
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, customer experience, testing, simulation, Lambda function

Summary: Amazon Connect Customer now offers an enhanced feature that allows users to validate outcomes of customer experience flow actions during testing and simulation. This functionality goes beyond merely confirming the initiation of an action, enabling verification of the data returned upon completion, including responses from Lambda functions, resolved intents from Amazon Lex, or variables set by Agentic CX blocks. When testing fails, users can easily identify the specific action that produced an unexpected result, rather than having to trace back through subsequent steps. This targeted troubleshooting helps in addressing issues more effectively, leading to faster resolutions. Consequently, organizations can implement flow changes with increased confidence, knowing that they can validate their customer experience flows. To learn more about this new feature, users can refer to the Connect Customer administrator guide. Additionally, a comprehensive list of testing and simulation capabilities available by AWS Region can also be found. For further insights into Amazon Connect Customer, an AI-driven solution designed to enhance customer experiences, interested parties are encouraged to visit the official website.

Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to validate the outcomes of your customer experience flow actions during testing and simulation. In addition to confirming that an action started, you can now verify the data it returns when it completes, such as a Lambda function response, an Amazon Lex resolved intent, or the variables set by an Agentic CX block. When a test fails, you can pinpoint the exact action that returned an unexpected result instead of tracing it back from a downstream step, so you can resolve issues faster and launch flow changes with greater confidence.

To learn more about this feature, see testing and simulation in the Connect Customer administrator guide. For a complete list of testing and simulation capabilities available by AWS Region, refer to Availability of Connect Customer features by Region. To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer now lets you view metrics by customer lifetime value and repeat-caller status
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: customer segments, lifetime value, repeat callers, metrics, satisfaction

Summary: This article discusses the importance of analyzing customer segments, particularly focusing on customer lifetime value (LTV) and repeat callers. It highlights how different metrics can reveal variations in performance between repeat callers and other contacts, allowing businesses to identify trends before they become apparent in overall data. By monitoring these segments, organizations can pinpoint areas of underperformance and take proactive measures. For instance, high-LTV customers can be routed to the most effective team members to enhance service quality. Additionally, businesses can optimize knowledge bases and self-service options that repeat callers might be struggling with, ensuring these resources remain effective. The article also emphasizes the need to refine agent guidance for segments experiencing a decline in customer satisfaction. By leveraging the insights gained from segment analysis, companies can identify specific areas requiring attention or improvement. This targeted approach allows organizations to focus their efforts on the segments that need it most, ultimately leading to enhanced customer experience and satisfaction.

Now you can view your metrics across customer segments: customer lifetime value (LTV) and repeat callers. See how any metric differs for repeat callers versus the rest of your contacts, or how results hold up among your highest-LTV customers; so you can spot the groups trending the wrong way before it shows up in the aggregate. Where a segment is underperforming, you can act. Route high-LTV customers to your most effective people, adjust the knowledge bases and self-service flows that repeat callers are falling back from, or refine agent guidance for segments where satisfaction is slipping. The segment tells you where to look; the metrics tell you what to fix.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer now measures the outcomes that drive retention and revenue
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, customer interactions, metrics, analytics, success.

Summary: Amazon Connect now allows customers to score the outcomes of their interactions, providing insights into customer satisfaction, churn risk, purchase behavior, and self-service resolution. This enhancement enables businesses to evaluate not only the efficiency of interactions but also their effectiveness in meeting customer needs. Each interaction metric is accompanied by a default definition, which businesses can customize to align with their specific success criteria, ensuring a tailored approach to performance measurement. These metrics are accessible through both analytics dashboards and application programming interfaces (APIs), offering companies flexible options for tracking customer engagement and satisfaction over time. This development marks a significant shift in how businesses can analyze customer interactions, moving beyond traditional operational metrics to focus on real results and outcomes that matter to the customer experience. By integrating these scoring capabilities into their operations, companies can better understand their performance in relation to customer expectations, leading to improved strategies for enhancing satisfaction and reducing churn. Overall, Amazon Connect's new features provide a powerful toolset for businesses to better understand their customer interactions and drive effective outcomes.

Amazon Connect Customer now scores the outcome of your customer interactions. It shows whether the customer left satisfied, is at risk of churning, made a purchase, or resolved their need in self-service. You can now see whether an interaction worked, not just how efficiently it ran. Each metric comes with a default definition you can adjust to match how your business defines success and are available both through the analytics dashboards and APIs.

item.title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: trusted identity propagation, AWS Regions, permissions, IAM Identity Center, fine-grained access control

Summary: Trusted identity propagation allows a user's identity to accompany their requests, enabling AWS services to grant permissions based on individual user identities and group associations. This capability enhances auditing by logging access activity per user. With the introduction of cross-Region support, identity context can now be propagated to AWS services operating in different AWS Regions, providing users with increased flexibility in architecture and deployment across regions. Customers often utilize multiple AWS Regions to better manage workloads, whether for separating compute from data queries or ensuring disaster recovery. Previously, trusted identity propagation was limited to services within the same region, necessitating broad IAM roles or regional consolidation. Now, with cross-Region trusted identity propagation, a user's identity seamlessly travels with requests, allowing for precise access control and detailed auditing across regions. This feature is available at no extra cost in all AWS Regions that support IAM Identity Center. Refer to the IAM Identity Center User Guide for a complete list of eligible regions.

Trusted identity propagation carries a user's identity with their request, so AWS services can grant permissions based on who the user is and their underlying group associations, and log that user's access for auditing. With cross-Region support, this identity context can now be propagated to AWS services running in different AWS Regions, giving you greater flexibility in how you architect and deploy across AWS Regions.

Customers often distribute workloads across AWS Regions for many reasons including separating the compute from the data it queries, to running workloads where capacity is available, or for disaster recovery and global scale. Previously, trusted identity propagation required all of the AWS services accessing a user's identity to reside in the same AWS Region. To reach services in another AWS Region, customers had to either grant access through broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users or consolidate all their services into a single AWS Region. With cross-Region trusted identity propagation, a user's identity travels with the request across AWS Regions automatically, so you can grant access based on who the user is and their underlying group associations, and audit who accessed which resources, while preserving fine-grained access control for every individual user.

Cross-Region trusted identity propagation is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. For the list of Regions where IAM Identity Center is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region.  For more information, see Trusted identity propagation in the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

item.title: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, KMS, ML-KEM, post-quantum cryptography, shared secret

Summary: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now incorporates the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), a post-quantum cryptography standard established by NIST, aimed at enhancing secure key exchange. ML-KEM is designed to supersede traditional key-establishment mechanisms like Diffie-Hellman (DH), Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), and RSA-based key transport. It specifically mitigates the "harvest now, decrypt later" vulnerability that allows future adversaries with quantum capabilities to compromise previously recorded exchanges. KMS supports three ML-KEM specifications defined in NIST FIPS 203: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. The Encapsulate API generates a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext using the public key, while the Decapsulate API retrieves the shared secret via the corresponding private key. Security is enhanced as KMS safeguards the private key within FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). The public key can be retrieved using the GetPublicKey API for distribution to partners or external systems for local encapsulation using cryptographic libraries like AWS-LC, OpenSSL, or Bouncy Castle. ML-KEM is currently available in all AWS Regions, except the Middle East (UAE), Middle East (Bahrain), and China Regions.

AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now supports Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), a post-quantum cryptography standard under NIST FIPS 203, which enables two parties to establish a shared secret. NIST designed ML-KEM to replace the classical key-establishment schemes, like DH/ECDH key agreement, and RSA-based key transport, in their strategic cryptographic roadmap (see NIST IR 8547). ML-KEM addresses the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat to those classical schemes, where an adversary records the key-establishment exchange today and recovers the shared secret once sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available.

KMS supports all three ML-KEM key specs defined in NIST FIPS 203: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. The Encapsulate API uses the public key to produce a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext form. The Decapsulate API recovers the shared secret from ciphertext using the corresponding private key. KMS protects the private key of an ML-KEM key pair in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). You can use the GetPublicKey API to export the public key and distribute it to partners, client applications, or external systems for performing the encapsulate operation locally using cryptographic libraries like AWS-LC, OpenSSL, or Bouncy Castle.

ML-KEM is available in all AWS Regions where KMS is available, except the the Middle East (UAE), Middle East (Bahrain), and China Regions. For more information, see Key spec reference in the AWS KMS Developer Guide.

item.title: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now supports Launch Before Terminate at account-level to replace instances
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, EC2, Auto Scaling, Launch Before Terminate, account settings

Summary: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling has introduced a feature called Launch Before Terminate, which allows users to set it as the default behavior for all Auto Scaling groups within an account. When activated, this feature ensures that a new replacement instance is launched and fully passes health checks prior to terminating the instance it is set to replace. This functionality is crucial for maintaining optimal application capacity and availability during various instance replacement events, such as instance refreshes, rebalancing, health checks, and maximum-instance-lifetime replacements. Users can enable Launch Before Terminate via the AWS EC2 Auto Scaling account settings, allowing for a streamlined configuration process done at the account level instead of managing it for each group separately. This setting can be controlled using the new `PutAccountSetting` and `DescribeAccountSettings` APIs, accessible through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Importantly, the Launch Before Terminate feature is available across all AWS Regions and incurs no additional costs for users. For further information, users are encouraged to reference AWS documentation.

AWS EC2 Auto Scaling now lets you enable Launch Before Terminate as the default replacement behavior across all Auto Scaling groups in your account. When enabled, Auto Scaling launches a replacement instance and waits for it to pass health checks before terminating the instance it replaces, helping your applications maintain full capacity and availability during instance replacement events. This applies to replacement events such as instance refreshes, rebalancing, health checks, and maximum-instance-lifetime replacements.

You can enable Launch Before Terminate through AWS EC2 Auto Scaling account settings, which let you configure the behavior once at the account level instead of on each Auto Scaling group individually. You can manage the setting with the new `PutAccountSetting` and `DescribeAccountSettings` APIs, available through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs.

Launch Before Terminate is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost.

To learn more, see Launch Before Terminate in the AWS EC2 Auto Scaling User Guide and AWS EC2 Auto Scaling API Reference Guide.

item.title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Microsoft SQL Server, Cumulative Updates, General Distribution Release, RDS version, upgrades

Summary: The latest release now supports the recent Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates for Microsoft SQL Server. It includes support for the following versions: SQL Server 2017 CU31+GDR (RDS version 14.00.3550.4.v1), SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR (RDS version 15.00.4490.9.v1), SQL Server 2022 CU27 (RDS version 16.00.4295.3.v1), and SQL Server 2025 CU9 (RDS version 17.00.5005.3.v1). Users are encouraged to review the Microsoft documentation for detailed information on the improvements and fixes associated with these updates, referencing KB5122774, KB5122772, KB5104824, and KB5122048 for specifics. To ensure optimal performance and security, it is recommended that users upgrade their Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to include these updates. This can be accomplished through the Amazon RDS Management Console or by utilizing the AWS SDK or CLI. Additionally, more information on the process for upgrading your database instance can be found within the AWS documentation.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for Microsoft SQL Server 2017 CU31+GDR KB5122774 (RDS version 14.00.3550.4.v1), SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR KB5122772 (RDS version 15.00.4490.9.v1), SQL Server 2022 CU27 KB5104824 (RDS version 16.00.4295.3.v1) and SQL Server 2025 CU9 KB5122048 (RDS version 17.00.5005.3.v1).

For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5122774, KB5122772, KB5104824 and KB5122048. We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine.

item.title: AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports OAuth for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog APIs
item.content:encoded:
AWS Glue Data Catalog now supports OAuth 2.0 bearer token authentication for Apache Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) APIs using AWS Sign-In. The Apache Iceberg REST Catalog specification defines OAuth 2.0 as its standard authentication mechanism, and query engines such as Apache Spark, Trino, and Apache Flink implement it natively. These engines and external integration partners can now authenticate to the Glue Data Catalog Iceberg endpoint using standard OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens, in addition to AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4).

You can now grant partners federated access to your Iceberg tables without distributing AWS credentials. Using OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), you exchange an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity token for a short-lived, Glue-scoped bearer token and include it in IRC requests following the same standards-based pattern used across the Iceberg ecosystem. Access remains governed by AWS IAM and AWS Lake Formation permissions. Common use cases include enabling third-party analytics and data cloud platforms to query tables in the Glue Data Catalog through a single, consistent authentication path.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Glue and Lake Formation are available. To learn more, see the AWS Glue User Guide and AWS Sign-In User Guide.

Summary: The program highlights the importance of nurturing dreams in children, emphasizing that many young individuals aspire to careers as doctors, inventors, or writers. The speaker, reflecting on their own childhood in East Tennessee, recalls the dreams that motivated them and expresses a genuine belief that the same potential exists within children in the community today. By focusing on the power of literature, the program stresses that books can plant the seeds of these dreams, inspiring children to reach for their aspirations. It encourages community involvement in supporting literacy initiatives, suggesting that small contributions can lead to significant impacts over time. The message is clear: by helping children discover and nurture their dreams through reading, individuals can foster growth not just locally, but globally as well. The program serves as a reminder of the vital role that education and support play in shaping the futures of young dreamers, and it calls upon community members to take action in empowering the next generation to pursue their passions.

With today's news, I thought I'd share this great program:

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.

The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

I was playing around with visualising the S&P 500 by market cap and decided to add employees to each company's bubble.

What surprised me was how empty some of the biggest companies looked.

Nvidia is worth $5.2 trillion but employs only 42,000 people. That's around $124 million in market cap per employee. Meanwhile, Accenture employs 814,000 people and is worth $146 billion.

Each stick figure represents 10,000 employees. You can zoom in and explore individual companies.

I wrote a bit more about what I found here: https://bigwhalehunting.com/blog/workforce/

item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Flight script, Turbopack, lockfile, chunk groups, parallelize

Summary: The inline Flight script has been rebuilt using React's strings, eliminating the need for re-encoding. Additionally, adjustments were made to the dist directory lockfile to ensure compatibility with filesystems that have limited or no lockfile implementations, such as NFS. In terms of performance improvements, Turbopack has seen enhancements where chunk group indices are now looked up through a keyed cell, allowing for more efficient tracking of availability by chunk group. Furthermore, the chunk groups have been refactored and organized by key, and Turbopack is now able to consume graph-derived chunk groups effectively. The turbo-tasks-backend has also benefitted from several updates, including a reduction in SnapshotCoordinator's operation count through striped processing and a polling mechanism for the drain. Large batch lookups have been parallelized to improve decoding efficiency. Finally, in turbo-persistence, it has been noted that the shard count should not shrink before the initial bottom merge takes place. Overall, these changes and improvements contribute to better performance and functionality across the system.

Core Changes

  • Build the inline Flight script from React's strings instead of re-encoding them: #100142
  • Fix dist dir lockfile on filesystems with no or limited lockfile implementations (e.g. NFS): #100684

Misc Changes

  • perf(turbopack): look up chunk group indices through a keyed cell: #99050
  • Turbopack: track availability by chunk group: #98685
  • refactor(turbopack): chunk chunk groups by key: #99750
  • Turbopack: consume graph-derived chunk groups: #98734
  • turbo-tasks-backend: stripe SnapshotCoordinator's operation count and poll for the drain: #100280
  • turbo-tasks-backend: parallelize decoding of large batch lookups: #100453
  • turbo-persistence: don't shrink the shard count before the first bottom merge: #100424

Credits

Huge thanks to @sokra, @lukesandberg, @gaearon, and @bgw for helping!

Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location controls
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Bedrock, domain filtering, user location, Web Search, OpenAI Responses API

Summary: AWS Bedrock has introduced two new controls for the Web Search feature, enhancing the precision of model responses. The first control, domain filtering, allows users to restrict search results to a specific set of domains. By using the filters parameter, you can specify up to 100 allowed_domains to focus on trusted sources or up to 100 blocked_domains to exclude unwanted sites. This functionality is particularly beneficial for ensuring that responses are grounded only in reliable information or for avoiding specific domains. The second control is user location, which enables the specification of location parameters to return geographically relevant results. This feature is especially useful for questions that depend on location, like regional availability or local services. Both domain filtering and user location controls are available in all AWS Regions that support Web Search, including US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). For more information on how to get started, users can check the Web Search section in the respective documentation, while pricing details can also be found in the relevant section.

Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports two new controls that give you more precision over the results that ground a model's response: domain filtering and user location. Both are configured directly on the web_search tool in your existing OpenAI Responses API request.

With domain filtering, you can restrict Web Search results to a set of domains you choose. Using the filters parameter, you specify up to 100 allowed_domains to limit results to trusted sources, or up to 100 blocked_domains to exclude sources you don't want. This is useful when you want responses grounded only in specific sites, or when you need to keep certain domains out of results.

With user location, you can optionally specify location parameters so that Web Search can return results relevant to that geography. This helps with location-dependent questions, such as regional availability or local services.

Domain filtering and user location are available in all AWS Regions where Web Search is supported: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). To get started, see the Web Search section in the AWS Bedrock User Guide. For pricing, see the AWS Bedrock pricing page.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now supports persistent chat across linked AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, Global Resiliency, chat experiences, AWS Regions, conversation history

Summary: Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency introduces a feature that enables long, persistent chat experiences across linked AWS Regions. This capability allows end users to resume previous chats seamlessly, maintaining the full context, metadata, and transcripts as they move between regions. As a result, users no longer need to repeat information, enabling agents to deliver a more personalized service with complete access to the conversation history. For example, a user can start a chat in the US-East (N. Virginia) and later continue the same discussion in the linked US-West (Oregon) Region, without losing any context or chat attachments. This feature is designed to enhance customer experience by allowing continuity in conversations even when switching between regions. To take advantage of this functionality, users need to onboard to the service, which is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect is supported. This innovation reflects Amazon's commitment to improving customer interactions by providing reliable and resilient chat solutions across its global infrastructure. For further details, interested parties are encouraged to visit the relevant resources provided by Amazon.

Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now provides customers a mechanism to deliver long, persistent chat experiences across linked AWS Regions. With this capability, end users can resume previous conversations with full context, metadata, and transcripts carried over across Regions, eliminating the need for end users to repeat information and allowing agents to provide personalized service with access to the entire conversation history across AWS Regions.

For example, an end user can start a chat in US-East (N. Virginia) and later come back to it in the linked US-West (Oregon) Region, continuing the same conversation with an agent with full conversation history and chat attachment. To adopt this capability, onboard to Global routing.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency is supported. To learn more, visit Amazon Connect Customer Admin Guide.

item.title: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now support 1:1 NAT
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transit Gateway, AWS Cloud WAN, Network Address Translation, overlapping CIDR blocks, Regional Private NAT Gateway

Summary: AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now offer managed one-to-one network address translation (NAT) via integration with the Regional Private NAT Gateway. This feature allows the interconnection of private networks with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) blocks without the need for IP address renumbering, NAT appliances, or return-traffic rules. This improvement addresses a common issue in mergers, acquisitions, and multicloud connectivity where two networks cannot communicate due to shared IP ranges. Customers can easily create address-translation rules on AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN attachments to define how source CIDR addresses should be translated across various services, including Amazon VPC and AWS Direct Connect. The automatic bidirectional translation eliminates the need for additional return-traffic rules. AWS manages and scales this NAT capability, enabling swift setup via the Management Console, AWS CLI, SDKs, or CloudFormation. Monitoring of translated traffic is available through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Amazon EventBridge. The service is available in all AWS commercial regions. Detailed pricing and further information can be found on the respective product pages and documentation.

AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN now provide managed one-to-one network address translation (NAT) directly on their attachments, through integration with Regional Private NAT Gateway. This enables customers to connect private networks that share the same IP address ranges without renumbering either network, deploying a NAT appliance, or writing return-traffic rules.

Networks with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) blocks have long been unable to communicate, a common blocker during mergers and acquisitions, when connecting partner networks over AWS Site-to-Site VPN, in multicloud connectivity, and when independently provisioned VPCs need to interconnect. Using this capability, customers can define address-translation rules on a AWS Transit Gateway or AWS Cloud WAN attachment, specifying the private IP range each source CIDR translates to, across Amazon VPC, AWS Site-to-Site VPN, AWS Direct Connect, and SD-WAN appliances connected through Transit Gateway Connect. Both services apply translation automatically in both directions, with no separate return-traffic rule and no NAT appliance to deploy. AWS operates, scales, and manages the NAT capability as part of the attachment. For example, if a customer acquires a business and both VPCs use 10.0.0.0/16, they translate one VPC's addresses to a non-overlapping range on its attachment and connect the networks immediately. Customers set it up in minutes using the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, and AWS CloudFormation, and monitor translated traffic through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and Amazon EventBridge events.

AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Cloud WAN offer 1:1 NAT through Regional Private NAT Gateway in all AWS commercial regions where they operate. For full pricing details, see  Amazon VPC pricing . To learn more, see the  AWS Transit Gateway  and  AWS Cloud WAN  product pages, and the AWS Transit Gateway  and AWS Cloud WAN  documentation.

item.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service introduces intelligent ingestion for logs and documents in Amazon S3
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon OpenSearch, intelligent ingestion, documents, S3, processing

Summary: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless has introduced intelligent ingestion, a fully managed feature that transforms logs and documents stored in Amazon S3 into searchable content within OpenSearch Serverless collections. Users can easily set up ingestion via the AWS Management Console or a single API call, eliminating the need to manage ingestion infrastructure. This feature supports various data formats, including observability logs, structured data in JSON, and unstructured files like PDFs and Word documents. Users select an S3 source and a collection index, while intelligent ingestion automatically detects data types, parses documents, and generates vector embeddings for indexing. The tool accommodates both one-time ingestion jobs and streams to keep indexes updated with new objects. It processes unstructured data while maintaining its format and creating searchable descriptions of visual content through a vision-language model. Intelligent ingestion is available in seven AWS Regions, and users can access it from the Amazon OpenSearch Service console by selecting the Ingestion tab. For more details, users can refer to the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. Pricing information is also available for users interested in the service.

Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now offers intelligent ingestion, a fully managed feature that turns logs and documents stored in Amazon S3 into searchable content in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) collections . With intelligent ingestion, you can set up ingestion with a few clicks in the AWS Management Console or a single API call, with no ingestion infrastructure to manage. Intelligent ingestion supports observability logs and structured data in JSON, NDJSON, and JSON array formats, and unstructured files in PDF, Word, plain text, and Markdown formats.

You choose an S3 source and a collection index, and intelligent ingestion handles the rest. It automatically detects data types, parses documents, describes images, chunks text, generates vector embeddings, and indexes the results. You don't need to manage ingestion or document-processing infrastructure, or size capacity in advance. Use ingestion jobs for one-time loads such as migrations and backfills, or ingestion streams to keep an index in sync as new objects arrive in your bucket. Capacity scales with your workload up to the collection's configured limit, and you pay only for active processing. Source S3 buckets can be in the same AWS account as the collection or in a different account.

For logs and structured data, intelligent ingestion applies transformations and optionally adds embeddings, with no pipeline code. For unstructured data, it parses PDF, Word, plain text, and Markdown files while keeping headings, reading order, and tables intact, so the content lands in an index ready for semantic and hybrid search. When documents contain charts, diagrams, screenshots, or photos, a vision-language model generates text descriptions that are indexed with the surrounding content, making visual information searchable too.

Intelligent ingestion is available today for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless (NextGen) collections, with Amazon S3 as the source, in seven AWS Regions. To get started, open the Amazon OpenSearch Service console, choose your collection, and select the Ingestion tab. To learn more, see Intelligent ingestion in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide. For pricing, see Amazon OpenSearch Service pricing.

item.title: Amazon MSK Connect now supports pausing and resuming connectors
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon MSK Connect, connectors, pause, resume, costs

Summary: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) Connect now allows users to pause and resume connectors, providing enhanced control over data processing. This feature is particularly beneficial for maintaining a source database or sink target or investigating issues without needing to delete and recreate connectors, which was a previously disruptive process. By pausing a connector, users can halt record processing temporarily while retaining the connector's configuration, capacity settings, and committed offsets. When resumed, the tasks will continue from where they left off, minimizing operational overhead and risk. This capability is offered at no additional cost and is accessible through various platforms including the Amazon MSK Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDK, and AWS CDK. It is available in all AWS regions where Amazon MSK Connect operates. This new feature enhances the management of connectors, making it easier to handle various operational situations. For more information or to get started, users are encouraged to visit the relevant AWS resources.

Amazon MSK Connect (Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka Connect) now supports pausing and resuming connectors, letting you temporarily pause a connector from processing records and resume it later. This is useful when you need to stop data flow during maintenance on a source database or a sink target, or to pause processing while you investigate an upstream or downstream issue.

Amazon MSK Connect is a fully managed service that allows you to deploy, monitor, and scale Apache Kafka Connect connectors with Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka). Previously, pausing a connector meant deleting it and recreating it - a more disruptive operation, adding risk and operational overhead. With this launch, you can pause a running connector and resume it in place when you are ready — a paused connector keeps its configuration, capacity settings, and committed offsets, and its tasks continue processing from the offsets they last committed when you resume.

This capability is available at no additional cost through the Amazon MSK Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDK, and AWS CDK in all AWS Regions where Amazon MSK Connect is available. To learn more, visit the Amazon MSK Connect documentation. To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Console.

item.title: v16.5.0-canary.26
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Turbopack, caching, tests, deployment, trace

Summary: The core changes include a significant update to Turbopack, which has transitioned to the TRACEv1 format for its trace headers. Additionally, the staged fallback parameters are now passed directly to adapter renders. A fix has been implemented to ensure proper navigation from global-not-found pages to app routes, and the cache-signal read will end appropriately when encryptActionBoundArgs interacts with the RDC. Furthermore, the CI now ignores the flaky turbo-tasks-fs watcher tests to enhance stability. In terms of miscellaneous changes, the testing suite has been improved with new build-error cases enabled in deploy mode and deploy-excluded suites verified against deployments. Turbopack has also received fixes for trace crates following concurrent change issues and added delta-encoding for trace timestamps. Documentation has been updated to clarify that the Turbopack team has the authority to approve releases. New development guidance for turbo_tasks agents is now available. There are fixes for pnpm new-test unit types generating no test file, and efforts have been made to reproduce and cover cache-sharing bugs after handler failures. A special acknowledgment goes to the contributors for their support in these developments!

Core Changes

  • Turbopack: bump trace format header to TRACEv1: #99781
  • Pass staged fallback params directly to adapter renders: #100456
  • Fix navigation from global-not-found to app routes: #100592
  • End the cache-signal read when encryptActionBoundArgs hits the RDC: #100622
  • Ignore flaky turbo-tasks-fs watcher tests in CI: #100627

Misc Changes

  • test: enable build-error suites in deploy mode: #100482
  • test: enable deploy-excluded suites verified against deployments: #100484
  • Turbopack: fix trace crates after concurrent trace format changes: #100656
  • [cd] Document that Turbopack team can also approve releases: #100650
  • Turbopack: delta-encode trace timestamps: #99809
  • docs: add turbo_tasks development guidance for agents: #100581
  • Fix pnpm new-test unit type generating no test file: #100641
  • [test] Reproduce two cache-sharing bugs: #100510
  • [test] Cover cache sharing after handler failures: #100519

item.title: v16.5.0-canary.25
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: webpack, cache, bundle, analysis, dependencies

Summary: The article discusses a recent technical update involving changes to the management of build dependencies within webpack loaders. A key change is the reversion of a previous update that aimed to bring more parity across webpack loader build dependencies. This decision reflects an effort to ensure better consistency and stability in the build process. Additionally, the new approach focuses on caching bundle analysis for each output file, which enhances performance and efficiency when dealing with large projects. The caching mechanism allows developers to access previously analyzed data, reducing the need for redundant processing and speeding up the build times. This update is particularly beneficial for teams that rely on complex builds, as it minimizes delays and improves the overall development experience. The article also expresses gratitude to individuals who contributed to these improvements, acknowledging their support and collaboration in refining the webpack build process. This highlights the importance of teamwork and community in driving advancements in software tools. Overall, these changes aim to optimize the workflow of developers working with webpack, making the build process more streamlined and effective.

Misc Changes

  • Revert "More parity for webpack loader build dependencies (#99549)": #100634
  • Cache bundle analysis per output file: #100475

Credits

Huge thanks to @mischnic and @wbinnssmith for helping!

    • fix(core): end sse responses to head requests once headers are sent
    • fix(core): do not send the message of an unexposed http error

    • fix(core,websockets): run transient enhancers bound to static gateways
    • fix(core): run guards bound as classes without a name

    • fix(core): run interceptor, pipe and filter classes without a name
  • @nestjs/platform-express
    • fix(express): run wildcard middleware on "/api/" for a named wildcard
    • fix(express): apply middleware to controller root routes in strict mode
    • fix(express): map multer array index and invalid field name codes to 400 — backport of #17857
    • fix(express): destroy the StreamableFile source on client disconnect — backport of #17973
    • fix(express): send object error bodies with a json content type

    • fix(express): stop reading a streamable file for a head request
  • @nestjs/platform-fastify
    • fix(fastify): treat an empty route parameter as a route miss
    • fix(fastify): answer request targets that are not a path with 404
    • fix(fastify): pass middleware rejections to the error handler
    • fix(fastify): pass version extractor errors to the error handler
    • fix(fastify): match middleware paths like a case-insensitive router
    • fix(fastify): apply middleware to plugins registered before init
    • fix(fastify): run cors before nest middleware — backport of #18217

  • @nestjs/microservices

    • fix(microservices): keep sibling event handlers running on error
    • fix(microservices): reject tcp data too long to be a content length
    • fix(microservices): keep reading tcp replies during client backpressure — backport of #18162
    • fix(microservices): drop tcp peers that stop reading their responses
    • fix(microservices): reply to a request only from its message handler
    • fix(microservices): stop tcp observable responses when the peer leaves
    • fix(microservices): route message handler rejections to handleError — backport of #17785
    • fix(microservices): reject mqtt topics longer than 65535 bytes

    • fix(microservices): drop rmq replies that amqp cannot address

    • fix(microservices): limit the length of pattern keys

    • fix(microservices): limit the size of kafka messages the parser decodes
    • fix(microservices): limit the number of kafka header values
    • fix(microservices): let only the exact message handler answer a request — backport of #18229
    • fix(microservices): honor mqtt topic filter boundaries — backport of #18221
