Amazon Connect Customer now supports customizing the Customer Profiles app on the agent workspace
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, Customer Profiles, Profile Explorer, agent workspace, layouts

Summary: Amazon Connect Customer Profiles now enables administrators to customize the customer data visible to agents in the agent workspace through layouts built in Profile Explorer. This feature offers a real-time, unified view of customer interactions, merging contact history with data from various sources. Different agents handling various requests can access tailored data sets; for instance, an airline baggage claims agent receives information on contact history, active flights, and baggage ticket details, while a loyalty agent sees loyalty status, preferences, and upcoming flights. Administrators can create and save distinct layouts of Customer Profiles widgets, which may include elements such as contact information and lifetime value attributes, and assign them to agents to replace the legacy view. Additionally, layouts can feature an AI Profile Summary that highlights essential customer insights, directing the agent's focus on key information. Profile Explorer is available in multiple AWS Regions, including US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and several locations across Africa, Asia Pacific, Canada, and Europe. For further details, refer to the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

Amazon Connect Customer Profiles now allows administrators to customize which customer data that agents see in the agent workspace, and how it is displayed, using layouts they build in Profile Explorer. Customer Profiles provides agents with a real-time, unified view of each customer during interactions, combining contact history with customer data from multiple sources. Agents who handle different kinds of requests need different customer data in front of them.

Within Profile Explorer, administrators can create and save each layout of Customer Profiles widgets, such as contact history, contact information, and lifetime value calculated attributes, and assign it to agents in place of the legacy Customer Profiles view. For example, an airline baggage claims agent sees contact history, active flights, and baggage ticket information, while a loyalty agent sees loyalty status, preferences, and upcoming flights. Layouts can also include an AI Profile Summary that focuses the agent's attention on key customer insights by summarizing the customer profile.

You can use Profile Explorer in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more about Profile Explorer, see Profile Explorer in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

item.title: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Continuum, code vulnerabilities, remediation, AI model

Summary: Today, AWS announced the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities, a tool designed to discover, validate, prioritize, and remediate code vulnerabilities at machine speed. Continuum builds a context graph that encompasses the AWS environment, capturing resource topology, identity relationships, and network reachability. It identifies which resources are part of an application and assesses the real business risk associated with various findings. The tool ingests existing vulnerability findings and conducts code scans, confirming exploitability through testing in an isolated sandbox. Findings are then prioritized based on business impact, and remediation patches are provided as pull requests integrated into developer workflows, complete with exploitability proof and blast radius assessments. Continuum utilizes various AI models for its tasks, beginning in 'Learn' mode for proposing remediation fixes that require approval. Once a level of trust in its precision is established, users can switch to 'Enforce' mode, allowing the system to act autonomously within set guardrails. AWS Continuum is designed to work in conjunction with other AWS security services, including Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub. For details about AWS Regions where it’s available, additional information can be found on the AWS site.

Today, AWS announces the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. Continuum for code vulnerabilities discovers, validates, prioritizes, and remediates code vulnerabilities at machine speed.

Continuum for code vulnerabilities builds a context graph from your AWS environment, including resource topology, identity relationships, and network reachability. It knows which resources are part of your application, and which findings carry real business risk. It ingests your existing vulnerability findings, scans your code, and then confirms which findings are exploitable by testing them in an isolated sandbox. The findings are prioritized by business impact. And finally, it provides remediation patches as pull requests directly to developer workflows with exploitability proof and blast radius assessment attached.

Continuum for code vulnerabilities picks the right AI model for each task. Continuum starts in Learn mode where it proposes the remediation fixes that you approve. When it builds sufficient trust in its precision, you switch to the Enforce mode and let it act autonomous within the guardrails you set. 

AWS Continuum works alongside your existing AWS security services, including Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Continuum is available, see the AWS Region table. To learn more, see the AWS Continuum product page.

item.title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports a 5-second default refresh interval
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, refresh interval, search collections, near real-time, data retrieval

Summary: Starting today, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless reduces the default refresh interval to 5 seconds for search and vector collections, previously set at 10 seconds. This change allows newly ingested documents to be searchable more quickly, enhancing applications’ read-after-write visibility without requiring any configuration changes. The update applies to the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless across all regions where it is available. The faster refresh rate is particularly advantageous for workloads that continuously ingest data and require near real-time access to information, such as full-text search over frequently updated content and vector applications like retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, and recommendation systems. Consequently, applications and AI agents can now retrieve and act on the most recent data more rapidly, leading to improvements in the relevance and accuracy of search results and RAG responses. Overall, the default 5-second refresh interval offers significant benefits for users managing dynamic datasets and enhances overall search functionality in diverse applications.

Starting today, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless reduces the default refresh interval to 5 seconds for both search and vector collections. The refresh interval controls how quickly newly ingested documents become available for search. By lowering the default from 10 seconds to 5 seconds, newly written data becomes searchable faster, giving applications quicker read-after-write visibility automatically, with no configuration changes and no action required on your part.

This improvement applies to the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and takes effect by default on both search and vector collections. Faster refresh is valuable for workloads that continuously ingest data and need near real-time retrieval, including full-text search over frequently updated content as well as vector use cases such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, and recommendation and personalization systems. This means applications and AI agents can retrieve and act on the most recently ingested data sooner, improving the relevance and accuracy of search results and RAG responses for datasets that change frequently.

The 5-second default refresh interval is available in all 24 regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is available today. To learn more, see the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless documentation.

item.title: AWS CloudFormation now simplifies stack update rollback operations
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: update rollback, force rollback, CloudFormation, deployable state, AWS

Summary: AWS CloudFormation has simplified the process of performing update rollbacks, allowing users to revert their stack to a known good state more efficiently. Starting today, the introduction of the force rollback feature enables users to complete the rollback process in a single operation, even if some resources cannot roll back automatically. This enhancement works across multiple CloudFormation workflows, including the console, SDKs, and AI agents. With force rollback, CloudFormation promptly finishes the update rollback, bringing the stack back to a deployable state without the need to identify and manually retry affected resources. Any resources that require attention, such as those impacted by changes outside of CloudFormation, will be noted for further review and resolution prior to the next deployment. Users can initiate this by running the continue update rollback command with the force rollback option and creating a configuration difference report before proceeding. This feature is available in all AWS regions without additional costs, and users can refer to the AWS CloudFormation User Guide for more detailed information on using this new capability.

AWS CloudFormation now makes it simpler to complete an update rollback and get back to deploying. An update rollback returns your stack to a known good state. Starting today, if some resources cannot roll back automatically, force rollback enables you to complete the rollback it in a single operation. It works across every CloudFormation workflow, from the AWS CLI, and SDKs to AWS CDK and AI agents.

With force rollback, CloudFormation completes the update rollback and returns your stack to a deployable state in a single operation, instead of requiring you to identify, list, and retry the operation for each affected resource. Any resource that still needs attention, such as one affected a change outside CloudFormation, is recorded for you to review and resolve it before your next deployment.

To get started, run continue update rollback with the force rollback option, then create a drift-aware change set to review any configuration differences before your next deployment. To learn more, see  Continue rolling back an update  in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide.

Force rollback is available in all Regions at no additional cost. Refer to the  AWS Region table  for service availability details.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI announces training session APIs for serverless model customization
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, training session APIs, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, GPU infrastructure

Summary: Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced serverless model customization with training session APIs, allowing customers to control their post-training algorithms without managing GPU infrastructure. Users can select managed techniques such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Data Programming Optimization (DPO), enabling them to run training sessions seamlessly. The APIs allow customers to write their training loops, whether recreating established methods like SFT and DPO or implementing custom algorithms based on the latest research. Key operations like forward_backward(), optim_step(), and sample() are available as API calls within a live session, providing flexibility in composing training procedures while SageMaker handles critical tasks like GPU allocation, model loading, distributed execution, fault recovery, checkpoint storage, and security. Customers can integrate these operations into their Python code to facilitate various objectives, including reinforcement learning and custom training goals, with built-in checkpointing and resume features. Billing is token-based, which means local computations, such as reward scoring, are not charged as GPU time. Additionally, SageMaker AI offers ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes to help users get started with their training loops. Training session APIs are available in multiple regions, including US East, US West, and Asia Pacific.

Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization now supports training session APIs, giving customers full control over their post-training algorithm without provisioning or managing GPU infrastructure. Managed techniques, including SFT, DPO, and other reinforcement learning methods, let customers pick a technique and a model and have SageMaker AI run the training. With training session APIs, teams get to write the training loop, whether that's reproducing SFT or DPO on their own terms or implementing a custom loss, a new RL reward signal, a data curriculum, or an algorithm straight from the latest research. Operations such as forward_backward(), optim_step(), and sample() become API calls against a live, stateful session, so customers compose whatever training procedure their technique requires while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, model and LoRA loading, distributed execution, fault recovery, checkpoint storage, and security.

Customers can call these operations directly from their own Python code to drive reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, or custom training objectives against a live session, with checkpointing and resume built in. Billing is per token processed, so local computation like reward scoring isn't billed as GPU time. SageMaker AI is also releasing the SageMaker training sessions cookbook, a set of ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes customers can use as blueprints for their own training loops.

Training session APIs are generally available today in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Asia Pacific (Mumbai). To get started, install the SageMaker Python SDK and clone the cookbook, or launch a notebook in SageMaker Studio and connect a coding agent. To learn more, visit the documentation and the Amazon SageMaker AI webpage.

item.title: AWS Direct Connect announces 100G expansion in Bangalore, India
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Direct Connect, Bangalore, 100 Gbps, private connection

Summary: Today, AWS announced the expansion of 100 Gbps dedicated connections at the existing Netmagic DC2 data center near Bangalore, India. This expansion allows customers to establish private, direct network access to all public AWS Regions (excluding those in China) and AWS GovCloud Regions from this location. The Direct Connect service enables organizations to create a private, physical network connection between AWS and their data center, office, or colocation environments. These connections provide a more reliable and consistent network experience compared to those using the public internet. Businesses looking to enhance their connectivity options now have greater flexibility and performance potential with this service. For detailed information on the more than 150 Direct Connect locations globally, users can refer to the relevant section of the Direct Connect webpage. Additionally, AWS provides resources on its site to guide customers in purchasing and deploying Direct Connect, catering to diverse needs and infrastructure requirements. This expansion is part of AWS's commitment to improving network services and connectivity for its customers in the region and beyond.

Today, AWS announced the expansion of 100 Gbps dedicated connections at the existing AWS Direct Connect location in the Netmagic DC2 data center near Bangalore, India. You can now establish private, direct network access to all public AWS Regions (except those in China), AWS GovCloud Regions, and AWS Local Zones from this location.

The Direct Connect service enables you to establish a private, physical network connection between AWS and your data center, office, or colocation environment. These private connections can provide a more consistent network experience than those made over the public internet.

For more information on the over 150 Direct Connect locations worldwide, visit the locations section of the Direct Connect product detail pages. Or, visit our getting started page to learn more about how to purchase and deploy Direct Connect.

item.title: AWS announces AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport
item.content:encoded:
AWS, Interconnect, Megaport, connectivity, SDN

Summary: AWS has launched AWS Interconnect - last mile in collaboration with Megaport, offering a fully managed connectivity solution that simplifies network setup for connecting branch offices, data centers, and remote locations to AWS. This service leverages Megaport's extensive Software Defined Network, comprising over 1,200 data centers across 31 countries. Users can initiate private and high-speed connections through the AWS Management Console by selecting their preferred AWS Region, bandwidth, Direct Connect Gateway ID, and partner subscriber ID. Upon initiation, AWS generates an activation key for provisioning connectivity with Megaport. The service automates complex configurations such as BGP peering, VLAN setup, and ASN assignment, enhancing the overall connectivity experience. Customers will have the capability to dynamically scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps via the AWS Console, and the service is designed with high availability in mind, featuring zero downtime maintenance and a 99.99% SLA. Currently, AWS Interconnect - last mile is available in the San Jose (us-west-1) and N. Virginia (us-east-1) metros through Megaport. Users can create a preview Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, CLI, or API, ensuring easy adaptation for partners.

AWS launches AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Megaport, a fully managed connectivity offering that allows customers to connect their branch offices, data centers, and remote locations to AWS with just a few clicks, eliminating the friction and complexity of network setup. As a milestone collaboration between AWS and Megaport, AWS Interconnect - last mile combines AWS cloud innovation with Megaport operating one of the world's largest Software Defined Networks (SDN), with 1,200+ enabled data centers across 31 countries.

Through the AWS Management Console, customers can now instantly establish private, high-speed connections to AWS by simply choosing their preferred AWS Region, bandwidth speed, Direct Connect Gateway ID and partner subscriber ID. Once initiated, AWS generates an activation key to complete connectivity provisioning with Megaport. The launch simplifies the connectivity experience by pre-provisioning capacity and automating complex network configuration including BGP peering, VLAN configuration, and ASN assignment. At GA, customers will also be able to dynamically scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps through the AWS Console. The service is designed for high availability, with zero down-time maintenance, backed by a 99.99% SLA. 

AWS Interconnect - last mile is available in the San Jose (us-west-1) and N. Virginia (us-east-1) metros through Megaport. You can create a preview Interconnect using the AWS Management Console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or API. Partners can also easily adopt via a published open API package on GitHub. For more information, see the AWS Interconnect - last mile documentation and pricing pages.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports serverless model customization for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8 and Ministral 3 models
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, serverless customization, model adaptation, fine-tuning, infrastructure management

Summary: Amazon SageMaker AI now offers serverless model customization for several advanced models, including Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8 27B, and Ministral 3 (3B, 8B, and 14B). Users can deploy these models and tailor them to specific domains using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) techniques. Customization options include low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full fine-tuning methods. This new capability expands the array of models available for serverless customization on SageMaker AI, which already includes options from the Nova, Gemma 4, Nemotron 3.5, Qwen, Llama, gpt-oss, and DeepSeek families. By customizing models with proprietary data, organizations can achieve frontier-model quality with smaller, cost-effective models, thus minimizing latency. SFT aids in enhancing accuracy for specific tasks, DPO aligns model outputs with an organization's tone through preference data, and RFT uses reward signals for boosting performance on new tasks. The serverless approach simplifies infrastructure provisioning and training orchestration, allowing users to concentrate on data and evaluation while only paying for what they utilize. Availability spans key regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

Amazon SageMaker AI now supports serverless model customization for Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8 27B, and Ministral 3 3B, 8B, and 14B models. In addition to deploying these models on SageMaker AI, you can now adapt them to your specific domains and workflows, using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) techniques. You can also adapt these models with either low-rank adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning techniques. This launch adds these models to a wide variety of models available for serverless customization on SageMaker AI, including models from the Nova, Gemma 4, Nemotron 3.5, Qwen, Llama, gpt-oss, and DeepSeek families.

Model customization lets you tailor foundation models with your proprietary data so a smaller, right-sized model can match frontier-model quality on your tasks, while also reducing cost and latency. You can use labeled data with SFT to improve accuracy on domain-specific tasks, preference data with DPO to align outputs with your organization's tone, or reward signals with RFT to improve performance on new tasks. With serverless customization, SageMaker AI handles all infrastructure provisioning and training orchestration, so you can focus on your data and evaluation rather than cluster management, and only pay for what you use.

Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To get started, navigate to the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio to launch a customization job, use the SageMaker Python SDK or use our Agent skills with your choice of coding assistant. To learn more and see the full supported list of models, see the Amazon SageMaker AI model customization documentation.

item.title: AgentCore Gateway now supports Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, InvokeModel, fallback routing, inference endpoint, SDK integration

Summary: The Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway now supports the InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream APIs, enhancing the inference endpoint capabilities. With the InvokeModel feature, users can integrate their existing Amazon Bedrock SDK easily, directing traffic to any model provider through a single governed endpoint, eliminating the need to rewrite client code for each provider. Moreover, the gateway introduces model fallback routing, which ensures that requests are automatically routed to alternative models or providers if the primary is throttled, at capacity, or unreachable. This feature enhances the availability of agents without requiring clients to implement their own retry logic. For fallback routing, users can establish an ordered chain of alternative destinations in a gateway rule, specifying conditions for activation, such as server errors or timeouts. Additionally, a built-in circuit breaker facilitates faster routing by bypassing failing destinations, thus minimizing latency. All these features are accessible in all AWS regions where the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is available, with exceptions for regions in China. For more detailed information, users are encouraged to refer to the official documentation.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream APIs on its inference endpoint, along with model fallback routing for inference traffic. With InvokeModel support, you can point your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK integration at the gateway and reach any model provider through one governed endpoint, without rewriting client code for each provider. With model fallback, the gateway automatically routes a request to an alternative model or provider when the primary destination is throttled, out of capacity, or unreachable, so your agents stay available without each client implementing its own retry logic.

For fallback routing, you define an ordered chain of alternative destinations in a gateway rule, along with the conditions that trigger a switch, such as throttling, server errors, or response timeouts. A built-in circuit breaker skips destinations that are currently failing, so requests reach a healthy destination faster and you avoid added latency for failed attempts. Fallback routing happens behind the scenes, which means you send one request and receive one response, regardless of the internal trial and error on a given request.

These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is available (except those in China). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway User Guide.

item.title: AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 4 additional AWS regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Lambda, MicroVMs, Regions, serverless, isolation

Summary: AWS Lambda MicroVMs are now available in four additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Europe (Spain), making it a total of 14 Regions. Lambda MicroVMs offer a serverless compute environment with VM-level isolation, quick launch speeds, and state preservation for executing user or AI-generated code. Developers can utilize MicroVMs to provide each user or job with a managed, isolated compute environment without the need for virtualization infrastructure, balancing isolation, speed, and state retention. This service is ideal for applications such as AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners. With the recent expansion, developers can position Lambda MicroVMs closer to end-users, aiding latency and data residency compliance. Users can begin by creating a MicroVM image from their Dockerfile and launching MicroVMs from this image, assigning each user or task a dedicated HTTPS URL that supports various protocols like HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets. Access to MicroVMs is facilitated through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or preferred Agentic development tools.

AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Europe (Spain). With this launch, you can use Lambda MicroVMs in a total of 14 AWS Regions.

Lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume speeds, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code.  Developers can use Lambda MicroVMs to give each user or job their own isolated compute environment without managing virtualization infrastructure or choosing between isolation, speed, and state retention. MicroVMs enable secure, stateful, and responsive code execution for applications including AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners.

With today's launch, developers can run Lambda MicroVMs closer to their end-users in 4 additional Regions, helping meet latency and data residency requirements. To get started, create a MicroVM image from your Dockerfile, then launch MicroVMs from that image. Give each user or job their own MicroVM with a dedicated HTTPS URL that supports popular connectivity protocols such as HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets. You can use MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred Agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS.

To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide. For information on pricing, see Lambda MicroVMs pricing. Visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page for the latest region availability.

item.title: Amazon Quick Now Available in the AWS Singapore Region
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Quick is now available in the AWS Asia Pacific (Singapore) region (ap-southeast-1). This launch allows customers in Singapore to access the full power of Amazon Quick while meeting local requirements for data sovereignty.

Amazon Quick provides business users an agentic teammate that quickly answers questions at work and turns those answers into actions. With Amazon Quick, every user is empowered to make better decisions faster and take actions without switching applications using AI they can trust. Today’s launch allows customers to take advantage of Amazon Quick’s capabilities including AI-powered chat, Research, Spaces, and QuickSight dashboards — with their data stored and processed locally within the AWS Singapore region. 

For a full list of AWS regions where Amazon Quick is available, visit the Quick regional availability page. To learn more, visit the Amazon Quick documentation or product detail page.

item.title: AWS Service Reference Information now supports global condition keys, service names, and data plane classification
item.content:encoded:
AWS is expanding programmatic service reference information to help you automate IAM policy management and keep your policies aligned with the latest service updates. The service reference now includes all aws:-prefixed global condition keys in a single machine-readable file, a ServiceName field mapping service identifiers to human-readable names, and an IsDataPlane property identifying which actions are data plane operations.

You can automate retrieval of this information to eliminate manual effort, and incorporate it directly into your existing policy management tools and processes. This feature is available at no additional cost. To get started, refer to the documentation on programmatic service reference information.

item.title: AWS Transform now builds new networks and modernizes security groups
item.content:encoded:
AWS Transform for migrations now gives you three ways to bring your network to AWS. In addition to migrating and modernizing your existing network, you can build a new network from scratch or convert your on-premises access rules into optimized security groups and deploy them into existing VPCs. Whichever path you choose, you arrive on AWS with a secure and scalable network foundation.

On-premises networks accumulate years of definitions and access rules that you may not want to carry to AWS as-is. For a clean start, AWS Transform builds a new network aligned to AWS best practices. To bring your access rules with you, AWS Transform converts them into security groups and modernizes them as it goes, detecting stale rules and recommending optimizations, then deploys the groups into your existing VPCs without redeploying your network stack.

These capabilities allow you migrate to any AWS commercial or GovCloud Region.

To get started, see Migrate networks. To learn more, visit AWS Transform for migrations.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.20
item.content:encoded:
v8.0.0-rc.20

ORM commands run on @prisma/cli-engine 0.9.0, so a piped command prints tab-separated data lines and JSON needs --json. A type alias in PSL can set @default, @onCreate and @onUpdate, and the contract stores each column's real type instead of the alias name. Postgres migrations can rename, move and remove namespaces, and can change a relation's actions or a primary key. A failed migration check now names the object it expected.

The upgrade recipes for this hop: the app recipe and the extension recipe. Each breaking change below names the change ids to look for in them.

Breaking changes

  • A piped ORM command prints data lines, not JSON, unless you pass --json. The ORM toolchain now requires @prisma/cli-engine 0.9.0, up from 0.7.0, the engine the prisma CLI ships since 8.0.0-rc.25. This engine picks the output format from flags only. When stdout is a pipe, a file, $(…), a CI log or an agent, a command used to print JSON. It now prints the human output on stderr and plain data lines on stdout. Add --json to every script, CI step or program that reads JSON from prisma contract …, prisma db …, prisma migration … or prisma orm init. A project that depends on @prisma/cli-engine itself moves to 0.9.0. Data lines are a stable interface: fields are tab-separated in a documented order, and new fields are only added at the end. For example, migration list prints space, name, from, to and operation count, one line per migration. db init, db update, db verify, db schema and migration ref delete print nothing on stdout; read their exit code, or pass --json. See piped-output-needs-json and engine-pin-moves-to-0-9-0 in the app recipe and the extension recipe. (#30835)

    Before:

    prisma migration status | jq '.envelope.result'

    After:

    prisma migration status --json | jq '.envelope.result'
prisma migration list | cut -f2   # or read the data lines: one migration name per line

  • The contract stores a column's type, not the type alias it was written with. A column typed by a types {} alias now stores the alias's codec and parameters itself, and the contract no longer has the alias in storage.types. Every contract that uses an alias gets a new storage hash. A stored contract whose columns still name an alias in typeRef no longer loads. Run the app recipe's script, which rewrites stored contracts and migration snapshots, then run prisma contract emit, then prisma db sign against every database. The database does not change. In the TypeScript builder, the types key is removed and field.namedType(...) takes only an enum: write an alias as a constant field.column(type.VarChar(64)). The Supabase extension's contract changes hash for the same reason, so sign a Supabase database too. See stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases, ts-types-key-removed and supabase-contract-expanded in the app recipe. Extension authors run the same script from the package root and re-emit the bundled contract. A contract space that registers a database type writes it under databaseTypes instead of types. ColumnTypeDescriptor.typeRef, StorageColumn.typeRef and ExecutionContext.types are removed. See stored-contracts-expand-type-aliases, types-key-is-database-types and column-type-ref-removed in the extension recipe. (#30819)

    Before:

    const types = { Embedding1536: type.pgvector.Vector(1536) } as const;
const Post = model('Post', {
  fields: { embedding: field.namedType(types.Embedding1536).optional() },
});
return { types, models: { Post } };

    After:

    const Embedding1536 = field.column(type.pgvector.Vector(1536));
const Post = model('Post', {
  fields: { embedding: Embedding1536.optional() },
});
return { models: { Post } };

  • A SQL builder insert must include every column the database requires. In db.sql.<namespace>.<table>.insert(rows), leaving out a column that is not nullable and has no default is now a type error that names the column. Such an insert used to compile and then fail in the database. A value typed T | undefined for such a column is an error too; check it before the insert. In ORM create and upsert, a field that is not nullable, has no default and generates a value only on update, such as one with @onUpdate(...) and no @onCreate(...), is now required. See sql-builder-insert-required-columns and orm-create-on-update-only-field in the app recipe, and sql-builder-insert-required-columns in the extension recipe. (#30830)

    Before:

    // User.displayName is `String` with no default; this compiled, then failed in the database
db.sql.public.user.insert([{ email: 'admin@example.com', kind: 'admin' }]);

    After:

    db.sql.public.user.insert([{ email: 'admin@example.com', kind: 'admin', displayName: 'Admin' }]);

  • MongoDB enum members and discriminator values are written in the syntax of their data type. A MongoDB PSL enum member is read as a value of its codec's data type, as on SQL, so a quoted member is text. A quoted member on a type that does not take text is refused with PSL_VALUE_TYPE_INCOMPATIBLE: write numbers, NaN and the infinities unquoted, and dates and binary values with their tags. An Int32 or Int64 member written with a fraction, such as 1.0, is refused; write 1. A @@discriminator field must be required and hold one value, on SQL and MongoDB alike. When an enum types a discriminator, each @@base value must be one of its members. A value the receiving type refuses now reports PSL_VALUE_REFUSED. A Decimal128 value with leading zeros in contract.json, such as "007.5", is refused when the contract loads; re-emit the contract. See mongo-quoted-enum-members, mongo-integer-enum-members-with-a-fraction, discriminator-optional-or-list, discriminator-base-value-not-a-member, psl-value-refused-code and decimal128-spelling in the app recipe. Extension authors: AuthoringEntityContext takes dataTypes in place of dataTypeLookup, the readWrittenValueForCodec hook is removed, and an enum block needs writtenValues. See entity-context-data-types and enum-block-members-written-values in the extension recipe. (#30832)

    Before:

    enum Ratio {
  @@type("mongo/double@1")
  Unknown = "NaN"
  Half    = 0.5
}

    After:

    enum Ratio {
  @@type("mongo/double@1")
  Unknown = NaN
  Half    = 0.5
}

  • Supabase runs every role operation through forRole(binding), and its pg option takes a pool only. SupabaseRuntime no longer has queryWithRole, executeWithRole, preparedQueryWithRole or preparedExecuteWithRole. Call runtime.forRole(binding) once and use its query, execute and connection members. The pg option of supabase() takes a pg.Pool; a pg.Client fails with SUPABASE.CONFIG_INVALID. db.close() does not end a pool you pass in. RoleBoundDb, ServiceRoleDb and the transaction context gain enums and nativeEnums, so test doubles of them must add those members. After db.close(), a query on any role-bound client rejects with DRIVER.NOT_CONNECTED "Runtime is closed", and close() waits for open role transactions. See supabase-for-role-replaces-with-role-methods, supabase-role-types-gain-members, supabase-pg-takes-a-pool and supabase-close-waits-for-work in the app recipe. Extension authors: SqlRuntimeBase.acquireRawConnection() now follows the close rule of connection(), and a runtime that shares its driver is built with ownsDriver: false. See supabase-for-role-replaces-with-role-methods, supabase-role-types-gain-members, supabase-pg-takes-a-pool and raw-connection-obeys-close in the extension recipe. (#30828)

    Before:

    const rows = await runtime.queryWithRole(plan, { role: 'anon' }).toArray();
const db = await supabase({ contract, pg: new Client({ connectionString }), jwtSecret });

    After:

    const rows = await runtime.forRole({ role: 'anon' }).query(plan).toArray();
const db = await supabase({ contract, pg: new Pool({ connectionString }), jwtSecret });

  • A removed Postgres namespace is asked about, and accessWidening is renamed accessChanges. When the contract no longer declares a namespace, migration plan and db update now ask about each model in it, as for any removed model. They used to leave its tables in place without a word. Answer with --rename <old>:<new> if you renamed it, or --delete <namespace> to drop its tables and the schema. A run without a terminal fails with CLI.CONSENT_REQUIRED until you answer. The list of operations that change who can read or write a model's data is now accessChanges, in db update --dry-run --json and the control API, and the option acceptAccessWidening is now acceptAccessChanges. The question ends with "who can read and write its data" in place of "its rows". See removed-namespace-questions and access-changes-rename in the app recipe. Extension authors: SchemaTables gains hasNamespace, SchemaOwnership gains namespaceDeclaringSpaces, and a resolved rename can name a namespace. See access-changes-rename, statement-planning-target-namespaces, schema-ownership-namespace-spaces and namespace-rename-statement in the extension recipe. (#30823)

    Before:

    const result = await client.dbUpdate({ contract, mode: 'apply', migrationsDir, acceptAccessWidening: true });
if (result.ok) console.log(result.value.accessWidening);

    After:

    const result = await client.dbUpdate({ contract, mode: 'apply', migrationsDir, acceptAccessChanges: true });
if (result.ok) console.log(result.value.accessChanges);

  • db verify --json and db sign --json report schema differences in meta.schemaIssues. The CONTRACT.SCHEMA_VERIFICATION_FAILED diagnostic carried label strings in meta.issues. It now carries issue objects in meta.schemaIssues, the same key and shape as MIGRATION.SCHEMA_VERIFY_FAILED. Each issue has a path, and expected and actual. A failed apply also lists each way out as a separate entry in nextActions, and some entries change kind. See schema-verification-failed-schema-issues in the app recipe. (#30814)

Features

  • A type alias in PSL can set @default, @onCreate and @onUpdate, and each field typed by it gets them, such as types { UpdatedAt = TimestampString(3) @onCreate(now()) @onUpdate(now()) }. Postgres, SQLite and MongoDB provide temporal.CreatedAt and temporal.UpdatedAt, and Postgres also has String and JsDate variants. MongoDB schemas can now use aliases. The TypeScript builder has a type.* helper for every type PSL can write, such as type.VarChar(64). (#30819)
  • Postgres migrations can rename and move namespaces. --rename billing:finance renames the schema, and --rename public.Invoice:billing.Invoice moves a table into another schema with its rows, constraints, indexes and policies. migration.ts gains this.renameSchema, this.setTableSchema and this.dropSchema. (#30823)
  • prisma migration plan can change a relation's onDelete or onUpdate, and can change or remove a primary key, on Postgres. It drops the foreign key or primary key and adds it back, dropping and restoring every foreign key that points at an old primary key. It used to refuse both changes with MIGRATION.PLANNING_FAILED. (#30774)
  • Prisma 7's prisma migrate dev, deploy, status, diff, reset and resolve exit with CLI.COMMAND_MOVED and name the Prisma 8 command to use. (#30774)
  • A failed migration check names the object it expected, such as the database already has table "user", in place of a generic sentence. Each check can carry an expectation in ops.json, and a check you write in a rawSql operation can carry one too. Migrations already written keep their hashes and the generic sentence. (#30814)
  • A failed apply reports meta.databaseUnchanged, and its message says whether the database changed. On MongoDB, which has no transaction around a migration, it says so once anything was written. (#30814)
  • A MongoDB discriminator may be a type alias of String. (#30832)

Fixes

  • A Supabase client's internal runtime for Supabase's own tables is now closed by db.close(), so its queries after close reject with "Runtime is closed" instead of a driver error you could not act on. (#30828)
  • In the TypeScript builder, passing undefined to skip a preset argument no longer loses the arguments after it, so field.temporal.timestamptz(undefined, 'now') types correctly. (#30830)
  • db migrate no longer says a failed apply changed nothing on MongoDB when operations before the failure stayed applied. (#30814)

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.20-dev.1: chore(release): bump to 8.0.0-rc.20 (#30838)
item.content:encoded:
Version 8.0.0-rc.19 → 8.0.0-rc.20. Merging this PR publishes the
release.

The main change: the ORM's commands run on @prisma/cli-engine 0.9.0,
the engine the prisma CLI 8.0.0-rc.25 ships (#30835). A piped ORM
command now prints tab-separated data lines on stdout; scripts that read
JSON must pass --json. This release lets prisma/composer and
prisma/prisma-cli drop their engine 0.7.0 pins.

What to review

  • Release notes:
    docs/releases/v8.0.0-rc.20.md,
    which becomes the GitHub Release body. It covers 11 merged PRs: 7
    breaking changes, 7 features, 3 fixes. CHANGELOG.md has the same
    entry.
  • App upgrade guide:
    skills/prisma-8/upgrading/app/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.19-to-8.0.0-rc.20/instructions.md,
    24 changes, opening with the order to run the steps in, and one script
    (expand-type-aliases).
  • Extension upgrade guide:
    skills/prisma-8/upgrading/extension/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.19-to-8.0.0-rc.20/instructions.md,
    19 changes, the same script.

What the commits do

  1. Version bump to 8.0.0-rc.20 in every workspace package.json,
    the lockfile's workspace: pins, the library_version stamp in
    skills/prisma-8/SKILL.md, and the Supabase extension version stamped
    in contract artefacts.
  2. Upgrade guides. All 11 pending fragments are combined into the
    two guides; the originals move unchanged to
    upgrade-instructions/releases/8.0.0-rc.19-to-8.0.0-rc.20/sources/.
    Every entry's "before" form exists at v8.0.0-rc.19, so none was
    dropped. The upgrade-instruction tests read the published guides and
    script; the expand-type-aliases tests no longer call live framework
    code (its fixture generator and the tests that compared fixtures with a
    live emit are removed; hashes are recorded constants).
  3. Release notes, as above.

Checks run locally

  • pnpm check:upgrade-coverage --mode publish --prev v8.0.0-rc.19 --head HEAD and --mode pr pass.
  • pnpm check:release-notes --mode pr and pnpm lint:skills pass.
  • Upgrade-instruction tests: 56 files, 1,010 tests pass.
  • Every change id the notes cite exists in a guide.

How the release ships

When this merges, the Publish to npm workflow publishes 8.0.0-rc.20
under latest and creates a pre-release GitHub Release from the notes
file. See
docs/oss/versioning.md.
The prisma/web docs PR for rc.20 follows and merges after the publish.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.19-dev.10: TML-3693: Each database's packages move into one folder (#30829)
item.content:encoded:
This PR moves each database's packages into one folder per database.
After it, everything Postgres needs is here:

packages/3-targets/postgres/
  1-target/          @internal/target-postgres
  2-adapter/         @internal/adapter-postgres
  3-driver/          @internal/driver-postgres
  4-codec-testkit/   @internal/postgres-codec-testkit
  9-facade/          @internal/postgres

Before, the same five packages were spread over four folders:

Package Was in Now in
target pack packages/3-targets/3-targets/postgres/
packages/3-targets/postgres/1-target/
adapter packages/3-targets/6-adapters/postgres/
packages/3-targets/postgres/2-adapter/
driver packages/3-targets/7-drivers/postgres/
packages/3-targets/postgres/3-driver/
codec testkit
packages/3-targets/6-adapters/postgres-codec-testkit/
packages/3-targets/postgres/4-codec-testkit/
facade packages/3-extensions/postgres/
packages/3-targets/postgres/9-facade/

SQLite moves the same way. Mongo moves from packages/3-mongo-target/
and packages/3-extensions/mongo/ into packages/3-targets/mongo/. The
SQL family folder packages/2-sql/ becomes packages/2-sql-family/, to
match packages/2-mongo-family/.

No package is renamed. @internal/target-postgres is still
@internal/target-postgres, so no import, published package or
generated file changes. Only folders move.

Why we're doing this

Each database used to be spread over four folders. The target pack,
adapter and driver each sat in their own role folder (3-targets/,
6-adapters/, 7-drivers/), and the facade sat in a fourth,
3-extensions/. Working on one database meant moving between all four.

The numbers 3, 6 and 7 looked like layers that the build checks, but
nothing checked them. pnpm lint:deps decides what each file may import
from globs in architecture.config.json, not from folders. The role
folders cost something and bought nothing.

Mongo already kept its packages together, but under a top-level folder
of its own, 3-mongo-target/. Copying that for every database would add
a top-level folder per database.

So every database, in every family, now gets one folder under
packages/3-targets/. Inside it, the numbers give the dependency order:
the adapter imports the target pack, the facade imports the target pack,
adapter and driver, and the driver imports none of them. Adding a
database means adding one folder. MySQL and MariaDB are next, in the
MySQL proof-of-concept project
(projects/mysql-poc/). This PR lands
first so their PRs only add files.

ADR 278 records the decision.

What changed, step by step

  1. The move. Four commits do nothing but git mv: one for the
    2-sql rename, then one each for Postgres, SQLite and Mongo. git show --stat -M <commit> shows only renames.
  2. Paths. One commit updates every file that names a folder:
    architecture.config.json, the publish mapping in shells.ts,
    coverage.config.json, tsconfig.base.json, scripts, tests, fixtures,
    examples and READMEs. The facades and Mongo packages are one folder
    deeper, so their relative paths gain a ../. The publish mapping
    produces exactly the same published entrypoints as before.
  3. Registration. architecture.config.json must give every source
    file a plane: shared, control (migration) or runtime. Postgres had
    registered only six of its core files, so lint checked almost none of
    its target. Every target now registers its files the same way. Doing
    that showed some files filed as shared that are really control or
    runtime code, so they moved:
  • Control-only code went to src/core/migrations/. That covers the
    SQLite control target, the schema verifiers, the control mutation
    defaults and the Mongo control adapter.
  • Runtime-only code went to a new src/core/runtime/. That covers the
    SQLite runtime target, adapter and driver.
  • The Postgres constraint-name helpers moved out of migrations/. They
    are plain functions that shared code needs.
  1. Two new checks in pnpm lint:deps, so the layout stays honest:
  • Every source file under packages/ must match exactly one glob
    (scripts/lint-architecture-registration.mjs). It found 68 files that
    matched none, and they are now registered.
  • A package in a database folder may depend only on lower-numbered
    packages of the same database (scripts/lint-target-layering.mjs). This
    replaces the separate layering test each target had, so a new database
    is covered without writing a test. I checked that it fails when a
    forbidden import is added.
  1. Upgrade notes. The upgrade-coverage check used to require
    extension notes for changes under packages/3-extensions/, where the
    facades lived. It now also covers packages/3-targets/*/9-facade/. Two
    pending declarations say this PR needs no user action.
  2. Docs. The layout docs, the directory-layout rule and the
    onboarding recipe for adding a target are rewritten. ADR 278 is new, ADR
    140 points to it, and other ADRs' paths are updated.

A gap this found, which this PR does not fix

pnpm lint:deps has never checked an import from one package to
another. A workspace import such as @internal/target-sqlite resolves
to the package's dist/ folder, which the config excludes, so the
import disappears. Only imports between files of the same package are
checked. That is true on main today.

Reading the imports by hand found seven plane violations the check
should have caught. One example: the adapter's control-codecs.ts is
control code that imports @internal/sql-runtime. Fixing the resolution
will surface more, so it is its own issue, TML-3700. Until then, the
ordering check in step 4 is what checks dependencies between one
database's packages.

Effect on other open PRs

41 open PRs touch the moved folders. Git follows renames when it merges,
so a PR that only edits existing files merges as before. Trial merges
into six open PRs added 0 to 3 conflicts to typical ones. Most of those
are files a PR adds inside a moved folder, which need accepting git's
suggested new location and sometimes fixing an import. We resolve
conflicts on our own PRs as they come up.

Verification

All of these pass locally:

  • pnpm build, pnpm typecheck, pnpm lint, pnpm lint:deps
  • pnpm lint:publishability, pnpm lint:docs, pnpm fixtures:check
  • pnpm test:scripts (623 tests)
  • pnpm check:upgrade-coverage --mode pr
  • the tests of every moved package
  • the one integration test that read the old folder

The full integration suite runs in the merge queue.

Alternatives considered

  • Keep the role folders. They check nothing and spread each database
    over four folders.
  • Copy Mongo's layout for every database, such as
    packages/3-postgres-target/1-postgres-target/. It adds a top-level
    folder per database and repeats the database's name in every folder.
  • Move only new databases, and leave Postgres, SQLite and Mongo for
    later.     That avoids conflicts with open PRs now, but leaves two layouts
    side by side. The move only gets more expensive as more code lands.
  • Move single-database extension packs, such as pgvector, under their
    database.     They use the same extension points a third-party pack would,
    and keeping them in 3-extensions/ shows that.

Refs: TML-3693

item.title: v2.269.0
item.content:encoded:
Features

  • bedrockagentcore: graduate Policy submodule to stable (#38687) (2b95e32), closes #37219
  • update L1 CloudFormation resource definitions (#38784) (1b5e2e0)
  • logs: support DELIVERY log group class (#38703) (b7a057a), closes #34338
  • s3-deployment: expose deployed object version IDs (#38766) (09342df), closes #38765

Bug Fixes

  • awslint: use a default import for chalk (#38110) (36d14e0), closes #38109 #38058
  • core: cdk-nag warnings cannot be suppressed (#38787) (211029f)
  • core: cdk-nag's findings duplicated in multi-environment apps (#38707) (4b7b2e7), closes #38483 #38135
  • core: tree.json generation is quadratic in the number of subtrees (#38761) (3d034b6), closes #38762
  • core: unnecessary warnings around builtins and AZs (#38673) (6860777)
  • core: upgrade CloudFormation validation to latest version (#38804) (d703eb6)
  • dynamodb: TableV2 emits internal grants deprecation warnings (#38806) (57b3043), closes #38709 #38399 #37892
  • ecs: allow ephemeralStorageGiB for Windows Fargate platform version 1.0.0 (#37589) (855dfeb), closes #37510
  • ecs: removing the last target group from a service is not deployed (#38776) (73100f6), closes #35446 #35446 #35452
  • lambda-go: escape generated go build path arguments (#38785) (279d101)
  • s3-deployment: sanitize all log outputs to mitigate CWE-117/93 (#37670) (47a3a38), closes #37671 #30746 #28469 #30211

Alpha modules (2.269.0-alpha.0)

⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

  • glue-alpha: Glue job constructs now reject construct-managed and Glue-reserved
    arguments passed through defaultArguments. Previously, a managed argument set via
    defaultArguments was silently honored in SparkJob and PythonShellJob (customer
    value won over the construct default) and silently ignored in RayJob (construct
    default won). Both behaviors let a caller bypass the construct's security and
    observability defaults with no error. Passing any of the following through
    defaultArguments now throws a ValidationError at synthesis time:
  • construct-managed arguments — --enable-continuous-cloudwatch-log,
    --continuous-log-logGroup, --continuous-log-logStreamPrefix,
    --continuous-log-conversionPattern, --enable-continuous-log-filter,
    --enable-metrics, --enable-observability-metrics, --enable-spark-ui,
    --spark-event-logs-path, --job-language, --class, --extra-jars,
    --user-jars-first, --extra-py-files, --extra-files, library-set
  • Glue-reserved arguments — --debug, --mode, --JOB_NAME, --endpoint

A managed argument is rejected whether or not the current configuration emits it, so a
disabled feature (e.g. enableMetrics: false) cannot be re-enabled through
defaultArguments. Configure these through their dedicated props instead
(continuousLogging, enableMetrics, enableObservabilityMetrics, sparkUI,
className, extraJars, extraJarsFirst, extraPythonFiles, extraFiles). For
example, replace defaultArguments: { '--enable-continuous-cloudwatch-log': 'false' }
with continuousLogging: { enabled: false }. Arguments without a dedicated prop (e.g.
--enable-glue-datacatalog) are unaffected and remain settable via defaultArguments.

The checkNoReservedArgs(defaultArguments?) method on the Job base class was removed.
It is replaced by two protected members: setManagedArgument(key, value?), which each
job class calls to declare (and, when a value is present, emit) a managed argument, and
mergeDefaultArguments(defaultArguments?), which validates the caller-supplied
defaultArguments against the accumulated reserved set and returns the merged map.

  • route53resolver-alpha: FirewallRuleGroupAssociation now honors the previously-ignored mutationProtection and name props. Stacks that set mutationProtection: true will enable mutation protection on redeploy (which blocks further CloudFormation update/delete until it is set back to false); stacks that set name will write it to the template, which may replace the association.
  • glue-alpha: trigger Action and Condition are no longer plain objects — use Action.job(...) / Action.crawler(...) and Condition.job(...) / Condition.crawler(...). Jobs are referenced via IJobRef and crawlers via ICrawlerRef (a CfnCrawler instance or CfnCrawler.fromCrawlerName(...)) instead of a CfnCrawler field or crawler-name string; IJob now extends the generated IJobRef. addDailyScheduledTrigger/addWeeklyScheduledTrigger/addCustomScheduledTrigger are replaced by addScheduledTrigger(id, { schedule, ... }) (use TriggerSchedule.daily()/weekly()/cron(...)). addNotifyEventTrigger is renamed addEventTrigger (NotifyEventTriggerOptions → EventTriggerOptions). All addXxxTrigger methods now return ITriggerRef instead of CfnTrigger.
  • glue-alpha: PartitionProjectionConfiguration's variant fields (integerRange, dateRange, interval, digits, format, intervalUnit, values) are no longer public; DATE projection now takes step: { interval, intervalUnit } instead of top-level interval/intervalUnit.
  • glue-alpha: ConnectionOptions no longer has subnet, vpc, or vpcSubnets; use network: ConnectionNetwork.subnet(...) or network: ConnectionNetwork.vpc(...) instead.

Features

  • glue-alpha: ensure job parameters consistency (#38480) (bc7dc0c)
  • glue-alpha: model Connection VPC placement as a value object (#38729) (f72e9fe)
  • glue-alpha: model partition projection variants as internal state (#38726) (16527cd)
  • glue-alpha: overhaul the workflow trigger API (#38579) (c8f917d)

Bug Fixes

  • route53resolver-alpha: association silently ignored mutationProtection and name (#38795) (5ab40b2)
