AWS Transform adds storage migration assessments for Amazon S3, EBS, EFS, and FSx
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transform, storage migration, workload mapping, cost projection, assessment tool

Summary: AWS Transform simplifies the process of evaluating on-premises storage for migration to AWS by allowing users to upload a storage inventory. Instead of manually analyzing numerous volumes, the tool automatically maps each workload to the most suitable AWS service, sizes the recommendations, and projects associated costs to create a comprehensive total cost of ownership business case. This service accommodates various storage types, including NAS shares, SAN LUNs, direct-attached disks, and backup repositories, using formats like NetApp Digital Advisor exports and RVTools files. AWS Transform intelligently routes workloads to optimal services such as Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx, which includes options like NetApp ONTAP, Windows File Server, OpenZFS, and Lustre. Users can also explore various deployment scenarios, comparing factors such as Single-AZ vs. Multi-AZ configurations and performance vs. cost optimization. Follow-up questions can be addressed through chat for further clarification. Storage migration assessments are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered, enhancing accessibility and usability for organizations considering cloud migration.

Migration assessments in AWS Transform now evaluate on-premises storage for migration to AWS. Instead of manually analyzing thousands of volumes across protocols, capacity, and performance, you upload a storage inventory and AWS Transform does the mapping for you. It matches each workload to the best-fit service, sizes the recommendation, and projects costs to produce a total cost of ownership business case. Bring NAS shares, SAN LUNs, direct-attached disks, or backup repositories via a NetApp Digital Advisor export, RVTools file, or other inventory. AWS Transform routes workloads across Amazon S3, Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx (NetApp ONTAP, Windows File Server, OpenZFS, Lustre). Run what-if scenarios to compare deployment options such as Single-AZ vs. Multi-AZ or cost-optimized vs. performance-optimized, then ask follow-up questions about any result in chat.

Storage migration assessments are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is available. To learn more, see the AWS Transform User Guide.

item.title: AWS Direct Connect announces 100G expansion in Manchester, England
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Direct Connect, 10 Gbps, MACsec, Manchester

Summary: Today, AWS announced the expansion of its 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps dedicated connections with MACsec encryption capabilities at the Equinix MA3 data center, located near Manchester, England. This upgrade allows customers to establish private, direct network access to all public AWS Regions (excluding those in China) and AWS GovCloud Regions from this location. Notably, this facility becomes the third AWS Direct Connect location in England to offer 100 Gbps connections equipped with MACsec encryption. The AWS Direct Connect service facilitates a private, physical network connection between AWS and users' data centers, offices, or colocation environments, ensuring a more consistent network experience compared to public internet connections. For those looking to explore the vast network options, there are over 150 Direct Connect locations available worldwide. Interested parties can find more information about the service in the Direct Connect section and learn how to purchase and deploy it on the relevant page dedicated to the process. The announcement emphasizes AWS's commitment to providing secure and efficient networking solutions for its customers.

Today, AWS announced the expansion of 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps dedicated connections with MACsec encryption capabilities at the existing AWS Direct Connect location in the Equinix MA3 data center near Manchester, England. You can now establish private, direct network access to all public AWS Regions (except those in China), AWS GovCloud Regions, and AWS Local Zones from this location. This is the third AWS Direct Connect location in England to provide 100 Gbps connections with MACsec encryption capabilities.

The Direct Connect service enables you to establish a private, physical network connection between AWS and your data center, office, or colocation environment. These private connections can provide a more consistent network experience than those made over the public internet.

For more information on the over 150 Direct Connect locations worldwide, visit the locations section of the Direct Connect product detail pages. Or, visit our getting started page to learn more about how to purchase and deploy Direct Connect.

item.title: Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS now support On-Demand Capacity Reservations
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: On-Demand, Capacity Reservations, Amazon Aurora, RDS, Availability Zones

Summary: Starting today, AWS allows users to reserve compute capacity for Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS DB instances in one or more Availability Zones for any duration they need. This capability ensures that operations like creating, restoring, scaling, and starting DB instances do not fail due to insufficient capacity. On-Demand Capacity Reservations cater to workloads requiring guaranteed availability, particularly for business-critical events such as migrations, product launches, seasonal spikes, high availability, or disaster recovery. Users can choose the DB instance class, engine, and Availability Zones while specifying the reserved capacity for each zone, including support for Multi-AZ deployments. Reservations can be used immediately, can be canceled at any time without commitment, or scheduled to begin between 5 to 120 days later with a minimum commitment. The billing is at On-Demand rates during the active reservation period, regardless of whether instances are running. Existing discounts from Reserved DB Instances or Database Savings Plans will automatically apply. On-Demand Capacity Reservations are available for Amazon Aurora and RDS in all AWS commercial regions. For more details, refer to the relevant documentation.

Starting today, you can reserve compute capacity for your Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS DB instances in one or more Availability Zones for as long as you need it. Reserving capacity helps ensure that DB instance create, restore, scale-compute, and start operations don't fail because of insufficient capacity.

On-Demand Capacity Reservations are designed for workloads that need assurance that specific DB instance capacity will be available when they need it for business-critical events, such as migrations, product launches, seasonal peaks, high-availability deployments, or disaster recovery. You choose the DB instance class, engine, Availability Zones, and reserved capacity per Availability Zone, and RDS holds that capacity for you. Capacity can be reserved in two or more Availability Zones to support Multi-AZ deployments. To use the reserved capacity, reference the reservation when you create, restore, modify, or start a DB instance.

You can reserve capacity for immediate use with no commitment and cancel at any time, or schedule a reservation to begin 5 to 120 days in the future with a minimum commitment. Reserved capacity is billed at On-Demand rates while the reservation is active, whether or not DB instances within the reservation are running. Discounts from your existing Reserved DB Instances or Database Savings Plans apply automatically.

On-Demand Capacity Reservations are available for Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS in all AWS commercial Regions. To learn more about On-Demand Capacity Reservations, visit the documentation for Amazon Aurora and Amazon RDS.

item.title: Amazon Cognito extends multi-Region replication to AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Cognito, multi-Region replication, AWS GovCloud, user pools, resilience

Summary: Amazon Cognito's multi-Region replication (MRR) now includes support for AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, enhancing resilience for various workloads. MRR allows for the synchronization of user and machine identity data—such as credentials, user pool configurations, and federation setups—to a designated secondary user pool in a standby Region. This synchronization occurs in near real-time, ensuring that user data is readily available in the standby Region. In the event of a disruption in the primary Region, traffic can be redirected, maintaining continuous authentication services. Previously, MRR was limited to 16 commercial Regions, but it now extends to more AWS Regions, helping businesses achieve their resilience, data residency, and compliance objectives. MRR is available as an add-on for user pools within the Essentials or Plus feature tiers and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). Users interested in utilizing MRR can find a complete list of available AWS Regions and detailed instructions for getting started, along with pricing information, on the official AWS site.

Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication (MRR) now supports AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, extending the resilience benefits of MRR to more workloads. MRR lets you synchronize user and machine identity data, including credentials, user pool configurations, and federation setups, to a secondary user pool in a standby Region you designate, in near real-time. With user data in the standby Region, you can redirect traffic and keep authentication available if there is a disruption in your primary Region.

Previously, MRR was available in 16 commercial Regions. You can now also use MRR to replicate between additional AWS Regions, helping you meet resilience, data residency, and compliance requirements in the Regions that best align with your business needs.

MRR is available as an add-on for user pools in the Essentials or Plus feature tiers, and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). For the full list of AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region. To get started, visit the developer guide for instructions and the pricing page for pricing details.

item.title: AWS Neuron 2.33 adds native PyTorch support, Neuron Observer, and other new features
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Neuron, TorchNeuron, PyTorch, Trainium, Neuron Observer

Summary: AWS Neuron 2.33 has launched with several new features, including the public beta of TorchNeuron, a native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Users can now run models on Amazon EC2 Trn2 and Trn3 instances with both eager mode and with torch.compile. Additionally, Neuron Observer is introduced in public beta, capable of detecting Trainium health issues in under a second and pinpointing the affected node or device. The vLLM Neuron plugin has been upgraded to vLLM 0.29.0, and the new vLLM Omni Neuron plugin for video generation has been added, supporting native PyTorch compilation. A new Neuron Deep Learning AMI and Deep Learning Container for PyTorch training now include TorchNeuron, PyTorch 2.14, and TorchTitan. Neuron Explorer allows users to analyze profiles captured by torch.profiler, enabling them to attribute memory allocations to specific Python source lines. Finally, the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) has been enhanced to support full Python language capabilities for metaprogramming, along with the addition of 25 new experimental kernels, including those for DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, and Kimi Delta Attention.

AWS Neuron 2.33 is now available, introducing TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, in public beta. You can run models written with the standard PyTorch APIs on Amazon EC2 Trn2 and Trn3 instances, in eager mode or with torch.compile. This release also introduces Neuron Observer in public beta, which detects Trainium health issues in under a second and identifies the affected node or device.

The vLLM Neuron plugin upgrades to vLLM 0.29.0, and the vLLM Omni Neuron plugin for Wan2.2 video generation is now part of the Neuron release. Both support native PyTorch compilation through TorchNeuron. A new Neuron Deep Learning AMI and Deep Learning Container for PyTorch training include TorchNeuron, PyTorch 2.14, and TorchTitan. Neuron Explorer opens profiles captured with torch.profiler. From a PyTorch memory snapshot, it now attributes allocations to the Python source lines that made them, for debugging out-of-memory errors in eager mode.

Kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) can now use the full Python language for metaprogramming, including generators and class inheritance. The NKI Library adds 25 new experimental kernels, including kernels for DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, and Kimi Delta Attention.

To get started, see the following resources:

  • AWS Neuron 2.33.0 Release Notes

  • AWS TorchNeuron documentation

  • AWS Neuron Observer documentation

  • AWS Neuron Kernel Interface documentation

  • AWS Neuron

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer launches two new layouts for agent workspace
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, agent workspace, Modern layout, Classic layout, AWS regions

Summary: Amazon Connect now provides two optimized layouts for the agent workspace, enhancing screen space and agent efficiency. The Modern layout positions contact controls at the top, allowing for a more spacious area below for applications during voice calls. This layout is particularly beneficial for agents handling chat, email, and task contacts, as it provides a taller and wider area for reading and responding. In contrast, the Classic layout retains a familiar experience for existing agents, featuring expandable and contractible contact controls based on the channel used and a resizable agent assist application. Administrators have the flexibility to assign the Modern layout to teams transitioning from other desktops or stick with the Classic layout for those already accustomed to it. The new layouts are available in multiple AWS regions, including US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London). For more information on how to implement these layouts, users can refer to the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

Amazon Connect Customer now offers two different layouts that optimize screen space on the agent workspace. Contact center agents spend hours each day in the agent workspace, which includes all of the contact controls and applications they need to resolve customer issues. Agents who handle different channels and workflows want the workspace arranged differently, so that they can quickly read, respond, and access their tools. Now, administrators can choose the best layout for each team, maximizing agent efficiency and satisfaction.

On the Modern layout, contact controls are at the top of the workspace, maximizing screen space for the applications beneath during voice calls. When agents handle chat, email, and task contacts on the Modern layout, they now have a taller, wider area to read and respond. The Classic layout offers a familiar experience for agents already using the agent workspace, now with contact controls that expand and contract by channel and a resizable agent assist application. Administrators can assign the Modern layout to a team migrating from another agent desktop with controls at the top, while teams already familiar with the agent workspace can use the Classic layout.

You can use the new layouts for the Amazon Connect Customer agent workspace in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more and get started, see the agent workspace in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

item.title: Amazon S3 server access log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs now available in five additional AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon S3, CloudWatch Logs, access logs, AWS GovCloud, monitoring

Summary: Amazon S3 server access log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS China Regions. This feature allows users to query access logs as they arrive, set alarms, and encrypt them with AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keys. It complements the existing delivery of server access logs to S3 general-purpose buckets, providing greater flexibility for monitoring and analyzing access to data. With CloudWatch Logs, users can set alarms for error rates, monitor traffic patterns, investigate access incidents, and correlate S3 access activity with other operational data. The capability enhances the ability to track and respond to access patterns and potential security issues in a more integrated manner. Additionally, S3 server access log delivery to CloudWatch Logs is now available across all AWS Regions. Please note that Amazon CloudWatch Logs charges for vended logs apply, and users can find pricing details on the AWS website. To learn more about this new delivery path and its benefits, the AWS documentation provides additional information.

Amazon S3 server access log delivery to Amazon CloudWatch Logs is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, AWS European Sovereign Cloud, and AWS China Regions. With your access logs in CloudWatch Logs, you can query them as they arrive, set alarms, and encrypt them with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys. This new delivery path complements the existing delivery of server access logs to S3 general purpose buckets, giving you more flexibility in how you monitor and analyze access to your data.

With delivery to CloudWatch Logs, you can set alarms on error rates, monitor traffic patterns, investigate access incidents, and correlate S3 access activity with the rest of your operational data.

S3 server access log delivery to CloudWatch Logs is now available in all AWS Regions. Amazon CloudWatch Logs charges for vended logs apply. For pricing details, visit Amazon CloudWatch pricing. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 User Guide.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports custom sequence lengths for serverless model customization jobs
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, serverless model customization, sequence length, fine-tuning, open-weight models

Summary: Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced a new feature that allows users to configure the sequence length during serverless model customization jobs. This enhancement supports fine-tuning for various open-weight models, including popular families like gpt-oss, Gemma, Llama, Nemotron, and Qwen. Previously, fine-tuning recipes were restricted to fixed sequence lengths that could not be altered, limiting customers' ability to optimize for their specific use cases. Now, users can set the sequence length parameters within hyperparameters, allowing for customization up to the published maximum for their selected model and technique. For SFT and DPO jobs, the dataset_max_len hyperparameter can be set, while max_prompt_length and max_response_length hyperparameters are used for RFT jobs. This flexibility enables users to align training data characteristics, whether dealing with short question-answer pairs or extensive documents, with published maximums reaching up to 16K tokens for many models based on the technique. Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in regions including US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Users can start customization jobs via the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio or use coding assistants.

Today, Amazon SageMaker AI announces the ability to configure the sequence length used during your serverless model customization job. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization supports fine-tuning for many open-weight models, including models from popular families including gpt-oss, Gemma, Llama, Nemotron, and Qwen. Previously, each fine-tuning recipe ran at a fixed sequence length that customers could not modify. Customers sometimes need to modify these parameters to achieve better results for their use case. Customers also asked for longer sequence lengths than the static defaults we supported on some models.

Now, you can set sequence length parameters as part of the customization job's hyperparameters, anywhere up to the published maximum for your chosen model and technique. You can set the dataset_max_len hyperparameter for SFT and DPO jobs or set max_prompt_length and max_response_length hyperparameters for RFT jobs. This gives you more control to match your training data characteristics, whether you are working with short question-answer pairs or multi-page documents. Published maximums are up to 16K tokens for many models depending on model and technique.

Serverless model customization on SageMaker AI is available in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). To get started, navigate to the Models page in Amazon SageMaker Studio to launch a customization job, use the SageMaker Python SDK or use our Agent skills with your choice of coding assistant. To learn more, and see the list of models and supported sequence lengths per technique, see the SageMaker AI documentation.

item.title: AWS Network Firewall now supports Route 53 Resolved IP Validation
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Network Firewall, IP validation, domain filtering, SFTP, DNS security

Summary: AWS Network Firewall has introduced IP validation, enhancing domain-based filtering capabilities to include protocols such as SFTP and SSH, beyond just HTTP/HTTPS. This feature ensures that a connection's destination IP address is resolvable via the VPC's Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver, addressing security vulnerabilities where clients might circumvent domain rules. With this advancement, organizations can create domain filtering rules for various protocols, leading to more flexible security policies compared to solely IP-based rules. It bolsters protection against Server Name Identifier (SNI) spoofing by confirming that the resolved IP addresses match the SNI, allowing traffic to only reach verified destinations. This allows for the consistent application of domain-based security policies across all outbound traffic types, ranging from web applications to file transfers, without the need for complex workarounds. Furthermore, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall can be utilized in conjunction with the VPC Resolver to provide enhanced DNS security. The resolved IP validation feature is available in all commercial AWS regions supporting AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, at no extra cost. Users can find a complete list of supported regions on the AWS website.

AWS Network Firewall now supports IP validation, extending domain-based filtering beyond HTTP/HTTPS to protocols such as SFTP and SSH. This new capability validates that a connection's destination IP address was resolved through your VPC's Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver, closing security gaps where clients could bypass domain rules.

This feature enables Network Firewall customers to implement domain filtering rules for any protocol, not just HTTP/HTTPS, providing more flexible security policies than IP-based rules alone. It simplifies protection against Server Name Identifier (SNI) spoofing by validating the IPs resolved by the Route 53 VPC Resolver against the SNI, ensuring traffic only reaches legitimately resolved destinations. Organizations can now enforce consistent domain-based security policies across all outbound traffic types, from web applications to file transfer protocols, without complex workarounds. Additionally, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall can be used with your VPC Resolver for extended DNS security.

Resolved IP validation is available in all AWS commercial regions where AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available, at no additional charge. For a full list of supported regions, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page.

To learn more, visit AWS Network Firewall product page and service documentation.

item.title: Amazon WorkSpaces simplifies secure AI agent access to enterprise cloud desktops with less infrastructure to operate and manage
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: WorkSpaces, AI agents, authentication, MCP, applications

Summary: WorkSpaces for AI agents now facilitates authentication and desktop connections via the managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) service, eliminating the need for custom coding. This enhancement allows agents to access governed cloud desktops seamlessly. Previously, connecting an agent required managing presession needs and manually handling streaming URLs, adding complexity each time a session expired. The new setup allows the creation of sessions using existing AWS credentials through OAuth 2.0 while managing the connection lifecycle automatically. Users configure the desktop stack once, enabling agents to connect without dealing with the underlying streaming connection. Furthermore, session states can be queried for insights into which desktop stack and fleet the agents are using, providing real-time observability. Additionally, with the MCP Tool, agents can discover and launch applications more efficiently, listing available apps and switching between them programmatically. WorkSpaces operates within the same compliance and network isolation measures applicable to human workers, ensuring security. The service has expanded to four new AWS Regions: São Paulo, Milan, Spain, and Malaysia. To start operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit the provided resource link.

WorkSpaces for AI agents now handles authentication and desktop connections as part of the managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) service, so you can connect agents to governed cloud desktops, removing the need to write custom code. This makes it easy to use WorkSpaces with any client that supports MCP.

Connecting an agent to a desktop previously required you to manage presession requirements; generate, invoke, and rotate streaming URLs manually, adding complexity every time a session expired. You can now create sessions with your existing AWS credentials through OAuth 2.0, and the service handles the connection lifecycle. You configure once which desktop stack to use, and your agents reach the right desktop without ever seeing or handling the underlying streaming connection. You can also query session state to see which desktop stack, fleet, and session an agent is connected to, and generate a link for real-time observability of your agent. This gives you visibility and auditability over active agent work to know what your agents are doing and where.

To help your agents work with multiple applications, they can now discover and launch applications through a catalog MCP Tool rather than navigating menus. Using these new tools, agents can list the available applications, launch one or several at runtime, and switch between them, replacing the start-menu and taskbar navigation with a programmatic, deterministic path that improves accuracy and reduces token cost. 

WorkSpaces for AI agents runs agent sessions inside the same network isolation and compliance boundaries that govern your human workforce, inheriting the VPC controls, data-loss prevention policies, and session-level security posture that enterprises have already configured. The service is also now available in four additional AWS Regions: South America (São Paulo), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia).

To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/agent-access.html.

item.title: Amazon CloudWatch Alarms now supports tags in alarm actions payload
item.content:encoded:
Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces support for including alarm tags in action payloads and Amazon EventBridge events, enabling customers to route and filter alarm notifications by tag without additional lookups. When enabled on an alarm, CloudWatch adds the alarm tags to the messages it sends to Amazon SNS, AWS Lambda, and Amazon EventBridge each time the alarm changes state. This option is designed for customers who route many alarms through a shared notification pipeline and need to identify the owning team, environment, or service directly from the message.

With tags in actions payloads, customers can avoid the extra work of correlating tag metadata with alarm events after the fact. For example, a team that routes hundreds of alarms through a single SNS topic to a Lambda function previously had to call ListTagsForResource for each event to find the owning team before paging. With this feature, the tags arrive in the notification, so the function can route directly from the message. The setting is off by default and configurable per alarm, and customers can include all tags, only selected tag keys, or all tags except selected keys. It is supported for metric, composite, and log alarms.

Tags in actions and events for CloudWatch Alarms are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch is available except Middle East (UAE), and Middle East (Bahrain).

To get started, see  Alarm tags in action payloads  in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide. To learn more about Amazon CloudWatch Alarms, visit the  Amazon CloudWatch  product page.

item.title: v16.5.0-canary.22
v8.0.0-rc.19
item.content:encoded:
v8.0.0-rc.19

@default now means a database default, and values the client generates are written @onCreate(...) and @onUpdate(...). Every default is stored in one form owned by its column's data type, so date, time and bytes defaults are written with tags. Clients take the contract as a typed value, can render any plan as SQL without a database, and run each ORM call as one activity that middleware and the cache can see. A column of any database type can be declared with Raw(sql`...`), and Prisma 7 schemas with Unsupported(...) fields now load.

The upgrade recipes for this hop: the app recipe and the extension recipe. Each breaking change below names the change ids to look for in them.

Breaking changes

  • Client generators are written @onCreate(...) and @onUpdate(...), and @default means a database default. @default(uuid()), @default(cuid(2)), @default(ulid()) and @default(nanoid()) are refused with PSL_GENERATOR_IN_DEFAULT. Write @onCreate(uuid()) and so on instead. The app recipe ships a script that rewrites your Prisma 8 schema files. The contract does not change, so there is nothing to re-emit, sign or migrate. @default(now()) and @default(autoincrement()) are unchanged. contract print now writes generated values as @onCreate(...) and @onUpdate(...). See client-functions-move-from-default-to-on-create and contract-print-writes-generator-attributes in the app recipe. (#30780)

    Before:

    model Post {
  id   String @id @default(uuid(7))
  slug String @default(nanoid(12))
}

    After:

    model Post {
  id   String @id @onCreate(uuid(7))
  slug String @onCreate(nanoid(12))
}

  • A client takes the contract as a typed value. The contractJson option and the type argument on the client call are removed from postgres(), postgresServerless(), sqlite(), supabase(), mongo(), postgresStatic(), sqliteStatic(), mongoStatic() and mongoQuery(). Turn the emitted JSON into a value once with contractFromJson<Contract>(contractJson) from the facade's /static entry, and pass { contract }. The app recipe ships a script that moves your source files; move test files by hand. The *OptionsWithContract and *OptionsWithContractJson types are replaced by PostgresOptions<Contract> and the matching types of the other facades. See client-takes-contract-value in the app recipe. (#30748)

    Before:

    export const db = postgres<Contract>({ contractJson, url: process.env['DATABASE_URL']! });

    After:

    import { contractFromJson } from '@prisma/orm-postgres/static';

export const contract = contractFromJson<Contract>(contractJson);
export const db = postgres({ contract, url: process.env['DATABASE_URL']! });

  • Date, time, interval and bytes defaults are written with tags, and each default has one stored form. contract emit refuses a quoted date, time, interval or bytes default and names the tag to write. A bytea default takes hexadecimal, not base64. A PostgreSQL contract that stores a default in another form than its column's type gives, such as "1.5" on numeric(10,2), is refused by the CLI: run prisma contract emit, then prisma db sign. On SQLite, datetime and JSON columns get their own data types; run the app recipe's script before the next CLI command, because the CLI refuses the old contract. Reading a value that its column's type cannot hold now throws RUNTIME.DECODE_FAILED. A SQLite DateTime text with no UTC offset is read as UTC. Run prisma db sign against every database after the upgrade. See date-time-interval-and-bytes-defaults-use-tags, sqlite-contracts-name-datetime-and-json-data-types, postgres-defaults-stored-in-another-spelling, prisma7-datetime-default-finer-than-column, stored-values-a-column-type-does-not-hold, sqlite-datetime-without-offset-read-as-utc, text-array-min-max-return-arrays and sign-databases-after-data-type-values in the app recipe. (#30750)

    Before:

    at      DateTime @default("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z")
day     Date     @default("2024-03-15")
payload Bytes    @default("AQID")

    After:

    at      DateTime @default(timestamptz`2024-01-01T00:00:00Z`)
day     Date     @default(date`2024-03-15`)
payload Bytes    @default(bytea`\x010203`)

  • @noCheck is removed, and a list that allows null elements is written T?[]. A stored contract with a noCheck key no longer loads. First run the app recipe's script, which rewrites stored contracts and migration snapshots, then run prisma db sign against every database. Then replace T[] @noCheck(elementNotNull) with T?[] and delete @noCheck(membership); in TypeScript, use .many({ elementsNullable: true }). A contract read from a Prisma 7 schema now types list elements as T | null, and the Supabase extension's four text[] columns allow null elements; both change the storage hash, so sign your databases. See stored-contracts-drop-nocheck, psl-nocheck-removed, ts-nocheck-method-removed, prisma7-lists-allow-null-elements and supabase-contract-lists-allow-null-elements in the app recipe. Extension authors run the same script from the extension package root, then re-emit the bundled contract; see stored-contracts-drop-nocheck, psl-nocheck-removed and ts-nocheck-method-removed in the extension recipe. (#30741)

    Before:

    tags String[] @noCheck(elementNotNull)

    After:

    tags String?[]

  • Type-constructor arguments are values. A quoted number, such as VarChar("255") or Timestamp("3"), is refused with PSL_VALUE_TYPE_INCOMPATIBLE; write the number without quotes. On Postgres a whole number written with a fraction, such as VarChar(255.0), is refused too, and so is a number the type cannot hold. The same applies to a field preset's precision, such as temporal.timestamp("3"). See type-constructor-arguments-are-values in the app recipe. (#30801)

    Before:

    name VarChar("255")

    After:

    name VarChar(255)

  • Enum members are values of their data type. A PSL enum member is read as a value of the enum codec's data type, as a @default is. A quoted member is refused on a codec whose type is not text, such as pg/numeric@1 or pg/int8@1; write numbers unquoted and dates and times with their tag. Enums typed by pg/jsonb@1, pg/timetz@1, pg/enum@1, arktype/json@1, pg/vector@1 or pg/geometry@1 are refused; use a text enum, or a native enum instead of pg/enum@1. Members of a pg/numeric@1, pg/interval@1 or mongo/decimal128@1 enum compare as values, so 0.5 and 0.50 are duplicates. Columns of more enum codecs are now typed as the union of their members; re-emit the contract. See psl-enum-members-read-by-the-cast-rule, more-codecs-refused-for-enums, enum-members-compare-by-their-data-type and enum-columns-typed-by-member-literals in the app recipe. (#30790)

    Before:

    enum Ratio {
  @@type("pg/numeric@1")
  Half  = "0.5"
}

    After:

    enum Ratio {
  @@type("pg/numeric@1")
  Half  = 0.5
}

  • Generator arguments are checked, and a generator must fit its column. An argument uuid, cuid or nanoid does not take, such as uuid(5), is now refused, in Prisma 8 PSL with PSL_INVALID_GENERATOR_ARGUMENT and in a Prisma 7 schema with PSL.PRISMA7_UNKNOWN_DEFAULT; it used to be read as something else. A number with a fraction, such as nanoid(8.0), is refused too. A generator on a Postgres column too short for what it writes, such as VarChar(5) @onCreate(uuid()), is refused when the contract is built instead of failing at the first insert. A SQL @@discriminator that is not text has a new message. See prisma7-default-function-arguments-checked, generator-function-argument-diagnostics, generator-function-argument-with-fraction, generator-fits-column and discriminator-must-be-text in the app recipe. (#30792)

  • Re-emit contract.d.ts, and expect more precise types from defineContract. prisma contract emit writes field and column types as generics applied to the contract, so a SQL contract.d.ts emitted by an earlier release no longer compiles; re-emit it. A contract built with defineContract now gets the same ORM types as an emitted one: typed include rows, aggregates, query operations, parameterized types such as Varchar<50>, index names in where and orderBy callbacks, unique keys in whereUnique, and its enums. A Mongo defineContract contract types lists and value objects as readonly, and its factory form no longer types every field as never. Casts that only worked because a type was unknown or never may now fail to compile. See typescript-contract-include-row-types, typescript-contract-aggregates-and-operations, typescript-contract-parameterized-output-types, typescript-contract-index-references, typescript-contract-storage-and-domain-types, typescript-contract-enums-in-domain, emitted-contract-types-from-generics, emitted-field-types-from-shared-generic, mongo-define-contract-readonly-rows, mongo-define-contract-factory-field-types, value-object-enum-fields-narrow and mongo-update-accessors-take-input-types in the app recipe. (#30709, #30747)

  • A MongoDB field keeps its schema name in code. A field declared id ObjectId @id @map("_id") is the field id in the contract, in ORM rows and in where, select, orderBy and write data, where it was _id. The contract records the stored name in model.storage.fields, and a contract without it is refused with CONTRACT.VALIDATION_FAILED. Run prisma contract emit, then the app recipe's script, which rewrites migration snapshots. Storage hashes do not change. --rename and --delete name fields by their schema names. @map on a field of a composite type is now refused, because it was always ignored. In the TypeScript builder, set a stored name with .mongo({ field: '_id' }). See mongo-contracts-record-stored-field-names, mongo-orm-uses-field-names, mongo-statements-name-fields, mongo-composite-field-map-refused and mongo-typescript-stored-field-names in the app recipe. (#30779)

    Before:

    await db.orm.users.where({ _id: user._id }).update({ name: 'Ada' });

    After:

    await db.orm.users.where({ id: user.id }).update({ name: 'Ada' });

  • MongoDB contracts written in TypeScript get a collection validator. A defineContract contract now gets the same closed $jsonSchema validator as a PSL contract, and its storage hash changes once. defineContract refuses what a validator cannot describe, such as an _id that can hold an array or null. MongoDB does not check existing documents when a validator is added, so fix documents the validator would refuse, then apply it with prisma db update, or with prisma migration plan and prisma db migrate. A collection shared by several models now gets a validator that accepts each of them; apply it the same way. See mongo-typescript-contract-validator and mongo-shared-collection-validator in the app recipe. (#30773)

  • Each SQL ORM call is one orm-call activity, and ORM annotations live on it. The statements an ORM call sends carry no user annotations, so a middleware that reads an annotation from a statement plan finds nothing; read it in activityStarted from the orm-call activity. The cache middleware caches an annotated ORM read as a whole, keyed by cacheAnnotation({ key }) or by the call's content hash; deriveKey applies only to SQL builder queries. If your deriveKey separates tenants or users, give each annotated ORM read a tenant-prefixed key, or one tenant's cached ORM read can be served to another. A custom cache store holds CachedValue instead of CachedRows. A hand-built object passed to orm() that copies only query and execute now fails with ORM.ACTIVITY_SOURCE_MISSING. An ORM call still pending at close() now completes instead of rejecting. See orm-annotations-on-the-call, cached-orm-reads-key-on-the-call, cache-store-holds-cached-values, orm-needs-a-runtime-queryable and close-lets-open-orm-calls-finish in the app recipe. (#30749)

    Before:

    async beforeEncode(plan) {
  const actor = auditAnnotation.read(plan);
  if (actor) log(actor);
},

    After:

    async activityStarted(activity) {
  if (activity.kind !== 'orm-call') return;
  const actor = auditAnnotation.read(activity);
  if (actor) log(actor);
},

  • Migration checks require the full effect of an operation, so plan unapplied migrations again. The runner skips an operation only when its checks show the whole effect is already in place. On PostgreSQL, SQLite and MongoDB these checks now compare the full definition, not just a name. An ops.json written by an earlier release keeps its old checks: run migration.ts again for each migration that is not applied yet. On PostgreSQL, this.setDefault no longer takes operationClass; delete the option. Widening an autoincrement() column now also widens its sequence; for a migration already applied, run ALTER SEQUENCE … AS bigint yourself. this.alterColumnType with using on a column that already has the new type is refused; write the conversion as a dataTransform. See setdefault-operation-class-derived, setdefault-has-no-postcheck, the postgres-postcheck-* entries, postgres-alter-column-type-unchanged-refused, postgres-autoincrement-sequence-follows-column-type, sqlite-postchecks-check-full-definition and mongo-postchecks-check-full-definition in the app recipe. (#30752)

  • A failed migration reports the runner's own error code. MIGRATION.RUNNER_FAILED no longer exists. A failed apply reports codes such as MIGRATION.SCHEMA_VERIFY_FAILED, MIGRATION.PRECHECK_FAILED or MIGRATION.POSTCHECK_FAILED, with typed meta.schemaIssues and meta.failedCheck. On a control client, dbInit, dbUpdate and migrate take a required invocation option, and their failures are CliStructuredErrors. See runner-failures-report-own-codes and control-client-apply-takes-invocation in the app recipe. (#30791)

  • prisma db schema --json names a column's type typeText. It holds the type as the database reports it, such as integer, in place of nativeType, and resolvedNativeType is gone. The tree output shows the same text. CONTRACT.DEFAULT_INVALID carries meta.typeText instead of meta.nativeType. See db-schema-json-names-type-text and default-invalid-meta-type-text in the app recipe. (#30777)

  • String timestamp columns are filled with text. The Postgres temporal.*String presets, and every @updatedAt field a prisma7Schema(...) contract reads, now fill the column with text instead of a Date. Re-emit the contract; only the execution hash changes. The pg/timestamp-string@1 and pg/timestamptz-string@1 codecs refuse a Date at runtime with RUNTIME.ENCODE_FAILED. See string-timestamp-presets-write-text and string-timestamp-codecs-take-text-only in the app recipe. (#30742)

  • using is a reserved member of every ORM collection. A custom collection class with its own member named using no longer compiles; rename it. See orm-collection-member-using-reserved in the app recipe. (#30717)

  • Objects that implement client or transaction types need the new members. Clients and transactions gain query, execute, toSql and other members (see Features). Code that only uses these types needs no change. Code that builds its own object of one of them, such as a test double, must add the new members. supabase() now creates its pool on the first query. See client-query-and-to-sql in the app recipe and transaction-query-members in the extension recipe. (#30802, #30789)

  • Extension authors: activities, codecs and generator functions. RuntimeActivity is renamed Activity and now includes client activities, which an extension starts with startActivityOn; queryables and transactions carry an activity source. A codec implements toWire, fromWire, toDataTypeValue and fromDataTypeValue instead of encode, decode, encodeJson and decodeJson, and a data type's read replaces toCanonicalForm. A default function can no longer generate a value in the client; contribute a generator function instead, and stop registering the identifier generators the SQL family now registers. A SQL target declares the uuid, cuid and nanoid signatures with sqlIntegerArgumentGeneratorFunctions. See runtime-activity-is-activity, activity-includes-client-activities, start-a-client-activity, runtime-connections-carry-an-activity-source, begin-transaction-on-takes-a-parent, transaction-activity-takes-a-parent, orm-runtime-objects-carry-an-activity-source, orm-annotations-on-the-call, cache-store-holds-cached-values, queryable-carries-the-activity-source, codecs-read-wire-and-data-type-values, data-types-own-parameter-limits, json-helpers-renamed, stored-form-helpers-renamed, projections-read-by-from-wire, empty-result-json-renamed-empty-result-wire, default-functions-lower-to-database-defaults-only, applicable-codec-ids-and-build-phases-removed, sql-family-registers-identifier-generators, sql-target-declares-integer-argument-generators, generator-signature-from-data-types, generator-function-field-length, build-contract-definition-takes-lookups, arg-binding-spec-label, one-of-refuses-data-type-value and text-data-types in the extension recipe. (#30706, #30749, #30750, #30780, #30742, #30792)

  • Extension authors: type constructors, column types, contract types and MongoDB. A type constructor's value argument is declared { kind: 'value', dataType }, and the string, boolean and stringArray kinds are removed. Columns are compared by data type, so the type-name normalisers and SqlTypeLookups and MongoTypeLookups are removed, schema IR columns have typeText, and the Postgres and SQLite control adapters take the stack's data types. A codec whose output type depends on its type parameters declares a type function instead of renderOutputType, and FieldTypesFromDomain moves to @prisma/orm-framework/contract/types. A MongoDB model's storage records each field's stored name, and deriveJsonSchema is replaced by deriveCollectionValidators. See value-arguments-name-a-data-type, value-argument-types-in-typescript, psl-and-print-helpers-take-data-types, composed-helpers-take-no-data-type-lookup, helper-codec-invariants, type-lookups-one-framework-type, type-name-normalisers-removed, introspected-type-text, schema-ir-column-type-text, default-resolver-takes-the-column, alter-type-postcheck-by-data-type, control-adapters-take-declared-data-types, resolved-sql-type-carries-the-data-type, typescript-contract-pack-type-slots, parameterized-output-types-declared-once, psl-interpreter-contract-capabilities, field-types-expression-removed, field-types-generic-moved, resolve-field-value-set-renamed, mongo-parameterized-output-types, family-codec-templates-render-no-literals, enum-block-written-values, mongo-model-storage-fields, mongo-validator-derivation-moves-to-mongo-contract, mongo-derive-json-schema-replaced-by-derive-collection-validators and aggregate-operation-using-reserved in the extension recipe. The app-facing changes above also apply to extensions that build clients, write migrations or ship contracts. (#30801, #30777, #30709, #30747, #30790, #30779, #30733, #30773, #30717)

Features

  • @onCreate(fn()) and @onUpdate(fn()) set the values the client generates, and each function resolves for the column's codec: uuid() works on String, VarChar(n), Char(n) and Uuid. A column may have both a database @default and a generator. The TypeScript builder has .onCreate(gen.uuid(7)) and .onUpdate(gen.now()). (#30780)
  • Every Postgres date and time type has a now() generator, including date, time and timetz, so @updatedAt works on @db.Date, @db.Time and @db.Timetz. A generator on an optional field generates a value the client leaves out and stores an explicit null. (#30742)
  • Raw(sql`ltree`) declares a column of a database type no data type in the stack knows, on Postgres and SQLite. Migrations create it from the text, db verify compares that text with the database, and the ORM reads and writes its values as unknown. The TypeScript builder has type.Raw(sql`...`) and rawColumn(sql`...`). (#30745, #30801)
  • A Prisma 7 schema with Unsupported(...) fields now loads through prisma7Schema(). Each such field becomes a raw column with no field on the model, as in Prisma 7's client. (#30788)
  • A Prisma 7 schema with @updatedAt beside @default(now()), or with a generator on an optional field, now loads, signs and verifies against the database Prisma 7 built. (#30742)
  • A client can be created with no database. db.toSql(plan) renders any plan as { sql, params }, and db.query(plan) and db.execute(plan) run a plan directly. postgres(), postgresServerless(), sqlite() and supabase() take mode: 'strict' | 'permissive'. (#30802)
  • Every SQL client takes custom collection classes as the collections option, and uses them on db.orm, on every transaction's tx.orm, on serverless connections and on Supabase role-bound clients. (#30776)
  • A transaction offers the client's query members (sql, orm, raw, prepare, query, execute) on every SQL client. A Supabase role-bound client gains prepare, and SQLite's db.orm gains fragment. (#30789)
  • Packages contribute collection methods computed from a model, under using. The Postgres package adds a search method for each full-text index, such as db.orm.public.Post.using.post_search(query), and pgvector adds a nearest-neighbour search for each vector field. The methods chain with where, orderBy and limit. (#30717)
  • Middleware sees each SQL ORM call as one orm-call activity, with its statements as children, and can answer the whole call through intercept.onActivity. The cache middleware uses this to cache an annotated ORM read as a whole, so a cache hit sends no statement. (#30706, #30749)
  • ORM filters and writes take each field's input type, so a Varchar<50>, Char<36> or Numeric<10, 2> field accepts a plain string in where, create, update and the other write methods. (#30709)
  • A pg.enum column can name a native_enum declared in another namespace, such as pg.enum(auth.OrderStatus). (#30721)
  • prisma contract infer reads each column's type from the data types of the configured target and extensions. It writes the shortest matching type constructor, and when columns have types no pack declares, it fails once and lists every one of them instead of writing a schema that cannot emit. New Bit, VarBit and Interval type constructors let those columns infer. (#30735)
  • prisma db verify and the migration planner compare column types as data types with their parameters, so numeric(10) matches numeric(10,0). A database column of a type no configured pack declares gets a message that says so. (#30777)
  • A SQL @@discriminator field may be a Char(n) or VarChar(n) column on Postgres, or a sql.String(n) column on SQLite. (#30792)

Fixes

  • A hand-written setDefault that changes an existing default is applied instead of skipped, and the runner no longer skips an operation because an object of the same name but another definition exists. (#30752)
  • Widening a Postgres autoincrement() column from int4 to int8 now also widens its sequence, which used to stop at 2147483647. (#30752)
  • When a raw SQL default fails the schema check because the database stores it in another form, the error shows both texts and the sql literal to write. (#30740)
  • The MongoDB ORM's typed where accepts null, an empty list and a whole list on list fields, and null on a nullable field. A null filter on a list field matches only a null or missing list, not a list that holds a null item. (#30769)
  • A MongoDB PSL contract with a composite type that contains itself now emits, where it failed with Maximum call stack size exceeded. (#30733)
  • A MongoDB collection that stores several unrelated models gets a validator that accepts all of them, where it described only the last model. (#30773)
  • An enum field inside a value object is typed by its enum's members, as an enum field of a model is. (#30747)
  • The language server no longer leaves an unhandled rejection when it removes a file watcher after the editor connection has closed. (#30787)
  • A cache store's get and unset take optional fields, so code that calls a store directly passes only the fields it needs, where it had to pass undefined for the others. cache.invalidate and cacheAnnotation accept undefined for their optional fields under exactOptionalPropertyTypes. Stores written against the old shape still fit. (#30822)

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.19-dev.1: chore(release): bump to 8.0.0-rc.19 (#30821)
item.content:encoded:
Version 8.0.0-rc.18 → 8.0.0-rc.19. Merging this PR publishes the
release.

What to review

  • Release notes:
    docs/releases/v8.0.0-rc.19.md.
    This file becomes the GitHub Release body. It covers 51 merged PRs: 19
    breaking changes, then features and fixes. CHANGELOG.md has the same
    entry.
  • App upgrade guide:
    skills/prisma-8/upgrading/app/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.18-to-8.0.0-rc.19/instructions.md.
    It has 82 changes and five scripts, and it opens with the order to run
    the steps in.
  • Extension upgrade guide:
    skills/prisma-8/upgrading/extension/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.18-to-8.0.0-rc.19/instructions.md.
    It has 81 changes and two scripts.

What the commits do

  1. Version bump. It sets 8.0.0-rc.19 in every workspace
    package.json and the workspace: pins in pnpm-lock.yaml. It also
    changes the library_version stamp in skills/prisma-8/SKILL.md and
    the Supabase extension version stamped in contract artefacts.
  2. Upgrade guides. All 38 pending fragments are combined into the
    two guides above. The originals are moved unchanged to
    upgrade-instructions/releases/8.0.0-rc.18-to-8.0.0-rc.19/sources/. The
    upgrade-instruction tests now read the published guides and scripts.
    Tests that called live framework code were made to read committed
    fixtures or were deleted, as in earlier releases.
  3. Release notes, as above.

While combining the fragments, I made these changes:

  • Dropped raw-columns-take-a-sql-literal. Raw(...) is new in
    this release, so nobody upgrading from rc.18 has the quoted form it
    tells you to change.
  • Dropped print-generated-values-through-generator-functions. It
    said not to add printArguments, which never shipped in rc.18.
  • Corrected a fragment: an ORM call fails with
    ORM.ACTIVITY_SOURCE_MISSING when its queryable has no activity source.
    One fragment said the call just starts no activity.
  • Corrected a fragment: a SQL contract.d.ts from rc.18 still
    compiles. One fragment said it does not compile.

Checks run locally

  • pnpm check:upgrade-coverage --mode publish --prev v8.0.0-rc.18 --head HEAD passes.
  • pnpm check:release-notes --mode pr passes.
  • The upgrade-instruction tests pass: 44 files, 744 tests.

How the release ships

When this merges, the push to main carries the new root version. The
Publish to npm workflow then publishes 8.0.0-rc.19 under the
latest dist-tag and creates a pre-release GitHub Release from the
notes file. See
docs/oss/versioning.md.

A docs PR for prisma/web follows. It must merge only after this release
is on npm.

Agent: rochester-20

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • New Features
  • Added typed contract values, raw columns, custom collections,
    transaction query members, database-free plan execution, Prisma 7
    Unsupported support, and improved type inference.
  • Bug Fixes
  • Improved migration verification, MongoDB field and validator handling,
    recursive composites, enum behavior, sequence handling, and
    language-server cleanup.
  • Documentation
    • Added release notes and upgrade guidance for Prisma 8.0.0-rc.19.
  • Breaking Changes
  • Updated defaults, validation, migration metadata, ORM activity and
    caching semantics, extension APIs, and removed noCheck support.

Signed-off-by: willbot w.a.madden+machine@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Will Madden madden@prisma.io

item.title: 19.3.0 (September 9, 2026)
item.content:encoded:
Below is a list of all new features, APIs, and bug fixes.

Read the React 19.3 release post for more information.

New React Features

  • <ViewTransition />: Adds <ViewTransition /> and addTransitionType APIs to power View Transition animations in React (@sebmarkbage, @jackpope, @gaearon: #31975, #31987, #31996, #31999, #32001, #32002, #32028, #32029, #32031, #32034, #32038, #32041, #32050, #32090, #32105, #32254, #32379, #32422, #32462, #32540, #32545, #32585, #32599, #32611, #32612, #32617, #32651, #32653, #32656, #32664, #32699, #32723, #32734, #32751, #32752, #32760, #32761, #32764, #32772, #32790, #32819, #32820, #32822, #32833, #32849, #33094, #33191, #33200, #33206, #33293, #33330, #33331, #33332, #33357, #33362, #33433, #33576, #34374, #34450, #34481, #34500, #34502, #34510, #34511, #34539, #35567, #35564, #35485, #35380, #35063, #35060, #34676, #36917, #35337, #35520)
  • Fragment Refs: Add Refs to <Fragment /> to support composable platform behavior (@jackpope, @sebmarkbage, @eps1lon, @Dhakshin2007, @chirokas, @teamleaderleo, @fallintoplace: #32465, #32613, #32619, #32654, #32660, #32682, #32722, #32813, #32814, #33056, #33058, #33093, #34069, #34103, #34544, #34545, #37062, #37061, #37060, #36047, #36010, #35642, #35641, #35637, #35630, #34935, #37457, #37408, #37326, #37251, #37171, #37169, #37168, #37167, #37166, #37165, #37164, #37163, #37162, #37161, #37160, #37125, #37063)

New React DOM Features

  • browser(): a new react-dom API that returns a usable which errors during server rendering and resolves in the browser. use(browser()) inside a <Suspense> boundary marks a subtree as browser-only without reporting a recoverable error (@gnoff: #37143, #37241)
    • Added an onBrowserBailout option to the react-dom/server APIs to observe when a subtree defers to the browser (@gnoff #37193)

Notable changes

  • Enable Trusted Types API integration (@rickhanlonii #35816)
  • Transitions now render independently instead of being entangled into a single render, so a slow transition no longer holds up unrelated ones (@acdlite #37290)
  • Added a DEV-only warning when a component appears to have been unblocked by calling use() conditionally (@hoxyq, @eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)

All Changes

React

  • Fast Refresh Fixes
    • Fix Fast Refresh to find and remount edits to components wrapped behind lazy() (@sophiebits #36965)
    • Fix Fast Refresh so edits to a memo() comparison function take effect (@sophiebits #36964)
    • Fix Fast Refresh crash when an edit changes the kind of a component's type (@sophiebits #36963)
    • Unify hot reload type resolution for Fast Refresh (@sophiebits #36962)
    • Fix Fast Refresh to remount correctly when an edit changes the component kind (@sophiebits #36950)
    • Double invoke effects in StrictMode after Fast Refresh (@eps1lon #35962)
  • Performance Track Fixes
    • Prevent crash when accessing $$typeof in Performance Tracks (@eps1lon #35679)
    • Handle non-string function names in Performance Tracks (@eps1lon #35659)
    • Use minus (-) instead of en dash for removed props in Performance Tracks (@eps1lon #35649)
    • Handle arrays with bigints in deep objects in Performance Tracks (@eps1lon #35648)
    • Don't enumerate typed array props in Performance Tracks in DEV (@UditDewan #36913)
    • Bail out of diffing wide objects and arrays in Performance Tracks (@eps1lon #34742)
    • Clear potentially large performance measures in DEV (@hoxyq #34803)
    • Fix missing else branch for renders with no props change in Performance Tracks (@hoxyq #34837)
  • Activity Fixes
    • Fix useSyncExternalStore missing store mutations that happened while an Activity tree was hidden (@sophiebits #36947)
    • Hide portal contents when an Activity is hidden (@acdlite #35091)
    • Prevent metadata hoisting in hidden <Activity> trees (@ronnakamoto #34983)
    • Prevent errors thrown inside a hidden Activity from escaping to the visible UI (@acdlite #35074)
    • Don't unhide a node if a direct parent Offscreen is still hidden (@sebmarkbage #34821)
    • Don't show internal <Offscreen> component in error messages (@rickhanlonii #35763)
  • Warn in DEV when a component appears to have been unblocked by a conditional use() (@hoxyq, @eps1lon: #37104, #37203, #37491)
  • Render transitions independently instead of entangling them into a single render (@acdlite #37290)
  • Fix hang when updating a dehydrated boundary inside a hidden tree (@gaearon #37135)
  • Don't reacquire Host Singletons during dev effect validation (@gnoff #37113)
  • Only remove properties from Host Singletons on release (@gnoff #37112)
  • Don't invoke effects on moved children in StrictMode (@sophiebits #36948)
  • Throw a clearer error when a rejected Promise is incorrectly instrumented (@eps1lon #36328)
  • Fix context propagation into Suspense fallbacks (@acdlite #36160)
  • Fix context propagation through suspended Suspense boundaries (@acdlite #35839)
  • Fix useDeferredValue getting stuck (@gaearon #36134)
  • Update useActionState error message to say "action state" instead of "form state" (@rickhanlonii #35790)
  • Don't warn when rendering data block scripts (@eps1lon #35953)
  • Treat fibers with alternates as mounted in getNearestMountedFiber (@sebmarkbage #35578)
  • Always instrument the lazy initializer thenable (@gnoff #35521)
  • Annotate cascading updates for DevTools performance tracks in DEV (@huntie #34961)
  • Resolve the .default export of a React.lazy as the canonical value (@sebmarkbage #34906)
  • Limit owner stacks to 10 frames (@eps1lon #34864)
  • Ensure useEffectEvent reads latest values in forwardRef and memo() components (@eps1lon #34831)

React DOM

  • Copy source onto the synthetic toggle event (@lazerg #37389)
  • Update HTML parser rules for the new <select> parser (@josepharhar #34804)
  • Update defaultValue for type="number" inputs to match other input types (@sophiebits #36980)
  • Avoid setting innerHTML when it hasn't changed (@sophiebits #36949)
  • Forward the nonce option in ReactDOM.preloadModule() (@UditDewan #36851)
  • Support fetchPriority for module resources (@TheAlexLichter #36835)
  • Track stylesheet preloads when explicitly preloaded to avoid unnecessary suspension (@gnoff #36386)
  • Suggest correct casing for the misspelled credentialless iframe attribute (@vmx906 #36322)
  • Add credentialless as a recognized boolean attribute for iframes (@vmx906 #36148)
  • Prevent reentrant finishedTask from calling completeAll multiple times (@gnoff #36287)
  • Update the CSS shorthand property list (@kidonng #35636)
  • Support the maskType SVG prop (@sleitor #35921)
  • Add support for onFullscreenChange and onFullscreenError events (@chirokas #34621)
  • Include submitter in submit events (@eps1lon #35590)
  • Fire onReset when automatically resetting forms (@eps1lon #35176)
  • Use the FormData submitter parameter (@jenseng #29028)
  • Fix form status reset when component state is updated (@eps1lon #34075)
  • Batch updates from resize events until the next frame (@eps1lon #35117)

React Server

  • Add nonce to rendered import maps (@mattcosta7 #37339)
  • Add an onBrowserBailout option to observe subtrees that defer to the browser (@gnoff #37193)
  • Stop the caller's signal from retaining a finished render (@unstubbable #37315)
  • Construct the render lifetime controller only when it is needed (@unstubbable #37357)
  • Fix react-dom/server hanging on Deno (@fraidev #35235)
  • Extend stack overflow recovery to retries in SSR (@jackpope #36977)
  • Fix false-positive hydration mismatch on nonce attributes (@MaxwellCohen #37030)
  • Guard shell-error callbacks instead of nulling them out on the request (@eps1lon #36916)
  • Stop firing onAllReady after the shell errored (@eps1lon #36903)
  • Treat an incomplete tree as an error during error recovery (@acdlite #36911)
  • Fix non-script modulepreload tracking (@fallintoplace #36564)
  • Finalize postponed nextSegmentId after the prelude flush (@gaojude #36779)
  • Preserve referrerPolicy in image preload headers (@ulises-jeremias #36803)
  • Allow pending work to specialize abort reasons (@gnoff #36586)
  • Abort tasks that suspend after aborting during render (@gnoff #36585)
  • Finish abort in a scheduled task (@gnoff #36580)
  • Fix aborts during resumed rendering (@gnoff #36584)
  • Track abort state on the request (@gnoff #36583)
  • Model external work scheduling explicitly in the fb bundle (@gnoff #36576)
  • Continue reporting aborted task errors after a fatal abort (@gnoff #36575)
  • Disallow abort reentrancy (@gnoff #36574)
  • Stop transpiling computed property names (@eps1lon #36542)
  • Fix crash when capturing the callsite of a stalled use() of a rejected Flight chunk (@lubieowoce #36544)
  • Double invoke effects in Strict Mode during hydration (@eps1lon #35961)
  • Add additional task reentrancy protections in Fizz (@gnoff #36291)
  • Don't outline Suspense boundaries with suspensey CSS during shell flush (@gnoff #35824)
  • Push a stalled use() to the owner stack and debug task (@eps1lon #35226)
  • Fix useId tracking on replay (@gnoff #35518)
  • Correctly handle replaying when hydrating (@gnoff #35494)
  • Simplify the createSuspenseBoundary path (@sebmarkbage #35087)
  • Unify preamble-only fields to save a field on Suspense boundaries (@sebmarkbage #35068)
  • Unify prerender-only fields to save a field on Suspense boundaries (@sebmarkbage #35067)
  • Push halted awaits to the owner stack for late-arriving I/O info (@unstubbable #35019)
  • Include all Node.js APIs in the Bun entrypoint for react-dom/server (@RiskyMH #34193)
  • Detach a Suspense boundary after flushing its segment (@gnoff #34694)

React Server Components

  • Keep an element pending while a referenced row is resolving (@unstubbable #37542)
  • Fix RangeError from exponential debug info growth (@unstubbable #37481)
  • Abort the cache signal when debug objects are retained (@unstubbable #37342)
  • Transfer key validation of lazy nodes when they are unwrapped (@unstubbable #37258)
  • Add pending_weak to the Flight thenable protocol (@acdlite #37154)
  • Outline and dedupe repeated strings (@gaearon #37147)
  • Port Reply Server traversal guards to the Flight Client (@eps1lon #37144)
  • Define Flight chunk .then with Object.defineProperty (@eps1lon #37109)
  • Support Turbopack's experimental array format for chunks (@sampoder #37095)
  • Limit fake JSX call site stacks to 10 frames (@timneutkens #37086)
  • Improve performance when decoding Flight replies (@gnoff #37090)
  • Recognize Node 22+ V8 frames for Promise statics in debug info (@gaearon #36969)
  • Tailor the warning for binary data serialized through toJSON (Node Buffer) (@unstubbable #36873)
  • Resolve models before JSON.stringify for faster serialization (@mhart #36795)
  • Prune debug info when chunks error (@gnoff #36782)
  • Avoid main-thread stalls from large debug strings (@unstubbable #36570)
  • Fix stranded row content under Node stream backpressure (@unstubbable #36516)
  • Fix dropped FormData entries in decodeReplyFromBusboy (@unstubbable #36468)
  • Harden types and improve performance of Flight replies (@eps1lon #36425)
  • Add more cycle protections to Flight replies (@eps1lon #36236)
  • Transport AggregateError.errors (@eps1lon #36156)
  • Bail out early when a backing entry for Blob deserialization is not a Blob (@eps1lon #36055)
  • Clear chunk reason after successful module initialization (@unstubbable #36024)
  • Add support for transporting Error.cause (@eps1lon #35810)
  • Walk parsed JSON instead of using a reviver for faster RSC payload parsing (@timneutkens #35776)
  • Skip transferReferencedDebugInfo during debug info resolution (@unstubbable #35795)
  • Add unstable_allowPartialStream option to Flight Client (@unstubbable #35731)
  • Fix encodeReply for JSX with temporary references (@unstubbable #35730)
  • Fix debug channel flag in Node.js renderToPipeableStream (@feedthejim #35724)
  • Fix stack overflow in visitAsyncNode with deep async chains (@unstubbable #35612)
  • Allow Server Components to render context providers from client modules (@rickhanlonii #35675)
  • Allow overriding request.timeOrigin via options.startTime (@lubieowoce #35598)
  • Warn once if eval is disabled in the dev environment (@eps1lon #35661)
  • Restore original function name in dev server callstacks served with unsafe-eval (@eps1lon #35650)
  • Fix react-markup types for server references (@eps1lon #35634)
  • Add more DoS mitigations to Flight replies and harden Flight (@unstubbable #35632)
  • Allow cyclic references to be serialized when unwrapping lazy elements (@unstubbable #35471)
  • Improve cyclic thenable detection in Flight reply server (@cvan20191 #35369)
  • Add extra loop protection to Flight reply server (@sebmarkbage #35351)
  • Patch Promise cycles and toString on Server Functions (@sebmarkbage #35345)
  • Move react-server-dom-webpack/*.unbundled to private react-server-dom-unbundled (@eps1lon #35290)
  • Never parse then functions in Flight replies (@sebmarkbage #35289)
  • Patch Flight reply server with fixes from Flight Client (@sebmarkbage #35277)
  • Complete the list of Node.js internal Promise awaits (@eps1lon #35161)
  • Reduce risk of maximum call stack exceeded when emitting async sequences (@eps1lon #35159)
  • Fix pending chunks count for streams and async iterables in DEV (@unstubbable #35143)
  • Fix broken byte stream parsing caused by buffer detachment (@unstubbable #35127)
  • Fix hasReadable flag in Node.js clients' debug channel (@unstubbable #35039)
  • Fix debug info filtering to include later resolved I/O (@unstubbable #35036)
  • Cache the value when visiting the same I/O or Promise along different paths (@sebmarkbage #35005)
  • Clone subsequent I/O nodes when resolved more than once (@sebmarkbage #35003)
  • Fix hang after resolving cyclic references (@unstubbable #34988)
  • Allow passing DEV-only startTime as an option (@sebmarkbage #34912)
  • Ignore bound-anonymous-fn resources as they're not considered I/O (@sebmarkbage #34911)
  • Fix detached ArrayBuffer error when streaming typed arrays (@unstubbable #34849)
  • Exclude RSC stream if the stream resolves in a task (@sebmarkbage #34838)
  • Forward the current environment when forwarding I/O entries (@sebmarkbage #34836)

item.title: v1.17.0
item.content:encoded:
1.17.0 (October 21, 2026)

NEW FEATURES:

  • Terraform now supports variables and locals in provider requirements (#39153)

  • A new -minimal-refresh planning option has been added, which will only refresh resources that have proposed changes. (#35290)

  • policy: Terraform Policy is now generally available. The -policies flag for plan, apply, and query no longer requires an experimental build or the -allow-experimental-features flag. Query policies evaluate resources discovered by list blocks and report human-readable or JSON results. See https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/policy for more information. (#38970)

ENHANCEMENTS:

  • command/init: Enrich log messages with provider versions (#38918)

  • test: Add mock_provider support for ephemeral resources (#38928)

  • command/login: display warning after successful login if user is subject to an organization's TTL policy

BUG FIXES:

  • funcs: pow and log no longer panic when result is not a number (#38912)

  • ephemeral: Terraform will now use and display diagnostics raised when renewing an ephemeral resource. This may cause warnings to appear that previously were lost. We expect that any error diagnostics that were previously lost would have caused confusing downstream errors, so we do not anticipate this change to be breaking. (#38989)

  • test: Deterministic dependency ordering in cleanup graph (#38247)

  • query: report Unknown and N/A results for policy evaluations of discovered resources (#39058)

  • query: terraform query -policies now rejects a path that is not a directory, instead of passing it on to the policy engine (#39238)

  • funcs: The log and pow functions now raise errors when they return +/- Infinity, as this result is not usable in downstream code. (#39304)

  • show: Read variable values from the plan file when showing a local plan (#39362)

NOTES:

  • version: JSON output now includes a new format_version field, which will enable safer future changes of the command's JSON output format. It is assumed existing tooling ignores unknown fields and therefore this change should not be breaking in itself but we advice consumers to pay attention to format_version in future releases and/or use latest version of hashicorp/terraform-json & hashicorp/terraform-exec which does. (#38930)

  • Terraform is now built with Go 1.26.10, which no longer trusts certificates issued through a set of compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs (CVE-2026-111943) (#39417)
