Announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a managed ingress solution for your ECS services
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon ECS Gateway, ingress networking, Application Load Balancers, centralized governance, ALB metrics

Summary: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) has introduced the ECS Gateway, a resource designed to simplify ingress networking for containerized applications. The ECS Gateway dynamically provisions and manages Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources within your AWS account. With this feature, platform teams can define organizational networking standards once and associate them with multiple clusters, offering a centralized method to govern traffic routing to ECS services. Application teams can easily inherit these standards without needing specialized networking knowledge. ECS Gateway supports host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share a single ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and provides each service with a unique DNS hostname. It automates the lifecycle management of infrastructure, provisioning ALBs as needed based on service connections and scaling down when they're no longer required. Users can inspect resources and route paths for request tracking while utilizing standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring. To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and add the gateway connector parameter through various AWS tools. ECS Gateway is available at no extra charge across all commercial AWS Regions.

AWS announces Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Gateway, a new resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized applications by dynamically provisioning and managing Application Load Balancers (ALBs) and their supporting resources directly in your account.

With ECS Gateway, platform teams define organizational networking standards once on a gateway and associate it with one or more clusters, giving organizations a centralized way to govern how traffic reaches their ECS services. Application teams simply opt in to inherit those standards without requiring networking expertise. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing, allows up to 25 services to share an ALB to optimize infrastructure costs, and gives each service a unique Domain Name System (DNS) hostname. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs when capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. You can inspect these resources and the gateway route to each service to see exactly how requests reach your applications. For traffic and health monitoring, you can use standard ALB metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and target health information from Elastic Load Balancing.

To get started, create an ECS Gateway, associate it with a cluster, and opt in your ECS service by adding the gateway connector parameter using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types. It is available now in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when your services connect to the gateway. To learn more, refer to the AWS News blog and our documentation page.

item.title: Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating replicas
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: global tables, replicate, disassociate, multi-account, eventual consistency

Summary: Global tables in Amazon DynamoDB now allow users to disassociate a replica without losing the associated table or data. This feature enhances the functionality of fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active replication. Users can stop replication both to and from a replica while continuing to operate the table as a single-Region table. With this update, accounts can exit a shared multi-account global table and maintain their tables independently. Additionally, users now have the ability to halt replication to a specific Region while still utilizing its table for localized workloads, validation, or auditing purposes, eliminating the need to create a new table or transfer data. The ability to disassociate replicas is supported across all AWS Regions for both same-account and multi-account global tables that implement multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC). To get started with these features, users can utilize the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, DynamoDB API, or AWS CloudFormation. For further details, refer to the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide.

Amazon DynamoDB global tables now support disassociating a replica without deleting its table or data. Global tables provide fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active replication. You can now stop replication to and from a replica and continue using the same table as a single-Region table.

An account can leave a shared multi-account global table and continue using its table independently. You can also stop replication to a Region while keeping its table for local workloads, validation, or audit, without creating a replacement table or copying data.

DynamoDB supports disassociating replicas in all AWS Regions for same-account and multi-account global tables that use multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC).

To get started, use the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, DynamoDB API, or AWS CloudFormation. For more information, see Disassociating replicas in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide.

item.title: Polly Generative engine upgraded with more natural speech, 14 new voices, and 2 new languages
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Polly, Generative engine, voice portfolio, new languages, low latency

Summary: Amazon Polly has launched an upgraded Generative engine that enhances the quality of speech output, making it more natural-sounding and accurate with low latency. This upgrade introduces a broader voice portfolio, including 14 new voices across nine locales and two new languages—Hindi and Finnish—now available for the first time. New voices feature US English options Kenneth and Nate, Australian English voices Russell and Curtis, Indian English and Hindi voices Kiara and Arjun, along with others like Tina (German) and Carlos (US Spanish). The service handles complex text inputs like numbers and addresses more effectively, reducing the need for manual adjustments. Users can continue leveraging Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tags to control speech output. The low-latency streaming API facilitates real-time applications in contact centers, chatbots, and voice-based LLMs, making it suitable for news, media, and accessibility applications. Additionally, the updated Amazon Polly offerings are now accessible in AWS GovCloud, catering to public sector and regulated industries, with new voices available in various AWS Regions including the US, Europe, and Asia Pacific.

Today, we are introducing a new model behind the Amazon Polly Generative engine that delivers more natural-sounding, accurate speech output with low latency. With this upgrade, you get access to an enhanced voice portfolio with higher overall quality, 14 new voices across nine locales, and two new languages—Hindi and Finnish—now generally available on the Generative engine for the first time. New voices include Kenneth and Nate (US English), Russell and Curtis (Australian English), Kiara and Arjun (Hindi and Indian English), Tina (German), Carlos (US Spanish), Leo and Carolina (Brazilian Portuguese), Hyunduk (Korean), and Suvi (Finnish).

Amazon Polly is a fully managed service that turns text into natural-sounding speech. This drop-in model upgrade makes Generative voices more natural and accurate. Complex content such as numbers, email addresses, and street addresses is designed to sound more reliable, reducing the need to fine-tune speech output. You can continue to use Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tags to control speech output on the Generative engine, just as before. The low-latency streaming API makes it easy to build contact center experiences, chatbots, and large language model (LLM) based agentic voice applications for real-time conversations. The richness and variety of voice options are also well suited for news, media, entertainment, e-learning, and accessibility use cases. This launch also expands the Amazon Polly Generative offering to AWS GovCloud, providing more options for public sector and regulated industries.

All new Generative voices are now available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West).

To hear how Polly voices sound, go to Amazon Polly Features. For more details on the Polly offerings and use, see the Amazon Polly documentation and pricing page.

item.title: AWS announces TorchNeuron: Native PyTorch Support for AWS Trainium (Public Beta)
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: TorchNeuron, AWS Trainium, PyTorch, open source, deep learning

Summary: AWS has launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, a new open source native PyTorch backend optimized for AWS Trainium, a series of AI chips designed for high performance and cost-effective deep learning AI training and inference workloads. With TorchNeuron, AI scientists and researchers can easily adapt their PyTorch code to run on Trainium by simply using the .to('neuron') method, ensuring full compatibility with PyTorch’s eager execution, torch.compile, and standard APIs. This user-friendly integration allows developers to transition their existing workflows without significant modifications. Moreover, TorchNeuron works alongside the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which supports the implementation of custom operators and enhances performance optimization specifically for Trainium hardware. The open-source version of TorchNeuron can be utilized on Amazon EC2 Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances, allowing users to exploit the capabilities of AWS's advanced AI infrastructure. For further information about TorchNeuron and the AWS Trainium accelerators, users are encouraged to visit the official website.

Today, AWS launched the public beta of TorchNeuron, an open source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium. Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed to deliver high performance and cost efficiency for deep learning AI training and inference workloads. TorchNeuron enables AI scientists and researchers to experiment and build models with PyTorch natively on Trainium.

With TorchNeuron, developers can enable their PyTorch code on Trainium simply by switching to .to('neuron') while maintaining full PyTorch compatibility with eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware.

TorchNeuron is available as open source through the TorchNeuron github repo for Amazon EC2 Trainium2 instances and Amazon EC2 Trainium3 instances.

To learn more about TorchNeuron and AWS Trainium accelerators, visit the AWS Neuron page.

item.title: Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, structured outputs, Claude models, schema-compliant, automation

Summary: Amazon Bedrock now includes support for structured outputs across all Anthropic Claude models, available through both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints. Users can access Claude via boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or the Messages API, receiving schema-compliant JSON responses that follow a defined structure, eliminating the need for custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. This feature enables reliable automation of schema-compliant tasks across various industries. Use cases include efficient extraction of essential fields from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, as well as updating clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR). It can also enhance product catalogs with consistent and validated data. Furthermore, users can analyze contracts for critical terms, parties involved, and obligations, which supports intelligent routing of support tickets where intents, sentiments, and entities align with the application's data model. For more details, users are encouraged to check the Amazon Bedrock's structured outputs information, which is available wherever Claude models are supported.

Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models across both the bedrock-runtime and the bedrock-mantle endpoint. Whether you call Claude through boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing.

With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application's data model.

To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation . Structured outputs is available where claude models are available. For more information check the regional availability details page.

item.title: AWS Clean Rooms now supports Databricks as a data source
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Clean Rooms, Databricks, Delta Sharing, collaboration, data analysis

Summary: AWS Clean Rooms now supports collaboration with Databricks, enabling members to analyze data securely without the need to move or reveal source data. Previously, users had to export or replicate data from Databricks to Amazon S3 for use within a collaboration, which required additional pipeline work and management of duplicate data. Now, members can directly register a Databricks table by providing necessary details, including the workspace URL, schema, and table, alongside a Delta Sharing share for collaboration access. This enhancement allows for streamlined collaboration, exemplified by a retailer managing customer data in Databricks working with a media partner to measure campaign effectiveness using AWS Clean Rooms. The platform is designed to facilitate analysis and collaboration on collective datasets without compromising the privacy of the underlying data from either party. AWS Clean Rooms supports multiple data sources, including AWS Glue, Snowflake, and Amazon Athena, making it a versatile tool for organizations. For further details about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available and how to collaborate effectively, additional resources are provided through the AWS website.

AWS Clean Rooms now supports Databricks as a data source, so collaboration members and their partners can securely analyze data managed in Databricks without moving or revealing the source data. Members query a Databricks table shared through Delta Sharing directly in a collaboration. Databricks joins AWS Glue, Snowflake, and Amazon Athena as supported data sources in AWS Clean Rooms.

Previously, members with data in Databricks had to export or replicate it into Amazon S3 to use it as a table in a collaboration, which added pipeline work and an extra copy of the data to govern. Now members can register a Databricks table directly by providing the workspace URL, schema, and table along with a Delta Sharing share, and make it available to a collaboration. For example, a retailer that manages its customer data in Databricks can collaborate with a media partner on campaign measurement in AWS Clean Rooms, running approved analyses against its Databricks data without first building and maintaining an export to S3.

AWS Clean Rooms helps companies and their partners easily analyze and collaborate on their collective datasets without revealing or copying one another’s underlying data. For more information about the AWS Regions where AWS Clean Rooms is available, see the AWS Regions table. To learn more about collaborating with AWS Clean Rooms, visit AWS Clean Rooms.

item.title: AWS IAM Identity Center simplifies identity source changes from Active Directory
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, IAM Identity Center, identity source, workforce identities, external identity provider

Summary: AWS IAM Identity Center now retains workforce identities and their assignments when switching the identity source to an external identity provider (IdP), such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, or to the Identity Center directory. This feature retains users, groups, group memberships, permission sets, and application assignments, eliminating the need to recreate them in IAM Identity Center. IAM Identity Center connects workforce identities to AWS and enables centralized access management across AWS applications and accounts. When changing from Active Directory, the existing identity store remains intact, allowing users and groups to retain the same IDs, thus preserving their access to AWS accounts and applications. Policies referencing user IDs, group IDs, or the identity store ID continue to function. To implement this change, configure the new identity source for user sign-in, after which the workforce can sign in via the dual-stack AWS access portal URL. Changing the identity source back to Active Directory operates as before. This feature is available for organization instances of IAM Identity Center across all AWS Regions where it is offered and comes at no additional cost. For more information, visit the IAM Identity Center console and user guide.

AWS IAM Identity Center now retains your workforce identities and their assignments when you change your identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP), such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, or to the Identity Center directory. Specifically, it preserves your users, groups, group memberships, permission set assignments, and application assignments. Previously, this change required you to recreate them in IAM Identity Center.

IAM Identity Center helps you connect your workforce identities to AWS once and manage their access centrally across AWS applications and accounts. When you change your identity source from Active Directory, your existing identity store remains in place, so your users and groups keep the same IDs. As a result, users retain their access to AWS accounts and applications, and policies that reference your user IDs, group IDs, or identity store ID continue to work.

To make this change, configure your new identity source with the standard setup required for users to sign in. After the change, your workforce signs in through your dual-stack AWS access portal URL. Changing your identity source in the other direction, to Active Directory, works as before. This feature is available for organization instances of IAM Identity Center in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. IAM Identity Center is provided at no additional cost.

To get started, navigate to the IAM Identity Center console. For more information, see Change your identity source in the IAM Identity Center User Guide. To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page.

item.title: AWS Partner Central launches Program Navigator, Case Study Generator, and streamlined specialization review
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Partner Central, Program Navigator, Case Study Generator, specialization, application review

Summary: AWS Partner Central introduces Program Navigator, a centralized platform for partners to discover, apply for, and track applications for AWS Specialization programs. It features a guided workflow for browsing designation requirements and benefits. Additionally, the Case Study Generator offers three paths for case study creation: AI-assisted development, importing from existing URLs, or auto-populating from opportunities. These case studies can be published directly to AWS domains for go-to-market purposes with a streamlined review process. However, case studies linked to Program Navigator applications undergo a deeper specialization review. Furthermore, the specialization application review process is expedited through Program Navigator, providing partners with quicker feedback and detailed insights on requirements. Non-specialization program applications can still be submitted via the existing platform. To access these new features, partners can navigate to Program Navigator and Case Studies within the Go to Market section of the left navigation panel in AWS Partner Central.

AWS Partner Central now features Program Navigator, a unified experience that lets partners discover, apply for, and track AWS Specialization program applications in one place. Partners can browse specialization designations, view requirements and benefits, and submit applications through a guided, step-by-step workflow.

The new Case Study Generator in AWS Partner Central gives partners a redesigned creation experience with three starting paths: build a case study directly with AI assistance, import from an existing customer success story URL, or auto-populate from an opportunity. Case studies created for go-to-market purposes now follow a streamlined review path, a lightweight policy validation that lets partners publish directly to AWS domains without a specialization review. The deeper specialization-level review applies only to case studies associated with Program Navigator applications.

Additionally, AWS has streamlined the specialization application review process through Program Navigator. Partners submitting applications can expect faster review times and more detailed, requirement-level feedback throughout the process. Partners applying for non-specialization programs continue to access those programs through the existing experience.

Program Navigator and Case Study Generator are available to all AWS Partners in AWS Partner Central. To get started, navigate to Program Navigator and Case Studies under the Go to Market section in the left navigation panel.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now supports Standard tier for contextual grounding checks
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, Guardrails, Standard tier, contextual grounding, API

Summary: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails has introduced a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, aimed at detecting and filtering hallucinations by ensuring that model responses are grounded in reference sources and relevant to user queries. This Standard tier is more robust than the previous Classic tier, supporting reasoning and conversational content. It also provides more consistent scoring for differently worded responses with the same meaning and offers comprehensive language support. Configurable safeguards for generative AI applications can be implemented via the ApplyGuardrail API. Previous contextual grounding checks were mainly suited for tasks like summarization and paraphrasing, but the Standard tier extends its applicability to conversational applications and reasoned responses. Users can select the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API, with existing guardrails maintaining the Classic tier until changed. The pricing remains the same for both tiers. To utilize the Standard tier, cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile is required. The Standard tier is currently available in multiple AWS regions, including various locations in the US and Europe, as well as Asia Pacific. For further details, users can refer to the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails now offers a Standard tier for contextual grounding checks, which detect and filter hallucinations by checking whether a model response is grounded in your reference source and relevant to the user's query. The Standard tier is more robust than the Classic tier. It supports responses that include reasoning or conversational content, scores differently worded responses with the same meaning more consistently, and provides more comprehensive language support, matching the Standard tier for content filters and denied topics. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provides configurable safeguards for generative AI applications on any foundation model through the ApplyGuardrail API.

Until now, contextual grounding checks applied strict grounding suited to summarization, paraphrasing, and question answering. With the Standard tier, you can also apply contextual grounding checks to conversational applications and to responses that reason over the source. You choose the tier for each guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock console or API. Existing guardrails keep the Classic tier until you change them. Pricing is the same for both tiers. To use the Standard tier, your guardrail must use cross-Region inference with a guardrail profile.

The Standard tier for contextual grounding checks is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Milan), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation on contextual grounding checks and safeguard tiers, or visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails product page.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening
item.content:encoded:
Prompt Shortening, Amazon Bedrock, Advanced Prompt Optimization, Token Costs, Evaluation Scores

Summary: Amazon Bedrock's Advanced Prompt Optimization now features prompt shortening, an optional setting designed to reduce the length of prompts while maintaining or enhancing evaluation scores. Previously, the optimization process focused solely on quality, often resulting in longer prompts that increased input token costs and latency for applications. With prompt shortening enabled, the optimizer will condense the prompt’s length, returning it only if the new version is shorter and performs equally well or better on established evaluation criteria. If the optimized prompt fails to meet these requirements, the original prompt is retained, ensuring that users do not end up with less effective or longer prompts. The output includes the compression ratio and original versus optimized token counts, providing transparency regarding the efficiency of the adjustments. The feature supports various evaluation methods, including custom Lambda evaluators and LLM-as-a-judge rubrics. Available in all AWS Regions offering Advanced Prompt Optimization, users can activate this feature for prompt templates in their input datasets and proceed with creating optimization jobs as per the usual process. Additional information can be found in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide and related documentation.

Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization now supports prompt shortening, an optional setting that reduces the length of your prompt while maintaining or improving your evaluation scores. Advanced Prompt Optimization optimizes prompts for any model on Amazon Bedrock against your own evaluation criteria. Until now, optimization focused on quality alone. Optimized prompts were often longer than the original. Longer prompts raise input token costs and can increase time to first token, which matters at scale and in latency-sensitive applications.

When you turn on prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset, the optimizer reduces the prompt's length. The optimized prompt is returned only when it is shorter than your original prompt and scores at least as high on your evaluation. Otherwise your original prompt is returned, so the setting never leaves you with a longer or lower-scoring prompt. Results include a compression ratio and the original and optimized token counts, in the output file and on the console results page. For example, a compression ratio of 0.7 means the optimized prompt uses 30% fewer tokens. Prompt shortening works with any evaluation method, including steering criteria, LLM-as-a-judge rubrics, and custom Lambda evaluators.    

Prompt shortening is available in all AWS Regions where Advanced Prompt Optimization is available. To get started, enable prompt shortening for a prompt template in your input dataset and create an optimization job as usual. To learn more, see Shorten prompts in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, the Amazon Bedrock pricing page, and the Amazon Bedrock product page.

item.title: AWS Transform for migrations expands support for existing landing zones
item.content:encoded:
AWS Transform now supports more types of existing AWS environments when building landing zones for your migration, including AWS Control Tower landing zones and landing zones built with AWS Organizations. AWS Transform runs a foundation gap analysis of your current environment against AWS best practices and expands your landing zone on top of what's already in your target accounts, so your team can start migrating sooner.

AWS Transform also now supports an Infrastructure as Code (IaC)-only mode for building landing zones for your migration. In this mode, AWS Transform analyzes your organization, generates recommendations, and produces IaC tailored to your migration plan in AWS CDK, Terraform, or Landing Zone Accelerator (LZA) format. IaC-only mode is designed for organizations that prefer not to grant AWS Transform direct access to their management account. AWS Transform can now connect through a delegated administrator (DA) account instead. It also benefits customers who manage their own deployment pipeline and don't need the agent to deploy automatically.

The AWS Transform for migrations landing zone agent automates landing zone design end to end, including foundation setup, organizational unit (OU) and account structure, service control policies (SCPs), and workload accounts aligned to your migration planning and waves. You can deploy directly or generate IaC for your own pipeline.

These new capabilities are available in all target AWS Regions supported by AWS Transform for migrations.

To learn more, please visit the AWS Transform User Guide.

item.title: Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime
item.content:encoded:
Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration from self-managed Valkey and Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 with zero downtime. Zero downtime means zero Errors returned to the client during migration, measured the same way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. Your application continues reading and writing through cutover, and you do not need third-party replication tools.

Online migration runs in three steps. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, and complete the cutover. ElastiCache gives you a migration endpoint your application can point to when you prepare the migration, and data replicates continuously from your source once you start the sync. You choose when writes move to the serverless cache, with a manual cutover or an automatic one once your data is in sync. ElastiCache records each step as an event on the cache’s Events tab, with the reason for any failed step.

Online migration connects to your source using encryption in transit (TLS) and authentication, and reads credentials from AWS Secrets Manager, so your existing security controls stay in place. Online migration supports self-managed caches in cluster mode on Amazon EC2 running Redis OSS 4.0 through 7.2 or Valkey 7.2 through 8.1, and you can migrate them straight to Valkey 9.0.

Migration usage is free for the first 180 days per AWS account, starting when the account first prepares a migration. After that, you pay per node-hour for the migration nodes that ElastiCache runs to replicate your data, for as long as a migration is active. The ElastiCache Serverless cache is billed separately at standard data storage and ECPU rates, including during the free period. For pricing details, see Amazon ElastiCache pricing. Online migration is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. 

To get started, create or select an empty ElastiCache Serverless cache to migrate into, then start the migration from the ElastiCache console or the AWS CLI. To learn more, see the documentation.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now supports configurable time-to-live for long-term memory
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory now lets you set a time-to-live (TTL) on long-term memory records, so they are automatically deleted after a retention period you define. By default, long-term memory records do not expire. With this launch, you can configure a TTL to meet data-retention requirements, control storage growth, and ensure that stale insights age out of a memory over time.

You can configure retention on the resource or specific records. Configuring or removing a TTL requires the new bedrock-agentcore:UpdateMemoryRecordExpirySpecification permission, giving you independent control over who can set record retention.

To learn more, see Set a time-to-live for long-term memory records in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory is supported.

Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now provides business users visibility into resiliency readiness across linked Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, Global Resiliency, Region switch, administrators, resources

Summary: Amazon Connect has introduced a Global Resiliency page within the admin website, allowing administrators to assess their readiness for a Region switch in one centralized location. This page provides an overall readiness status and details the resources that Global Resiliency replicates natively. It indicates which resource types are in sync, which are pending synchronization, and which require administrator action. For example, if resources such as phone numbers or users are not linked to a traffic distribution group, this page highlights these issues and enables administrators to associate the affected resources directly from that interface. The new feature assures administrators that they can evaluate their resiliency posture at any time to ensure their instance is prepared for a Region switch. It is noteworthy that this capability is available across all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect operates. To gain a deeper understanding and learn more about this functionality, administrators are encouraged to refer to the respective admin guide provided by Amazon.

Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency now provides a Global Resiliency page in the admin website, giving administrators a single place to review their Region switch readiness. The page shows an overall readiness status and lists the resources that Global Resiliency natively replicates, including which resource types are in sync, which are still pending synchronization, and which need action. For example, if a phone number or user is not associated with a traffic distribution group, the page flags it and lets the administrator associate the affected resources directly from the page. With this readiness overview, administrators can review their resiliency posture at any time and verify that their instance is ready for a Region switch.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Connect Customer Global Resiliency is supported. To learn more, see Amazon Connect Customer admin guide.

item.title: Amazon CloudWatch Omni is now available in additional AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: CloudWatch Omni, AI-powered, observability, AWS Regions, telemetry

Summary: Amazon CloudWatch Omni is now available in eight additional AWS Regions, enhancing its AI-powered observability capabilities. This tool organizes observability around teams and their applications, enabling easier monitoring and troubleshooting in a single interface. It combines OpenTelemetry's interoperability with CloudWatch's robustness, available as a standalone web experience with single sign-on (SSO) or as a local IDE extension. Users can create spaces in their central accounts to view telemetry across AWS accounts, different Regions, and other cloud platforms like Azure and GCP. CloudWatch Omni automatically discovers services, maps dependencies, and highlights golden metrics. Users can interact with the telemetry through chat, point-and-click, or their tools via the Agent Toolkit for AWS. The solution also supports an evaluation-driven workflow for various frameworks including LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK. With this expansion, CloudWatch Omni is now accessible in Canada (Central), multiple Asia Pacific locations, Europe, and South America, in addition to existing US Regions. To begin, users can create their Omni space from the CloudWatch console, configure SSO, and sign in. Agent developers can also install free tools like Cursor and Kiro for improved functionality.

AWS announces that Amazon CloudWatch Omni is now available in eight additional AWS Regions. CloudWatch Omni is an AI-powered observability experience, organized around your teams and the applications they run, that helps you observe and troubleshoot your applications and agents in one place. It combines the interoperability of OpenTelemetry with the scale and reliability of CloudWatch, and meets you where you work — a standalone web experience with single sign-on (SSO), or a local IDE extension.

With CloudWatch Omni, You create spaces in your central accounts to see telemetry across your AWS accounts, Regions, and other clouds, including Azure and GCP. Omni discovers services, maps dependencies, and surfaces golden metrics automatically and you can interact with telemetry through chat, point-and-click, or your own tool via Agent Toolkit for AWS to find signals, build dynamic views, and reach root cause powered by AWS DevOps Agent. A dedicated agent observability experience adds an evaluation-driven workflow for frameworks including LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, Vercel AI SDK, and Strands.

With this expansion, CloudWatch Omni is now available in Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), and South America (São Paulo), in addition to US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland).

To get started, create your Omni space from the CloudWatch console, configure SSO, and sign in. Agent developers can install the free CloudWatch Omni extension for VS Code, Cursor, and Kiro. To learn more, see the Amazon CloudWatch Omni product page and documentation. For pricing, see the CloudWatch Omni pricing page.

item.title: EC2 Image Builder now integrates with ASG for faster image builds
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: EC2 Image Builder, Auto Scaling Group, existing instances, faster builds, no additional cost

Summary: EC2 Image Builder now offers a feature that enables the use of existing instances from an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) for image building. This innovation increases build speed by eliminating the need to launch and bootstrap new instances, allowing for the reuse of already-running EC2 instances. Users can configure ASG in their Image Builder infrastructure setup, which allows Image Builder to select active instances instead of initiating new ones during the build process. As instances are utilized for builds, the ASG automatically replenishes its pool to ensure that there are always available instances for future pipeline executions. Importantly, this feature is entirely opt-in, meaning that existing pipelines will remain unaffected if no ASG is configured, continuing to use the default launch method without any changes in behavior. This capability is accessible across all AWS Regions and comes at no additional cost to users. For detailed steps on configuring ASG integration in Image Builder pipelines, users can refer to relevant AWS documentation.

EC2 Image Builder now supports using existing instances from an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) for building images, enabling faster builds by eliminating the time spent in launching and bootstrapping new instances and reusing already running EC2 instances.

With this feature, you can provide an ASG in your Image Builder infrastructure configuration. Instead of launching a new instance at the build time, Image Builder selects an already-running instance from this ASG, applies your build components, and creates the image. The ASG continuously replenishes the pool as instances are used for builds, ensuring instances are always available for subsequent pipeline runs.

This feature is fully opt-in and does not affect existing pipelines. Pipelines without an ASG configured continue to use the default launch path with no behavior change.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. To configure ASG integration in your Image Builder pipelines, see the EC2 Image Builder documentation.

item.title: Amazon GuardDuty adds optional threat detection rules for Runtime Monitoring
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon GuardDuty, Runtime Monitoring, detection rules, MITRE ATT&CK, exfiltration

Summary: Amazon GuardDuty has introduced optional detection rules for Runtime Monitoring, enabling users to activate over 50 rules that identify process, file, and network activities indicative of compromises in various environments. Key activities detected include altering sudoers files and disabling audit logging. These new rules cater to Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon EKS, and Amazon ECS (both on EC2 and AWS Fargate), encompassing 13 finding types aligned with MITRE ATT&CK® tactics such as persistence, privilege escalation, execution, defense evasion, discovery, exfiltration, and command and control. Notably, four new finding types have been added: CommandAndControl:Runtime/SuspiciousCommand, CredentialAccess:Runtime/SensitiveFileRead, Discovery:Runtime/SensitiveFileRead, and Exfiltration:Runtime/SuspiciousCommand. To begin, users can visit the GuardDuty console and enable rules in dry-run mode to assess detection efficacy before activating live monitoring. This feature is available across all AWS commercial Regions and in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. For more details, users are encouraged to explore the provided resources, and they can subscribe to receive programmatic updates on new Amazon GuardDuty capabilities and threat detections.

Amazon GuardDuty now supports optional detection rules for Runtime Monitoring. You can enable more than 50 Runtime Monitoring rules that help detect process, file, and network activity that might be routine in one environment but a sign of compromise in another, such as modifying sudoers files or disabling audit logging.

The new rules provide detections for Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon EKS, and Amazon ECS on both EC2 and AWS Fargate, and span 13 finding types mapped to MITRE ATT&CK® tactics including persistence, privilege escalation, execution, defense evasion, discovery, exfiltration, and command and control. This release introduces four new finding types: CommandAndControl:Runtime/SuspiciousCommand, CredentialAccess:Runtime/SensitiveFileRead, Discovery:Runtime/SensitiveFileRead, and Exfiltration:Runtime/SuspiciousCommand.

To get started, visit the GuardDuty console. You can enable rules in dry-run mode to evaluate detection efficacy before enabling live detection.

Custom Detection Rules for Runtime Monitoring is available in all AWS commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, see Amazon GuardDuty Custom Detection Rules. To receive programmatic updates on new Amazon GuardDuty features and threat detections, subscribe to the Amazon GuardDuty SNS topic.

item.title: Grok 4.7 is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)

Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, SpaceXAI, Grok 4.7, coding, AWS GovCloud

Summary: Amazon Bedrock has expanded its capabilities by integrating SpaceXAI's Grok 4.7 model, specifically designed for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work within the AWS GovCloud (US). Grok 4.7 improves upon its predecessor, Grok 4.6, by offering enhanced mixed-document handling, which allows users to process various document types more effectively. Additionally, it features more reliable repo-scale coding capabilities, including improved planning and error recovery mechanisms to aid developers. The model also introduces improvements in browser-usage agents, enabling enhanced functionalities for form filling and portal navigation, which can streamline user interactions with web applications. To begin utilizing Grok 4.7, users can access the service directly or programmatically through the supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For more detailed information regarding supported endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles, and pricing, users are encouraged to refer to the official documentation. This upgrade signifies a substantial enhancement in the tools available for developers, facilitating a more efficient coding process and broader application scenario coverage.

Amazon Bedrock now supports SpaceXAI Grok 4.7, a frontier model built for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work in AWS GovCloud (US).

Grok 4.7 builds on Grok 4.6 with better mixed-document handling, more dependable repo-scale coding with planning and error recovery, and enhanced browser-use agents for form fills and portal navigation.  

Get started with Grok 4.7 in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation. To learn more, read the launch blog post.

item.title: AWS IAM Identity Center now supports optimistic locking for users and groups in its identity store
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: IAM Identity Center, users, groups, Revision, ConflictException

Summary: IAM Identity Center facilitates the single sign-on experience for AWS accounts and applications. It now incorporates optimistic locking for users and groups in the identity store, ensuring that updates and deletions succeed only if the user or group's attributes haven't changed since the last read. This mitigates issues when multiple administrators or automated workflows attempt modifications concurrently, preventing one write from unintentionally overwriting another. Each user and group is assigned a Revision value that updates with every modification, whether through SCIM provisioning, Active Directory sync, or the IAM Identity Center console. Operations such as create, describe, update, and list return the current Revision, which can be used in subsequent requests like UpdateUser, UpdateGroup, DeleteUser, or DeleteGroup. The request will only succeed if the provided Revision matches the current one; otherwise, a ConflictException is returned, prompting the workflow to re-read the user or group for the latest details. Supplying a Revision is optional, and requests without it function as before, ensuring compatibility with existing integrations. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center operates and incurs no additional cost. To learn more, visit the product detail page.

IAM Identity Center helps you configure the single sign-on experience of your workforce to AWS accounts and applications. You can now use optimistic locking for users and groups in the identity store, so that update and delete requests succeed only if the user or group hasn't changed since you last read it. This helps when multiple administrators or automated workflows modify the same user or group at nearly the same time, where previously one write could silently overwrite another.

Each user and group now has a Revision value that changes every time the user's or group's attributes are modified, including through SCIM provisioning, Active Directory sync, or the IAM Identity Center console. Create, describe, update, and list operations return the current Revision, and you can pass it on a later UpdateUser, UpdateGroup, DeleteUser, or DeleteGroup request. The request succeeds only if the supplied Revision matches the current Revision. Otherwise, it returns a ConflictException, so your workflow can re-read the user or group and retry with the latest values.

Providing a Revision is optional. Requests that omit it behave as before, so existing integrations continue to work without changes. Conditional requests are supported through the Identity Store API, not the SCIM endpoint. Group membership operations don't accept a Revision, and adding or removing members doesn't change the Revision of the user or the group. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where IAM Identity Center is available. IAM Identity Center is provided at no additional cost.

To learn more about IAM Identity Center, visit the product detail page. To get started, see UpdateUser in the Identity Store API Reference.

item.title: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports high bitrate mode
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Elemental, MediaConnect, high bitrate, broadcast, VSF TR-07

Summary: AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router has introduced high bitrate modes, offering two new tiers: 250 Mbps and 500 Mbps. This enhancement is designed for professional broadcasters who require higher bitrates to convey high-value content without sacrificing quality or reliability. The new high bitrate mode enables industry-standard workflows, including VSF TR-07 compliant transport stream distribution, which is essential for broadcast contribution, content distribution, and remote production activities. Additionally, the high bitrate mode incorporates support for up to two redundant sources, ensuring reliability during transmission. It also features data plane optimizations that significantly reduce jitter, thereby enhancing overall performance. Broadcasters can now transport their content more effectively, thus meeting the demands of modern broadcasting environments. By utilizing this capability, content providers can ensure a higher standard of service while promoting a more efficient operational workflow. For further details on this update and its implications for the industry, additional resources can be accessed through the pertinent links.

AWS Elemental MediaConnect Router now supports high bitrate modes with two new tiers: 250 Mbps and 500 Mbps. This allows professional broadcasters that need higher bitrates to transport high-value content without compromising quality or reliability.

This enhancement enables industry-standard workflows such as VSF TR-07 compliant transport stream distribution for broadcast contribution, content distribution, and remote production. High bitrate mode supports up to two redundant sources for reliability and includes data plane optimizations that reduce jitter for improved performance.

To learn more, visit the AWS Elemental MediaConnect product page and the MediaConnect pricing page.

item.title: Amazon RDS Custom now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: SQL Server, Cumulative Updates, Amazon RDS, upgrades, GDR

Summary: Amazon RDS for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates. This includes support for SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR (RDS version 15.00.4490.9.v1) and SQL Server 2022 CU26 + GDR (RDS version 16.00.4275.2.v1). These updates come with improvements and fixes that are detailed in the Microsoft documentation for KB5122772 and KB5122768. Users can upgrade their Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server instances to incorporate these recommended updates. This can be accomplished through the Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. For users interested in upgrading their database instances, further information is available to guide them through the process. The importance of keeping SQL Server instances up to date with the latest releases and updates cannot be overstated, as it ensures better performance, security, and access to new features.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) Custom for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR KB5122772(RDS version 15.00.4490.9.v1) and SQL Server 2022 CU26 + GDR KB5122768 (RDS version 16.00.4275.2.v1).

For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5122772 and KB5122768. You can upgrade your Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server instances to apply these recommended updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. To learn more about upgrading your database instances, see Amazon RDS Custom User Guide.

item.title: Amazon RDS for SQL Server now supports snapshots on read replicas
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: DB snapshots, read replica, Multi-AZ, automated backups, SQL Server

Summary: Amazon RDS now allows the creation of DB snapshots directly on read replica instances, enhancing flexibility for backup and disaster recovery workflows. Previously, snapshots were limited to standalone and primary instances. This update means you can snapshot a read replica without promoting it first. Furthermore, enabling Multi-AZ on a promoted read replica was traditionally delayed by the need for an initial full snapshot, especially on larger storage configurations like io2 volumes up to 64 TiB. With the new feature, snapshot data is maintained on the read replica throughout its lifecycle, allowing for faster completion of the first snapshot post-promotion. This improvement aids in enabling Multi-AZ quickly and makes disaster recovery timelines more predictable. Users can now take manual snapshots of a read replica, activate automated backups by setting a non-zero backup retention period, and retain backups even after deleting the replica. However, point-in-time recovery (PITR) from a read replica remains unsupported. This feature applies to both in-region and cross-region read replicas and is available for SQL Server Enterprise Edition across all supported versions and AWS Regions, including the GovCloud (US) Regions.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports creating DB snapshots directly on read replica instances. Previously, you could create snapshots only on standalone and primary DB instances. You can now snapshot a read replica without promoting it first, giving you more flexibility in your backup and disaster recovery (DR) workflows.

Previously, enabling Multi-AZ on a promoted read replica meant waiting for an initial full snapshot to finish before the conversion could begin. On larger storage configurations—such as io2 volumes up to 64 TiB—that first snapshot could take a long time, making DR timelines hard to predict. Now, Amazon RDS for SQL Server maintains snapshot data on the read replica throughout its lifecycle, so the first snapshot after promotion completes faster. This shortens the time to enable Multi-AZ and helps you plan DR exercises with more predictable recovery timelines. You can take manual snapshots of a read replica, turn on automated backups by setting a backup retention period greater than zero, and retain automated backups when you delete the replica; however, point-in-time recovery (PITR) from a read replica isn't supported.

This feature works for both in-region and cross-region read replicas. It's available for SQL Server Enterprise Edition on all SQL Server versions that support read replicas, in all AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for SQL Server read replicas are available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

To learn more, see Working with read replicas for Microsoft SQL Server. For pricing details, see Amazon RDS for SQL Server Pricing.

item.title: AWS Partner Central adds Solution Matching Engine performance insights
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Partner Central, Solution Matching Engine, Partner Analytics, opportunities, visibility

Summary: AWS Partner Central has enhanced visibility for AWS Partners through its Solution Matching Engine (SME), which now provides insights into the co-sell pipeline. The SME performance section in Partner Analytics allows partners to understand their individual performance regarding SME and AWS Marketplace listings. Key metrics available include recommendations, SME-attributed opportunities, and the share of AWS-originated opportunities, in addition to stall rates and pipeline data attributed to SME. Partners can utilize filters by recommendation type or AWS Marketplace listing to analyze their data further. Moreover, they can explore top customer profiles categorized by region, industry, and segment, which enables them to assess their market visibility comprehensively. This functionality equips partners with the necessary insights to identify areas for improvement in their listings and opportunity information. All eligible partners can access these features located on the Opportunity pipeline analysis page within Partner Analytics. To gain a deeper understanding of the SME and enhance visibility with AWS sellers, partners are encouraged to read additional resources provided.

AWS Partner Central now gives AWS Partners more visibility into how the Solution Matching Engine (SME) contributes to their co-sell pipeline. The Solution Matching Engine performance section in Partner Analytics helps partners understand how SME performs for their company and AWS Marketplace listings.

Partners can view recommendations, SME-attributed opportunities, their share of AWS-originated opportunities, stall rate, and pipeline attributed to SME. They can filter by recommendation type or AWS Marketplace listing and explore top customer profiles by Region, industry, and segment. These insights help partners assess their visibility and decide where to improve their listings and opportunity information.

All partners eligible for APN Customer Engagements (ACE) can find the section on the Opportunity pipeline analysis page under Partner Analytics in AWS Partner Central. To learn more about SME and how to strengthen your visibility with AWS sellers, read Solution Matching Engine: Your Gateway to AWS Sellers.

item.title: Amazon EMR Serverless now supports IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity
item.content:encoded:
Amazon EMR Serverless now supports IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity, expanding beyond the IPv4-only connectivity that was previously available. You can now run your Apache Spark and Apache Hive jobs over IPv6 in your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) by supplying dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6) or IPv6-only subnets. This gives you greater flexibility in how your applications connect to data stores and services, while maintaining full backward compatibility with your existing IPv4 workloads.

As Spark and Hive workloads scale to many workers, the IPv4 address space in your VPCs and subnets can become a constraint, and a growing number of organizations face compliance mandates that require IPv6 adoption. With dual-stack connectivity, your EMR Serverless applications accept both IPv4 and IPv6, making it easy to adopt IPv6 gradually while maintaining backward compatibility with your existing IPv4 workloads. With IPv6-only subnets, you can eliminate the need for IPv4 addresses entirely, overcoming IPv4 address exhaustion and meeting the networking standards and compliance requirements that call for IPv6, while your jobs reach IPv6 endpoints and services both inside and outside your VPC.

IPv6 and dual-stack connectivity for Amazon EMR Serverless is available at no additional cost in all AWS Regions where Amazon EMR Serverless is available. IPv6 and dual-stack subnets are supported on all EMR Serverless release versions. To get started, see Configure IPv6 subnets for EMR Serverless applications and Configuring VPC access for EMR Serverless applications.

item.title: v12.2.0
item.content:encoded:
v12.2.0 (2026-10-19)

Notable changes

New options

  • @Sse({ maxPendingDataLength }) sets how many characters of event data may wait for a client that is not reading its events (4M by default; 0 or Infinity lifts the limit) – 2f05ad954e
  • IoAdapter and WsAdapter take maxConcurrentMessages, the number of a client's messages handled at once (1000 by default; Infinity lifts it) – 0bd0810ed7
  • ValidationPipe takes maxErrorMessagesLength (1,000,000 characters by default); messages past it are replaced by a "Further validation errors were omitted" entry – 086c1c514f
  • Kafka: parser.maxMessageSize (16 MiB after decompression by default); larger messages are logged and skipped – 9bdf844fca
  • TCP server: drainTimeout (30 s by default, 0 disables) disconnects a peer that leaves its responses unread – 583d6077ad
  • MQTT server: reconnectOnConnackError is now enabled by default, so a refused connection attempt is retried; set it to false for the previous behaviour – a63cea600a
  • HttpServer.getRouteMatchingOptions(), an optional adapter hook that tells core how the router matches paths (see "Middleware exclusions" below) – 08d8677c8d

New defaults and behaviour changes

  • @nestjs/platform-express, @nestjs/platform-fastify: fieldNestingDepth and fieldArrayIndexLimit (#18074) now default to 32 and 1000; set them to Infinity to lift the limits – 94fcc93770
  • ValidationPipe validates with validationError.target: false unless the options set it, so an exceptionFactory that reads error.target gets undefined; set validationError.target to true for the old errors – 8c5a59bf63
  • ValidationPipe answers an array or a primitive sent for a validated class with a 400 – 197371c1f3
  • FileTypeValidator matches a string fileType up to the end of a name (e.g. font/woff no longer accepts font/woff2; use a RegExp for that) – 770c6f1a19
  • @SerializeOptions({}) on a handler no longer turns off the class schema – d27cb7017f
  • BaseExceptionFilter answers http-errors errors created with expose: false (the default from 500) with the standard reason phrase instead of their message – 9ed572f853
  • A StreamableFile error still gets a 400, but the body no longer carries the error message – 2f28d91afb
  • Files uploaded with a request that a pipe rejected are removed from storage – acb98de89e
  • @nestjs/platform-fastify: a route with fileSize: undefined (or null) falls back to the plugin's limit; set it to Infinity to keep uploads unlimited – dd549e1a74
  • @nestjs/platform-express: object error bodies are sent as application/json on routes with a non-JSON Content-Type – 7dc6e349d5
  • ConsoleLogger in JSON mode cuts a record short past about a million characters – ad4915eaa3
  • A global enhancer that the injector failed to instantiate now fails the application at startup – ae78524ced
  • A request- or transient-scoped APP_FILTER now logs a startup warning, as it only applies to exceptions thrown from controllers – df5275c5e1
  • Microservices: a pattern key longer than 256 characters matches no handler – accd27e66c
  • Kafka: a message may carry up to 10,000 header values (e419ff540b); headers given as a string or array are not sent (312777743f); reply headers are decoded as text (ee94f6aaae)
  • gRPC: request streams are paused while their replies wait to be written – 37e5cf7706
  • Deprecation: on TCP, Redis, NATS, MQTT and RabbitMQ, an @EventPattern() handler that replies to ClientProxy#send() now logs a deprecation warning. The reply is unchanged; in the next major version event handlers will not reply to send(), as on Kafka already – ba3668d36b

Middleware exclusions

  • MiddlewareConsumer.exclude() now compiles excluded routes with the router's case and trailing-slash matching (08d8677c8d). Update @nestjs/core together with @nestjs/platform-express / @nestjs/platform-fastify: with an adapter that does not implement getRouteMatchingOptions(), excluded routes are matched exactly (f5aa875e40), so on a lenient router other spellings of an excluded path run the middleware.
  • With header, media type or custom versioning, exclude({ path, method, version }) and enableCsrfProtection({ exclude }) apply only to requests that ask for one of the excluded versions – 1a7a31fa46
  • @nestjs/platform-fastify: the request hook used by enableCsrfProtection() and useSecurityHeaders() now runs before Nest and app.use() middleware with NestFactory.create() too, including middleware registered before either call, as it already did with Test.createNestApplication() – 8351806290

Bug fixes

    • 614d1ac7ea fix(fastify): send the status of an exception whose body is an error (@kamilmysliwiec)
    • 8b420f788f fix(fastify): apply middleware to plugins registered before init (@kamilmysliwiec)

Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
item.content:encoded:
I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...

> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too?

How are you handling this?

v12.1.1
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: bug fixes, enhancements, microservices, core, common

Summary: The release of version 12.1.1 on September 28, 2026, focuses on bug fixes across several components including common, core, microservices, and testing. Key fixes in the common module address logger bugs in JSON output and the handling of string enum values. In microservices, multiple issues are resolved, such as allowing the MQTT client to retry upon failed connections, preserving TCP event listeners during reconnects, and ensuring newer NATS and Kafka connections are maintained when stale ones fail. Additionally, the RMQ client is allowed to retry, and improvements are made for handling Redis wildcard events. The core module sees enhancement in detecting circular dependencies involving more than two providers, while testing features are improved by honoring class and factory overrides of value providers. Enhancements in the common module include rejecting non-numeric items in ParseArrayPipe. The microservices module also introduces a new feature that exports deserializers from the package root. Overall, these changes enhance reliability and functionality across the platform, benefiting developers and users alike.

item.title: Updates to site guidelines and AI/LLM tags
item.content:encoded:
vibecoding, AI, self-promotion, community, guidelines

Summary: The Lobsters community, focused on computing discussions, is making updates to enhance user engagement and encourage thoughtful content. The about page will clarify what constitutes topical content, specifically narrowing down on computing-related material and encouraging submissions that deepen understanding or spark discussions. Code repositories will no longer be accepted to reduce low-effort self-promotions that don’t foster conversation. Off-topic subjects like entrepreneurship and careers are explicitly listed to maintain focus. Self-promotion guidelines will limit personal promotions to under 25% of contributions from established users and prohibit new users from self-promotional posts. Additionally, the vibecoding tag has been made inactive due to its overloaded nature, which included various AI-related discussions and criticisms. A new tag, ai-tooling, has been introduced to focus on the design and development of AI tools specifically. The administrator emphasizes the importance of respectful discourse, asserting that frustrations towards technology should not be directed at individuals within the community. These changes aim to foster a more constructive environment as the community navigates the evolving landscape of AI and computing.

Hey folks,

I've been having to perform an increasing number of moderation actions surrounding the vibecoding tag and AI/LLM related content. I started reading Lobsters because it had the most interesting viewpoints related to computing. During that time, I've found that this community is at it's best when it's trying to, in good faith, help others grow. In lieu of a larger and more rambling discussion on this point, we would like to try two changes encourage that behavior again and re-focus topicality around ensuring that content submitted to the site should, at a minimum, be respectful of a reader's time and intelligence. 

The first adjustment is two updates to the about page, which try to provide a bit more clarity in what we consider topical and what constitutes self promotion:

Intro:

Lobsters is a computing-focused community centered around discussing links. Our goal is to learn, craft, collaborate, and share interesting viewpoints.

The administrator is Peter Bhat Harkins ("pushcx"), contact him or another moderator with any support issues. Lobsters was launched on July 3rd, 2012 by joshua stein (who is no longer running it, so please quit bugging him with site stuff) with careful design touches to encourage a healthy community:

At this risk of writing a mission statement, it seemed worth explaining what the site is and hopes to be to visitors from the first sentence of /about. (This original text came from an intro post.)

Then the Guidelines:

Topicality: Lobsters is focused pretty narrowly on computing; tags like art don't imply every piece of art is on-topic.  Some rules of thumb for great stories to submit: Will this improve the reader's next program? Will it deepen their understanding of their last program? Will it be more interesting in five or ten years? Is this compelling material that will seed a discussion, or is it just an artifact?

Pending an upcoming deploy, we no longer allow submissions which are code repositories. While, at first blush, this may seem odd for a community which is primarily centered around programming but it does eliminate the bulk of the "low effort, self promotional" submissions we've been seeing on the site. We've also found that being dropped into a new codebase doesn't start discussions because the reader has to have enough subject matter experience to immediately recognize what's novel or otherwise worth talking about. Instead, we are more interested in content around code bases which cover why it was created, the purpose it serves, the challenges overcome, and the reasons why it's a useful artifact in the ecosystem.

Some things that are off-topic here but popular on larger, similar sites: entrepreneurship; management; careers; news about companies that employ a lot of programmers; investing; world events; anthropology; self-help; personal productivity systems; last-resort customer service requests via public shaming; "I wanted to see what this site's amazing users think about this off-topic thing"; and defining the single morally correct economic and political system for the entire world when we can't even settle tabs vs. spaces.

We're listing "careers" as off-topic to try to head off posts about interviewing, promotions, burnout, and farming. We have the job tag because it's nice to help people connect to jobs, but the topic of getting a good job, weaving jobs into a career over your lifetime, and work is a different thing than the actual programming itself.

Self-promotion: It's great to have authors participate in the community, but we do not want the community to be exploited as a write-only tool for product announcements or driving traffic to their work. As a rule of thumb, self-promotional activity should be less than a quarter of one's stories and comments in the last year. New users (first 70 days) are not allowed to submit self-promo.

This is how we've been enforcing the rule for a while, better to be explicit. It's unfortunately common that authors see their work posted, join the site, but then only use us for traffic. Hopefully this time helps them understand the difference between a symbiotic and parasitic relationship.

The second adjustment is that the vibecoding tag is now marked as inactive. It still appears on old stories but can't be applied to new ones. From my perspective, the tag was overloaded with six differing responsibilities:

  • First, it was the tag which was trying to capture the discussions related to the use and implementation of AI/LLM tools.

  • Second, it was a marker for content which is partially related to AI/LLM tools, tooling or companies.

  • Third, it was a marker for content which includes a discussion on or output from AI/LLM tools in a part of a larger work.

  • Fourth, it was a marker for content which was generated using AI/LLM tools.

  • Fifth, it was being used in competition to the spam flag, for really low-quality content which was generated via AI/LLM tools but without apparent significant human authorship.

  • Sixth, it was being used as a tag of shame by people who really dislike AI/LLM tools and used it to insult people at every passing mention.

The last couple years have been the biggest upheaval in the field for decades. While it's acceptable, within limits, to express frustration towards circumstance or technology, it's not acceptable to direct that behavior towards individuals whether they be members of the community or not. Other people can't be your punching bags and Lobsters can't be your boxing ring. That's not acceptable.

While `vibecoding` is no longer an active tag, we still feel that a subset of the tooling related discussions are relevant to the site. While this is reaching far back into the annals of computing history, tools like compilers, databases, testing, and vcs had similar points of consternation and concern when they were introduced. I'm not going to claim that I'm able to guess how the industry is going to shape up, but my gut feeling is that but my gut feeling is that it's going to be closer to something like we've seen with systemd than compilers. This new tag `ai-tooling` covers "The design, ux, development of AI/LLM-powered tools themselves".

As a fun addendum, there's a variant of Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs which exist for websites, we kinda fell on the wrong side of that trying to migrate the site and get this out on a Saturday. Whoops!

Thanks, 355E3B

item.title: It's enough - vibecoding tag crossed from useless to harmful
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: vibecoding, LLMs, software engineering, community, original content

Summary: The vibecoding tag has lost its original purpose as the landscape of software engineering and LLMs has evolved. Initially meant to signal relevant content, it now encompasses a wide array of posts, including those that only mention LLMs in passing. This broad usage has diluted its significance and is driving valuable community members away. Over time, the excessive tagging of posts related to LLMs has made it challenging for individuals to find original technical content, which many users prefer. Despite the support for filtering out LLM-centric posts, the current state is detrimental for everyone involved. Original articles relevant to software engineering are getting filtered out simply because they touch on LLMs, while community members are becoming frustrated with the persistent tagging issues and leaving the platform. The situation calls for a reevaluation or separation of the vibecoding tag to restore its effectiveness. In conclusion, maintaining the current tagging system is counterproductive, and improving the categorization could lead to a more vibrant and focused community that encourages original contributions.

The vibecoding tag has been getting more and more useless for a while now. It lost the original meaning as the culture of software engineering with LLMs matured a bit. It got silly when posts talking about LLMs in general got tagged. It got useless when posts even mentioning some project created with LLMs in passing got tagged. Now it actually got harmful to the community when tagging posts turns away very valuable members https://lobste.rs/c/vecuxj

I sighed and moved on for a while now as almost everything gets tagged - you can skip a word. But now it not only carries no signal whatsoever, it turns away people creating original technical content - which is what I assume anti-vibecoding people would actually like to see more of.

Please split it or kill it. But we'd be better off without what exists today.

Added: To be clear, I totally support people filtering out llm-generated or llm-centric posts. But right now everyone loses. And every day we lose a little bit more. Whether it's an original, interesting article that turns out to be nth-degree related to llms and filtered out, or a community member annoyed by this recurring problem and leaving us with even fewer actual non-llm-centric entries.
