item.title: Amazon Braket now in scope for FedRAMP Class C
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Braket, FedRAMP, quantum computing, AWS, US Regions

Summary: Amazon Braket has received FedRAMP Class C authorization for AWS US Regions where it is offered, allowing government customers and associated organizations to explore quantum computing securely. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) standardizes security assessments and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by U.S. government entities. With Class C authorization, Amazon Braket enables users to operate within an authorized security boundary. The AWS components of Braket, including the API, SDK, job orchestration, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are all within the FedRAMP-certified environment. However, quantum workloads are processed on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs), which are outside of this secured boundary. All data transmitted to QHPs complies with AWS's stringent privacy and security measures, including the removal of personally identifiable information, and the encryption of data both in transit and at rest. Additionally, AWS maintains its standard policies regarding data retention and deletion. For further details, users can explore the AWS FedRAMP services, the FedRAMP Marketplace, and the Amazon Braket product page. Regional availability includes US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), and US West (Oregon).

Amazon Braket is now in scope for FedRAMP Class C in AWS US Regions where Braket is available. The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program that delivers a standard approach to the security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products and services.

With FedRAMP Class C authorization, government customers and the organizations that serve them can use Amazon Braket to explore quantum computing within an authorized boundary. The AWS-operated components of Braket, including the API and SDK, job orchestration and management, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are within the FedRAMP-certified boundary, while quantum workloads execute on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs) outside that boundary. All data sent to QHPs meets AWS' privacy and security requirements including removal of all personally identifiable information, data encryption in transit and at rest, and adherence to AWS' standard data retention and deletion policies.

To learn more about FedRAMP, visit AWS FedRAMP services and the FedRAMP Marketplace. To learn more about Amazon Braket, visit the Braket product page and Getting Started on Braket resources.

Regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon)

item.title: v16.5.0-canary.17
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: turbo-persistence, prefetching, SST blocks, MADV_WILLNEED, optimization

Summary: The article discusses enhancements related to turbo-persistence, particularly focusing on prefetching strategies for multi-page SST (Sorted String Table) blocks. It highlights the use of the MADV_WILLNEED flag, which is designed to optimize memory management and improve performance by indicating to the operating system that certain data will be accessed soon. This proactive approach can significantly reduce latency when retrieving data, as it prompts preloading of necessary pages into memory. The implementation of this feature is aimed at increasing efficiency in data access patterns, which is crucial for applications that handle large datasets. The article also acknowledges the contributions of individuals or teams who supported the initiative, showing appreciation for their collaborative effort in bringing about these advancements. By leveraging these techniques, systems can enhance their overall responsiveness and performance, particularly in scenarios that involve frequent data retrieval and processing. The combined efforts towards refining these functionalities illustrate the ongoing commitment to optimizing software performance and memory management practices.

Misc Changes

  • turbo-persistence: prefetch multi-page SST blocks with MADV_WILLNEED: #100283

Credits

Amazon CloudWatch log centralization now available in AWS GovCloud and additional commercial Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: CloudWatch, log centralization, AWS GovCloud, Regions, organizations

Summary: Amazon CloudWatch log centralization is now provided in AWS GovCloud (US) and 13 additional commercial Regions, enabling organizations to consolidate log data from various AWS accounts and Regions into a single destination. This feature integrates seamlessly with AWS Organizations, which facilitates efficient log aggregation without requiring custom solutions. Users can create centralization rules that apply organization-wide, to specific organizational units, or to selected accounts. Logs are copied to a single account, preserving the source context through enriched system fields. The feature is available in multiple new Regions including Africa (Cape Town), several Asia Pacific locations, Canada West (Calgary), and various European locations such as Milan, Spain, and Zurich, among others, as well as Middle Eastern Regions like Bahrain and UAE. Getting started is easy—users can create a centralization rule through the Amazon CloudWatch console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. Customers can centralize one copy of logs for free, with additional copies billed at $0.05 per GB. For full details, users can refer to the Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide.

Amazon CloudWatch log centralization is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) and 13 additional commercial Regions. CloudWatch log centralization copies log data from multiple AWS accounts and Regions into a single destination account, integrating with AWS Organizations for efficient aggregation without the need for custom solutions.

With this launch, organizations in the AWS GovCloud (US) partition and commercial partition can each centralize logs across their accounts and Regions for centralized monitoring. You can scope centralization rules to your entire organization, specific organizational units, or selected accounts and copy logs into a single account while preserving source context through enriched system fields.

CloudWatch log centralization is now additionally available in Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Melbourne), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan), Europe (Spain), Europe (Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Middle East (Bahrain), Middle East (UAE), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). For a complete list of supported Regions, see the AWS Region table.

To get started, create a centralization rule in the Amazon CloudWatch console, or by using the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, see Log centralization in the Amazon CloudWatch Logs User Guide. Customers can centralize one copy of logs for free; additional copies are charged at $0.05/GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing.

item.title: AWS Lambda durable functions are now available in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Lambda, durable functions, GovCloud, compliance, orchestration

Summary: AWS Lambda durable functions are now accessible in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. These functions allow developers to create reliable multi-step applications and AI workflows within the Lambda developer experience. Durable functions enhance the Lambda programming model by introducing new primitives such as "step" and "wait", which help in checkpointing progress, recovering from failures automatically, and pausing executions without incurring compute charges for on-demand functions. With their availability in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, government customers and those in regulated industries can effectively handle complex processes like order workflows, user onboarding, and AI-assisted tasks while adhering to strict compliance and security standards. Developers can activate durable functions for various languages, including Python (versions 3.13 and 3.14), Node.js (versions 22 and 24), Go (versions 1.24 or later), .Net (version 2.2), and Java (17+) using several platforms: the AWS Lambda API, AWS Management Console, and AWS SDK. Additionally, tools like AWS CloudFormation, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), and the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) can be utilized for infrastructure as code.

AWS Lambda durable functions are now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. Lambda durable functions enable developers to build reliable multi-step applications and AI workflows within the Lambda developer experience.

Lambda durable functions extend the Lambda programming model with new primitives in your event handler, such as "step" and "wait", allowing you to checkpoint progress, automatically recover from failures, and pause executions without incurring compute charges for on-demand functions. With availability in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, government customers and regulated industries can orchestrate complex processes such as order workflows, user onboarding, and AI-assisted tasks while meeting stringent compliance and security requirements.

You can activate durable functions for new Python (versions 3.13 and 3.14), Node.js (versions 22 and 24), Go (versions 1.24 or later), .Net (version 2.2), or Java (17+) based Lambda functions using the AWS Lambda API, AWS Management Console, or AWS SDK. You can also use infrastructure as code tools such as AWS CloudFormation, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM), and the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK).

For more information on durable functions, visit the AWS Lambda durable functions product page or the AWS Lambda Developer Guide. To learn about pricing, visit AWS Lambda pricing. For region availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page.

item.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: NVIDIA, Nemotron 3.5, multimodal, SageMaker, AI solutions

Summary: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now offered on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, enhancing the range of foundation models for AWS users. This vision-language model accepts various inputs, including images, videos, and text, and generates text, making it suitable for multimodal AI applications. It features a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a vision encoder, accommodating up to 1 million tokens in context. Designed for tasks like document intelligence, GUI understanding, and video question answering, it employs a Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head for faster text generation and configurable reasoning. The model supports ten languages: English, French, Spanish, German, Japanese, Hindi, Korean, and Chinese. It has undergone extensive post-training with multimodal supervised fine-tuning and GRPO reinforcement learning to produce structured JSON outputs and facilitate tool calling for enterprise workflows. SageMaker JumpStart provides two deployment variants optimized for specific instances and customization options. Users can easily deploy the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model via the SageMaker console or the SageMaker Python SDK, streamlining the process of addressing specific AI use cases.

NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, expanding the portfolio of foundation models available to AWS customers. This vision-language model from the Nemotron 3.5 family accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text, enabling customers to deploy multimodal AI solutions on AWS infrastructure.

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is designed for document intelligence, GUI understanding, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. It pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a vision encoder, supporting context lengths of up to 1 million tokens. The model includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head for speculative decoding to accelerate text generation, with reasoning configurable per request. It supports ten languages including English, French, Spanish, German, Japanese, Hindi, Korean, and Chinese. Post-trained with multimodal supervised fine-tuning on image, video, document, chart, and GUI data followed by GRPO reinforcement learning, it delivers structured JSON output, tool calling, and configurable reasoning for enterprise agent workflows. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4 for optimized inference on G7 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, and BF16 reference weights on ml.p5en.48xlarge for customization including SFT, RL, distillation, and domain adaptation.

With SageMaker JumpStart, customers can deploy Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with just a few clicks to address their specific AI use cases.

To get started with these models, navigate to the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog in the SageMaker console or use the SageMaker Python SDK to deploy the models to your AWS account. For more information about deploying and using foundation models in SageMaker JumpStart, see the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart documentation.

item.title: Beam model by Reflection is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart and AWS Trainium
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Beam, Reflection, Amazon SageMaker, open weight model, AI

Summary: Beam, an open weight model from Reflection, is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, enhancing its capabilities in reasoning, coding, and automated workflows. This model allows businesses to create advanced coding agents while maintaining control over their data and infrastructure. Beam is designed to work alongside existing models in SageMaker AI and is optimized for AWS Trainium, ensuring high performance and cost efficiency for deployments. Reflection emphasizes the control developers have with Beam, as it can be run in private AWS accounts, ensuring data privacy and compliance. Engineering teams can leverage Beam for tasks such as resolving software issues, code generation, and automating operations. Additionally, it supports complex workflows and advanced reasoning in math and science. As Beam is released under the Apache 2.0 license, businesses can customize and inspect the model freely. Available initially in the US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio) regions, users can find Beam in SageMaker JumpStart within Amazon SageMaker Studio. The introduction of Beam in SageMaker represents a significant advancement in maintaining openness and providing managed infrastructure for AI solutions.

Beam, the first open weight model offered by US-based Reflection, is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, the model hub in Amazon SageMaker AI. According to Beam, they operate at the frontier of open weight models in its class, with strong performance across reasoning, coding, and agentic benchmarks. With it, customers can now build advanced coding agents and automated workflows on a frontier open weight model while keeping control of their data and infrastructure and adapting the model to their business. Beam runs alongside other models that customers already use in SageMaker AI and scales to meet production demand with the same controls, audit trails, and monitoring built into every SageMaker AI deployment. Additionally, Beam was ported and optimized for AWS Trainium3, giving customers a high-performance, cost-efficient option for deploying and scaling the model from day one. “Reflection is delivering frontier AI that developers can actually control, not just rent through an API. Bringing Beam to SageMaker AI puts that capability in front of millions of developers on infrastructure they already trust, running in their own AWS account, on their own data, fully in their control," said Misha Laskin, co-founder and CEO, Reflection.

Engineering teams can use Beam to resolve software issues, generate and review code, and automate routine operations work. Businesses can also use it for complex workflows that span many steps and tools, and for advanced math and science reasoning. Because Beam is released under the Apache 2.0 license, customers can inspect and customize the model, while also running it in their own AWS accounts, so data stays private and under their control, protected by the same AWS security and compliance capabilities they already rely on.  “Advanced AI models like Beam, now available on Amazon SageMaker, let us run open weight frontier AI entirely inside our own secure environments, with full visibility into the weights, the data, and the pipeline. In the age of multi-model AI, the pairing of openness and managed infrastructure is an essential addition to the AI ecosystem. The freedom to deploy and adapt advanced AI, tailored to mission problems with client-specific security and controls, gives more agencies greater flexibility to deploy advanced AI across their enterprise." said Garrett Berntsen, Chief AI Officer, Accenture Federal Services.

Beam is initially available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). To start, search for "Beam" in SageMaker JumpStart within Amazon SageMaker Studio, or deploy it directly on SageMaker AI.  To learn more, read the AWS/Beam launch blog, SageMaker AI documentation and SageMaker JumpStart documentation.

item.title: AWS Transform announces Azure-to-AWS cloud-native code conversion
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transform, Azure SDK, code conversion, cloud-native applications, modernization agent

Summary: AWS has announced the general availability of its application code conversion feature in AWS Transform, enabling users to migrate their Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS effectively. The AWS Transform .NET modernization agent identifies Azure service code within submitted source code and provides conversion options in an assessment report and modernization plan. Users have the flexibility to accept the suggested options or modify them as per their preferences prior to executing the modernization process. The service converts Azure Functions to AWS Lambda functions, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS. Additionally, a preview conversion from Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB is also available. AWS Transform ensures that the changes are validated and integrated into the newly transformed code. This feature is currently accessible across eight AWS Regions, including US East (N. Virginia), various Asia Pacific locations (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London). For those interested, more information can be found in the AWS Transform User Guide.

Today, AWS announced the general availability of application code conversion from Azure SDK to AWS SDK in AWS Transform, giving you an accelerated path to migrate Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS. The AWS Transform .NET modernization agent identifies Azure service code and converts it to equivalent AWS service code. For example, an Azure Functions serverless function that uses Azure Cosmos DB can be converted to an AWS Lambda function that uses Amazon DynamoDB.

AWS Transform discovers the Azure SDK in your submitted source code and presents the conversion options in the assessment report and modernization plan. You can accept the options provided or adjust them based on your preferences before running the modernization. AWS Transform then converts the identified Azure service code to the equivalent AWS SDK calls, and validates that the changes are incorporated into the transformed code. The feature supports conversion of Azure Functions to AWS Lambda functions, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS, with Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion available in preview.

AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London).

To learn more, see Convert cloud-native code to AWS in the AWS Transform User Guide.

item.title: AWS End User Messaging adds registration improvements for faster, higher-quality submissions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Messaging, Registrations, Compliance, RCS

Summary: AWS End User Messaging has introduced enhancements to assist users in completing messaging registrations accurately from the outset. Key improvements include clearer guidance, explicit field requirements, and tools to avoid common rejection reasons. Registration submissions now require compliance evidence such as opt-in proof and sample messages. Frequently, registrations face delays or denials due to incomplete evidence or missed required fields. To streamline this process, AWS has added mock-up examples of compliant opt-in and sample messages for US 10DLC, US short code, US toll-free, and RCS registrations. This allows users to see compliant submissions before creating their own. Additionally, the registration API response has been updated to include conditional logic, specifying required fields based on the values entered. This feature eliminates guesswork for users and their AI agents. Lastly, RCS registration now provides a step-by-step walkthrough for recording compliant videos needed for agent registrations. These enhancements are implemented across all AWS Regions where End User Messaging registrations are available, making the registration process smoother and more efficient. To learn more and get started, visit the End User Messaging documentation.

AWS End User Messaging now makes it easier to complete messaging registrations correctly the first time, with clearer guidance, explicit field requirements, and help avoiding the most common rejection reasons. Registrations ask for compliance evidence such as opt-in proof and sample messages, and submissions are often delayed or denied when that evidence is incomplete or a required field is missed. These improvements give you worked examples, surface exactly which fields you must provide, and walk you through the content that most often causes denials.

First, example mock-ups of a compliant opt-in and sample messages are now included for US 10DLC, US short code, US toll-free and RCS registrations, so you can see what a compliant submission looks like before you build your own. Second, the registration API response now surfaces conditional logic, so you and your AI agents no longer have to guess which fields are required based on other field values. The response tells you which fields are required for your specific registration. Third, RCS registration now includes a walkthrough for recording the compliant video that agent registrations require.

These improvements are available in all Regions where AWS End User Messaging registrations are available.

To learn more and get started, see the End User Messaging User Guide.

item.title: AWS End User Messaging now supports Brand Profiles
item.content:encoded:
Brand Profiles, AWS End User Messaging, registration, messaging channels, AI matching

Summary: Today, AWS End User Messaging introduced Brand Profiles, a feature that simplifies the process of storing and reusing brand and company information for messaging registrations across SMS, RCS, and WhatsApp. Traditionally, brands have to manually fill in their details, such as company name, address, and contact information, for every registration, which is time-consuming and prone to errors that could result in rejection. With Brand Profiles, users can input their information once and apply it to multiple registrations, expediting the process and ensuring consistency across different channels and countries. When starting a registration with a Brand Profile, the service automatically populates the relevant fields with saved information, allowing users to review a draft before submission. It features a smart match option that uses AI to fill in fields even when their names differ. Users can create a Brand Profile from scratch or build it upon existing registrations. Brand Profiles are available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging is offered, facilitating easier management for users who send messages for their own brands or multiple brands under a single AWS account.

Today, AWS End User Messaging announces Brand Profiles, which let you store your brand and company information once and reuse it across your messaging registrations. To send messages on SMS, RCS, and WhatsApp, you register your brand with carriers and messaging providers, and today you fill in the same company details, address, contact information, and use case by hand on every form, for each channel and country. That repeated entry slows every new registration, and a typo or other error can get one rejected and delay when you can start sending. With Brand Profiles, you enter this information once and apply it to each new registration, so you register faster and keep your details consistent across channels and countries. You can use Brand Profiles whether you send for your own brand or manage several brands in a single AWS account.

When you start a registration with a Brand Profile, the service fills in the matching fields from the information you saved and gives you a draft to review before you submit. By default, it matches standard fields such as company name, tax ID, address, and contact details. You can also turn on smart match, which uses AI to fill in fields even when their names differ. You can build a Brand Profile from scratch or start from your existing registrations.

Brand Profiles is available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging is available.

To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

item.title: AWS End User Messaging now offers managed OTP verification end-to-end
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Notify, OTP, verification, messaging

Summary: AWS End User Messaging has introduced an end-to-end managed one-time passcode (OTP) verification feature in Notify, enabling users to establish a comprehensive OTP solution in less than five minutes. This new functionality eliminates the need to set up a phone number, register with carriers, or manage message delivery. Previously, users were responsible for generating, storing, and expiring passcodes, but now Notify takes care of code generation, delivery, and verification. Users can send OTPs through text, voice, and WhatsApp. Setting up the verification process involves configuring rules in a notify code configuration, including defining the code type, length, expiration time, and the number of attempts allowed for recipients. Additionally, users can customize message templates for each communication channel. Once configured, sending a code to a recipient and verifying the code they enter require only a simple API call. This feature is now available across all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging services are offered, simplifying the implementation of secure verification processes for developers and businesses alike. To learn more and get started with this service, AWS suggests visiting the AWS End User Messaging documentation.

Today, AWS End User Messaging announces end-to-end managed one-time passcode (OTP) verification in Notify. You get a working OTP solution in under five minutes, including AWS phone numbers and code verification, without setting up a phone number, registering with carriers, or managing how messages are delivered. Before, you generated the passcode yourself and passed it to Notify to send, and you built and maintained the logic to create, store, and expire codes. Now Notify generates the code, delivers it, and verifies the code the recipient enters, so you ship a complete verification flow and skip that work entirely. You can deliver codes over text, voice, and now WhatsApp.

You set the rules once in a notify code configuration: the code type, length, how long it stays valid, and how many attempts a recipient gets, along with your templates for each channel. From then on, one call sends a code to a recipient on the channel you choose, and another checks the code they enter.

Notify is available in all commercial AWS Regions where AWS End User Messaging is available.

To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

item.title: AWS End User Messaging adds a guided wizard for RCS registration videos
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, RCS, video capture, registration, wizard

Summary: AWS End User Messaging has introduced a new wizard that simplifies the video capture process for RCS agent registration. This change addresses a key requirement in multiple countries, including the United States, where a screen recording demonstrating the messaging experience is necessary for RCS registrations. Previously, users had to manually script a specific sequence of messages to send to a test device, a process that often led to errors and mismatched or incomplete video submissions. The newly implemented wizard automates this process by driving each step of the video capture for users. It ensures that the correct messages are sent in the right order, which increases the chances of recording a compliant video on the first attempt. This improvement facilitates quicker approvals for RCS agent registrations. The wizard is now available on all RCS registration forms that necessitate video submissions. For more information on how to utilize this new feature and streamline your registration process, users are encouraged to visit the AWS End User Messaging documentation.

Today, AWS End User Messaging adds a wizard that orchestrates the entire video capture for your RCS agent registration. RCS registrations in multiple countries, including the United States, require a screen recording that demonstrates your messaging experience. To record it, you have to send a specific sequence of messages to a test device, and until now you scripted those messages yourself, which easily introduced errors and made a mismatched or incomplete video one of the hardest parts of registering for RCS.

The wizard now drives each step of the capture for you, sending the right messages in the right order, so you record a compliant video the first time and get your agent approved sooner. The wizard is on all RCS registration forms that require a video submission.

To learn more and get started, see the AWS End User Messaging User Guide.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.18-dev.16: Test that PSL merges several types blocks (#30753)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a — small change

At a glance

types {
  Email = String
}

model User {
  id Int @id
  email Email
  slug Slug
}

types {
  Slug = VarChar(191)
}

prisma contract emit accepts this schema: the named types from both
blocks are in the contract. If a name is bound in two types blocks,
the second one is reported as PSL_DUPLICATE_DECLARATION and the first
binding is kept.

Summary

A schema has been able to contain several types blocks since the
legacy PSL parser was replaced by the symbol table in #851. The legacy
parser reported "Only one top-level types block is allowed per
document". buildSymbolTable instead reads every types block and
checks each binding name against the same set of names as models and
composite types. Nothing tested this. This PR adds tests at each level
and documents it in the psl-parser README. It does not change any
implementation code.

Behavior changes & evidence

  • Bindings from several types blocks are merged into namedTypes.
    Implementation:
    packages/1-framework/2-authoring/psl-parser/src/symbol-table.ts.
    Evidence:
    psl-parser/test/symbol-table.test.ts,
    contract-psl/test/interpreter.types.test.ts.
    In the interpreter test, one block is declared after the model that uses
    it.
  • A name bound in two types blocks is a duplicate declaration. The
    diagnostic points at the later name. Evidence: the same two unit test
    files, plus the provider-level diagnostics fixture
    test/integration/test/authoring/diagnostics/duplicate-named-type-across-types-blocks/.
  • contract emit succeeds on a schema with two types blocks.
    Evidence: emits a psl schema with several types blocks in
    test/integration/test/cli.emit-command.test.ts.
    It runs the real CLI command and checks for exit code 0.
  • Docs:
    packages/1-framework/2-authoring/psl-parser/README.md
    now says that a schema can have any number of types blocks.

Testing performed

  • pnpm test in psl-parser (symbol-table.test.ts, 61 tests) and
    contract-psl (interpreter.types.test.ts)

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.18-dev.15: Remove 945 redundant and declaration-restating unit tests (#30731)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a. This continues the test-suite audit from #30729.

At a glance

This is a typical removal, from
packages/1-framework/3-tooling/migration/test/find-path-with-invariants.test.ts:

-  it('unreachable target → null', () => {
-    const graph = reconstructGraph([pkg('A', 'B', 'm1')]);
-    expect(findPathWithInvariants(graph, 'A', 'Z', new Set(['X']))).toBeNull();
-  });

The same file keeps a test with an identical body, at line 145:

  it('returns null when target is structurally unreachable', () => {
    const graph = reconstructGraph([pkg('A', 'B', 'm1')]);
    expect(findPathWithInvariants(graph, 'A', 'Z', new Set(['X']))).toBeNull();
  });

Summary

This is the second batch from the test audit. It removes 945 it/test
declarations from package, example, app and script tests. It changes
only test files: no production code, no src/, and nothing in the
integration suite.

Decision

The batch takes only the audit entries that are both rated
high-confidence and marked "remove". It includes two kinds of test:

  • Redundant: another test makes the same assertion through the same
    code path.
  • Trivial: a type test that restates a declared type; a test that
    compares an id, kind, capability flag or constant with its own literal;
    a getter test that reads back a constructor argument; a "hook is a
    function" or toBeDefined check; or a test of a test-only helper.

It does not include:

  • unreachable-input entries, because each one needs a judgement about
    whether the input can actually happen;
  • integration tests;
  • anything that would need a test rewritten or production code changed.

The audit was written against an older main, so every entry was
checked again against current code. A test was removed only when the
test it duplicates still asserts the same thing or more. About 90
entries were skipped in whole or in part: the test had already gone, the
kept test turned out to check less, or the removed test was the only
check of some behaviour.

Reviewer notes

  • There is one commit per package area: sql, tooling, adapters and
    drivers, cli, targets, framework and mongo, and extensions and examples.
    Each commit can be reviewed or reverted on its own.
  • Some removals are partial. In a few tests, one duplicated assertion
    was dropped and the rest of the test stays:
    • the second "reprint stability" verify in check-lifecycle-e2e;
  • redundant .not.toEqualTypeOf<number | string>() lines in the example
    type tests.

Three tests were renamed after an assertion was dropped, so that the
name matches what the test still checks.

  • 18 files are deleted outright. In each of them, every test was either
    a duplicate or a restatement. Examples:
    • default-functions.test.ts;
    • the codec-factory* tests of the test-only defineTestCodec;
    • is-ci.test.ts;
    • the mongo and sqlite create-*-control-client tests;
    • several *.test-d.ts files that restate declared types.
  • Test-only helpers and fixtures that became unused were removed with
    the tests that used them, for example
    test/fixtures/exact-prefix-import.ts in the CLI.

Testing performed

All on the final HEAD:

  • pnpm build, pnpm lint and pnpm lint:deps pass.
  • pnpm typecheck passes, except prisma7-adoption#typecheck, which
    cannot download the Prisma 7 schema-engine binary for linux-nixos
    (404) in this environment.
  • pnpm coverage:packages ran 24,844 passed, 40 failed and 36 skipped.
    Then pnpm coverage:report gave 0 threshold failures; the 6 warnings
    are all packages already on the warning-only list. The 40 failures are
    in files this PR does not change:
  • 39 are environment-specific: CLI init-prisma7* tests (EACCES
    copying fixtures), and the tarball and module-identity tests (pnpm
    trust policy on @vercel/detect-agent).
  • 1 is no-parallel-ci-detection, which hit its 500 ms timeout under
    load and passes when run alone.
  • The language-server, cli-telemetry and postgres-adapter round-trip
    suites also timed out during the parallel run. Each passes in full when
    run alone.
  • The example tests in mongo-demo, prisma-8-demo and retail-store pass,
    and so does pnpm test:scripts.
  • apps/telemetry-backend handler.test.ts fails here because
    ingestedAt comes back as a Temporal.Instant where the test expects a
    Date. This PR does not change that test or that app's source; the only
    file it touches in the app is rate-limit.test.ts.

Skill update

n/a — internal only.

Alternatives considered

  • Include the unreachable-input and medium-confidence entries. Left
    for a later batch. They need a judgement call on each test, while this
    batch is limited to deletions that can be checked directly against the
    code.
  • Rewrite per-value test groups as table-driven tests. Not done
    here, for example the 36 1-core/errors factory tests. A rewrite
    changes what each test asserts and needs its own review.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated.
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form. No
    Linear ticket exists for this work.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in.

item.content:encoded:
I've been writing notes as plain text files since forever, and it occurred to me that note-taking could benefit from the typical features that a language server provides: clickable links, autocomplete, hover previews, formatting, diagnostics, refactoring, etc. So I built a little language server and a vscode extension which adds syntax highlighting. Note-taking now feels more like writing code, and I get to use my favorite vscode keybindings (vim). Feedback is welcome!

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore expands to AWS GovCloud and 3 Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, Web Search, AWS Regions, compliance

Summary: Amazon Bedrock's Web Search feature is now accessible in four additional AWS Regions: US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). This fully managed tool enhances AI agents by providing them with real-time information sourced from the web, which ensures that responses are more accurate and up-to-date. It's particularly useful for tasks that involve research, summarization, and question answering. With this geographical expansion, customers can deploy agents that fetch web data closer to their applications and end users, leading to reduced latency in accessing information. Additionally, customers operating within government workloads can leverage the Web Search capability in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region, ensuring they meet stringent compliance and data residency requirements. This expansion reflects a commitment to enhancing the versatility and accessibility of AI solutions powered by Amazon Bedrock. For further information on Web Search, pricing details, and Region availability, customers are encouraged to check the provided resources.

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available in four additional AWS Regions: US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). Web Search is a fully managed tool that provides AI agents with current grounding from the web, enabling more accurate and up-to-date responses for tasks such as research, summarization, and question answering.

With this expansion, customers can build agents that retrieve web information closer to their applications and end users with lower latency. Customers with government workloads can now use Web Search in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region to meet compliance and data residency requirements. 

To learn more about Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, see the Web Search tool documentation. To learn about pricing, visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing. For Region availability, visit Supported AWS Regions.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Studio simplifies getting started for new AI/ML builders with new sign-in options
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker Studio, sign-up, Google, free credits, collaboration

Summary: Amazon SageMaker Studio now allows new customers to sign up using Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials, providing immediate access to a pre-configured Studio environment. Previously, users faced a complex multi-step AWS account creation process that included providing credit card information and navigating the AWS Console. With recent enhancements, the environment setup was reduced to twenty seconds and now includes pre-configured model customization permissions. New sign-in options further simplify the process, allowing users to complete sign-up without a credit card and receive free credits through the AWS Free Tier. Once inside SageMaker Studio, users can fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy foundation models swiftly. Teams can collaborate by inviting members via email, enabling shared access to models, notebooks, and endpoints without the need to set up IAM users or permissions. As projects expand beyond free credits, customers have the option to upgrade to paid plans and set spending limits. Verified customers can access GPU resources for various tasks without needing quota increases. This feature is currently available in all AWS Commercial Regions supporting Amazon SageMaker Studio. To get started, users can visit supported models or the SageMaker AI page.

Amazon SageMaker Studio now lets new customers sign up with their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials and land inside a fully configured Studio environment - no traditional AWS account setup and no console navigation required.

Previously, new customers who discovered a model on Hugging Face or an AWS product page had to complete a multi-step AWS account creation process, provide a credit card, navigate the AWS Console to find SageMaker AI, configure an environment, and set up IAM permissions before they could begin working. With earlier launches, we reduced environment setup to twenty seconds, pre-configured model customization permissions, and introduced deep links from Hugging Face and AWS product pages so customers could land directly inside Studio with a model pre-loaded. Now, with new sign-in options, customers complete a simplified sign-up using an existing identity, receive free credits as part of the AWS Free Tier with no credit card required in most cases, and arrive inside a ready-to-use SageMaker Studio environment where they can immediately fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy foundation models. Customers can invite team members by email, and collaborators sign in with their own email credentials to access the shared Studio environment, including shared models, notebooks, and endpoints without configuring IAM users or permissions. When a project grows beyond free credits, customers can upgrade to a paid plan and set a spend limit to stay within budget. Verified customers continue to receive default GPU access to G5, G6, G6e, and G4dn instances across endpoint deployments, training jobs, and notebooks without requesting quota increases.

This feature is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is supported. To get started, visit any supported model on Hugging Face and select "Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI" or "Deploy on SageMaker AI," or click Get Started from the SageMaker Studio page. To learn more, see the AWS sign-up documentation and SageMaker Studio setup guide.

item.title: Amazon EC2 T8i instances are now available in South America (São Paulo)
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: T8i instances, Amazon EC2, price performance, Intel Xeon, workloads

Summary: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) T8i instances have launched in South America (São Paulo) and are powered by custom sixth generation Intel Xeon processors on the latest AWS Nitro cards. T8i instances offer up to 30% better price performance than the previous T3 generation and are available in four sizes: nano, micro, small, and medium. These instances are ideal for workloads with low to moderate CPU utilization, including data processing, login gateways, small databases, batch processing, event-driven functions, CI/CD pipelines, microservices, and low-traffic websites. T8i instances boast up to 70% higher compute performance, 1.25 times higher network bandwidth, and 2.4 times higher EBS bandwidth compared to T3 instances. They utilize a CPU credit system similar to T3 with Standard and Unlimited modes, allowing existing T3 customers to upgrade easily and reduce total cost of ownership (TCO). They are available in multiple AWS regions, including the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Canada, and South America. Customers can purchase T8i instances via On-Demand and Spot instances, with a Savings Plan option arriving soon. To learn more, visit the AWS website.

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) T8i instances are now available in South America (São Paulo). These instances are powered by custom sixth generation Intel Xeon 6 processors, available exclusively on AWS, and built on the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards. T8i instances deliver up to 30% better price performance compared to previous generation T3 instances, and offer four sizes: nano, micro, small, and medium. These instances are designed for workloads requiring low to moderate CPU utilization, including data processing, login gateways, small databases, batch processing, event driven functions, CI/CD pipelines, microservices, and low traffic websites.

T8i instances deliver up to 70% higher compute performance, 1.25x higher network bandwidth, and 2.4x higher EBS bandwidth compared to T3 instances. They use the same CPU credit system as T3 with Standard and Unlimited modes, so existing T3 customers can upgrade to T8i and immediately benefit from better price performance, enabling them to lower their TCO.
