item.title: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: DynamoDB Streams, timestamp-based processing, Kinesis Client Library, point-in-time recovery, AWS Regions

Summary: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now includes a timestamp-based stream processing feature, allowing users to read stream records beginning at a specified point in time. Previously, stream consumption could only commence from the oldest retained record within the last 24 hours or from new records written after the start of consumption. The new capability enables you to specify a timestamp and begin processing from the earliest record that was written at or after that time using the AT_TIMESTAMP shard iterator type. This functionality is compatible with the Amazon Kinesis Client Library through the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis adapter. It facilitates several use cases, including recovery from interruptions, debugging, auditing by replaying data from a specific past point, and synchronizing after a restore. Additionally, it allows users to skip backlogs by resuming from a recent timestamp near the latest records. The feature is available across all commercial AWS Regions, AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and China Regions, with no extra charges beyond standard GetRecords API requests. To begin using this feature, consult the DynamoDB developer guide.

Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing, enabling you to begin reading stream records from a specific point in time. Previously, you could only start from the oldest retained record (up to 24 hours old) or from new records written after you start consuming the stream. Now, you can supply a timestamp and begin processing at the first record written at or after that time using the AT_TIMESTAMP shard iterator type.

Timestamp-based stream processing can be used with the Amazon Kinesis Client Library (KCL) through the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis adapter. It helps you avoid reprocessing entire retained streams or missing records when resuming stream consumption, supporting common use cases such as recovery after an interruption, data replay for debugging and auditing by reading from a specific point in the past, skipping a backlog by resuming from a recent timestamp near the latest records, and synchronizing after a restore by beginning at the export timestamp following a point-in-time recovery (PITR) export.

Timestamp-based stream processing is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. There is no additional charge for this feature beyond standard GetRecords API request charges. To get started, see Amazon DynamoDB Streams timestamp documentation in the DynamoDB developer guide.

item.title: AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go is now generally available
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Lambda, Durable Execution SDK, Go, workflows

Summary: AWS has announced the general availability of the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go, which allows Go developers to create resilient, long-running workflows using Lambda durable functions. This SDK facilitates the development of multi-step applications, such as infrastructure automation and deployment rollouts, directly within Go code without the need for custom progress tracking. Lambda durable functions enhance the event-driven programming model of Lambda by automatically checkpointing progress and allowing execution to pause for up to a year while waiting for external events. The SDK offers a native Go experience, including features for progress tracking, callback integration, durable invocation for reliable function chaining, and efficient suspension for waits. Developers can easily add the SDK to their Go modules using the go get command and deploy their functions as static binaries on the provided.al2023 runtime, just like other Go functions on Lambda. Additionally, the durabletest package allows for local testing of complete workflows without network access or AWS credentials, while the durablelint analyzer helps identify code that could disrupt a workflow upon resumption. For more information, developers can refer to the Lambda durable functions documentation and related resources.

Today, AWS announces the general availability of the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go, enabling Go developers to build resilient, long-running workflows using Lambda durable functions. With this SDK, developers can create multi-step applications like infrastructure automation, deployment rollouts with approval gates, and pipelines that call AI models and pause for human review directly in their Go code without implementing custom progress tracking.

Lambda durable functions extend Lambda's event-driven programming model with operations that checkpoint progress automatically and pause execution for up to an year when waiting on external events. The AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go provides a native Go experience for building with Lambda durable functions. It includes steps for progress tracking, callback integration for human and agent-in-the-loop workflows, durable invocation for reliable function chaining, and waits for efficient suspension.

The SDK works with the Go tools developers already use. Developers add it to a Go module with go get and deploy their function as a single static binary on the provided.al2023 runtime, like any other Go function on Lambda. Before deploying, they can locally test complete workflows on their own machine with the durabletest package, without requiring network access or AWS credentials, and use the durablelint analyzer to catch code that could break a workflow when it resumes.

To get started, see the Lambda durable functions developer guide and the AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go on GitHub. For Regional availability and pricing details for Lambda durable functions, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page and AWS Lambda Pricing.

item.title: Muse Spark Open model now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Meta, Muse Spark Open, SageMaker, foundation models, coding workflows

Summary: Meta's Muse Spark Open is now accessible through Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, enhancing the variety of foundation models for AWS users. This model is tailored for coding-optimized agent workflows in enterprise software engineering, particularly on AWS infrastructure. It employs a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, containing 816 billion total parameters with 42 billion active per token, striking a balance between large capacity and efficient per-token compute. The model features a remarkable 1 million-token context window, allowing it to process entire projects, including dependencies and legacy code, seamlessly. It supports multiple input types—text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video—and can generate text outputs. Muse Spark Open is trained on real-world developer tasks like multi-file refactors and extensive debugging, enabling it to plan, act, observe outcomes, and self-correct over extended periods. Two model variants are available in SageMaker JumpStart: BF16 and NVFP4 quantized, with the latter being memory-efficient. Customers can deploy Muse Spark Open within their AWS accounts via the SageMaker console or Python SDK, offering complete control over source code and prompts. For further details, users can consult the SageMaker JumpStart documentation.

Meta's Muse Spark Open is now available on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, expanding the portfolio of foundation models available to AWS customers. This coding-optimized open-weight model from Meta is purpose-built for agentic coding workflows, bringing multi-step reasoning and tool calling to enterprise software engineering on AWS infrastructure.

Muse Spark Open is designed for long-running coding agents and multimodal engineering workflows. Built on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 816B total parameters and 42B active per token, it delivers the capacity of a very large network while keeping per-token compute closer to that of a much smaller dense model. The model holds a 1M-token context window, enabling it to ingest an entire project—including dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files—without splitting tasks into smaller pieces. It accepts text, images, documents, audio, and audio-video as input and generates text output. Trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions, it plans, acts, observes results, and self-corrects over long horizons rather than making single tool calls. SageMaker JumpStart offers two variants: BF16 (Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B) and NVFP4 quantized (Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4), with the NVFP4 variant requiring roughly a quarter of the memory for cost-efficient deployment.

With SageMaker JumpStart, customers can deploy Muse Spark Open with just a few clicks, with the endpoint running in their own AWS account for full control over source code and prompts.

To get started with this model, navigate to the SageMaker JumpStart model catalog in the SageMaker console or use the SageMaker Python SDK to deploy the model to your AWS account. For more information about deploying and using foundation models in SageMaker JumpStart, see the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart documentation.

item.title: AWS HealthOmics now supports shared VPCs
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS HealthOmics, shared VPCs, bioinformatics, HIPAA-eligible, network management

Summary: AWS HealthOmics now allows sharing of Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) across different accounts, facilitating workflow access to resources managed by other AWS accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM). As a HIPAA-eligible service, it aids healthcare and life sciences clients in accelerating bioinformatics workflows. Shared VPCs enable centralized networking management by allowing subnets and security groups to be shared from a single VPC across multiple accounts. This functionality integrates workflows from different accounts into the same centrally managed VPC, eliminating the need for separate endpoints in individual VPCs. With cross-account sharing, workflows can access data privately, reducing the requirement for VPC peering connections or duplicated AWS PrivateLink VPC endpoints. Previously, maintaining individual route tables and separate endpoints added complexity. This new capability simplifies network management while allowing researchers and developers to conduct their bioinformatics operations within their respective accounts. The shared VPCs feature is available in all regions where AWS HealthOmics operates, including various locations in the US, Europe, Israel, and Asia Pacific. For further guidance, users are encouraged to refer to the AWS documentation.

AWS HealthOmics now supports sharing VPCs across accounts, enabling your workflows to access resources in Amazon Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) managed by other AWS accounts with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM). AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows.

With shared VPCs, customers can centralize networking administration by sharing subnets and security groups from a single VPC across multiple accounts in their organization, and HealthOmics then places each account's workflows directly into those shared subnets. With cross-account VPC sharing, multiple accounts run inside one centrally managed VPC, instead of duplicating endpoints across VPCs. Workflows in participating accounts can access data privately without separate VPC peering connections or duplicated VPC endpoints. Previously, customers with centralized networking had to create separate AWS PrivateLink VPC endpoints in each VPC and maintain individual route tables using VPC peering. Cross-account VPC sharing reduces infrastructure overhead and simplifies network management for organizations with centralized networking while allowing researchers and developers to run bioinformatics workflows in their own accounts.

Shared VPCs is available in all Regions where AWS HealthOmics is available: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Singapore, Seoul, Tokyo). To get started, see the AWS HealthOmics User Guide.

item.title: Amazon Time Sync Service adds support for microsecond-accurate time on 135 additional EC2 instance types in all commercial regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Time Sync Service, microsecond-accurate time, EC2 instance types, Precision Time Placement Group, AWS Nitro System

Summary: Amazon Time Sync Service now supports microsecond-accurate time on 135 additional EC2 instance types across 12 instance families in all commercial regions. This enhancement is built on Amazon’s reliable network infrastructure and the AWS Nitro System. The service leverages reference clocks within the Nitro System to provide microsecond accuracy and nanosecond-precision hardware timestamps, allowing customers to efficiently order application events, measure one-way network latency, and speed up transactions in distributed applications. The newly supported instance families comprise eight Gen8 families (C8a, C8i, C8i-flex, C8id, M8i, M8i-flex, R8a, and X8i) and four Gen9 families (C9g, C9gd, M9g, and M9gd). Starting today, customers can enable microsecond-accurate time by creating a Precision Time Placement Group (PTPG), a new placement strategy that activates Precision Time Protocol hardware clock (PHC). Additionally, customers requiring low network latency and precision time can associate a PTPG with their Cluster Placement Group (CPG), allowing their low-latency workloads to benefit from microsecond-accurate time. For more information, refer to the AWS documentation.

Amazon Time Sync Service introduces support for microsecond-accurate time on 135 additional EC2 instance types—spanning 12 instance families—in all commercial regions. Built on Amazon's proven network infrastructure and the AWS Nitro System, microsecond-accurate time and nanosecond-precision hardware timestamps leverage the reference clocks running in the Nitro System directly, enabling customers to easily order application events, measure 1-way network latency, and increase distributed application transaction speed.

The newly supported families include eight Gen8 families (C8a, C8i, C8i-flex, C8id, M8i, M8i-flex, R8a, and X8i) and four Gen9 families (C9g, C9gd, M9g, and M9gd).

Starting today, customers can access microsecond-accurate time on these additional instance types by creating a Precision Time Placement Group (PTPG), a new placement strategy that allows customers to launch instances with Precision Time Protocol hardware clock (PHC) enabled. Customers that require both low network latency as well as precision time can associate a PTPG with their Cluster Placement Group (CPG), so that their low-latency workloads also benefit from microsecond-accurate time.

For more information, refer to the Amazon Time Sync Service documentation.

item.title: AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization now supports Aurora PostgreSQL cross-region deployment in 7 more Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transform, Windows modernization, Aurora PostgreSQL, cross-region deployment, .NET applications

Summary: AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization has introduced support for cross-region deployment of converted Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL databases, enhancing customer control over database deployment locations. This feature is now available in seven additional AWS Regions, aligning with data residency, latency, and disaster recovery requirements. Customers can upload SQL Server Database Design Language (DDL) files alongside a transformation plan specifying the target AWS Region. This process converts the database and deploys the resulting Aurora PostgreSQL cluster in a different region. Additionally, the same workflow ensures that dependent .NET applications are made PostgreSQL compatible by updating their connection strings and Entity Framework data-access calls. With this expansion, the service is now accessible in the following Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Canada (Montreal). To get started with AWS Transform, customers are encouraged to visit the provided links or resources.

Today, AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization adds support for cross-region deployment of converted Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL databases and is available in seven additional AWS Regions. Together these changes give customers more control over where their modernized databases are deployed after SQL Server modernization, supporting data residency, latency, and disaster recovery requirements.

Customers can upload SQL Server Database Design Language (DDL) files and set a target AWS Region in the transformation plan to convert the database and deploy the resulting Aurora PostgreSQL cluster to a different AWS Region. The same workflow makes dependent .NET applications PostgreSQL compatible, updating connection strings and ADO.NET and Entity Framework data-access calls.

With this expansion, AWS Transform for full-stack Windows modernization is now available in the following Regions:

US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Canada (Montreal).

To get started, you can go to AWS Transform product page or see AWS Transform for full-stack Windows documentation.

item.title: Amazon MSK Connect and AWS Glue Schema Registry are now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, European Sovereign Cloud, MSK Connect, Apache Kafka, data validation

Summary: Starting today, new features are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region, enhancing support for Apache Kafka applications. With the introduction of MSK Connect, customers can now run fully managed Kafka Connect clusters alongside existing Amazon MSK Standard brokers. This feature allows for seamless deployment, monitoring, and scaling of connectors that facilitate data movement between Apache Kafka and external systems without requiring infrastructure provision. MSK Connect offers automatic scaling and a pay-as-you-go pricing model for convenience. Complementing this, there is a new serverless feature that enables users to validate and control streaming data evolution using various schema formats like Apache Avro, JSON, and Protobuf. This serverless option serves as a centralized repository for data structure, which helps reduce data validation logic, enhances cross-team coordination, and minimizes downstream issues. It integrates easily with applications developed in C# and Java, streamlining the management of data formats across decoupled applications. For those interested in leveraging these capabilities, relevant documentation can be found on the AWS website.

Starting today, Amazon MSK Connect and the AWS Glue Schema Registry are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. Together with Amazon MSK Standard brokers, already available in the region, these launches give customers running streaming workloads on the AWS European Sovereign Cloud a more complete set of tools to build, connect, and govern their Apache Kafka applications.

MSK Connect lets you run fully managed Kafka Connect clusters with Amazon MSK - deploy, monitor, and scale connectors that move data between Apache Kafka and external systems like databases, file systems, and search indices, with no infrastructure to provision, automatic scaling, and pay-as-you-go pricing. Complementing it, the AWS Glue Schema Registry - a serverless, free feature of AWS Glue - lets you validate and control the evolution of streaming data using Apache Avro, JSON, and Protobuf schemas. Acting as a centralized repository for data format and structure across decoupled applications, it reduces data validation logic, cross-team coordination, and downstream failures, and integrates with C# and Java applications built for Amazon MSK, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and AWS Lambda.

To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Developer Guide and the AWS Glue Schema Registry documentation.

item.title: Amazon CloudFront announces dual-stack support for VPC origins
item.content:encoded:
Amazon CloudFront now supports end-to-end IPv6 delivery to origins inside your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with the new dual-stack VPC origins. With VPC origins, customers keep their Application Load Balancers (ALB), Network Load Balancers (NLB), and EC2 instances in private subnets that only their CloudFront distributions can reach. With dual-stack support, customers can now send IPv6 traffic all the way to these private origins to meet their IPv6 architecture and regulatory requirements, without exposing origins to the internet.

Previously, CloudFront supported dual-stack for public origins but connected to VPC origins over IPv4 only. Customers faced a tradeoff: move origins to public subnets for IPv6 and give up VPC origin security or keep them private and stay on IPv4. Now, with this launch, customers can configure their VPC origins as dual-stack and get end-to-end IPv6 without sacrificing security.

Dual-stack VPC origins are available in all AWS Commercial Regions where VPC origins are supported. The full list of supported Regions is available here. There is no additional cost for using dual-stack VPC origins. To learn more, visit CloudFront VPC origins.

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 RC1 is now available in Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment
item.content:encoded:
Starting today, Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 19 Release Candidate 1 (RC1) is available in the Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment, allowing you to evaluate the pre-release of PostgreSQL 19 on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.

PostgreSQL 19 RC1 focuses on stability, with bug fixes and improvements from the Beta 4 testing period. This release improves error handling for complex text-search expressions, hardens parallel autovacuum, and improves reliability of GIN index maintenance. Refer to the PostgreSQL community announcement for more details.. Refer to the PostgreSQL community announcement for more details.

Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment database instances are retained for a maximum period of 60 days and are automatically deleted after the retention period. Amazon RDS database snapshots that are created in the Preview Environment can only be used to create or restore database instances within the Preview Environment. You can use the PostgreSQL dump and load functionality to import or export your databases from the Preview Environment. Amazon RDS Database Preview Environment database instances are priced as per the pricing in the US East (Ohio) Region.

item.title: Amazon Redshift long-term system table retention with Amazon S3 Tables is now available in additional AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Redshift long-term retention for system table data through native integration with Amazon S3 Tables is now available in additional AWS Regions. With this feature, you can configure your Redshift system table data retention beyond the current 7-day limit to meet your compliance, auditing, and observability requirements. Once enabled, AWS automatically writes system table data to S3 Tables in Apache Iceberg format and manages partitioning, compaction, and retention.

Customers use Redshift system tables to monitor query performance, audit data warehouse activity, and meet compliance requirements. With this feature, system table data is replicated automatically, eliminating the need for custom extract transform load (ETL) pipelines and any resource contention with your production workloads. If you operate multiple data warehouses, you can consolidate their system table data into a single location for cross-warehouse observability and analysis. Because the data is stored in the open Apache Iceberg format, you can query it through Redshift, Amazon Athena, DuckDB, or any Iceberg-compatible engine, and build observability dashboards using AWS services or third-party tools without additional operations overhead. Additionally, the AWS Agent Toolkit provides skills for querying system table data to surface performance insights and optimization recommendations.

This feature is available for Amazon Redshift Provisioned RG and RA3 instances and Amazon Redshift Serverless in the following additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (New Zealand), Canada West (Calgary), AWS GovCloud (US-East), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). To learn more, visit our documentation or the blog.

item.title: Amazon S3 Metadata now available in six additional AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Amazon S3 Metadata is now available in six additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (New Zealand), Asia Pacific (Taipei), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Mexico (Central).

S3 Metadata is a fast and easy way to instantly discover and understand your S3 data with automated, easily queried metadata that updates in near real time. This helps you curate, identify, and use your S3 data for business analytics, real-time inference applications, and more. S3 Metadata automatically populates metadata for both new and existing objects, providing you with a comprehensive, queryable view of your data. Annotations extend S3 Metadata, letting you attach rich business context directly to your objects in JSON, XML, or YAML, with up to 1 GB per object. To query annotations at scale, you can surface them in S3 Metadata annotation tables in these Regions.

With this launch, S3 Metadata is now generally available in 38 AWS Regions. For pricing details, visit the S3 pricing page. To learn more, visit the product page and documentation.

item.title: AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports the Cyber Risk Institute profile version 2.2
item.content:encoded:
AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports automated security checks that align with the Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) profile. The CRI Profile is a cybersecurity framework developed by the Cyber Risk Institute, a non-profit coalition of financial institutions and trade associations. The framework harmonizes cybersecurity and regulatory expectations that apply to the financial services sector into a common set of requirements, so that an organization can assess itself once and report against multiple regulations. AWS Security Hub CSPM provides 404 controls that support a subset of CRI Profile v2.2 requirements; the controls don't support requirements that require manual checks.

The new standard is now available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is currently available, including the AWS GovCloud (US) and the China Regions. To quickly enable the standard across your AWS environment, we recommend that you use Security Hub central configuration. With this approach, you can enable the standard in all or only some of your organization's accounts and across all AWS Regions that are linked to Security Hub with a single action.

To learn more, see CRI Profile v2.2 in the AWS Security Hub CSPM user guide. To receive notifications about new Security Hub CSPM features and controls subscribe to the Security Hub SNS topic. You can also try Security Hub CSPM at no cost for 30 days with the AWS Free Tier offering.

item.title: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus Collector now available in Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collector, a fully-managed agentless collector for Prometheus metrics, is now available in Asia Pacific (New Zealand). Customers in New Zealand can now run their Prometheus-compatible monitoring workloads in-region, with lower latency for local workloads and the ability to keep their data in-country.

Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collector discovers and collects Prometheus metrics from your container workloads without the need to run and operate collection agents yourself. Customers ingest the collected metrics into an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace, where they query and analyze the metrics. This fully-managed approach simplifies operational overhead by eliminating the need to maintain and scale collection infrastructure.

To learn more about Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collector, visit the user guide or product page.

item.title: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow now offers AI agent skills
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (MWAA) now integrates with the Agent Toolkit for AWS to provide built-in AI agent skills that let you author, debug, and test MWAA workflows and upgrade MWAA environments using any AI coding assistant that supports agent skills.

The four skills are authoring-mwaa-workflow, debugging-mwaa-workflow, testing-mwaa-workflow, and upgrading-mwaa-environments. Together they let your AI assistant interact directly with MWAA using natural language, reducing the manual effort of building and maintaining data pipelines. For example, you can describe an ETL pipeline in plain language and the authoring skill generates a working DAG complete with task dependencies and error handling.

The Amazon MWAA AI agent skills work with both Amazon MWAA Provisioned and Amazon MWAA Serverless environments, and are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available.

To get started, install the aws-data-analytics plugin and configure your AI coding assistant to use the MWAA agent skills. To learn more, see Using agent skills with Amazon MWAA in the Amazon MWAA User Guide and the Agent Toolkit for AWS documentation.

item.title: Oracle Database@AWS supports aggregate and default routes for ODB peering
item.content:encoded:
Oracle Database@AWS (ODB) now supports advertising aggregate routes and a default route (0.0.0.0/0) when configuring ODB peering between applications in an Amazon VPC and databases in an ODB network. This simplifies network operations as customers extend new VPCs or on-premises networks to reach their databases, without updating the advertised CIDRs for each network that needs connectivity to the ODB network.

Previously, customers had to advertise each network reaching the ODB network as a separate CIDR, and could not advertise a broad aggregate range or a default route. With this launch, customers can advertise any CIDR range, so a single aggregate or default route can cover all networks reachable through the peered VPC, such as those connected through an AWS Transit Gateway, without a separate entry for each one.

This capability is available on ODB networks that support multiple ODB peering connections, in all AWS Regions where Oracle Database@AWS is available. To learn more, visit Oracle Database@AWS and the Oracle Database@AWS User Guide. To get started, subscribe through AWS Marketplace.

item.title: Launch AWS DevOps Agent to review findings and test results from AWS Resilience Hub
item.content:encoded:
The next generation of AWS Resilience Hub now integrates with AWS DevOps agent allowing you to review failure mode assessment findings and implement mitigations to resolve findings and review resilience test results. AWS Resilience Hub is a central location in the AWS Management Console that helps platform engineering and site reliability teams assess and strengthen the resilience of their workloads running on AWS. It provides automated dependency discovery, generative AI-powered failure mode analysis, modular resilience policies, resilience testing, and organization-wide resilience posture reporting.

Resilience test investigations: When you run a resilience test, Resilience Hub now launches an AWS DevOps Agent investigation that observes the test and returns a structured analysis. You can uncover symptoms, root cause, and impact along with observed recovery actions, like ARC Region switch.

Interactive agent analysis from failure mode assessment findings: You can now start AWS DevOps Agent on demand task directly from a failure mode assessment finding in the Resilience Hub console, with the finding's context already in place. This allows for asking questions and investigating findings to create a mitigation plan.

To get started, visit the AWS Resilience Hub console, select a service and configure DevOps agent in the service configuration. Then launch the DevOps agent directly from a failure mode assessment finding or a resilience test. To learn more, see the product page or visit the documentation.

AWS Resilience Hub is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), and South America (São Paulo).

item.title: AWS HealthOmics expands container registry support for private workflows
item.content:encoded:
You can now use container images from registries such as Seqera (Wave), NVIDIA NGC, and Google Artifact Registry with AWS HealthOmics expanded support for third-party container registries. You can use the containerized tools your workflows already rely on, without manually migrating images into Amazon ECR or editing your workflow definitions. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows.

With expanded container registry support, you can now instruct HealthOmics to copy container images, on your behalf, from newly supported registries into your Amazon ECR when running your private workflows. Previously, AWS HealthOmics could pull images only from registries supported through Amazon ECR pull-through cache (PTC). Your private workflows can now access Amazon ECR pull-through cache registries and the newly supported third party container registries, so you do not need to pull, re-push, or rewrite image URIs yourself.

Expanded container registry support is now available in all AWS Regions where HealthOmics is available: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Singapore, Seoul, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the third-party container image support documentation.

item.title: AWS Lambda recursive loop detection now supports Amazon EventBridge Custom event buses
item.content:encoded:
AWS Lambda recursive loop detection now automatically detects and stops recursive loops between Lambda Event Functions and Amazon EventBridge Custom event buses, helping protect you against unintended usage and unexpected charges from runaway workloads. Lambda recursive loop detection, enabled by default on your AWS account, automatically identifies when a Lambda Event Function is invoked recursively by a supported AWS service and stops the loop.

You can use EventBridge Custom event buses to invoke Lambda Event Functions, building automation workflows and scheduling recurring tasks without managing any infrastructure. However, a misconfiguration or code defect can cause EventBridge rules to trigger your Event Functions recursively, resulting in runaway usage. Now, recursive loop detection supports EventBridge Custom buses, automatically stopping such loops and sending you an AWS Health Dashboard notification with troubleshooting instructions.

EventBridge Custom event buses now support recursive loop detection in every commercial AWS Region where they are available. This feature is enabled by default on your account and requires no configuration. If your Event Function uses recursive loops intentionally, you can use the PutFunctionRecursionConfig API to turn off recursive loop detection for that function.

To learn more about recursive loop detection, visit Lambda documentation.

item.title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Update for Microsoft SQL Server
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for Microsoft SQL Server 2025 CU8 KB5104822 (RDS version 17.00.4075.5.v1).

For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5104822. We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.18-dev.2: Close out the lsp-rename project (#30724)
item.content:encoded:
Closes the lsp-rename project: deletes projects/lsp-rename/. Stacked
on #30721; it will be rebased onto main when that merges.

Project outcome

Slice PR State
Rename symbol in the PSL language server, with @map / @@map where
a database name would change #30633 merged
The binder resolves entity names in type-constructor arguments
(pg.enum(X)), so rename edits them #30659 merged
A pg.enum column can name a native_enum of another namespace
#30721 in the merge queue
A named type over pg.enum (types { Status = pg.enum(X) }) —
not delivered; dropped from this project at close-out (see below)

Definition of Done

  • Rename for models, composite types, named types, blocks, fields and
    namespaces, from a declaration and from a reference, across files: met
    (#30633, language-server tests).
  • prepareRename ranges and refusals, refused non-identifier names: met
    (#30633).
  • Map attribute on rename for models, scalar fields and blocks whose
    descriptor sets nameIsStorageName; none for relation fields, @@base
    models and the other kinds: met (#30633).
  • Rename in apps/lsp-playground across scratch files, including one
    never selected: met (#30633, checked in a headless browser).
  • READMEs state that rename is supported: met (#30633).
  • native_enum rename edits its pg.enum(...) usages: met (#30659; QA
    run over stdio with the Postgres target).
  • References across namespaces produce a column: met by #30721 once it
    merges.
  • A named type over pg.enum gives the same column as the constructor
    on the field: not met. Dropped at close-out on the operator's
    request; no follow-up ticket exists.
  • Manual check in VS Code (F2 on each symbol kind): not recorded in
    the project. The script for it was in
    projects/lsp-rename/qa/manual-qa.md, deleted here.

Where the project's decisions live

Decision Home
Rename applies without a collision check, as TypeScript and Prisma 7
do the rename provider and its tests
Rename adds @map / @@map with the old name where a database name
would change; the rule for models and fields is in the language server;
blocks opt in with nameIsStorageName
language-server/src/rename.ts; the doc comment on
AuthoringPslBlockDescriptor.nameIsStorageName
An entity name in a type-constructor argument is bound by the binder
through entityRefArg psl-parser/src/binder.ts and its tests
A pg.enum column's type is qualified by the namespace of its
value-set reference contract-ts/src/target-authoring-hooks.ts and
the Postgres target tests (#30721)

None is architecturally durable enough for an ADR.

Deferred, with no ticket

  • A named type over pg.enum.
  • The TypeScript builder cannot express a pg.enum column naming an
    enum of another namespace; the Prisma 7 interpreter still refuses an
    enum of another schema.
  • After a native_enum rename with @@map, the contract's value-set
    entry is keyed by the block name, so the storage hash changes.
  • No completion or signature help inside type-constructor arguments.

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • New Features

  • PostgreSQL enum columns can now reference enum types in other
    namespaces. Generated column types include the appropriate namespace
    qualification, while references to the public namespace remain
    unqualified.

  • Cross-namespace enum references are preserved when contracts are
    printed and read again.

  • Bug Fixes

  • Invalid or unresolved enum references now produce more accurate
    diagnostics, including when a reference points to an entity of the wrong
    type.

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon CloudWatch, conditional log routing, chained parsers, log pipelines, event types

Summary: Amazon CloudWatch introduces enhanced features such as conditional log routing and chained parsers through its CloudWatch pipelines service. This fully managed service allows for the ingestion, transformation, and routing of telemetry data to CloudWatch without the need for infrastructure management. Log pipelines can handle a diverse mix of event types, making it essential to route them correctly. With conditional log routing, users can define specific routes that direct events to different CloudWatch log groups based on evaluated conditions such as severity, source, or type, allowing for tailored retention and access controls. Additionally, the use of chained parsers enables the sequential application of multiple parser processors, where later parsers can utilize fields produced by earlier ones. An example usage could include parsing a JSON envelope first and then applying a Grok parser to an extracted field. These combined features empower users to organize varied log formats and ensure they are routed to appropriate log groups within a single pipeline configuration. Both conditional routing and chained parsers are available in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch pipelines are generally available, and they can be configured via the AWS Management Console, CLI, or SDKs.

Amazon CloudWatch now supports conditional log routing and chained parsers via pipelines, giving you more control over how log data is transformed and which CloudWatch log group it's sent to. CloudWatch pipelines is a fully managed service that ingests, transforms, and routes telemetry to CloudWatch without managing infrastructure.

Log pipelines often carry a mix of event types that belong in different places, and individual events can nest one log format inside another. With conditional log routing, you define routes that send each event to a different CloudWatch log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so you can separate events by severity, source, or type and apply the right retention and access controls to each. With chained parsers, you can apply multiple parser processors in sequence, where later parsers consume fields produced by earlier ones. For example, you can parse a JSON envelope first, then apply a Grok parser to a field it extracts. Together, these capabilities let you structure diverse log formats and route them to the right log groups in a single pipeline.

Conditional routing and chained parsers are available in all commercial AWS Regions where CloudWatch pipelines is generally available. You can configure these capabilities using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDKs. To get started, see the Amazon CloudWatch pipelines documentation.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Studio simplifies getting started for new AI/ML builders with social sign-in
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker Studio, social sign-in, simplified sign-up, free credits, GPU access

Summary: Amazon SageMaker Studio now features a streamlined sign-up process for new customers using their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials, eliminating the need for traditional AWS account setup, credit card submission, and complex navigation within the AWS Console. Previously, users had to follow a lengthy account creation process and set up IAM permissions before accessing SageMaker. Recent enhancements have already reduced environment setup time to twenty seconds and introduced direct links from Hugging Face and AWS pages for easier access. The latest update allows new customers to receive free credits under the AWS Free Tier without providing a credit card and enter a pre-configured SageMaker Studio environment for quick fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment of foundation models. Team collaboration is simplified, enabling members to join by email and access shared resources using their social credentials without IAM configurations. For projects exceeding free credits, customers can upgrade to paid plans with spending limits. Verified customers get access to various GPU instances for various tasks without needing to request quota increases. This feature is available across all AWS Commercial Regions supporting SageMaker Studio.

Amazon SageMaker Studio now lets new customers sign up with their Google, GitHub, or Apple credentials and land inside a fully configured Studio environment - no traditional AWS account setup, no credit card, and no console navigation required.

Previously, new customers who discovered a model on Hugging Face or an AWS product page had to complete a multi-step AWS account creation process, provide a credit card, navigate the AWS Console to find SageMaker AI, configure an environment, and set up IAM permissions before they could begin working. With earlier launches, we reduced environment setup to twenty seconds, pre-configured model customization permissions, and introduced deep links from Hugging Face and AWS product pages so customers could land directly inside Studio with a model pre-loaded. Now, with social sign-in, new customers complete a simplified sign-up using an existing identity, receive free credits as part of the AWS Free Tier with no credit card required, and arrive inside a ready-to-use SageMaker Studio environment where they can immediately fine-tune, evaluate, and deploy foundation models. Customers can invite team members by email, and collaborators sign in with their own social credentials to access the shared Studio environment, including shared models, notebooks, and endpoints without configuring IAM users or permissions. When a project grows beyond free credits, customers can upgrade to a paid plan and set a spend limit to stay within budget. Verified customers continue to receive default GPU access to G5, G6, G6e, and G4dn instances across endpoint deployments, training jobs, and notebooks without requesting quota increases.

This feature is available in all AWS Commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is supported. To get started, visit any supported model on Hugging Face and select "Customize and Deploy on SageMaker AI" or "Deploy on SageMaker AI," or click Get Started from the SageMaker Studio page. To learn more, see the AWS sign-up documentation and SageMaker Studio setup guide.

item.title: ARC Region switch adds four new capabilities
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon ARC, Region switch, failover, service quotas, target group health

Summary: Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch enhances multi-Region application failover orchestration to ensure a limited recovery time during regional impairments. The latest features include: 1. **AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block** - This allows users to run commands on managed instances during failover, ensuring that command documents have valid targets and that IAM permissions are correctly set up. 2. **Payloads for custom action Lambda execution block** - Users can now pass payloads to custom Lambda functions, promoting reusability across different recovery plans. 3. **Service quota checks** - To address common failures related to service quotas, Region switch now checks for quota parity between primary and standby regions, automatically submitting requests for quota increases to mitigate risks during recovery. 4. **Wait for target group health** - This feature ensures that Amazon ECS and EC2 Auto Scaling blocks can provision compute capacity that is prepared to handle traffic, thus enhancing overall service reliability. For further information on getting started, please refer to the relevant documentation for these features.

Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch helps you orchestrate the failover of multi-Region applications to achieve a bounded recovery time during a Regional impairment. Today, Region switch adds four new capabilities: AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block, payloads for custom action Lambda execution block, service quota parity checks, and wait for target group health feature for compute scaling actions.

AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block. During failover, you often need to run commands on managed instances and VMs. This execution block lets you invoke Run Command actions on managed instances during failover, with plan evaluation verifying that command documents target valid instances and that IAM permissions are correctly configured.

Payloads for custom action Lambda execution block. ARC Region switch now lets you pass payloads to your custom action Lambda execution block, allowing reusability of your Lambda functions across recovery plans.

Service quota checks. Service quota limits are a common failure mode during recovery. Region switch now verifies quota parity between your primary and standby Region, and automatically submits quota limit increases, reducing the risk of insufficient service quotas during recovery.

Wait for target group health. Amazon ECS service scaling and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution blocks help you provision compute capacity during recovery, but provisioned capacity may not be ready to serve traffic. The optional wait for target group health feature verifies that your provisioned capacity is ready to serve traffic.

To get started, see the documentation for AWS Systems Manager Run Command execution block , custom action Lambda execution block , Service quota checks  and the Wait for target group health for Amazon ECS service scaling execution block  and Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution block .

item.title: AWS License Manager now supports license type conversions for Ubuntu Pro purchased through AWS Marketplace
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: EC2, Ubuntu Pro, in-place upgrades, security patches, AWS Marketplace

Summary: Ubuntu Pro now supports in-place upgrades for EC2 Ubuntu LTS instances available on AWS Marketplace. This enhancement allows customers to improve their security posture and comply with requirements without needing to rebuild their systems or migrate workloads to new instances or AMIs. With an Ubuntu Pro subscription, customers benefit from security patches for up to ten years, extendable to 15 years with the Legacy add-on. This coverage includes not only the base operating system but also thousands of additional packages, such as popular open-source applications like NGINX, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. Additionally, Ubuntu Pro features Kernel Livepatch, which enables critical kernel security fixes to be applied without rebooting the system, minimizing downtime. Customers who already have a Canonical Ubuntu Pro subscription can upgrade directly during the conversion workflow. New customers can subscribe to Canonical Ubuntu Pro through the AWS License Manager console. This new feature is accessible wherever AWS License Manager is available. To begin the process, customers can navigate to the specific sections within the AWS environment.

AWS License Manager  now supports in-place upgrades for EC2 Ubuntu LTS (Long Term Support) instances to Ubuntu Pro available on AWS Marketplace. This allows customers to strengthen their security posture and meet compliance requirements without rebuilding their fleet or migrating workloads to a new instance or AMI. With an Ubuntu Pro subscription, customers receive security patches for up to 10 years — extendable to 15 years with the Legacy add-on. This coverage extends beyond the base OS to thousands of additional packages, including widely used open-source applications such as NGINX, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. Ubuntu Pro also supports Kernel Livepatch, which applies critical kernel security fixes without rebooting to minimize downtime.

With this launch, customers, who have an existing Canonical Ubuntu Pro subscription through AWS Marketplace, can upgrade directly during the conversion workflow. Customers who do not yet have a subscription can subscribe to Canonical Ubuntu Pro from within the AWS License Manager console. The new feature is available in  all commercial regions  where AWS License Manager is available.

To get started, navigate to the  AWS License Manager console  and the  AWS License Manager User Guide .

item.title: AWS HealthOmics introduces resource fallback order for Nextflow workflows
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS HealthOmics, resource fallback, Nextflow workflows, accelerator types, CPU instances

Summary: AWS HealthOmics has introduced a new resource fallback directive for tasks within Nextflow workflows. This feature allows users to specify a prioritized list of preferred accelerator types, with the capability to fallback to CPU instances if necessary. This development aims to ease the workload of researchers and bioinformaticians by minimizing the time spent on diagnosing and resubmitting tasks due to accelerator availability issues, thereby ensuring that production workflows remain efficient. The resource fallback mechanism works by automatically cycling through the specified alternatives when the preferred accelerator is unavailable, without requiring resubmission. Each accelerator profile is equipped with a configurable timeout, allowing users to control the search duration for their preferred option—shorter timeouts result in quicker transitions through the fallback sequence, while longer timeouts increase the chances of securing the preferred accelerator. As a bonus, users can include a CPU profile as an ultimate fallback option. This feature is now available across all AWS HealthOmics Regions, including the US, Europe, Israel, and Asia Pacific. For further information, users are encouraged to consult the official documentation.

Today, AWS HealthOmics introduces the resource fallback directive for tasks in your Nextflow workflows, enabling you to define an ordered list of preferred accelerator types, including an option to fallback to CPU instances. Researchers and bioinformaticians can use this directive to reduce time spent diagnosing and resubmitting runs due to accelerator constraints and keep production workflows running. AWS HealthOmics is a HIPAA-eligible service that helps healthcare and life sciences customers accelerate scientific breakthroughs at scale with fully managed bioinformatics workflows. 

With resource fallback for Nextflow workflows, you can prioritize your preferred accelerator for your task. When your preferred accelerator is unavailable, HealthOmics automatically moves through your specified alternatives in the fallback without resubmission. Each accelerator profile has a configurable timeout, giving you control over how long HealthOmics searches for that accelerator before moving to the next. Shorter timeouts help you move quickly through the fallback order, while longer timeouts increase the probability of reserving your preferred accelerator. You can also include a CPU profile as a final fallback to increase the likelihood of your task reserving an instance. 

You can now use resource fallback for Nextflow workflows in all AWS HealthOmics Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London), Israel (Tel Aviv), and Asia Pacific (Seoul, Singapore, Tokyo). To learn more, visit the advanced resource configuration and Nextflow specifics documentation.

item.title: AWS Backup now supports Amazon FSx file systems in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Backup, Amazon FSx, Asia Pacific, data protection, file systems

Summary: AWS Backup has now expanded its support to include various Amazon FSx services—Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS, and Windows File Server—in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region. This means users can now centrally automate and manage data protection for their FSx file systems along with other supported AWS resources. The service allows for the creation of policy-based backup plans that enable the scheduling of backups and the implementation of retention rules, thus streamlining backup management. Furthermore, AWS Backup stores backups in encrypted vaults to ensure data security. In the event of data loss or a need to restore information, users can easily recover their file systems when necessary. This capability helps organizations achieve business continuity, disaster recovery, and compliance with regulatory requirements through a centralized platform. To begin using this service, users can access the AWS Backup console, utilize the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or leverage the AWS SDKs. For more detailed information on supported regions and features, users can visit the AWS documentation.

AWS Backup now supports Amazon FSx for Lustre, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, and Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region.

With this launch, you can use AWS Backup to centrally automate and manage data protection for your Amazon FSx file systems in the Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Region, alongside your other supported AWS resources. You can create policy-based backup plans to schedule backups and apply retention rules, store backups in encrypted vaults, and restore file systems when needed. This helps you meet business continuity, disaster recovery, and regulatory compliance requirements from a single, centralized service.

To get started, visit the AWS Backup console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), or AWS SDKs. For a complete list of supported Regions and features, visit the AWS Backup documentation. To learn more about AWS Backup, visit the product page and pricing page.

item.title: Announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS for node bootstrapping
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS, Blockchain Snapshots, Ethereum, Solana, Amazon S3

Summary: AWS has launched Blockchain Snapshots, an initiative for blockchain node operators running Ethereum or Solana. This service provides pre-synced public blockchain node chain data, allowing users to bootstrap their nodes from a snapshot rather than syncing via peer-to-peer methods. The snapshots are hosted on Amazon S3, ensuring reduced latency and optimized data transfers for customers operating nodes on AWS. Each network's authoritative snapshot is repackaged in a format designed for parallel extraction across multiple cores, significantly decreasing setup time for instances. The snapshots support both Ethereum and Solana and are available free of charge, refreshing in alignment with the upstream provider's schedule. This service is particularly useful for scaling a remote procedure call (RPC) fleet, recovering failed nodes, or re-syncing corrupted databases. AWS Blockchain Snapshots are accessible in specific regions, including US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Ireland), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To access these snapshots, users need an Amazon EC2 instance located in the same region and an Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint. For setup instructions and the latest snapshot downloads, users are encouraged to visit the provided link.

For blockchain node operators running Ethereum or Solana, AWS is announcing Blockchain Snapshots on AWS, an initiative that publishes pre-synced public blockchain node chain data in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) so you can bootstrap a node from a snapshot instead of peer-to-peer syncing from the network. These snapshots are hosted on Amazon S3 within AWS infrastructure, enabling customers running nodes on AWS benefit from reduced latency and optimized data transfer. Blockchain Snapshots on AWS republishes each network's authoritative snapshot in a format optimized for parallel extraction across multiple cores, reducing setup time, that an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance can use.

Snapshots cover Ethereum and Solana, are available at no charge, and refresh on the same cadence as the upstream provider. Use them to add capacity to a remote procedure call (RPC) fleet, recover a failed node, or re-sync a corrupted database.

You can use Blockchain Snapshots on AWS in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Europe (Ireland), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). Access requires an Amazon EC2 instance in the same Region with an Amazon S3 gateway VPC endpoint.

To get started, visit the Blockchain Snapshots on AWS documentation to access setup instructions and download the latest snapshots.

item.title: AWS Transfer Family console supports SVG logos and ICO favicons for web apps
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transfer Family, SVG files, ICO files, logo uploads, favicon uploads

Summary: The AWS Transfer Family console has introduced support for SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web applications, significantly enhancing branding flexibility. The upload limits for these files have been increased to 2 MB, allowing users to utilize larger and more complex graphics. Previously, the console only allowed JPG and PNG formats, with much stricter size limits—50 KB for logos and 20 KB for favicons. Additionally, the console automatically resized images and converted them to JPG or PNG formats upon saving, which has simplified the upload process for users. However, it's important to note that existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged. These enhancements are now available across all AWS Regions where Transfer Family web apps are offered, making it easier for organizations to customize their online presence without compromising on quality. This update represents a significant improvement over the previous limitations, providing users with more options for leveraging their existing branding assets effectively. For more detailed information, users are encouraged to consult the AWS documentation.

The AWS Transfer Family console now supports SVG files for logos and ICO files for favicons in web apps, with upload limits increased to 2 MB. This gives you more flexibility to use existing branding assets when customizing your web app.

Previously, the console accepted only JPG and PNG files and limited logo uploads to 50 KB and favicon uploads to 20 KB. The console automatically resizes images and converts them to JPG or PNG before saving them. Existing API upload limits and format requirements remain unchanged.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family web apps are offered. To learn more, see the Transfer Family web apps tutorial.

item.title: AWS Transfer Family now supports AWS Secrets Manager storage for SFTP server host keys
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transfer Family, SFTP, Secrets Manager, host keys, IAM policies

Summary: AWS Transfer Family now allows you to store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager within your account. This improves control over server identity and simplifies migrations and failover processes. Previously, host keys were stored within the service, making it impossible to retrieve the private key material. With this update, you can select Secrets Manager as the storage option when creating a server or importing a host key. You can access the private key material to reuse the same host key across different servers and AWS Regions. This is particularly beneficial for standby servers during failover or replacement servers during migrations, as it eliminates the need for clients to accept a new host key. Using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, you can manage permissions for retrieving stored keys. Additionally, there is an option to migrate existing host keys to Secrets Manager, which may involve extra steps as outlined in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where the Transfer Family is accessible. For more information, refer to the user guide and get started by visiting the specified AWS resource.

AWS Transfer Family now lets you store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in your own AWS account. This gives you greater control over your server identity and helps simplify server migrations and failover.

Previously, Transfer Family stored host keys within the service, so you could not retrieve the associated private key material. With this launch, you can choose Secrets Manager as the storage type when creating a server or importing a host key. You can then retrieve the private key material and reuse the same host key across servers and AWS Regions. For example, you can use it on a standby server for failover or on a replacement server during migration, without requiring clients to trust a new host key. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies let you control who can retrieve the stored keys. You can also migrate existing host keys to Secrets Manager, which may require additional steps; see the AWS Transfer Family User Guide for details.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transfer Family is available. To learn more, see Store SFTP server host keys in AWS Secrets Manager in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide. To get started, go to the AWS Transfer Family console.

item.title: Amazon RDS Proxy now supports SQL Server 2022
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon RDS Proxy, SQL Server 2022, Multi-AZ, IAM authentication, AWS Secrets Manager

Summary: Amazon RDS Proxy is a fully managed and highly available database proxy that now supports instances running SQL Server major version 2022. It acts as an intermediary between applications and databases, pooling and sharing established database connections to enhance database efficiency and application scalability. For Multi-AZ deployments of Amazon RDS for SQL Server, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserving application connections and significantly reducing failover times by up to 83%. Additionally, RDS Proxy facilitates standard IAM authentication, allowing applications to authenticate through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), while managing database connections using credentials securely stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Enabling Amazon RDS Proxy for SQL Server 2022 is a straightforward process via the Amazon RDS console, and applications can easily connect by pointing to the RDS Proxy endpoint. This functionality greatly simplifies the management of database connections and enhances application resilience during database instances failures. For further details on getting started, users are advised to check the related documentation on the Amazon RDS console.

Amazon RDS Proxy, a fully managed, highly available database proxy for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), now supports Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances running major version 2022.

Amazon RDS Proxy sits between your application and the database to pool and share established database connections, improving database efficiency and application scalability. For Amazon RDS for SQL Server Multi-AZ databases, RDS Proxy automatically connects to the standby database instance during a failure, preserves application connections, and helps reduce failover times by up to 83%. RDS Proxy supports standard IAM authentication for SQL Server, where your applications authenticate to the proxy using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and RDS Proxy manages database connections using credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

You can enable Amazon RDS Proxy for your SQL Server 2022 database in a few steps on the Amazon RDS console, then connect by pointing your application to the RDS Proxy endpoint. To get started, see our documentation.

item.title: Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel
item.content:encoded:
Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel. Developers can create and connect S3 resources in seconds without leaving their development environment, getting the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 through Vercel's streamlined provisioning workflow.

Millions of customers rely on S3 for low-cost, high-performance storage to power web and AI applications, but until now provisioning it from Vercel required navigating to the AWS Management Console. Now, S3 integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, automatically handling resource provisioning and connection configuration. You can choose from S3 general purpose buckets for virtually any use case, S3 Tables for fully managed Apache Iceberg tables optimized for analytics workloads, or S3 Vectors to natively store and query vectors at scale.

New AWS accounts created through Vercel include $100 in credits valid for up to six months, usable across Amazon S3, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, and AWS Database services. Existing AWS customers can link their account to use S3 with their Vercel projects.

Amazon S3 on Vercel is now available in all AWS Regions where Vercel is available. To get started, read the AWS News Blog, visit AWS on Vercel Marketplace, or launch v0 by Vercel.

item.title: AWS Lambda durable functions increases durable operation and checkpoint payload limits
item.content:encoded:
Starting today, AWS Lambda durable functions increases the maximum number of durable operations per execution from 3,000 to 30,000, and the maximum checkpoint payload size from 256 KB to 1 MB. Higher operation limits let you safely do more work in a single execution including expanding iterative loops, polling for longer time periods, and building more complex rollback paths that run when a step fails. At 1 MB, checkpoint payloads match the maximum payload size of asynchronous Lambda invocations, and integration services such as Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge, so a workflow can persist a full event from any of these sources in a single operation.

AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. Every durable operation counts toward the per-execution limit, including each step attempt, each poll of a wait-for-condition, and each branch of a parallel or map operation. With 30,000 operations, a single execution has more room to coordinate complex, multi-step workflows, iterate across thousands of items, or poll an external system for weeks, without exceeding checkpoint limits.

An agentic application can reason over thousands of model and tool calls, and with 1 MB checkpoints it persists larger conversation histories, model responses, and outputs from tools directly in the checkpoint instead of writing to external storage. For state larger than 1 MB, the JavaScript and Python SDKs include a FileSystem serializer that writes the payload to an Amazon EFS or Amazon S3 Files mount and checkpoints a pointer instead.

 The new limits apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more about these service limits, see the AWS Lambda developer guide.

item.title: Amazon EC2 M8id instances now available in Asia Pacific (Malaysia) and Asia Pacific (Sydney)
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) M8id instances with up to 22.8 TB of local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage are now available in Asia Pacific (Malaysia) and Asia Pacific (Sydney). M8id instances are designed for workloads that require a balance of compute and memory resources along with high-speed, low-latency local block storage, including data logging, media processing, and medium-sized data stores.

Amazon EC2 M8id instances offer 3 times more vCPUs, memory and local storage compared to previous sixth-generation instances. These instances deliver up to 43% higher compute performance and 3.3 times more memory bandwidth compared to previous sixth-generation M6id instances. They also deliver up to 46% higher performance for I/O intensive database workloads, and up to 30% faster query results for I/O intensive real-time data analytics compared to previous sixth generation instances.

Additionally, customers can now adjust the network and Amazon EBS bandwidth on these instances by 25% using EC2 instance bandwidth weighting configuration, providing greater flexibility with the allocation of bandwidth resources to better optimize workloads. These instances offer Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes.

Customers can purchase these instances via Savings Plans, On-Demand instances, and Spot instances. For more information visit the Amazon EC2 M8id page.

item.title: Amazon EC2 C9g, C9gd, M9g, and M9gd instances are now available in additional regions
item.content:encoded:
Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C9g and C9gd instances are available in the Asia Pacific (Malaysia, Seoul, Singapore) regions. Amazon EC2 M9g and M9gd instances are available in the Asia Pacific (Malaysia) and Europe (Spain) regions. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton5 processors, the fifth generation of custom-designed CPUs, which deliver the best price performance for a broad range of workloads running on Amazon EC2.

C9g and C9gd instances and M9g and M9gd instances deliver up to 25% better compute performance than AWS Graviton4-based C8g, C8gd, M8g, and M8gd instances. They are up to 30% faster for databases, up to 35% faster for web applications, and up to 35% faster for machine learning. These instances are built on the sixth-generation AWS Nitro System and are the first to feature the Nitro Isolation Engine. The Isolation Engine uses formal verification to provide mathematical assurance that customer workloads are isolated from each other and from AWS operators, pioneering a new standard for mathematically proven cloud security.

C9g instances are ideal for compute-intensive workloads such as high-performance computing (HPC), batch processing, gaming, video encoding, scientific modeling, distributed analytics, CPU-based machine learning (ML) inference, real-time analytics, and ad serving. M9g instances serve a broad range of general-purpose workloads, including application servers, microservices, gaming, caching, and containers. They also deliver the performance needed for agentic AI use cases like real-time reasoning, code generation, and multi-step orchestration. C9gd and M9gd instances add local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage for workloads that need high-speed, low-latency local storage for scratch space, temporary files, and caches.

C9g, C9gd, M9g, and M9gd instances are available for purchase in these regions via Savings Plans, On-Demand, Spot Instances, Dedicated Instances, or Dedicated Hosts. Level up your compute with AWS Graviton and get started today with C9g and M9g.

item.title: Amazon EC2 C8gd and M8gd instances are now available in additional regions
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) C8gd and M8gd instances with up to 11.4 TB of local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage are now available in additional regions. C8gd instances are now available in Europe (Stockholm), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), and Asia Pacific (Seoul). M8gd instances are now available in Europe (Stockholm), US West (N. California), and Asia Pacific (Singapore). These instances are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors, delivering up to 30% better performance over Graviton3-based instances. They have up to 40% higher performance for I/O intensive database workloads, and up to 20% faster query results for I/O intensive real-time data analytics than comparable AWS Graviton3-based instances. These instances are built on the AWS Nitro System and are a great fit for applications that need access to high-speed, low latency local storage.

Each instance is available in 12 different sizes. They provide up to 50 Gbps of network bandwidth and up to 40 Gbps of bandwidth to the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). Additionally, customers can now adjust the network and Amazon EBS bandwidth on these instances by 25% using EC2 instance bandwidth weighting configuration, providing greater flexibility with the allocation of bandwidth resources to better optimize workloads. These instances offer Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes.

C8gd instances are ideal for compute-intensive workloads such as high-performance web servers, batch processing, distributed analytics, ad serving, video encoding, and gaming servers. M8gd instances are well-suited for balanced workloads including application servers, microservices, enterprise applications, and small to medium databases.

To learn more, see Amazon C8gd Instances and Amazon M8gd Instances. To explore how to migrate your workloads to Graviton-based instances, see AWS Graviton Fast Start program and Porting Advisor for Graviton. To get started, see the AWS Management Console.
