item.title: v8.0.0-rc.18
item.content:encoded:
v8.0.0-rc.18

Raw SQL in a contract is now always a sql literal or value, a full-text index can span several weighted fields and is searched from the ORM by naming it, and middleware observes each statement and transaction as an activity. PSL gains mixins, the SQL ORM gains whereUnique and firstOrThrow, and MongoDB migrations carry out --rename.

The upgrade recipes for this hop: the app recipe and the extension recipe. Each breaking change below names the change ids to look for in them.

Breaking changes

  • Raw SQL in a contract is a sql literal. In PSL, @@index(where:), @@index(expression:), @@fullTextIndex(where:), @@check(expression:) and a policy's using and withCheck take a sql literal, and a quoted string is refused with PSL_VALUE_TYPE_INCOMPATIBLE. The app recipe ships a script that rewrites every .prisma file. In a TypeScript contract the same fields take a sql value, and a string does not compile; migration files keep strings. A text with shared indentation, blank lines at its ends or CRLF line breaks is stored as its canonical text, which changes the storage hash once. See raw-sql-is-a-sql-literal, builder-raw-sql-is-a-sql-value, psl-storage-hash-may-change-once and ts-storage-hash-may-change-once in the app recipe. (#30550, #30558)

    Before:

    @@index([email], where: "(archived_at IS NULL)", name: "users_email_active")

    After:

    @@index([email], where: sql`(archived_at IS NULL)`, name: "users_email_active")

  • Middleware hooks are activity hooks. The runtime runs every statement and transaction as an activity. beforeQuery and beforeExecute become beforeEncode; interceptQuery and interceptExecute become intercept.onQuery and intercept.onExecute; afterQuery and afterExecute become activityEnded; afterTransaction becomes activityFinalized. RuntimeMiddlewareContext is now ActivityContext, and ctx.planExecutionId is replaced by activity.id. activityEnded also fires for a statement the caller stopped reading and for one that failed before it ran, so a metrics middleware checks result.outcome. See middleware-hooks-are-activity-hooks and every-started-statement-is-ended-and-finalized in the app recipe, and statement-runners-replace-middleware-runners in the extension recipe. (#30703)

    Before:

    async afterQuery(plan, result, ctx) {
  if (result.latencyMs > 250) ctx.log.warn({ sql: plan.sql, rowCount: result.rowCount });
},

    After:

    async beforeEncode(plan, ctx) {
  ctx.state(statementSql)['sql'] = plan.sql;
},
async activityEnded(activity, result, ctx) {
  if (result.kind !== 'statement' || result.latencyMs <= 250) return;
  ctx.log.warn({
    sql: ctx.state(statementSql)['sql'],
    ...(result.returns === 'rows' ? { rowCount: result.rowCount } : {}),
  });
},

  • A full-text index is stored as data. @@fullTextIndex and fullTextIndex store an index of type fullText with its columns, weight groups and language, not a SQL expression. The schema source does not change, but the index's generated name and the storage hash do: re-emit the contract and run prisma migration plan, which renames the index in place. Avoid db update for a large index, because it drops and rebuilds it. See re-emit-contracts-with-a-full-text-index in the app recipe and render-full-text-index-document-takes-a-definition in the extension recipe. (#30562)

    Before:

    { "expression": "to_tsvector('english', \"title\")", "name": "post_title_search_724b05e5", "type": "gin" }

    After:

    { "columns": ["title"], "name": "post_title_search_e0dd1131", "options": { "language": "english", "weightGroups": [["title"]] }, "type": "fullText" }

  • A base model lists its variants by discriminator value. In contract.json and contract.d.ts, a polymorphic base's variants is keyed by discriminator value, and each entry names the variant model and its namespace. A contract in the previous form is refused with CONTRACT.VALIDATION_FAILED. Re-emit the contract and rewrite variants in the snapshots under migrations/snapshots/; the storage hash does not change. See re-emit-contracts-with-polymorphic-models and read-variants-by-discriminator-value in the app recipe. (#30696)

    Before:

    "variants": { "Bug": { "value": "bug" }, "Feature": { "value": "feature" } }

    After:

    "variants": { "bug": { "model": "Bug", "namespace": "public" }, "feature": { "model": "Feature", "namespace": "public" } }

  • The SQL ORM client accepts only field names. Every name passed to the SQL ORM client must be a field of the model, or of the variant the collection is narrowed to; any other name, including a column name that differs from its field name, throws ORM.FIELD_UNKNOWN. Rows no longer carry a column no field maps. See orm-refuses-names-that-are-not-fields in the app recipe. (#30667)

    Before:

    await db.orm.Post.where({ user_id: 1 }).all();

    After:

    await db.orm.Post.where({ userId: 1 }).all();

  • The query fragment types are renamed, and a fragment is made from the model's root collection. Fragment is now QueryFragment and FieldFragment is now DeclaredFieldsFragment. collection.fragment(body) throws ORM.ARGUMENT_INVALID on a collection with chained calls, which it used to ignore; chain on the collection directly, or move the calls into the fragment's body. See fragment-types-are-renamed and fragment-is-made-from-the-root-collection in the app recipe. (#30652, #30673)

    Before:

    const recentSummary = db.orm.public.Post.orderBy((p) => p.id.desc()).fragment((posts) =>
  posts.select('id', 'title'),
);

    After:

    const recentSummary = db.orm.public.Post.fragment((posts) =>
  posts.orderBy((p) => p.id.desc()).select('id', 'title'),
);

  • migration plan asks before a lossy type change, and writes placeholders only when asked. On Postgres and SQLite, a type change that can lose values fails with CLI.CONSENT_REQUIRED where nobody can answer, until --convert <Model.field> (write the conversion yourself) or --delete <Model.field> (accept the database's cast) answers it. A new required field gets a temporary value in existing rows; pass --backfill <Model.field> to fill them yourself. In a hand-written Postgres migration.ts, alterColumnType takes type and using directly instead of an options object. See lossy-type-changes-ask, placeholders-only-when-asked and postgres-alter-column-type-plain-options in the app recipe. (#30695)

  • Removing a field from a MongoDB model asks first. The plan now removes the field from every document that holds it, and migration plan and db update ask about it; add --delete <Model>.<field>, or --rename if the field was renamed, to scripts and CI. A MongoDB plan's preview writes db.getCollection("users") where it wrote db.users, and node migration.ts uses the config that owns the migration. See mongo-removed-field-asks, mongo-preview-get-collection and migration-ts-finds-its-config in the app recipe. (#30691)

  • A Prisma 7 schema's @ignore and @@ignore objects stay in the contract. prisma7Schema() keeps their columns, tables, keys and indexes in storage, so a schema that uses them gets a new storage hash, and a schema that loaded only because they were dropped can be refused. Emit the contract, then sign each database, or plan a migration first if Prisma 8 already manages your migrations. See prisma7-ignore-keeps-storage in the app recipe. (#30672)

  • Top-level PSL declarations belong to the default namespace. A top-level declaration and one inside namespace public { … } on Postgres share one set of names, so the same name declared both ways is PSL_DUPLICATE_DECLARATION, and a top-level declaration cannot be named like the default namespace (public, or unbound on SQLite and MongoDB). See psl-default-namespace-duplicate-declaration and psl-default-namespace-name-is-reserved in the app recipe. (#30700)

  • Stricter types for TypeScript contracts and the SQL ORM. A contract built with defineContract types its namespaces with exactly the keys it has at runtime, and its ORM rows with each field's codec type instead of unknown. A model with no fields has no keys, so reading or writing one fails to compile; generic update code types its data as ScalarUpdateInput. conflictOn, connect and disconnect no longer accept null for a nullable unique column, and prepared.all and prepared.aggregate must be called on the prepared object. See typescript-contract-namespace-keys, model-with-no-fields-has-no-keys, generic-update-data-uses-update-input-type, unique-criterion-rejects-null and prepared-all-and-aggregate-need-their-receiver in the app recipe. (#30663, #30705, #30670)

  • db.nativeEnums lists native enum types only. A domain enum (enum block or enumType()) is no longer listed there; read it through db.enums, which holds its values as a query returns them. See native-enums-leave-out-domain-enums in the app recipe. (#30661)

  • A MongoDB enum member must be written as its codec stores it. A member that your own codec stores as a value it reads back differently is refused, with a message that says what to write. The built-in MongoDB codecs are not affected. See mongo-enum-member-written-as-stored in the app recipe. (#30711)

  • Extension authors: SQL ORM collection state, MongoDB migration operations and the PSL symbol table changed. CollectionState requires tables, built with createCollectionTables, and names a variant by its discriminator value. The MongoDB DDL alphabet gains RenameCollectionCommand, and MongoDataTransformOperation is now MongoDmlOperation. buildSymbolTable requires defaultNamespaceId, and the symbol table places top-level declarations in its default namespace. See collection-state-carries-tables, sql-orm-state-names-a-variant-by-value, mongo-ddl-rename-collection, mongo-dml-operations and symbol-table-has-no-top-level in the extension recipe. (#30646, #30696, #30691, #30700)

Features

  • PSL mixins: declare shared fields, attributes or enum members once with model mixin, enum mixin or the mixin form of another block, and include them with +Name. The language server completes, navigates to, hovers, renames and colours them. (#30675, #30694, #30679, #30681)
  • A Postgres full-text index can cover several fields in weight groups, strongest first: @@fullTextIndex([[title, subtitle], body], name: "post_search"). (#30562)
  • ORM where and orderBy callbacks receive { fns, indexes } as a second argument, so a query can search a weighted full-text index by naming it: fns.fullTextMatches(indexes.post_search, q) and fns.fullTextRank(indexes.post_search, q). (#30676)
  • whereUnique on SQL ORM collections addresses at most one record by a unique key; a many-record call after it, such as all() or limit(), is a compile error. (#30670)
  • firstOrThrow() on SQL and MongoDB ORM collections and on the SQL prepared view reads one row with LIMIT 1 and rejects with RUNTIME.NO_ROWS when nothing matches. (#30644)
  • On MongoDB, migration plan and db update carry out --rename: a model rename renames its collection and keeps its documents, indexes and validator, and a field rename renames the field in every document. (#30691)
  • postgres(), postgresServerless(), sqlite() and supabase() take a log option, so lint warnings, contract-marker warnings and errors swallowed from middleware hooks reach your logger. (#30707)
  • A polymorphic base can have variants in other namespaces: @@base(a.Task, "chore"). (#30696)
  • The sql tag interpolates other sql values, so predicates compose as sql`${owner} AND deleted_at IS NULL` instead of joined strings. (#30558)
  • prisma migration plan writes a contract's raw SQL into migration.ts as sql values, as a TypeScript contract writes it. (#30677)
  • The PSL language server renames symbols, and go-to-definition, hover, find references and rename work on the entity name inside a type-constructor argument, such as OrderStatus in pg.enum(OrderStatus). (#30633, #30659)

Fixes

  • prisma db verify --strict passes on a database Prisma 7 built, and prisma contract infer no longer prints a model for Prisma 7's _prisma_migrations table. (#30671)
  • A repeated db update on a MongoDB database with a time-series collection no longer fails with "Cannot change immutable collection option 'timeseries'". (#30691)
  • The budgets() middleware enforces maxRows on the rows a query returns; the check never ran before, so a read over the limit now fails with BUDGET.ROWS_EXCEEDED. (#30703)
  • update({}) resolves the first matching row and updateAll({}) yields the matching rows, where they returned null and no rows. (#30680)
  • Two enum members are refused as duplicates only when their stored values are equal, so dates a millisecond apart and distinct object members are accepted. (#30661)
  • A migration that makes a field required while rows have no value for it fails with a summary that counts those rows and names the fix. (#30695)

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.18-dev.1: chore(release): bump to 8.0.0-rc.18 (#30720)
item.content:encoded:
8.0.0-rc.17 → 8.0.0-rc.18

Version policy:
docs/oss/versioning.md.

Review surface:
docs/releases/v8.0.0-rc.18.md
holds the user-facing notes, mirrored at the top of CHANGELOG.md. It
becomes the GitHub Release body verbatim.

Merging this PR ships the release. The push to main carries the
bumped root version; the Publish to npm workflow detects the change,
publishes 8.0.0-rc.18 under dist-tag latest, and creates a matching
GitHub Release marked pre-release.

Docs site: prisma/web#8498 updates the Prisma ORM 8 pages for this
release. Merge it only after this release is published.

What the diff contains

  • Version bump: every workspace package.json, the workspace:
    specifiers in pnpm-lock.yaml, the library_version stamp in
    skills/prisma-8/SKILL.md, and the Supabase extension's version stamp
    in its tracked contract.json / contract.d.ts artefacts.
  • Upgrade guides: the 25 pending fragments are synthesized into
    skills/prisma-8/upgrading/app/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.17-to-8.0.0-rc.18/ (41
    changes) and .../extension/upgrades/8.0.0-rc.17-to-8.0.0-rc.18/ (46
    changes), with the rewrite-sql-strings.mjs script copied under each
    guide's scripts/sql-expression-literals-psl/. The originals, including
    10 no-op declarations, moved unchanged to
    upgrade-instructions/releases/8.0.0-rc.17-to-8.0.0-rc.18/sources/. The
    app guide adds the usual contract-artifacts-restamp entry for the
    extension version stamp.
  • Release notes: docs/releases/v8.0.0-rc.18.md and the
    CHANGELOG.md entry.

Synthesis decisions to check

  • Both SQL expression literal fragments declared a change with the id
    storage-hash-may-change-once. In the guides they are
    psl-storage-hash-may-change-once and
    ts-storage-hash-may-change-once, and the TypeScript entry's pointer to
    "the PSL instructions in this release" now names the PSL id in the same
    guide.
  • The extension fragment for variants keyed by discriminator value said
    IncludeExpr.localVariantName became localVariantValue.
    localVariantName never shipped: in 8.0.0-rc.17 the field was
    localTableName, which the collection-state fragment already covers
    (include-expr-junction-table). The guide's entry now points there, and
    the localVariantName example lines and detection pattern are removed.
  • pnpm check:upgrade-coverage --mode publish --prev v8.0.0-rc.17 --head HEAD and pnpm check:release-notes --mode pr pass.

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • New Features
  • Added PSL mixins, weighted multi-field full-text search,
    cross-namespace polymorphic variants, and composable SQL values.
  • Added SQL ORM whereUnique and firstOrThrow, MongoDB field renames,
    configurable client logging, and PSL language-server symbol navigation.
  • Bug Fixes
  • Improved Prisma 7 verification and inference, MongoDB time-series
    updates, row-budget enforcement, empty updates, enum validation, and
    required-field migration errors.
  • Breaking Changes
  • Updated SQL, ORM, middleware, migration, MongoDB, enum, TypeScript
    contract, and extension-author requirements. See the upgrade guide for
    required changes.

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.43: sql-orm-client: run update and delete through a mutation graph (#30680)
item.content:encoded:
First slice of a restructuring of how the SQL ORM client executes
writes. Every write method is to build a mutation graph
(database-level nodes joined by edges) and hand it to one runner,
replacing the per-method statement code and, later, the nested-write
executor. This PR adds the graph and moves the six update and delete
methods onto it.

Changes

All under packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/mutation-graph/
unless noted.

  • Nodes (node.ts, find.ts, update.ts, delete.ts): a frozen
    class per statement kind. A node holds its statement as SQL AST
    (SelectAst, UpdateAst, DeleteAst) and has execute(inputs, run),
    which applies its inputs to the AST and runs it. A statement that
    returns columns runs as a row stream, one that returns nothing as an
    affected-row count.
  • Edges (edge.ts, filter-data.ts, after.ts): FilterData has
    output(sourceRow), which turns one row of its source into a condition
    on its target. After is order only.
  • Graph (graph.ts): a bidirectional adjacency list with stable
    positions. add(node, inputs) is typed by the node's input slots and
    returns a branded NodeId; adding a data edge makes its source return
    the columns the edge reads; after(from, to) adds an order edge.
  • Runner (run-graph.ts): a loop over the nodes in position order:
    resolve each input edge per source row, call execute, keep the result.
    It puts the caller's annotations on every statement, opens a transaction
    when the graph has more than one node, and shapes the result node's rows
    for the caller with the existing mapping, include-loading and
    read-consumer code.
  • Collection methods (collection.ts, 3,385 → 3,120 lines):
    update (without relation callbacks), updateAll, updateAndCount,
    delete, deleteAll, deleteAndCount build a graph
    (collection-graphs.ts) and call the runner. update() with relation
    callbacks, the create methods, upsert and mutation-executor.ts are
    unchanged.
  • Shared with existing code: the AST-building parts of the update,
    delete and select compile functions and the row mapping of
    dispatchMutationRows are extracted so the graph and the remaining
    callers use one implementation.

Graphs are asserted in tests as text, through a printer that lives in
the test directory:

n1 Find users where name = 'Ada' order by id asc limit 1
n2 Update users set email = 'ada@example.com' <- FilterData n1 (id->id)
result: n2 first row

Behaviour changes

  • update({}) resolves the first matching row and updateAll({})
    yields the matching rows.     On main they resolve null and no rows. A
    write with nothing to set is a Find on the same rows, so a call
    returns what it matches whether or not it sets anything.
    updateAndCount({}) still resolves 0. Two integration tests asserted
    the old results and were changed; the port of Prisma 7's
    extended-where › "update with where 1 unique (PK)" now passes and left
    the failing ledger.
  • The matching read of update() / delete(), the read of
    deleteAll() / delete() with includes, and the reload read of a write
    with includes carry the caller's annotations.
  • delete() with includes issues two statements (main: three).
  • update() maps fields and applies update defaults before the matching
    read, so a default generator runs even when no row matches.
  • update() / delete() after limit(0) open no transaction.

Why

The nested-write executor issues statements while it walks the input,
once per relation layout, and the plain and nested paths of create()
and update() differ in annotations, variant handling and returned
selection. A graph between the input and the statements can be tested
and reordered by its edges alone, and a new kind of node or edge is a
class, not a change to the runner. The design, the reason for each
decision and the rejected alternatives are in
projects/nested-mutations/mutation-graph.md; this slice's contract is
projects/nested-mutations/slices/graph-core/spec.md.

Verification

  • Package tests: 1,546 pass; typecheck, lint, lint:deps,
    check:upgrade-coverage pass.
  • Integration, run locally for the directories that reach the ORM's
    write methods (test/sql-orm-client, test/ports,
    test/temporal-defaults, test/value-objects, test/cross-package,
    the namespaced-accessors test): 453 files, 2,524 passed, 86 expected
    failures, none failed. The whole integration suite was not run locally.

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.40: Close out the PSL mixins project (#30718)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a. Close-out of the PSL mixins project.

At a glance

projects/psl-mixins/                    deleted (28 files)

Summary

The PSL mixins project has delivered: <keyword> mixin <Name> { … }
declares a set of members for one block kind, +<Name> includes it, and
the emitted contract is the same as for the members written inline. This
PR removes the project's working folder. The decisions are recorded in

item.title: v1.17.0-rc2
item.content:encoded:
1.17.0-rc2 (October 14, 2026)

NEW FEATURES:

  • Terraform now supports variables and locals in provider requirements (#39153)

  • A new -minimal-refresh planning option has been added, which will only refresh resources that have proposed changes. (#35290)

  • policy: Terraform Policy is now generally available. The -policies flag for plan, apply, and query no longer requires an experimental build or the -allow-experimental-features flag. Query policies evaluate resources discovered by list blocks and report human-readable or JSON results. See https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/policy for more information. (#38970)

ENHANCEMENTS:

  • command/init: Enrich log messages with provider versions (#38918)

  • test: Add mock_provider support for ephemeral resources (#38928)

  • command/login: display warning after successful login if user is subject to an organization's TTL policy

BUG FIXES:

  • funcs: pow and log no longer panic when result is not a number (#38912)

  • ephemeral: Terraform will now use and display diagnostics raised when renewing an ephemeral resource. This may cause warnings to appear that previously were lost. We expect that any error diagnostics that were previously lost would have caused confusing downstream errors, so we do not anticipate this change to be breaking. (#38989)

  • test: Deterministic dependency ordering in cleanup graph (#38247)

  • query: report Unknown and N/A results for policy evaluations of discovered resources (#39058)

  • query: terraform query -policies now rejects a path that is not a directory, instead of passing it on to the policy engine (#39238)

  • funcs: The log and pow functions now raise errors when they return +/- Infinity, as this result is not usable in downstream code. (#39304)

  • show: Read variable values from the plan file when showing a local plan (#39362)

NOTES:

  • version: JSON output now includes a new format_version field, which will enable safer future changes of the command's JSON output format. It is assumed existing tooling ignores unknown fields and therefore this change should not be breaking in itself but we advice consumers to pay attention to format_version in future releases and/or use latest version of hashicorp/terraform-json & hashicorp/terraform-exec which does. (#38930)

The DelightQL Query Language
item.content:encoded:
Hey all, I would like to present a programming language I have been developing for many years called delightql.

This is an alpha release so there will be rough edges, but I have used it at home and work and have liked it enough to now throw it out into the world and see if it sticks. It's always a good thing if you like the language you've developed.

Delightql transpiles to SQL and looks something like a cross between Prolog, Elixir and cough Perl.

I will try now to enumerate some features:

  • reusable functions, reusable higher-order predicates, reusable row-predicates
  • 99% of all SQL (this is a vibe estimation and not a guarantee)
  • some stuff you never knew you wanted (union corresponding, anonymous tables, tree-groups, the occassional prolog-like join)
  • ETL directives and a module system

Coding in delightql will feel like a concatenative language insofar as the meaning of the query is explicitly read from left to right.

The language is implemented in Rust and is Apache licensed. I used LLMs over the past year and a half to help me with the implementation. The design (syntax, semantics, and features) is all my own work.

To that last point, I note that out of pure happenstance my mode of working was exactly suited to this new world of LLMs. Back in 2020 I decided to stop implementing and just write. By 2025, I had finished writing the book about the language I wanted.

I'd love to hear what makes sense, what doesn't, and/or kudos/criticisms.

AWS Security Hub now supports resource criticality for prioritization
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Security Hub, resource criticality, exposure prioritization, automation rule, Security Hub Essentials

Summary: AWS Security Hub has introduced resource criticality to improve exposure prioritization, enabling central security teams to focus on threats to their most business-critical assets. Users can establish criticality levels through automation rules, such as designating all compute resources in a certain account as Very High. This rule is effective for both existing resources and newly discovered ones by Security Hub. Additionally, Security Hub can infer criticality based on resource tags and names without requiring user configuration, and it tracks the source of these criticality values. The criticality information is visible as a column on the Resources page, facilitating sorting, filtering, and grouping, and it is also accessible on the Impact assessment tab of exposure findings. Notably, resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no extra cost, and is automatically enabled for all customers, meaning there’s no new enablement needed. For more information on these features, customers are encouraged to explore the relevant AWS documentation and check the list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available.

Today, AWS Security Hub adds resource criticality to exposure prioritization, helping central security teams focus on the exposures that threaten their most business-critical resources.

You can set criticality with an automation rule, for example marking every compute resource in a specific account as Very High. The rule applies to resources already in your inventory and to new resources as Security Hub discovers them. Security Hub also infers criticality from resource tags and resource names, with no configuration required, and records which source determined the value. Criticality appears as a column on the Resources page for sorting, filtering, and grouping, and on the Impact assessment tab of an exposure finding. Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and is always on for all customers.

Resource criticality is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost and requires no new enablement. To learn more, see  AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page. For a list of AWS Regions where Security Hub is available, see the AWS Region table.

item.title: Amazon ECS adds LiveTaskCount and removes the charge for RunningTaskCount metric
item.content:encoded:
LiveTaskCount, Amazon ECS, CloudWatch Container Insights, RunningTaskCount, autoscaling

Summary: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) has launched a new service metric called LiveTaskCount, which reports the number of actively running tasks in a service. This metric is available to all customers at no extra charge. LiveTaskCount captures tasks in all desired states—ACTIVATING, RUNNING, and DEACTIVATING—making it ideal for autoscaling policies and capacity planning. It includes tasks that are still running even while transitioning to a stopped state, such as those involved in connection draining during a scale-in event. Additionally, the existing RunningTaskCount metric in Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights will no longer incur any charges, effective from October 1, 2026, for all users. This metric still serves as a health and stability indicator, tracking tasks where both the current and desired states are RUNNING. These updates are applicable across all AWS Regions where Amazon ECS operates and require no action from users. LiveTaskCount is part of ECS service utilization metrics and does not require opting in to CloudWatch Container Insights, enhancing the overall monitoring capabilities for users of Amazon ECS.

Today, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) announces LiveTaskCount, a new ECS service metric that reports how many tasks are actively running in your service, available to all customers at no additional charge. Additionally, the existing RunningTaskCount metric in Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights no longer incurs a charge.

LiveTaskCount reports the number of actively running ECS tasks across all desired states (ACTIVATING, RUNNING, and DEACTIVATING), including tasks still running while transitioning to a stopped state, for example, tasks undergoing connection draining during a scale-in event. This comprehensive state coverage makes LiveTaskCount well suited for autoscaling policies and capacity planning where a complete view of active, metric-generating tasks is required. It is available at no charge as part of ECS service utilization metrics and does not require opting in to CloudWatch Container Insights. The existing CloudWatch Container Insights RunningTaskCount metric tracks tasks where both the current and desired state are RUNNING, and continues to serve as a health and stability signal for customers who depend on it. With today's update, RunningTaskCount is now available at no additional charge for all CloudWatch Container Insights users.

These updates are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECS is available. No action is required, and the pricing change for RunningTaskCount takes effect beginning October 1, 2026, and applies automatically. To learn more, see ECS CloudWatch metrics and ECS Container Insights metrics. For a pricing example, see Amazon CloudWatch pricing.

item.title: AWS Agent Registry now supports custom metadata for registry records
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Agent Registry, custom metadata, governance, resources, filtering

Summary: AWS Agent Registry is a centralized catalog for managing agents, MCP servers, skills, gateways, and custom resources in an organization. As resource counts grow, simple names and descriptions become inadequate for governance and discovery. Custom metadata enhances each registry record with structured fields, aiding in consistent resource management for both individuals and automated systems. Publishers can record various fields such as team ownership, data classification, and review status directly on records. The schema is defined once per registry, with common attributes and type-specific extensions, such as model family for agent records. Each field can hold free text, a URL, a Boolean, or choices from a predetermined list. The registry ensures validation of required fields and values during the creation or update of records. Users can conveniently filter search results based on any custom metadata field through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the MCP endpoint. Custom metadata is supported in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is operational, including US East, US West, Asia Pacific, and Europe. For more information, further resources are provided for detailed setup guidance.

AWS Agent Registry is the centralized, governed catalog for agents, MCP servers, agent skills, gateways, and custom resources within your organization. As organizations scale to hundreds of such resources, a name and description alone are insufficient for effective governance and discovery. Custom metadata lets you extend every registry record with your organization's own structured fields, so both people and automated systems can find and govern resources consistently.

With custom metadata, publishers can record fields like team ownership, data classification, or review status directly on each registry record. You define a schema once per registry with common attributes, then extend it with type-specific fields — such as a model family for agent records. Each field supports free text, a URL, a Boolean, or a choice from a list of allowed values, and the registry validates required fields and values on every record creation or update. You can then filter search results on any custom metadata field from the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, the AWS SDKs, or the registry's MCP endpoint.

Custom metadata is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Agent Registry is available: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland).

To learn more, visit the AWS Agent Registry documentation. For detailed setup guidance, see Define a custom metadata schema and Set custom metadata values on a record.

item.title: Amazon DCV releases version 2026.0 with RHEL 10 support and new clients
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon DCV, RHEL 10, macOS client, performance improvements, URL redirection

Summary: Amazon DCV 2026.0 has been released, introducing support for new operating systems including RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04. This version allows Linux hosts and sessions to operate on the Wayland display server, enhancing the user experience. A new macOS client has been introduced, featuring gamepad support, alongside updated clients for Windows and Linux platforms. Additionally, users can benefit from URL redirection on Windows hosts, which enables configured links opened within a remote session to launch in the local browser on the client device. The update also includes printer preferences redirection on Windows, allowing remote sessions to access client-side printer settings easily. Performance has been significantly enhanced with the inclusion of H.264 frame slice support and slice-based multithreaded decoding on both Linux and macOS clients, leading to reduced latency. Lastly, this version supports new macOS server versions on Amazon EC2, ensuring compatibility for cloud-based services. For more detailed information on these features and enhancements, users are encouraged to refer to the official documentation and resources available.

Amazon DCV 2026.0 is now available, adding support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04 along with a new macOS client and updated Windows and Linux clients. Amazon DCV is a high-performance remote display protocol that enables customers to securely access remote desktops and application sessions across Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Amazon DCV 2026.0 includes the following key features and improvements:

  • Support for RHEL 10, Rocky Linux 10, CentOS 10, and Ubuntu 26.04, with Linux hosts and sessions running on the modern Wayland display server

  • A new macOS client with gamepad support, and updated Windows and Linux clients

  • URL redirection on Windows hosts, so configured links opened in a remote session launch in the local browser on the client device

  • Printer preferences redirection on Windows, giving remote sessions access to client-side printer settings

  • Performance improvements, including H.264 frame slice support and slice-based multithreaded decoding on the Linux and macOS clients for lower latency

  • Support for new macOS server versions on Amazon EC2

For more information about the new features and enhancements in Amazon DCV 2026.0, see the release notes or visit the Amazon DCV webpage to learn more and get started.

item.title: AWS Deadline Cloud now helps users find their accessible resources in the Deadline Cloud monitor
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Deadline Cloud, resource discovery, access permissions, compute-intensive workloads, monitor

Summary: AWS Deadline Cloud has introduced a new feature that enables users to find queues, fleets, or jobs they have access to directly from the Deadline Cloud monitor, rather than needing access to an entire farm. This is particularly beneficial for users who previously required an administrator to provide farm IDs for their specific queues. The updated monitor displays accessible queues, their corresponding parent IDs, and the user’s level of access, including both direct and group-inherited permissions. This allows teams to manage their resources more efficiently and share a single monitor entry point (URL) across varying permission levels without needing additional coordination. The resource discovery feature is accessible in all AWS Regions where Deadline Cloud operates. This enhancement streamlines workflows for teams involved in tasks such as visual effects, animation, product design, simulation, and gaming, making it easier for them to engage with computing resources relevant to their specific projects. For further information, users can visit the official Deadline Cloud webpage.

AWS Deadline Cloud now lets users who have access to specific queues, fleets, or jobs, rather than an entire farm, find the resources they can reach directly from the Deadline Cloud monitor. Deadline Cloud is a fully managed service that helps teams run compute-intensive workloads for visual effects, animation, product design, simulation, and gaming.

Previously, a user with access to only one queue had to get the farm ID from an administrator before they could reach their work. With this launch, the Deadline Cloud monitor displays to users queues they have access to, the parent IDs needed to reach them, and their level of access, covering both direct and group-inherited permissions. Teams now can share a single monitor entry point (URL) across different permission levels without additional coordination.

Resource discovery is available in all AWS Regions where Deadline Cloud is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Deadline Cloud user guide.

item.title: Amazon Location Service launches an interactive API Playground featuring Places, Routes and Maps APIs
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Location Service, API Playground, Places API, Routes API, Maps API

Summary: Amazon Location Service has introduced a new interactive API Playground, allowing developers to explore and test all of its Places, Routes, and Maps APIs without writing code. This Playground features all 14 APIs, including Geocode, ReverseGeocode, CalculateRoutes, and Dynamic Map, enabling users to make real API calls and see results visualized on an interactive map. Developers can adjust parameters easily and copy request snippets directly for use in their applications, streamlining the integration process. The Playground facilitates various use cases, such as validating addresses for deliveries, planning safe multi-stop routes for trucks, visualizing drive-time service areas, and embedding maps into applications, without the need for SDK setup or test scripts. The API Playground is accessible in multiple AWS Regions, including US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), and several Asia Pacific locations, among others. To get started with the API Playground, developers can access it via the AWS Console or learn more through the provided resources. This initiative aims to enhance the overall developer experience with Amazon Location Service's capabilities.

Amazon Location Service now offers a complete, interactive API Playground that lets developers explore and test every Places, Routes, and Maps API visually without writing code. With this release, all 14 Amazon Location Service Places, Maps and Routes APIs are available in an interactive API Playground, where developers can make real API calls, see results rendered on an interactive map, adjust parameters, and copy ready-to-use request snippets directly into their applications.

The API Playground covers Amazon Location Service's Places, Routes, and Maps APIs: search and geocoding (Geocode, ReverseGeocode, Autocomplete, Suggest, SearchText, SearchNearby, and GetPlace), route planning and optimization (CalculateRoutes, CalculateRouteMatrix, CalculateIsolines, OptimizeWaypoints, and SnapToRoads), and mapping (Dynamic Map and GetStaticMap). Customers can simulate validating delivery addresses, planning truck-safe multi-stop routes, visualizing drive-time service areas, or embedding maps into their apps — with no SDK setup or test scripts required.

The API Playground is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), and South America (São Paulo).

To get started, visit the Amazon Location Service API Playground in the AWS Console, or learn more in the Developer Guide.

item.title: Bring deep SageMaker AI expertise to your coding agent with the AWS AI/ML skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS

It also includes MLflow for experiment tracking and model lifecycle management, JumpStart for model deployment and recommendations, and the ability to handle data preparation and ETL with processing jobs on managed compute. The AWS AI/ML skill incurs no additional charge; users only pay for AWS resources consumed. To get started, install the skill from GitHub or access it through SageMaker Studio JupyterLab. For additional information, refer to the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

Your coding agent can select, train, optimize and deploy models on Amazon SageMaker AI while working across the rest of your AWS environment in a single natural-language workflow. The AWS AI/ML skill is now a core skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS, so it works alongside the toolkit's other AWS skills like EC2, Bedrock, and more.

The skill is also pre-installed into SageMaker Studio JupyterLab for use with Kiro or your coding agent of choice.

  • Serverful training for both traditional ML and generative AI

  • MLflow: experiment tracking and model lifecycle management

  • JumpStart model deployment and model recommendations: deploy pre-built JumpStart models and get guided recommendations on the right model for the use case

  • Processing jobs: data preparation and ETL on managed compute

The AWS AI/ML skill is available at no additional charge; you pay only for the AWS resources your agents use. To get started, install the skill from the Agent Toolkit for AWS on GitHub, or use it pre-installed in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab. To learn more about using a coding assistant with your SageMaker AI workflows, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation.

item.title: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports FSx for OpenZFS, NFS 4.2, and object metadata controls
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS DataSync, Enhanced mode, Amazon FSx, NFS 4.2, ObjectMetadata

Summary: AWS DataSync's Enhanced mode now supports Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, allowing users to transfer data with greater flexibility as both a source and destination. This update replaces the previous limitation of only using Basic mode for FSx for OpenZFS transfers. Additionally, Enhanced mode supports NFS version 4.2, permitting seamless data transfers from on-premises NFS servers and FSx for OpenZFS file systems without requiring a reconfiguration to an older NFS protocol version. Another significant enhancement is the introduction of the ObjectMetadata option for object storage transfers, which offers more control over the copying of an object's user metadata during the transfer process. This feature is particularly useful for ensuring that destination metadata remains intact, especially in setups using AWS Storage Gateway or when dealing with incompatible metadata keys across different storage solutions, like Azure Blob Storage. It's important to note that existing tasks will remain unaffected and continue to operate as scheduled. These new capabilities for Enhanced mode tasks are available across all AWS Regions where AWS DataSync Enhanced mode is supported.

AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports Amazon FSx for OpenZFS as a source or destination location, NFS version 4.2 for on-premises NFS servers and FSx for OpenZFS file systems, and a new ObjectMetadata option for object storage transfers. Previously, customers transferring data to or from FSx for OpenZFS were limited to Basic mode.

NFS 4.2 lets you transfer data from NFS servers on the latest version without reconfiguring them to an older protocol version. The ObjectMetadata option gives you control over whether an object's user metadata is copied to the destination, which helps when destination metadata must stay intact, such as buckets served by AWS Storage Gateway, or when source metadata keys are not compatible with the destination, such as Azure Blob Storage. Existing tasks remain unaffected and continue to run as scheduled.

These capabilities are available for Enhanced mode tasks in all AWS Regions where AWS DataSync Enhanced mode is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS DataSync documentation.

item.title: Amazon Route 53 now supports registrations, transfers, and renewals for Premium Domains
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Route 53, Premium Domain Names, register, manage, customers

Summary: Amazon Route 53 Domains has now introduced support for Premium Domain Names, enabling customers to search for, register, transfer, renew, and restore these sought-after domains directly within Route 53. Historically, many domain registries reserved a selection of "premium" domains—characterized by their brevity, memorability, and high demand. Prior to this update, customers had to navigate multiple registrars to manage these domains, causing fragmentation in their portfolios. With this new feature, customers can now discover and acquire premium domains within Route 53, streamlining the process of consolidating their existing premium domains from other providers. The platform offers a unified management experience for both premium and standard domains, simplifying the ownership process. Searching for and registering premium domains operates similarly to standard domains; they automatically appear in search results with clear upfront pricing, allowing customers to understand the cost before making a commitment. To explore Amazon Route 53 Domains and start acquiring premium domains, customers are encouraged to visit the relevant site. A complete list of supported top-level domains is also available for reference.

Amazon Route 53 Domains now supports Premium Domain Names. Customers can now search for, register, transfer, renew, and restore registry premium names directly through Route 53.

Most domain registries set aside a selection of "premium" domains - names that are short, memorable, or in high demand. Previously, Route 53 Domains did not support these premium names, which meant customers who wanted them had to register and manage them through other registrars, fragmenting their portfolios across multiple providers. With this launch, customers can now discover and acquire premium domains directly in Route 53 Domains, consolidate their existing premium domains from other registrars, and manage premium and standard domains together through a single, unified experience. Finding and registering a premium domain works just like it does for standard domains. Premium domains appear automatically in domain search and availability results, with pricing shown upfront, so customers know the cost before they commit.

To learn more about Amazon Route 53 Domains and start registering premium domains, visit the Amazon Route 53 Domains page. For a complete list of supported top-level domains, see the Route 53 TLD list.

item.title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest CU for Microsoft SQL Server
item.content:encoded:
**Keywords:** Microsoft SQL Server, Cumulative Updates, Amazon RDS, upgrades, improvements

Summary: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) for Microsoft SQL Server, specifically CU8 for Microsoft SQL Server 2025, version 17.00.4075.5.v1. This update incorporates various improvements and fixes that enhance the performance and security of SQL Server databases. For detailed information on the enhancements and resolved issues, users can refer to Microsoft's documentation associated with KB5104822. It is highly recommended that users upgrade their Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to implement these changes. The upgrade process can be conveniently carried out via the Amazon RDS Management Console, or by utilizing the AWS SDK or CLI. The upgrade to the most recent version ensures that users can leverage new features and performance improvements while maintaining optimal database functionality. Additionally, guidance on upgrading database instances can be found in AWS documentation, providing users with necessary instructions to smoothly transition to the updated version. This ensures their database environments remain secure, efficient, and up-to-date in alignment with the latest technological advancements.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for Microsoft SQL Server 2025 CU8 KB5104822 (RDS version 17.00.4075.5.v1).

For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5104822. We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.35: docs: close out cross-namespace inheritance (#30712)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a — no Linear ticket. Closes out the cross-namespace inheritance
project, delivered in #30577, #30646 and #30696.

Summary

Closes the project in the team's process docs. The project's working
folder was never committed, so there is nothing to migrate or delete in
the repo.

What changes

  • drive/calibration/dod.md: the project-DoD item "Artefact-format
    changes load the previous format" is removed.     It contradicts
    .agents/rules/no-backward-compatibility.mdc, and it is where this
    project's spec got a "released contracts stay loadable" requirement that
    was later dropped. The mitigation bullet in failure-modes.md (second
    F20) that repeated it is removed too.
  • drive/calibration/failure-modes.md: one new entry, F49. Guards,
    helpers and tests are written for inputs the public API cannot produce,
    then removed.

Project definition of done

Item Result Evidence
An authored and emitted cross-namespace MTI contract loads and
executes reads and supported writes against distinct namespaces Met
#30696,
test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/polymorphism-namespaces.test.ts
One base tells same-named derived models in different namespaces apart
by discriminator value; equal table names across namespaces are treated
as MTI Met #30696, same test file and its type tests (b.Epic /
c.Epic, a.tasks / b.tasks)
Reads, includes, prepared queries, aggregation and supported mutations
keep qualified identity and assert complete rows Met #30696
Type tests in both ORMs for variant inference and for rejecting model
names, undeclared values and non-polymorphic receivers Met #30577
Duplicate discriminator values are rejected by SQL and Mongo authoring
and cannot be expressed in a contract Met #30577 (authoring), #30696
(value-keyed variants)
Zero-argument custom helpers return precisely typed variant
collections Met #30577
Same-namespace STI/MTI and Mongo polymorphism regression suites pass
Met CI on #30696
A variant entry that is not a CrossReference is rejected by
structural validation in both families Met #30696
Consumers, fixtures, docs, upgrade instructions and ADR examples
describe the implemented behaviour Met #30577, #30646, #30696 (ADR
173, ADR 177, ADR 265, upgrade fragments)
Final retro Done F49 in this PR
ADR audit Done The contract decision (variants keyed by
discriminator value, referencing the variant by coordinate) is in ADR
  1. The SQL ORM's table scope is described in the sql-orm-client
    README. |
    | Manual QA script and run report per slice | Waived by the project
    owner.     | No manual QA was run. The evidence is the automated suites,
    including database tests. |
    | Linear close-out items | n/a | The project had no Linear project. |

Known gaps the project found and did not fix

These exist on main. None has a ticket.

SQL ORM:

  • Single-row update() and delete() on a multi-table variant return
    only the base table's fields, although the type promises the variant
    row.
  • updateAll / deleteAll with a filter on a multi-table variant's
    field do not join the variant table.
  • Cursor pagination ordered by a multi-table variant's field binds the
    column to the base table.
  • create() with nested relation callbacks on a variant collection
    skips the variant insert.
  • createAll on a multi-table variant runs each row in its own
    transaction.
  • aggregate() cannot reduce over a variant's field.
  • select() types do not accept a variant's field names, although they
    are read at run time.
  • select() is not scoped to the collection's namespace when two models
    in a contract share a name.
  • A base model's relation cannot be included after variant() in the
    types, although it works at run time.
  • A required field on a single-table variant is optional in that
    variant's create input.
  • The value a grouped having comparison is checked against is written
    into the SQL text without codec encoding.
  • Projected column labels (<alias>__<column>) are not bounded to the
    63-byte identifier limit.
  • Custom collection classes require a single-namespace contract.

Mongo ORM:

  • variant() narrows only create inputs. Read results, where(),
    select() and include keys stay typed against the base model, and a
    relation declared on a variant cannot be included.

Upgrade path:

  • Users with polymorphic models rewrite existing migration snapshots by
    a rule given in the upgrade instructions; no command does it.
  • Four superseded example migration snapshots (two in
    examples/prisma-8-demo, two in examples/retail-store) are still in
    the previous variants form. Nothing loads them.

Testing performed

Docs only. pnpm lint:rules, pnpm lint:rules:symlinks and pnpm lint:skills pass.

Skill update

n/a — internal only (team process docs under drive/).

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO. The DCO
    status check will block merge if any commit is missing a
    Signed-off-by: trailer.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (or n/a if the change is doc-only / refactor
    with no behavioural delta). n/a — doc-only.
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form. — Not
    ticked: there is no Linear ticket.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in (or stated n/a — internal only).

Notes for the reviewer

The removal of the definition-of-done item is the part to read: it takes
out a rule added on 2026-09-10.

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • Documentation
  • Updated project guidance for format changes, removing requirements to
    test compatibility with artifacts from a previous release.
  • Added guidance to avoid safeguards and related work for inputs that
    cannot arise through a supported public call path.
