item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.32: A polymorphic base can have variants in other namespaces (#30696)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a — no Linear ticket; third and last PR for cross-namespace
inheritance (after #30577 and #30646).

At a glance

namespace a {
  model Task {
    id        Int    @id
    title     String
    type      String
    projectId Int?   @map("project_id")

    @@discriminator(type)
    @@map("tasks")
  }
}

namespace b {
  model Chore {
    effort  Int
    ownerId Int? @map("owner_id")

    @@base(a.Task, "chore")
    @@map("tasks")
  }

  model Epic {
    size Int

    @@base(a.Task, "b-epic")
    @@map("epics")
  }
}
const tasks = orm({ runtime, context }).a.Task;
const rows = await tasks.orderBy((task) => task.id.asc()).all();

The statement joins each variant table in its own namespace. b.tasks
has the same name as the base table a.tasks, so it gets an alias:

LEFT JOIN "b"."tasks" AS "tasks_2" ON "tasks"."id" = "tasks_2"."id"
"tasks_2"."effort" AS "tasks_2__effort"

Trimmed from
contract.prisma
and the first test in
polymorphism-namespaces.test.ts;
the SQL lines are the fragments that test asserts. Before this PR a
base's variants named each variant by model name only, so a variant in
another namespace could not be referenced, and the SQL ORM looked every
variant up in the base's namespace.

Summary

A polymorphic base model can have multi-table variants in other
namespaces, including variants that share a model name or a table name
with something in another namespace. To make that possible, a base's
variants in the contract changes form: it is keyed by discriminator
value and each entry references the variant model by { namespace, model }.

Decision

This PR ships:

  1. A new contract form for variants. "variants": { "bug": { "namespace": "public", "model": "Bug" } } replaces "variants": { "Bug": { "value": "bug" } }, in contract.json and contract.d.ts,
    for both families. The entry type is CrossReference;
    ContractVariantEntry is removed. Nothing reads the previous form, and
    a contract in that form fails validation. Every tracked contract,
    fixture and current example migration snapshot is re-emitted.
  2. Every producer and consumer of that form. Framework types and
    domain validation, both structural schemas, SQL PSL, Mongo PSL, the
    Mongo TS builder (its authoring input is unchanged), the emitter and the
    Postgres PSL printer.
  3. Both ORMs identify a variant by its discriminator value.
    variant(value) is a direct variants[value] lookup. Collection state
    and the variant type helpers hold the value where they held the model
    name. VariantNames, VariantNameForValue and variantsByValue are
    removed.
  4. The SQL ORM resolves each variant in the namespace its reference
    names.     Storage lookups, joins and variant inserts use the variant's
    own namespace and table.
  5. A new diagnostic in SQL PSL.
    PSL_BASE_IN_OTHER_NAMESPACE_WITHOUT_MAP rejects a variant in another
    namespace that has no @@map.
  6. Docs and upgrade instructions. ADR
    173
    (examples and one decision paragraph), ADR 177, ADR 265, the
    CONTRACT.MODEL_VARIANT_MISSING entry in the error reference, one
    addition to the prisma-8 contract skill reference, a pending upgrade
    fragment variants-keyed-by-discriminator-value for apps and
    extensions, and an update to the still-pending collection-state-tables
    fragment.

Notes for the reviewer

  • Where the lines are. Of 4529 added and 1000 removed lines, emitted
    artifacts are about 2530 added and 150 removed; 2160 of those are the
    new fixture's contract.json and contract.d.ts, and the rest are
    re-emitted contracts whose only change is variants. Hand-written
    source is about 700 added and 570 removed across 32 files. Tests are
    about 1060 added and 220 removed. Docs and upgrade instructions are
    about 240 added and 60 removed.
  • About 400 of the changed source lines are a rename in
    sql-orm-client/src: variantName to variantValue in state and type
    state, and IncludeExpr.localVariantName to localVariantValue. The
    behaviour change in that package is concentrated in
    collection-contract.ts,
    collection-tables.ts
    and types.ts.
  • Breaking for anyone with polymorphic models. A contract.json in
    the previous form is rejected. An existing migration snapshot in the
    previous form makes prisma migration plan --from <hash> fail with
    CONTRACT.VALIDATION_FAILED. No CLI command regenerates a snapshot; the
    app upgrade fragment gives the rewrite rule for contract.json and
    contract.d.ts. The storage hash does not change, so no migration is
    needed.
  • Four superseded example snapshots stay in the previous form: two
    in examples/prisma-8-demo and two in examples/retail-store. The
    validator already refused them before this PR and nothing loads them.
    The planner-golden manifest records the new refusal for the two demo
    snapshots.
  • Domain validation no longer checks for duplicate discriminator
    values.     A map keyed by value cannot repeat one. SQL PSL, Mongo PSL and
    the Mongo TS builder still report two variants declaring the same value.
    Domain validation does reject a base that lists the same variant model
    under two values.
  • The Postgres PSL printer refuses the new fixture because the model
    name Doc appears in namespaces b and c. That refusal exists on
    main; the round-trip test lists the fixture with it.
  • Custom collection classes still require a single-namespace
    contract.
  • The new tests work around four gaps that exist on main for
    hierarchies in one namespace and are not changed here. They are listed
    under Follow-ups.

How it fits together

  1. Change the representation. ContractModelBase.variants is
    Record<string, CrossReference>. Domain validation follows each entry's
    reference to the variant model and checks that its base is the
    declaring model's coordinate, and checks the reverse direction by
    coordinate too
    (domain-types.ts,
    validate-domain.ts).
    Both structural schemas require each entry to be a CrossReference; the
    SQL schema also gives discriminator the shape { field: string }, and
    data-contract-sql-v1.json is regenerated (SQL
    validators.ts    ,
    Mongo
    contract-schema.ts    ).
  2. Write it from every authoring source. SQL PSL writes the
    variant's own namespace into the reference and names models with their
    namespace in diagnostics when a hierarchy spans namespaces (SQL
    interpreter.ts    ).
    Mongo PSL and the Mongo TS builder write the same form with the single
    Mongo namespace; the builder still takes variants: { Bug: { value: 'bug' } } (Mongo
    interpreter.ts    ,
    contract-builder.ts).
  3. Emit and print it. contract.d.ts emits each entry as a
    CrossReference under its value key, takes the discriminator literal
    union from the keys, and finds Any<Base> members through the
    references
    (model-types-emission.ts,
    domain-type-generation.ts).
    The Postgres PSL printer finds a variant's value by coordinate and
    prints @@base(ns.Base, "value") when the base is in another namespace
    (model-attributes.ts).
  4. Identify a variant by value in both ORMs. variant(value) reads
    variants[value]. SQL collection state, CollectionTables.variants,
    the variant an include names for its local columns, and the fourth type
    parameter of MongoCollection all hold the value. VariantModelRow,
    VariantCreateInput and the model accessor take the value and read the
    variant's model and namespace from the reference (SQL
    types.ts    , Mongo
    collection.ts    ,
    Mongo
    types.ts    ).
  5. Resolve SQL variants where their references point.
    resolvePolymorphismInfo records each variant's namespace and table. A
    variant is single-table only when both equal the base's; otherwise it is
    multi-table. Each variant table is aliased at its own storage coordinate
    through the table scope added in #30646, which is what gives b.tasks
    the alias tasks_2 beside a.tasks
    (collection-contract.ts,
    collection-tables.ts).
  6. Prove it against a database. The new PSL fixture
    polymorphism-namespaces has a same-namespace single-table variant, a
    same-namespace multi-table variant, a variant in another namespace whose
    table has the base table's name, two variants named Epic mapped to
    epics in two namespaces, and a relation declared on a variant. It has
    12 database tests and 4 type tests.

Behavior changes & evidence

  • variants in contract.json and contract.d.ts is keyed by
    discriminator value and each entry is { namespace, model }; the
    previous form is rejected.     Implementation:
    domain-types.ts,
    SQL validators.ts,
    Mongo
    contract-schema.ts    .
    Evidence:
    validators.test.ts,
    variant-schema.test.ts.
  • A variant may be in a different namespace from its base, and domain
    validation matches base and variant by coordinate.     Implementation:
    validate-domain.ts.
    Evidence:
    validate-domain.test.ts.
  • SQL PSL accepts @@base(a.Task, "chore") from another namespace and
    rejects it without @@map with
    PSL_BASE_IN_OTHER_NAMESPACE_WITHOUT_MAP.     Two variants named alike in
    different namespaces no longer overwrite each other in variants.
    Implementation: SQL
    interpreter.ts    .
    Evidence:
    interpreter.polymorphism.test.ts.
  • The SQL ORM reads, filters, includes, aggregates and writes variants
    in other namespaces.     create and createAll insert the variant row
    into the table in the variant's namespace. Implementation:
    collection-contract.ts,
    collection-tables.ts,
    query-plan-select.ts.
    Evidence:
    polymorphism-namespaces.test.ts.
  • SQL variant() accepts only the values declared by the base in the
    collection's own namespace, and two variants with the same model name
    have separate row and create-input types.     Implementation:
    collection.ts,
    types.ts.
    Evidence:
    polymorphism-namespaces.test-d.ts,
    polymorphism.test-d.ts.
  • ORM type helpers and state fields take a discriminator value.
    VariantModelRow<C, 'Task', 'bug'> replaces VariantModelRow<C, 'Task', 'Bug'>; VariantNames and VariantNameForValue are no longer
    exported; CollectionState.variantName is variantValue. Mongo
    behaviour is otherwise unchanged. Implementation: SQL
    types.ts    , Mongo
    types.ts    ,
    Mongo
    exports/index.ts    .
    Evidence:
    orm-types.test-d.ts,
    collection-variant.test.ts.
  • The Postgres PSL printer prints a base in another namespace as
    @@base(ns.Base, "value").     Implementation:
    model-attributes.ts,
    contract-model-index.ts.
    Evidence:
    refusals-models.test.ts.
  • Upgrade instructions.
    app/instructions.md,
    extension/instructions.md.

Testing performed

On the branch with the latest main merged:

  • root pnpm typecheck: all packages but prisma7-adoption, which
    fails locally on an engine download (known);
  • pnpm test:packages: 25338 passed; 3 tarball tests fail locally with
    ERR_PNPM_TRUST_DOWNGRADE (known);
  • integration typecheck and test/sql-orm-client (122 files, 878
    tests);
  • pnpm lint:deps, pnpm fixtures:check, pnpm check:upgrade-coverage.

Before the last three small commits, also the targeted integration runs
test/planner-golden, test/mongo, test/authoring,
test/upgrade-instructions, test/psl-print, CLI emit and prepared
polymorphism (with test/sql-orm-client: 312 files, 3620 tests).

The full pnpm test:integration is blocked by a local hook. CI is the
full run.

Skill update

skills/prisma-8/references/contract.md,
polymorphism section: a base in another namespace is written
@@base(ns.Model, "value"), and such a variant must set @@map. The
query references already describe variant('<discriminator value>')
since #30577.

Follow-ups

These exist on main for hierarchies in one namespace and are not
changed here:

  • Single-row update() and delete() on a multi-table variant return
    only the base table's fields.
  • aggregate() cannot reduce over a variant's field.
  • select() types do not accept a variant's field names, although they
    are read at run time.
  • select() is not scoped to the collection's namespace when two models
    in a contract share a name.

Also open: custom collection classes on a multi-namespace contract.

Alternatives considered

  • Keep variants keyed by model name and add a namespace to each
    entry.     A model name is not unique across namespaces, so two variants
    named Epic in b and c would need one key. A discriminator value is
    unique in a hierarchy, and it is what variant() already takes since
    #30577, so the lookup becomes a key access.
  • Read the previous form, or rewrite it on load. Not done: the
    repo's rule is no backward-compatibility code, and the rewrite is
    mechanical enough to give as an upgrade instruction.
  • Allow a single-table variant in another namespace. A table belongs
    to one namespace, so a variant in b cannot store its fields in
    a.tasks while being a model of b. PSL reports
    PSL_BASE_IN_OTHER_NAMESPACE_WITHOUT_MAP and asks for @@map.
  • Change the Mongo TS builder's variants input to the value-keyed
    form.     Not done: Mongo has one namespace, so the model-keyed input is
    unambiguous, and the builder writes the contract form from it without a
    change for its users.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO. The DCO
    status check will block merge if any commit is missing a
    Signed-off-by: trailer.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (or n/a if the change is doc-only / refactor
    with no behavioural delta).
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form (Linear
    ticket prefix + concise title naming the concrete deliverable). See
    .claude/skills/create-pr/SKILL.md for the full convention. — Not
    ticked: there is no Linear ticket, so the title has no TML- prefix.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in (or stated n/a — internal only).

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • Features
  • Polymorphic variants are identified by discriminator values and can
    reference models in different namespaces. SQL and MongoDB ORM
    operations—including filtering, selection, relations, and
    mutations—support this mapping.
  • Documentation
  • Updated architecture references and Prisma guidance describe
    cross-namespace variants and their storage requirements.
  • Upgrade Notes
  • Existing contracts using the previous variant format must be
    regenerated, with matching migration snapshots updated.

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.31: Include PSL mixins in models, types, enums and extension blocks (#30694)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a. Third slice of the PSL mixins project (projects/psl-mixins/); the
syntax landed in #30675. This replaces #30678, which resolved inclusion
names in the symbol table.

At a glance

model mixin Timestamps {
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt DateTime @default(now())
  @@index([createdAt])
}

enum mixin BaseRoles {
  ADMIN = "admin"
  USER  = "user"
}

model User {
  id    Int    @id
  +Timestamps
  email String
}

enum Role {
  @@type("pg/text@1")
  +BaseRoles
  GUEST = "guest"
}

User has the fields id, createdAt, updatedAt, email, in that
order, and the index on createdAt. Role has ADMIN, USER,
GUEST. The emitted contract is the one the same schema gives with the
members written inline. Before this PR both forms parsed and were
rejected with "Mixins are not supported yet".

Summary

Mixins now work. The binder resolves each inclusion's name, and the
mixin's members are then placed in the enclosing block's symbol, so the
interpreters read an ordinary block. This holds for models, composite
types, enums and extension blocks such as row-level security policies.

Decision

  1. The symbol table records what is written. It gains mixin symbols;
    a model, composite type or block symbol holds only the members written
    in it. The symbol table resolves no name.
  2. The binder resolves an inclusion's name like any other name, in
    its first pass, through the scope chain and qualified-name code that
    type references use: the including block's namespace, then the top
    level, and a nearer declaration of any kind hides an outer one. Whatever
    it finds that is not a mixin is reported as Cannot find mixin "X".
  3. Placement is one function, called between the binder's two
    passes.     For each block with a resolved inclusion it rebuilds the
    member records in source order, adding the mixin's fields or entries and
    its attributes at the inclusion's position. It fills the records of the
    existing symbols, so a symbol handed out earlier shows the placed
    members. The members are the mixin's own symbols and nodes, shared by
    every including block.
  4. A mixin body is bound once, where it is written. In its second
    pass the binder resolves a mixin's field types in the mixin's namespace
    and the field names in its attributes against the mixin's own fields. An
    including block binds only the members written in it; its own attributes
    see the placed fields.
  5. Errors about an inclusion are reported at the inclusion. From the
    binder: a name that is not a mixin, a mixin for a different block
    keyword, an inclusion inside a mixin. From placement: the same mixin
    included twice, and a member the block already has.
  6. The binder passes the mixin itself as the owner of a member
    written in a mixin. AttributeSpecContext.model,
    UnsupportedAttribute.owner and UnresolvedTypeReference.owner accept
    a MixinSymbol, and the SQL and Mongo unsupported-attribute messages
    say Mixin "<name>" for one.
  7. A mixin is not a type. A field typed with a mixin's name is an
    unresolved reference.
  8. The interpreters for Prisma 7 and Prisma 6 schemas reject mixins.
    The parser reads mixins under every grammar (#30675), so those
    interpreters report a mixin declaration (Unsupported top-level block "model mixin") and an inclusion (Unsupported mixin inclusion "+Timestamps").

Reviewer notes

  • Own versus placed members. The second pass runs after placement,
    so the binder treats a member as a block's own when its syntax node's
    parent is the block's node (isWrittenIn in
    binder.ts).
    No symbol shape carries this, so interpreters, attribute specs and block
    specs have no way to ask whether a member came from a mixin.
  • Changes in the default-grammar interpreters are four files, each a
    compile fix or the wording in decision 4:
    psl-column-resolution.ts
    (one case),
    psl-field-resolution.ts
    (the word, and nothing for a type mixin as for a composite type),
    sql-attribute-specs.ts
    (a parameter type),
    mongo-attribute-specs.ts
    (the word).
  • Creating a binder completes the symbol table. A block's member
    records are final only after createBinder returns. Every production
    path builds the table and the binder together; the Prisma 7 and Prisma 6
    interpreters create no binder, and they reject mixins. The parser
    README's binder section gains one sentence saying this.
  • The duplicate-name test exists twice. The symbol table checks the
    fields written in a block; placement checks a mixin's members against
    what the block already has, and reports a block's own field that follows
    an inclusion which provided its name, reusing the symbol table's message
    and location code.
  • Placement assigns new member records to the existing symbol.
    fields and attributes on model and composite type symbols, and
    entries and attributes on block symbols, are assignable for this;
    the symbol object keeps its identity, so a symbol the binder handed out
    earlier shows the placed members.
  • members() on the block AST classes returns inclusions too, in
    source order with fields or entries and block attributes. Its only other
    production callers are the language server's semantic-token walkers,
    which skip an inclusion in this PR.
  • Which duplicate is reported. First wins, as before. If a model's
    own field comes after an inclusion that provided the name, the existing
    "Duplicate declaration" is reported at the field. If the inclusion comes
    second, the error is at the inclusion and names the mixin and the
    member.
  • Entry keys are checked in the symbol table too. Block-spec
    interpretation rejects a repeated key in both struct and map mode, so a
    repeated key is an error for every generic block; dropping the mixin's
    duplicate here keeps that later check from reporting it again. A block's
    own repeated keys still reach the later check unchanged.
  • Attributes are not checked for duplicates here. Whether two
    @@index or two @@map are allowed is each interpreter's rule, and
    those errors are reported at the attribute, inside the mixin.
  • An interpreter error on a mixin's member is reported once per
    including block    , at the member in the mixin. A test pins this.
    De-duplication is out of scope.
  • Not in this PR: go-to-definition, hover, rename and completion for
    mixins, and semantic tokens inside a mixin body. The binder records what
    an inclusion refers to; the language server answers for it in the next
    slice.

Behavior changes & evidence

  • A schema using a mixin gives the contract of the inline schema, for a
    model, a composite type, an enum and an extension block. Members are
    placed at the inclusion's position; an enum's member list in the
    contract follows it, while a model's fields and a table's columns are
    sorted in the emitted contract either way.
    symbol-table.ts;
    interpreter.mixins.test.ts
    (SQL),
    interpreter.mixins.test.ts
    (Mongo).
  • A policy_select mixin holding roles and using, included by two
    policies with different targets, gives the contract of the policies
    written in full.
    psl-policy-mixin.test.ts.
  • A mixin in namespace auth with owner User, included in a model in
    billing that has its own User, relates to auth.User.
    binder.ts;
    binder.mixin.test.ts
    and the SQL contract test above.
  • Each inclusion error has a test asserting code, message, file and
    range.
    mixin-placement.test.ts.
  • One mixin with an error in its body, included by three models, reports
    each binder diagnostic once; a mixin nothing includes is still bound.
    binder.mixin.test.ts.
  • Type completion does not offer mixin names.
    completion-scope.ts.

Testing performed

  • pnpm test:packages: 1761 of 1765 files pass.
  • pnpm typecheck: 170 of 171 tasks pass.
  • pnpm lint:deps, pnpm fixtures:check (no fixture changed), pnpm lint:skills, and lint for psl-parser, language-server, the SQL
    and Mongo contract-psl, the Prisma 7 and Prisma 6 contract sources,
    and the Postgres target: pass.
  • Local failures: prisma7-adoption#typecheck and three tarball-install
    tests, which fail on my machine and pass in CI, plus the CLI telemetry
    end-to-end test, which timed out at 5 s under the full run and passes
    when run alone.

Skill update

skills/prisma-8/references/contract.md gains "Workflow — Mixins
(shared members)": the example above and the rules (one keyword per
mixin, a member provided twice is an error, a mixin's attributes can
name only its own fields, a mixin cannot include a mixin, names follow
namespaces, a mixin is not a type).

Alternatives considered

  • Resolving names in a mixin where it is included. A mixin's
    @@unique([tenantId, id]) could then use the including model's id.
    The binder stores one resolution per syntax node, so one node would need
    several meanings, a mixin could not be checked on its own, and hover
    inside a mixin would have no single answer.
  • Copying members per including block, so interpreter errors could
    point at the inclusion. Members would stop being shared symbols, which
    rename and go-to-definition across including blocks rely on, and errors
    that are the mixin's own fault would move away from it.
  • Building a model-shaped object around a mixin to pass to spec
    factories and the family callbacks without widening their types. The
    object would claim to be a model that is in no symbol record.
  • Resolving inclusion names in the symbol table (#30678). The symbol
    table needed its own scope chain and had to register every symbol before
    filling any, and names were resolved by two components.
  • Placing members after all binding. A block's own attributes can
    name a mixed-in field, so the binder would have to work out a block's
    placed fields before placement had run.
  • Letting interpreters expand inclusions. Two family interpreters,
    two legacy-schema interpreters and the language server would each need
    the logic.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (or n/a if the change is doc-only / refactor
    with no behavioural delta).
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form. No
    Linear ticket is used for this project.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in (or stated n/a — internal only).

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • New Features
  • Added support for defining and including PSL mixins across models,
    composite types, enums, key-value blocks, and policies. Included members
    appear at the point of inclusion, and mixin names resolve across
    namespaces.
  • SQL and MongoDB contracts interpret supported mixin members, including
    fields and attributes.
  • Bug Fixes
  • Improved diagnostics for invalid, unresolved, duplicate, and
    unsupported mixins and mixin members.
    • Prisma 6 and Prisma 7 contracts report mixins as unsupported.
  • Documentation
    • Added guidance and examples for declaring and using mixins.

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.30: TML-3468: Close the project Storage a model does not map (#30704)
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

This PR removes projects/unmapped-storage/, the planning files of the
project "Storage a model does not map". Its four slices have merged, and
its decisions live in ADR 267
(#30641). It also corrects
one stale phrase in the Prisma 7 source project's slice 1 spec: an
@ignore field used by an index is now kept, not refused.

Merge this after ADR 267
(#30641), because the
project's done conditions include that ADR, and after
#30705, which makes the code
match what ADR 267 says about a model with no fields.

What the project delivered

Slice PR Outcome
1 #30665 A contract
definition can hold columns and tables no model maps, lowered by the
same code as a model's table.
2 #30667 The SQL ORM
reads and writes only the columns a model's fields map; naming any other
column throws ORM.FIELD_UNKNOWN.
3 #30672 The Prisma 7
reader keeps @ignore fields and @@ignore models as columns and
tables, so adding or removing @ignore after the handover plans
nothing.
4 #30671 Prisma 7's
_prisma_migrations table is left out of introspection, so `db verify
--strict` passes on a database Prisma 7 built.

Done conditions

  • Adding @ignore to a field and @@ignore to a model in
    examples/prisma7-adoption plans no operations, and so does removing
    them. Met: examples/prisma7-adoption/test/handover.test.ts.
  • The handover test asserts strict verify reports nothing unclaimed.
    Met: same file, after every edit.
  • findMany() with no select returns no extra column, and create
    with its name throws ORM.FIELD_UNKNOWN. Met:
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/unmapped-storage.test.ts.
  • ADR 267 is merged. Open:
    #30641 awaits review.
  • The Prisma 7 project's slice 1 text no longer says ignored objects are
    omitted. Met by slice 3, plus the phrase corrected here.

Where the deferred items went

  • Many-to-many on.targetFields holds junction column names: TML-3570.
  • Whether validator tests may build malformed contracts by hand:
    TML-3571.
  • A model with no fields types its rows as accepting any key: fixed in
    #30705 (TML-3536), because
    ADR 267 states the fixed behaviour. Its review found TML-3572 (the SQL
    ORM builds inputs from the row type), TML-3573 (Mongo contracts built
    without emitting) and TML-3574 (other empty maps in emitted types).
  • Prisma 8 syntax for unmapped columns and tables, the polymorphic
    integration test, and rebuilding buildMixedPolyContract through a
    source: TML-3469.
  • A relation to a bare model name used in two namespaces resolves by
    list order: TML-3280.
  • A junction declared only by a table node is refused: kept as designed,
    per ADR 267.
  • A cross-space foreign key carries the target model's name as well as
    its table: checked and kept; the name is real information about the
    target (TML-3569, cancelled).

Retro

  • Every path an upgrade instruction describes needs a test. The
    slice 3 spec first described the post-handover upgrade order wrongly,
    then claimed migrating was unsafe. Tests for each path (sign, migrate --advance-ref db, migrate then sign, sign-first recovery) showed the
    real behaviour, and the instruction and ADR were corrected from them.
  • Run the cross-cutting test families on a merge of main before
    queueing.     Slices 2 and 3 each left the merge queue once. Tests on main
    had changed or been added after the PR's own CI: ported _count tests
    for slice 2, and print refusals plus Prisma 7 journeys for slice 3.
    Running the print round-trip and Prisma 7 CLI journey files after
    merging main would have caught both.
  • After merging a sibling slice, run the shared test file even when
    git merges it cleanly.     Slices 3 and 4 both edited handover.test.ts.
    The merge was clean apart from one comment, but left a call to a helper
    slice 4 had renamed.
  • Approved means queue it at once. Slice 2 sat approved but not
    queued for hours.

Project: Storage a model does not
map.

Agent: anansi-36

Signed-off-by: willbot w.a.madden+machine@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Will Madden madden@prisma.io

item.title: v1.17.0-beta2
item.content:encoded:
1.17.0-beta2 (September 23, 2026)

NEW FEATURES:

  • Terraform now supports variables and locals in provider requirements (#39153)

  • A new -minimal-refresh planning option has been added, which will only refresh resources that have proposed changes. (#35290)

  • policy: Terraform Policy is now generally available. The -policies flag for plan, apply, and query no longer requires an experimental build or the -allow-experimental-features flag. Query policies evaluate resources discovered by list blocks and report human-readable or JSON results. See https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/policy for more information. (#38970)

ENHANCEMENTS:

  • command/init: Enrich log messages with provider versions (#38918)

  • test: Add mock_provider support for ephemeral resources (#38928)

  • command/login: display warning after successful login if user is subject to an organization's TTL policy

BUG FIXES:

  • funcs: pow and log no longer panic when result is not a number (#38912)

  • ephemeral: Terraform will now use and display diagnostics raised when renewing an ephemeral resource. This may cause warnings to appear that previously were lost. We expect that any error diagnostics that were previously lost would have caused confusing downstream errors, so we do not anticipate this change to be breaking. (#38989)

  • test: Deterministic dependency ordering in cleanup graph (#38247)

  • query: report Unknown and N/A results for policy evaluations of discovered resources (#39058)

  • query: terraform query -policies now rejects a path that is not a directory, instead of passing it on to the policy engine (#39238)

NOTES:

  • version: JSON output now includes a new format_version field, which will enable safer future changes of the command's JSON output format. It is assumed existing tooling ignores unknown fields and therefore this change should not be breaking in itself but we advice consumers to pay attention to format_version in future releases and/or use latest version of hashicorp/terraform-json & hashicorp/terraform-exec which does. (#38930)

Previous Releases

For information on prior major and minor releases, refer to their changelogs:

  • v1.16
  • v1.15
  • v1.14
  • v1.13
  • v1.12
  • v1.11
  • v1.10
  • v1.9
  • v1.8
  • v1.7
  • v1.6
  • v1.5
  • v1.4
  • v1.3
  • v1.2
  • v1.1
  • v1.0
  • v0.15

  • v0.13

  • v0.11 and earlier

BUG FIXES:

  • cloud: Fixed a bug causing the CLI to pause indefinitely after a run task failure with pending policy evaluations (#38751)

item.title: v2.268.0
item.content:encoded:
⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

L1 resources are automatically generated from public CloudFormation Resource Schemas. They are built to closely reflect the real state of CloudFormation. Sometimes these updates can contain changes that are incompatible with previous types, but more accurately reflect reality. In this release we have changed:

  • aws-athena: AWS::Athena::Session removed.
  • aws-bcmdataexports: AWS::BCMDataExports::Table removed.
  • aws-bedrock: AWS::Bedrock::DefaultPromptRouter and AWS::Bedrock::ModelInvocationJob removed.
  • aws-bedrockagentcore: AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Browser, AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CodeInterpreter, and AWS::BedrockAgentCore::TokenVault removed; AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentConnector ConnectorType and AWS::BedrockAgentCore::PaymentCredentialProvider CredentialProviderVendor are now immutable; AWS::BedrockAgentCore::CapacityProvider OperatingSystem allowed values in the LaunchParameters type reduced from [LINUX_X86_64, LINUX_ARM64, MAC_ARM64, WINDOWS_X86_64] to [LINUX_X86_64, LINUX_ARM64].
  • aws-certificatemanager: AWS::CertificateManager::Certificate Id attribute removed.
  • aws-chime: on both AWS::Chime::AppInstance and AWS::Chime::AppInstanceBot, the CreatedTimestamp and LastUpdatedTimestamp attribute types changed from number to string.
  • aws-cloudformation: AWS::CloudFormation::ResourceScan removed.
  • aws-codeartifact: AWS::CodeArtifact::Package removed.
  • aws-codebuild: AWS::CodeBuild::Sandbox removed; AWS::CodeBuild::SourceCredential Id attribute removed.
  • aws-dax: AWS::DAX::ParameterGroup Id attribute removed; Description property is now immutable.
  • aws-dms: Id attribute removed from AWS::DMS::Endpoint, AWS::DMS::EventSubscription, and AWS::DMS::ReplicationSubnetGroup; AWS::DMS::ReplicationTask MigrationType property is now immutable.
  • aws-docdb: Id attribute removed from AWS::DocDB::DBClusterParameterGroup and AWS::DocDB::DBSubnetGroup.
  • aws-dynamodb: AWS::DynamoDB::Export removed.
  • aws-elasticache: AWS::ElastiCache::ReservedCacheNode removed.
  • aws-emr: AWS::EMR::NotebookExecution removed.
  • aws-events: AWS::Events::Replay removed.
  • aws-fis: AWS::FIS::SafetyLever removed.
  • aws-glue:
    • Id attribute removed from AWS::Glue::Classifier, AWS::Glue::Connection, AWS::Glue::CustomEntityType, AWS::Glue::DataQualityRuleset, AWS::Glue::MLTransform, AWS::Glue::SecurityConfiguration, AWS::Glue::TableOptimizer, and AWS::Glue::Workflow.
    • AWS::Glue::Connection: complex-property types AuthenticationConfigurationInput and OAuth2PropertiesInput renamed to AuthenticationConfiguration and OAuth2Properties respectively.
    • AWS::Glue::DataQualityRuleset: Name, TargetTable.DatabaseName, and TargetTable.TableName properties are now required; Name property is now immutable; Tags property type changed from json to map<string>.
    • AWS::Glue::CustomEntityType: Name property is now immutable; Tags property is no longer recognised as resource tags.
    • AWS::Glue::MLTransform: TransformEncryption property is now immutable.
  • aws-greengrassv2: AWS::GreengrassV2::Component and AWS::GreengrassV2::CoreDevice removed.
  • aws-identitystore: AWS::IdentityStore::AllGroupMemberships removed.
  • aws-imagebuilder: AWS::ImageBuilder::AllImageBuildVersions, AWS::ImageBuilder::AllWorkflowBuildVersions, AWS::ImageBuilder::WorkflowExecution, and AWS::ImageBuilder::WorkflowStepExecution removed.
  • aws-medialive: AWS::MediaLive::Offering removed.
  • aws-mediaconvert: AWS::MediaConvert::Preset Id attribute removed.
  • aws-mediapackage: AWS::MediaPackage::HarvestJob removed.
  • aws-memorydb: AWS::MemoryDB::MultiRegionParameterGroup and AWS::MemoryDB::ReservedNode removed.
  • aws-omics: AWS::Omics::Reference removed.
  • aws-osis: AWS::OSIS::PipelineBlueprint removed.
  • aws-personalize: AWS::Personalize::DataDeletionJob and AWS::Personalize::Recipe removed.
  • aws-redshiftserverless: AWS::RedshiftServerless::RecoveryPoint removed.
  • aws-route53: AWS::Route53::RecordSet GeoProximityLocation property removed, along with its supporting GeoProximityLocation and Coordinates complex-property types; Id attribute removed.
  • aws-sagemaker: AWS::SageMaker::ModelCardExportJob, AWS::SageMaker::MonitoringScheduleAlert, and AWS::SageMaker::TransformJob removed.
  • aws-ses: AWS::SES::ReceiptRuleSet Id attribute removed.
  • aws-signer: AWS::Signer::SigningJob removed.
  • aws-ssm: AWS::SSM::Session removed; AWS::SSM::Association InstanceId property is now immutable.
  • aws-sso: AWS::SSO::ApplicationProvider removed.
  • aws-stepfunctions: AWS::StepFunctions::MapRun removed.
  • aws-transcribe: AWS::Transcribe::MedicalTranscriptionJob removed.
  • aws-vpclattice: AWS::VpcLattice::ServiceNetwork SharingConfig property is now immutable.

Features

  • update L1 CloudFormation resource definitions (#38732) (53fdc99)
  • codebuild: add Node.js 24 Lambda build image constants (#38471) (41ca888), closes #38172 #34197
  • ec2: support CpuOptions on LaunchTemplate (#38193) (b0f7d9c), closes #38187
  • medialive: new AWS Elemental MediaLive L2 Construct with integration on MediaConnect L2 alpha (#38563) (730b2ee)
  • update L1 CloudFormation resource definitions (#38645) (e238f54)
  • update L1 CloudFormation resource definitions (#38693) (51234fd)
  • s3-deployment: run the deployment handler on arm64 (Graviton) (#37174) (c2df7a3), closes #29996

Bug Fixes

  • core: ignored external symlinks throw validation error (#38679) (8fd1ef6)
  • core: templates are not checked for circular dependencies (#38712) (688b0c1)
  • core: upgrade CloudFormation validation to latest version (#38668) (d5df2ee)
  • eks-v2: generate and export L1 constructs from aws-eks-v2 (#37640) (ecdafa9), closes #37563 #37350 #37350
  • s3-deployment: replace deprecated addDependency in integ test (#38684) (43c4921)

Alpha modules (2.268.0-alpha.0)

⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

  • glue-alpha: DataQualityTargetTable's constructor is removed — use DataQualityTargetTable.fromTable(database, table) or fromTableName(database, tableName); IDatabase now extends IDatabaseRef.
  • glue-alpha: DataQualityRulesetProps.clientToken is removed; use the CfnDataQualityRuleset L1 for request-level idempotency.
  • glue-alpha: S3Table.clientSideEncryptionKey is now kms.IKeyRef instead of kms.IKey.
  • glue-alpha: DataQualityRulesetProps.rulesetName is now required. AWS::Glue::DataQualityRuleset made Name a required property, so the name can no longer be left for CloudFormation to generate.

Features

  • glue-alpha: reference-typed DataQualityTargetTable and remove clientToken (#38730) (c8fafbd)

Code Refactoring

  • glue-alpha: use kms.IKeyRef for KMS key inputs where possible (#38725) (604ac23)

item.content:encoded:
Guitoro is a free browser guitar using recordings of real instruments. You can strum with your keyboard, mouse, or touchscreen, choose acoustic, classical, electric guitar or bass, and see chord fingering and each stroke. Song practice can be slowed to 20%, and there are free chord tools and tuners. No signup or download.

1 minute video demo: https://youtu.be/DtcluMLdSgs

I would love feedback on how the strumming feels and sounds.

Amazon CloudFront now supports AWS Lambda Web Functions as an origin
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Lambda, CloudFront, security, caching, global edge network

Summary: Starting today, AWS Lambda Web Functions can be delivered via CloudFront's global edge network. By placing CloudFront in front of a Lambda Web Function, users benefit from TLS termination at the edge, resulting in lower latency and faster connections. Additionally, caching is enabled for improved performance along with the use of custom domains that support managed TLS certificates, with no changes required to application code. The implementation of CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts access to the Lambda Web Function, ensuring that it's only reachable through CloudFront, thus preventing unintended requests from bypassing security measures. This setup also protects the function from network-layer DDoS attacks and allows for the integration of AWS WAF for enhanced application-layer security. For applications that have their own user authentication, OAC preserves the original credentials, maintaining existing sign-in flows. Importantly, CloudFront support for AWS Lambda Web Functions is available globally, except in the CloudFront China region. To begin, users can configure their Lambda Web Function as a CloudFront origin through various means, such as the CloudFront Console, SDK, CLI, or CloudFormation, with no additional fees for this feature.

Starting today, you can deliver web applications built on AWS Lambda Web Functions through CloudFront's global edge network.  

With CloudFront in front of a Lambda Web Function, you get TLS termination at the edge for lower latency and faster connections, caching for better performance, and custom domains with managed TLS certificates. No changes to application code are needed. CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts your Lambda Web Function so it's reachable only through CloudFront, so unintended requests that bypass your security protections do not reach your origin. With OAC in place, CloudFront's edge network protects your Lambda Web Function from network-layer DDoS attacks, and you can attach AWS WAF for additional application-layer security. For applications that authenticate their own users, OAC ensures that original credentials reach the application unchanged, so existing sign-in flows keep working.

CloudFront support for AWS Lambda Web Functions is available worldwide, except in the CloudFront China region. To get started, use the CloudFront Console, SDK, CLI, or CloudFormation to configure your Lambda Web Function as a CloudFront origin. For more information, refer to the CloudFront Developer Guide. There are no additional fees associated with this feature.

item.title: Amazon EC2 G7 instances now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: G7 instances, NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500, AI inference, GPU-accelerated, AWS Regions

Summary: Amazon EC2 has introduced G7 instances, powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, available in Europe (Frankfurt and Stockholm) and other AWS Regions including US West (Oregon) and US East (N. Virginia, Ohio). G7 instances provide significant performance improvements, delivering up to 4.6x higher AI inference performance and 2.1x graphics performance compared to G6 instances. These instances are ideal for deploying AI models for various applications, such as language translation, video and image analysis, and speech recognition, as well as enhancing graphics workloads for real-time, cinematic-quality graphics and game streaming. G7 instances feature a robust infrastructure that includes up to 8 NVIDIA GPUs with 32 GB memory per GPU, custom Intel Xeon 6 processors, and support for up to 192 virtual CPUs and 700 Gbps EFA networking bandwidth. They also offer up to 768 GiB of system memory and up to 7.6 TB of local NVMe SSD storage. G7 instances can be purchased as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or through Savings Plans. For more information, users can explore official AWS resources.

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) G7 instances powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs are now available in Europe (Frankfurt) and Europe (Stockholm) Regions. G7 instances deliver up to 4.6x AI inference performance and up to 2.1 graphics performance compared to G6 instances. G7 instances also deliver faster performance for GPU-accelerated data analytics workloads.

Customers can use G7 instances for deploying AI models for language translation, video and image analysis, speech recognition and recommender systems. They also accelerate graphics workloads such as creating and rendering real-time, cinematic-quality graphics and game streaming. Additionally, G7 instances support video transcoding, spatial computing, and data analytics workloads. G7 instances feature up to 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs with 32 GB of memory per GPU and custom Intel Xeon 6 processors. They support up to 192 virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and up to 700 Gbps of Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking bandwidth. They also support up to 768 GiB of system memory, and up to 7.6 TB of local NVMe SSD storage.

You can use G7 instances for Amazon EC2 in the following AWS Regions: US West (Oregon), US East (N. Virginia, Ohio) and Europe (Spain, Frankfurt, Stockholm). You can purchase G7 instances as On-Demand Instances, Spot Instances, or as part of Savings Plans.

To get started, visit the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (CLI), and AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the G7 instance page.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer now prefills step-by-step guides for after contact work
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, information extraction, step-by-step guides, agents, data accuracy

Summary: Amazon Connect now allows customers to streamline the after-contact processes for agents by automatically populating step-by-step guides with pertinent information extracted from customer conversations, such as booking identifiers, claim numbers, and conversation summaries. This feature enables managers to define which specific information will be extracted and used to fill out the relevant fields in these guides. As a result, contact center agents no longer need to manually input frequently used information, significantly reducing the time spent on after-contact work. For instance, an insurance agent can swiftly review and submit essential details like policy numbers and call summaries after each claim call. By implementing this automation, agents can efficiently check and correct any discrepancies in the extracted data before submission, minimizing data entry errors. This functionality is currently available in several AWS Regions, including US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and multiple Asia Pacific, Europe, and Canada regions. Additionally, contact summaries can be utilized in Africa (Cape Town). For more details and guidance, customers are encouraged to refer to the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

Amazon Connect Customer can now fill in the step-by-step guides that agents complete after a contact, using information extracted from customer conversations, such as booking identifiers, claim numbers, and conversation summaries. Managers can set which information populates each form field. Agents can review and submit rather than manually typing in each field, saving time and improving data accuracy during after contact work.

Contact center agents spend time after each contact entering frequently used information into a step-by-step guide. For example, an insurance agent who finishes a claims call might record the customer’s policy number, a summary of the call, and a disposition code. Now, managers can define rules for which information to extract from the conversation and which fields to automatically fill in the guide. The agent can then check the information, make any necessary corrections, and submit the guide, shortening after contact work and reducing data entry errors.

You can use step-by-step guides with information extraction in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London). Contact summaries are also available in Africa (Cape Town).

To learn more and get started, see step-by-step guides in the Amazon Connect Customer administrator guide.

item.title: AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Lambda, Web Functions, serverless, HTTP requests, Node.js

Summary: AWS Lambda has introduced Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute solution that allows developers to manage HTTP requests directly, similar to traditional HTTP servers. This feature supports popular frameworks such as Express and Hono without needing additional configuration. It's particularly suited for applications like AI inference, server-side rendered web apps, streaming APIs, and microservices. Users pay only for active CPU usage and memory, avoiding costs during idle times. Existing Lambda functions will be renamed to Lambda Event Functions without requiring code changes or redeployments. Lambda facilitates rapid production deployments without server management, enhancing efficiency for event-driven applications. The Node.js runtime supports these new web functions, and a single warm execution environment can handle multiple requests, minimizing cold start issues. Developers can create and manage Lambda Web Functions using various tools, including AWS CLI and Management Console. The feature also supports multi-Region routing to deliver requests from the nearest location to the user and provides VPC connectivity. Currently, Lambda Web Functions is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland) regions.

AWS Lambda announces Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute primitive where your code handles HTTP requests directly. Your code listens on a port and handles requests as it would on any HTTP server. You use frameworks you already know, such as Express or Hono, with no adapters or custom configuration. This enables you to serve workloads such as AI inference endpoints, server-side rendered (SSR) web apps, streaming API endpoints, microservices, and webhooks. You pay for active CPU time and the memory your environment holds, not for idle CPU time your code spends waiting on databases or downstream services. With this launch, we are also renaming existing Lambda functions to Lambda Event Functions, a naming change only that requires no code changes or redeployments for your existing functions.

Builders use Lambda to go from code to production quickly and without managing servers, across event-driven pipelines, request-response APIs, and data processing. As AI-driven development accelerates, they want to build locally and deploy with a familiar programming model and pay for workloads based on active CPU usage, while serving users with low latency. Lambda Web Functions delivers this. Today, Lambda Web Functions supports the Node.js runtime. A single warm execution environment can serve multiple concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts by orders of magnitude. You can stream results to clients incrementally with native HTTP streaming.

You can create and configure Lambda Web Functions using the AWS Lambda API, Agent Toolkit for AWS, AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, AWS CDK, or the AWS SDKs. With multi-Region routing, you can deploy once and serve each request from the Region closest to the end user. Web Functions support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

Lambda Web Functions is available today in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). For the current list, see the AWS Capabilities by Region page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions developer guide. For pricing details, see AWS Lambda Pricing.  To see Lambda Web Functions in action, see the AWS News Blog announcement.

item.title: Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, consumption-based pricing, short-term memory, AWS Regions

Summary: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore has introduced consumption-based pricing for its short-term memory (STM), moving away from a flat rate per event. This new pricing model is advantageous for developers whose agents frequently write small events, as they will only pay for what they actually use. STM pricing is divided into three components: ingestion costs $1.00 per GB, retrieval costs $0.20 per GB, and storage is billed at $0.10 per GB-month. Ingestion and retrieval are charged per event, with a minimum of 12 KB and a maximum of 64 KB for billable sizes, while storage fees reflect the actual size of each event. Many workloads can expect cost reductions under this new pricing, especially those with smaller payloads. To better manage expenses, users have the option to set a shorter time to live (TTL) for their memory resources. It's important to note that pricing for long-term memory remains unchanged. This new pricing structure is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is offered. For more information on how to implement this, developers are encouraged to visit the provided resources.

Announcing consumption-based pricing for short-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory now prices short-term memory (STM) based on the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store, replacing the previous flat rate per event. AgentCore memory gives agents in-session context through short-term memory and persistent knowledge across sessions through long-term memory. With consumption-based pricing, developers building agents that write frequent, small events pay in proportion to what they use.

STM is priced across three dimensions: ingestion at $1.00 per GB, retrieval at $0.20 per GB, and storage at $0.10 per GB-month. Ingestion and retrieval are billed per event with a 12 KB minimum and 64 KB maximum billable size, while storage is billed on each event's actual size. Most workloads see lower costs, with small-payload use cases seeing the largest reductions. You can manage storage costs by setting a shorter time to live (TTL) on your memory resources. Long-term memory pricing is unchanged.

Consumption-based pricing for AgentCore Memory short-term memory is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore Memory is offered. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing page.

item.title: AWS Transfer Family supports custom ports for public SFTP servers
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Transfer Family, SFTP servers, communication modes, custom ports, client-first

Summary: AWS Transfer Family now allows the configuration of custom ports on public SFTP servers, enabling support for clients requiring different ports or connection methods on a single server. Previously, public SFTP servers only accepted connections on port 22 with server-first communication. With the new feature, users can configure up to three ports (including port 22 and any port from 2000 to 65535), accommodating specific business or network requirements. This enhancement facilitates the management of multiple ports on one server. Additionally, it addresses issues with certain SFTP clients that initiate communication differently, which can lead to stalled connections on server-first ports. Users can now select either client-first or server-first communication modes for each port, directing clients based on their connection behavior. Utilizing a port other than 22 can also minimize unwanted connection attempts from automated scanners that typically target port 22. This feature is available across all AWS Regions where Transfer Family public SFTP servers are offered. To get started, users can access the AWS Transfer Family console or utilize the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. More information can be found in the documentation for creating an SFTP-enabled server.

AWS Transfer Family now lets you configure custom ports on public SFTP servers and choose a communication mode for each port. You can support clients that require different ports or start SFTP connections differently on a single server.

Previously, public SFTP servers accepted connections only on port 22 and used server-first communication. With this launch, you can configure up to three ports (22, or any port from 2000 to 65535), allowing you to use the port numbers your business or network requires and offer multiple ports on one server. Some SFTP clients initiate communication themselves, and their connections can occasionally stall on a server-first port. For each port, you can now select client-first or server-first communication and direct clients to the port that matches their connection behavior. Using a port other than 22 can also reduce unwanted connection attempts from automated scanners that target port 22.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where Transfer Family public SFTP servers are offered. To get started, visit the AWS Transfer Family console or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit Create an SFTP-enabled server in the AWS Transfer Family User Guide

item.title: Amazon S3 Express One Zone is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon S3, Express One Zone, storage class, AWS Regions, high-performance

Summary: Amazon S3 Express One Zone storage class has expanded into four additional AWS Regions: Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), and Africa (Cape Town). This storage class is designed for high-performance, operating within a single Availability Zone, providing consistent single-digit millisecond data access for frequently accessed data and latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone offers data access speeds up to 10 times faster and request costs that can be reduced by up to 80% compared to S3 Standard. This makes it ideal for workloads like machine learning training, interactive analytics, and key-value caching in AI search engines, allowing for rapid data access coupled with high durability and availability. With this recent expansion, S3 Express One Zone can now cater to a broader range of users and applications across these new regions. For those looking for pricing details, it is recommended to visit the official AWS pricing page, while additional information about S3 Express One Zone can be found on the AWS website.

The Amazon S3 Express One Zone storage class is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions: Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), and Africa (Cape Town).

Amazon S3 Express One Zone is a high-performance, single-Availability Zone storage class purpose-built to deliver consistent single-digit millisecond data access for your most frequently accessed data and latency-sensitive applications. S3 Express One Zone delivers data access speed up to 10x faster and request costs up to 80% lower than S3 Standard. It enables workloads such as machine learning training, interactive analytics, and key-value caching in AI search engines to achieve fast data access with high durability and availability.

With this expansion, S3 Express One Zone is now available in 19 AWS Regions. For pricing details, visit the S3 pricing page. To learn more, visit the product page and documentation.

item.title: AWS Secrets Manager adds managed external secrets support for Databricks and Twilio
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Secrets Manager, Databricks, Twilio, rotation, credentials

Summary: AWS Secrets Manager has expanded its managed external secrets capability to include Databricks and Twilio, providing automatic credential rotation for data pipelines and messaging applications. This feature allows users to set up rotation directly through the AWS Management Console or API, eliminating the need for custom rotation Lambda functions. Long-lived credentials often remain unrotated due to setup challenges, but with managed external secrets, users can rotate Databricks personal access tokens and service principal OAuth client secrets easily. Each new token maintains the scopes of the previous one, ensuring continued security. For Twilio, users can rotate API keys and Auth Tokens utilized for messaging and calling services. Both integrations enable storing credentials in Secrets Manager as managed external secrets with a defined rotation schedule. Secrets Manager ensures that applications automatically use the current credential, necessitating no code changes. These new integrations complement existing support for services such as BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, and others. Databricks and Twilio managed external secrets are now available in all AWS Regions where this feature is supported, allowing organizations enhanced security and operational efficiency. To learn more, users are encouraged to visit the AWS website.

AWS Secrets Manager now extends its managed external secrets capability to include Databricks and Twilio, enabling you to automatically rotate the credentials that your data pipelines and messaging applications use to call these services. You set up rotation directly from the AWS Management Console or API without writing or maintaining any custom rotation Lambda functions.

Long-lived credentials often stay unrotated because rotation is hard to set up and hard to distribute safely to the applications that use the updated credential. With managed external secrets, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the Databricks personal access tokens that your jobs and continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines use. You can also rotate the service principal OAuth client secrets that your automation workflows use. Each replacement personal access token retains the scopes of the token it replaces, so a narrowly scoped token stays narrowly scoped.

For Twilio, you can use Secrets Manager to rotate the API keys and Auth Tokens that your applications use to send messages and place calls. For both services, you store the credential in Secrets Manager as a managed external secret and set a rotation schedule. Secrets Manager always returns the current credential, so your applications pick up rotated values automatically, with no code changes required.

These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, and SonarQube.

Databricks and Twilio managed external secrets are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets is supported. To learn more, visit the  AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets documentation.

item.title: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey introduces ElastiCache Insights
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: ElastiCache Insights, Amazon CloudWatch, node-based clusters, metrics, dashboard

Summary: ElastiCache now offers ElastiCache Insights, a pre-built dashboard in Amazon CloudWatch designed specifically for node-based clusters. This feature consolidates essential metrics such as cluster health, memory usage, compute performance, network activity, command throughput, latency, keyspace, and errors into a single view. The data is derived from OpenTelemetry metrics that ElastiCache automatically publishes. Users can easily monitor their cache workloads across an entire Region, identify when nodes reach memory, network, or connection limits, and customize their views based on clusters, shards, nodes, or Availability Zones. The Insights dashboard also allows users to save a customized version to match their specific workload requirements. Additionally, detailed monitoring can be set up to publish metrics every 15 seconds, accessible through the Metrics tab or a personalized dashboard. To utilize ElastiCache Insights, users simply navigate to the Metrics tab for a cluster and select "View in ElastiCache Insights" or find it under Infrastructure Monitoring in the Amazon CloudWatch console. This feature is available for node-based Valkey clusters across all AWS Regions that support OpenTelemetry metrics. For more detailed information, users are directed to the Amazon ElastiCache User Guide.

Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey now features ElastiCache Insights, a pre-built dashboard in Amazon CloudWatch for your node-based clusters. ElastiCache Insights brings cluster health, memory, compute, network, command throughput, latency, keyspace, and errors into a single view sourced from a set of OpenTelemetry metrics that ElastiCache publishes automatically.

You can use ElastiCache Insights to check the health of your cache workloads across a Region at a glance, detect when a node nears its memory, network, or connection limits, and filter your view to a cluster, shard, node, or Availability Zone. You can also save a copy as the starting point for a custom dashboard tailored to your workload.

With detailed monitoring, you can choose metrics to publish every 15 seconds and view them on the Metrics tab or in your custom dashboard. CloudWatch pricing for OpenTelemetry metrics applies to ElastiCache detailed monitoring.

To get started, open the Metrics tab for a cluster in the Amazon ElastiCache console and choose View in ElastiCache Insights. You can also choose ElastiCache Insights under Infrastructure Monitoring in the Amazon CloudWatch console.

ElastiCache Insights is available for node-based Valkey clusters in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. To learn more about ElastiCache Insights, see Monitoring ElastiCache with OpenTelemetry metrics in the Amazon ElastiCache User Guide.

item.title: Amazon EMR now supports native data quality checks in Apache Spark jobs
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon EMR, Data Quality, Apache Spark, validation rules, AWS Glue

Summary: Amazon EMR now offers native data quality validation within Apache Spark jobs, enabling data engineering teams to identify quality issues before they affect downstream systems. This feature, called Amazon EMR Data Quality, is powered by AWS Glue and incurs no additional costs. It employs the same Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) and APIs as AWS Glue, ensuring a consistent user experience across both platforms. The feature supports data formats such as Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, and Delta Lake, and is compatible with various deployment modes including EC2, EKS, and Serverless. Users can author validation rules within their Spark scripts or reference those stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, applying them at any stage of their data pipeline. With over 30 available rule types—including dynamic rules for historical comparisons and ML-based anomaly detection—Amazon EMR Data Quality allows users to customize their validation approach. Based on evaluation results, users can take actions such as failing a pipeline, filtering out invalid records, or quarantining them. Detailed results are provided at the dataset, rule, and row levels, enabling efficient identification of quality failures. This feature is available on AWS runtime for Apache Spark (emr-spark-8.1.0) across all AWS regions.

Amazon EMR now validates data quality natively within Apache Spark jobs. Data engineering teams can catch quality issues inline before bad data reaches downstream systems, without building or maintaining separate validation infrastructure. Amazon EMR Data Quality, powered by AWS Glue, is available at no additional cost and uses the same declarative rules language (Data Quality Definition Language) and APIs as AWS Glue for a consistent experience across both engines, and works with Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi, and Delta Lake across EC2, EKS, and Serverless deployment modes.

With this feature, you can author validation rules in your Spark scripts or reference rules stored in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and then apply them at any stage of your pipeline i.e., after reading data, during transformation, or after processing. With 30+ rule types, including dynamic rules that compare against historical runs and ML-based anomaly detection for tracking drift over time without specifying fixed thresholds, Amazon EMR Data Quality provides the flexibility of choosing the validation framework that fits your needs. You can take actions like failing a pipeline, filtering invalid records, or routing them to quarantine based on the quality evaluation results. Results are produced at the dataset, rule, and row level, so that you can easily identify which records or rules are driving the quality failures.

Amazon EMR Data Quality is available on AWS runtime for Apache Spark (emr-spark-8.1.0) in all AWS Commercial, AWS GovCloud (US), and AWS China Regions.

To get started, visit Amazon EMR Data Quality documentation and add DQDL rules for data quality validation to the Spark scripts of your EMR workloads.

item.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption
item.content:encoded:
Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports index-level encryption, letting you encrypt each index at rest with its own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. This helps you protect data with different ownership or sensitivity under separate keys on the same domain. For example, you can encrypt each tenant's data with its own key in a multi-tenant application.

Index-level encryption builds on the existing encryption at rest capability in Amazon OpenSearch Service. To enable it, set the encryption mode to Native and specify a customer managed AWS KMS key when you create a new domain using the AWS Management Console or the AWS CLI. You can then register additional keys with the domain and use them to encrypt individual indexes.

Index-level encryption is available for domains running OpenSearch version 3.3 or later in 14 AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Paris), and South America (São Paulo). There is no additional charge for the feature. Standard AWS KMS and OpenSearch Service charges apply.

To get started, see Index-level encryption in the Amazon OpenSearch Service Developer Guide.

item.title: AWS now lets customers sign up for AWS and pay invoices using ACH direct debit
item.content:encoded:
Starting today, AWS customers in the United States can use a US bank account to sign up for AWS and pay for their AWS services through ACH direct debit. This feature provides a convenient and secure way to manage AWS payments directly from a USD bank account.

Customers can securely connect a personal or business US bank account and use it to pay AWS invoices. Previously, new AWS customers needed a credit or debit card to complete signing up for an account.

During sign-up, customers can choose Bank Account on the AWS sign-up page, select their bank, and authenticate using their bank's mobile app or online banking credentials. This securely verifies ownership and links their bank account to their AWS account. By default, the account will be used to pay future AWS invoices.

Existing customers can add a bank account from the Payment preferences page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. They choose Add payment method, select Link your bank account, and follow the same bank-selection and authentication flow. Once verified, the bank account is available as a payment method to pay future AWS invoices..

ACH direct debit is available at no additional cost to AWS customers for USD bank accounts. To learn more, see Managing ACH direct debit.
