item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.24: SQL ORM names every table in a statement through one scope (#30646)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a — no Linear ticket; second of three PRs for cross-namespace
inheritance (first: #30577). The third PR re-keys contract variants by
discriminator value and adds multi-table-inheritance (MTI) variants in
other namespaces, which needs two tables with the same name in one
statement.

At a glance

From
packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/include-table-aliases.test.ts:

collection
  .select('id')
  .include('invitedUsers', (invited) =>
    invited.select('id').where((user) => user.name.eq('Bob')),
  )
SELECT "users"."id" AS "id",
  (SELECT coalesce(json_agg(json_build_object('id', "invitedUsers__rows"."id")), json_build_array()) AS "invitedUsers"
   FROM (SELECT "users_2"."id" AS "id"
         FROM "public"."users" AS "users_2"
         WHERE ("users_2"."invited_by_id" = "users"."id" AND "users_2"."name" = $1)) AS "invitedUsers__rows") AS "invitedUsers"
FROM "public"."users"

Before this PR the included table was aliased invitedUsers__child, and
the refinement's filter was written against users and then renamed by
a string rewrite of the finished expression.

Summary

The SQL ORM named the tables of a statement with four unrelated alias
schemes and two string-based reference rewriters, and left several
repeated uses of a table unaliased. This PR replaces them with one table
scope held in collection state, so any table can appear more than once
in a statement under a distinct alias.

Decision

This PR ships one naming mechanism for every table and derived table the
SQL ORM puts in a statement, in packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client:

  1. A table scope that hands out aliases.
    TableScope.alias(preferred) returns the preferred alias on first use
    and <alias>_<n> (from 2) on later uses, at most 63 bytes.
    aliasTable(storage) returns an AliasedTable: the alias with the
    table's storage coordinate, which produces column references and table
    sources. The first use of a table gets an alias equal to its own name,
    and no AS is written.
  2. Collection state holds the scope and the aliased tables.
    CollectionState.tables has the scope, the root table and one entry per
    MTI variant table. Every planner, the model accessor, MTI joins, the row
    decoder, MTI create and row locks take table sources and column
    references from them.
  3. The old aliases and rewriters are removed. __orm_rel_<n>,
    __orm_junction_<n>, <relation>__child, <table>__write_filter, both
    createTableRefRemapper copies and resolveChildTableSource no longer
    exist.
  4. A bug fix that follows from it. A relation declared on a variant
    that targets its own hierarchy now returns correct rows.
  5. A changed exported surface. emptyState(tables), the required
    CollectionState.tables, the createModelAccessor signature, the
    optional IncludeExpr.junction, IncludeExpr.localVariantName in place
    of localTableName, and new exports createCollectionTables,
    CollectionTables, AliasedTable, TableScope,
    TableStorageCoordinate.

Notes for the reviewer

  • SQL alias text changes in cases that had no alias before. Two
    sibling relation filters over one table; names accumulating across
    separate where() calls on one chain; an include that returns to an
    ancestor's table (users → posts → author); a relation filter plus an
    include of the same table; a derived-table name needed twice, which gets
    _<n>. Names follow call order, so where(...).include(...) and
    include(...).where(...) name the two uses in opposite order.
  • A relation call that renders no SQL still takes a name.
    every({}) returns a constant-true expression, but the related table is
    bound when the call runs, so the next use of that table is numbered one
    higher. No test asserts this.
  • Count-mutation subquery. In updateAndCount / deleteAndCount on
    an MTI variant, the copy of the root table inside the EXISTS subquery
    takes a fresh name and the stored filters reference the mutation target
    directly, because neither renderer can alias an UPDATE / DELETE
    target. See buildCountMutationWhere in
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/query-plan-mutations.ts.
  • Values that were inline SQL literals are now parameters. Shorthand
    object filters, the discriminator filter and the filters nested writes
    build are created as parameters with the column's codec. In the mutation
    paths that never bound their filters this changes the SQL from a literal
    to $n: updateAndCount / deleteAndCount on a variant collection,
    the identity UPDATE of a nested update, child-owned connect /
    disconnect, and the junction DELETE of a many-to-many disconnect.
    The planner no longer re-binds stored filters, so a literal in a
    hand-built CollectionState.filters is rendered as written.
  • The 63-byte limit is a constant in the scope (MAX_NAME_BYTES in
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/table-scope.ts),
    not an adapter capability. Only table and derived-table aliases are
    bounded; projected column labels are not (see Follow-ups).
  • Largest diffs.
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/query-plan-select.ts
    (the include planner loses its remapper and the child-table-name
    parameters) and
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/model-accessor.ts.
    Most test changes are alias-text assertions and the new
    createModelAccessor / emptyState arguments.

How it fits together

  1. Codecs stop reading table names out of column references. Filters
    the ORM builds itself (shorthand object filters, cursor boundaries,
    identity filters, the discriminator filter, nested-write filters) used
    to find a parameter codec by treating ColumnRef.table as a storage
    table name, which fails once that string is an alias. Each is now built
    as a parameter with its codec, from the table's storage coordinate. The
    binder serves only expressions passed to where(), and resolves an
    alias through a map built from the collection's aliased tables. See
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/where-binding.ts.
  2. The scope.
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/table-scope.ts
    holds a set of taken aliases: it does not read the contract and knows
    nothing of relations, includes or variants. Its methods are alias,
    aliasTable and copy. The model accessor aliases relation targets and
    junction tables through it.
  3. The scope moves into collection state.
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/collection-tables.ts
    aliases a model's root table and its MTI variant tables
    (createCollectionTables). A collection's scope is never mutated:
    where(), orderBy(), grouped orderBy() and the planners allocate on
    a copy, and the copy is stored in the state they produce. Two
    collections derived from one parent therefore get the same names for the
    same calls and do not see each other's names.
  4. Includes take their aliases from the parent's scope. include()
    aliases the child's root, variant and junction tables in a copy of the
    parent's scope, runs the refinement, and the parent adopts the resulting
    scope so a later sibling cannot take the same name. combine branches
    share the child's alias. The parent adopts the scope of the collection
    the refinement was handed, so an alias a branch takes for itself stays
    within that branch and a later sibling may reuse it. The six
    derived-table names of the include planner (<relation>__rows,
    __distinct, __ranked, __scalar, __scalar_distinct,
    __combine__<branch>) are requested from the scope.
  5. No reference is renamed by table name. Both rewriters are gone
    and nothing replaces them. An expression passed to where() is used as
    written.
  6. Database tests, docs and upgrade instructions. A new PSL fixture
    with a polymorphic model related to its own hierarchy, a README section
    on the tables in collection state, and a pending upgrade fragment for
    extension authors.

Behavior changes & evidence

  • A variant-declared relation that targets its own hierarchy returns
    correct rows.     The child's variant join was unaliased and captured the
    parent correlation; the child's variant table now has its own alias.
  • Implementation:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/collection-tables.ts,
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/query-plan-source.ts
  • Evidence:
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/polymorphism-self-relation.test.ts,
    fixture
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/fixtures/polymorphism-self-relation/contract.prisma
  • Relation filters and relation orders name their tables <table>,
    <table>_2, …     in place of __orm_rel_<n> / __orm_junction_<n>, and
    two filters over one table get separate aliases.
  • Implementation:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/model-accessor.ts
  • Evidence:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/relation-filter-aliases.test.ts,
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/table-scope.test.ts
  • Includes name their tables from the parent's scope in place of
    <relation>__child, including an include that returns to an ancestor's
    table and sibling includes of one table.
  • Implementation:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/collection.ts,
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/query-plan-select.ts
  • Evidence:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/include-table-aliases.test.ts,
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/self-relations.test.ts
  • Count mutations on an MTI variant name the subquery's table copy
    <table>_<n>     in place of <table>__write_filter.
  • Implementation:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/query-plan-mutations.ts
  • Evidence:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/collection-tables.test.ts,
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/polymorphism-self-relation.test.ts
  • Filters the ORM builds are parameters with the column's codec,
    including in mutation statements that used to render the value inline,
    and a literal in an expression passed to where() binds there,
    including on an MTI variant column.
  • Implementation:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/src/where-binding.ts
  • Evidence:
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/mutation-executor.test.ts,
    packages/3-extensions/sql-orm-client/test/collection-tables.test.ts,
    test/integration/test/sql-orm-client/polymorphism-self-relation.test.ts

Compatibility / migration / risk

  • No contract, emitter, adapter or Mongo change. The shared SQL AST
    is unchanged; a reference is still a plain string in ColumnRef.table.
  • Query results are unchanged apart from the fix above. Generated
    SQL text changes (aliases, and some inline values becoming parameters).
  • Exported surface (re-exported by
    @prisma/orm-family-sql/orm-client): code that builds
    CollectionState, calls emptyState() or createModelAccessor(), or
    writes a many-to-many IncludeExpr by hand must change.
  • Upgrade instructions are pending for extension authors, covering
    the changed state shape only:
    upgrade-instructions/pending/collection-state-tables/extension/instructions.md.
    Generated SQL text is not public API and has no upgrade entry.

Testing performed

On the current branch:

  • sql-orm-client package: lint, typecheck and test (120 files, 1529
    tests)
  • Integration: typecheck, test/sql-orm-client (117 files, 822 tests)
    and the planner golden
  • pnpm lint:deps
  • pnpm fixtures:check
  • pnpm check:upgrade-coverage

The gates above ran after merging the latest main into the branch. The
full pnpm test:packages and pnpm test:integration last ran before
the rebases onto rc.16 and rc.17. Their only failures were
local-environment ones: the Prisma 7 engine download returning 404 on
NixOS, the ERR_PNPM_TRUST_DOWNGRADE tarball tests, and broken symlinks
in the local node_modules. CI is the first full run on the rebased
branch.

Skill update

No skill update is required, and the diff touches no skill. The change
is an internal naming mechanism. No public query API changes; an
extension author who builds ORM state by hand sees the changed state
shape, which the upgrade fragment and the README section cover.

Follow-ups

Known gaps this PR does not change:

  • updateAll / deleteAll with a filter on an MTI variant field: the
    filter reaches a base-table statement that does not join the variant
    table.
  • Cursor pagination ordered by an MTI variant field: the cursor column
    is bound to the base table.
  • The value a grouped having comparison is checked against is still an
    inline literal, because the grouped planner rejects a parameter there.
  • Base relations are not typed on a variant collection:
    tasks.variant('feature').include('subtasks') is a type error although
    it works at runtime.
  • Projected column labels (<alias>__<column>) are not bounded to 63
    bytes.

Alternatives considered

  • Name tables in a pass at statement assembly. References would have
    to stay unresolved until the statement is complete, which means a change
    to the shared SQL AST or a rename of stored references. Naming a table
    when it is bound keeps ColumnRef.table a plain string and leaves
    callback timing and error timing as they are.
  • A unique reference per combine branch. The branches are sibling
    subqueries that cannot see each other, so one shared reference is valid
    SQL. Unique names would require renaming references already stored in
    each branch's state.
  • Keep one rename for expressions passed to where() on an aliased
    child.     On main, the rewriter moved such an expression's references
    to <relation>__child. Keeping that would leave one string rename in
    the package for a case no code in the repo uses, so the expression is
    used as written; the extension upgrade note says so.
  • Keep shorthand and discriminator filters as literals and bind them
    at plan time.     That leaves the SQL of the unbound mutation paths
    unchanged, but those paths write the value into the SQL text without the
    column's codec. Building the parameter where the filter is built fixes
    that and removes plan-time re-binding.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO. The DCO
    status check will block merge if any commit is missing a
    Signed-off-by: trailer.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (or n/a if the change is doc-only / refactor
    with no behavioural delta).
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form (Linear
    ticket prefix + concise title naming the concrete deliverable). See
    .claude/skills/create-pr/SKILL.md for the full convention. — Not
    ticked: no Linear ticket exists for this work, so the title has no
    TML- prefix.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in (or stated n/a — internal only).

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Signed-off-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Steven McClankerton tatarintsev@prisma.io
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 noreply@anthropic.com

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.23: TML-3282: Close out the SQL expression literals project (#30690)
item.content:encoded:
At a glance

The SQL expression literals project is finished. Raw SQL is one value
everywhere:

@@check(expression: sql`
  owner_id > 0
    AND char_length(email) > 0
`, name: "profile_valid")
check({ expression: sql`owner_id > 0 AND char_length(email) > 0`, name: 'profile_valid' });
// generated migration.ts
checkExpression('profile_valid_5901ae2d', sql`owner_id > 0 AND char_length(email) > 0`)

This PR closes the project: it deletes
projects/sql-expression-literals/, after moving the decisions that
lived only there into ADR 268, and records two lessons from the project
in the team's Drive calibration.

Decision

The project's transient files go. What must outlive them now lives in
ADRs, the subsystem docs, Drive calibration and Linear:

  • ADR 268 gains four alternatives that were recorded only in the
    project's design notes: holding opaque SQL in DDL as the query AST's
    RawExpr, migration functions that take only sql values, leaving
    generated migration files on strings, and a public builder for sql
    values from computed strings. Its status line now lists sql values in
    generated migration files as built.
  • drive/calibration/failure-modes.md gains F47 (a stack of PRs
    outlives its base's squash merge, and the last PR passes 250 commits,
    which the DCO check cannot read) and F48 (a new committed contract
    fixture fails the planner golden test, which only the merge queue runs).
    drive/calibration/dod.md adds the planner golden step to the slice
    gate before queueing.
  • projects/data-types-completion/design-notes.md pointed at this
    project's design file; it now points at ADR 231, ADR 254 and TML-3367.

Where each project decision lives

Decision (project design notes) Durable home
Every place that holds raw SQL takes a sql literal ADR 268, ADR
129
Plain strings are refused ADR 268
A sql literal is a value of the data type sql/expression; only
@default checks the text ADR 268, ADR 254, ADR 129
The SQL family defines and registers sql/expression (the notes'
first version said each target registers it; the family does) ADR 268,
ADR 254
The only tag is sql ADR 268, ADR 129
Specs name the data type an argument receives (dataTypeValue) ADR
231, ADR 249, ADR 262
The TypeScript builder takes sql values ADR 268, ADR 129
contract infer prints sql literals, and skips or notes text that
would not read back ADR 129, ADR 268
Opaque SQL is its own DDL value, OpaqueSql Migration System
subsystem doc, "Opaque SQL in DDL"; ADR 268 (alternative)
Migration files write sql values when they read back unchanged ADR
195 ("Recorded exception"), ADR 268, Migration System doc
Wire names keep line breaks in bodies with -- ADR 234
One set of codes for cast-rule refusals ADR 268, ADR 254
The decision gets its own ADR ADR 268
The typed argument ships first, for the "Data types own column types"
project Delivered as TML-3367; the default-function argument work is
TML-3389
Grammar versus database values ADR 231

Project definition of done

  • Delivered: all seven slices merged.

    Slice PR Linear
    2a #30534 TML-3296
    2t #30539 TML-3367
    1 #30546 TML-3287
    4 #30554 TML-3290
    2b #30550 TML-3288
    3 #30558 TML-3289
    5 #30677 TML-3297

    Every Linear issue is Done.

  • Review and manual QA: every slice that changed what a user sees
    had design and code reviews, a fixes check, and a manual QA run.

  • Follow-ups filed:

  • TML-3554: two Postgres migration operations paste raw SQL into DDL as
    strings.

    • TML-3555: a raw SQL column default cannot hold a -- comment.

A gap found in QA, now() - interval '1 day' failing apply's default
check, is on TML-2362, which replaces that comparison. Two deferred
items need no ticket:

  • contract infer and defaults that do not read back: slice 3 decided
    and built it.
  • A builder for sql values from computed strings: recorded in ADR 268
    as not offered.
  • References: nothing outside the deleted folder points into it.

Testing performed

  • pnpm lint:docs, pnpm lint:legacy-name and pnpm check:upgrade-coverage --mode pr pass.
  • This PR changes only docs, Drive calibration and the deleted project
    folder.

Linked issue

Closes out the Linear project SQL expression
literals
(TML-3282).

Skill update

n/a — docs and project files only.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (n/a, docs only).
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in.

Alternatives considered

DataCube: A Relational Aggregation Operator Generalizing Group-By, Cross-Tab, and Sub-Totals (1997)
item.content:encoded:
Abstract: Data analysis applications typically aggregate data across many dimensions looking for anomalies or unusual patterns. The SQL aggregate functions and the GROUP BY operator produce zero-dimensional or one-dimensional aggregates. Applications need the N-dimensional generalization of these operators. This paper defines that operator, called the data cube or simply cube. The cube operator generalizes the histogram, cross-tabulation, roll-up, drill-down, and sub-total constructs found in most report writers. The novelty is that cubes are relations. Consequently, the cube operator can be imbedded in more complex non-procedural data analysis programs. The cube operator treats each of the N aggregation attributes as a dimension of N-space. The aggregate of a particular set of attribute values is a point in this space. The set of points forms an N-dimensional cube. Super-aggregates are computed by aggregating the N-cube to lower dimensional spaces. This paper (1) explains the cube and roll-up operators, (2) shows how they fit in SQL, (3) explains how users can define new aggregate functions for cubes, and (4) discusses efficient techniques to compute the cube. Many of these features are being added to the SQL Standard.

Microservices, Core, Enhancements, Dependencies, Bug fixes

Summary: The release v12.0.4 on September 21, 2026, includes various bug fixes across microservices and core functionalities. In the microservices section, several issues have been addressed, allowing the Kafka client to retry after a failed connection, ensuring pending RabbitMQ (RMQ) and NATS requests are appropriately failed when the client closes, and implementing graceful handling for missing gRPC package namespaces. Additionally, the processing hook envelope is now shared across transports, and the closure of both the Kafka and general request-response spans is ensured to occur exactly once. It also includes a fix for routing message handler rejections to the `handleError` method. In the core segment, a fix for hanging on sparse factory inject arrays has been made. Enhancements in the platform-express involve merging multer limits in a more granular way instead of an all-or-nothing approach. The common module marks options for the parse date pipe as optional. **Keywords:** React, Server Components, performance, decoding, improvements

Summary: React Server Components represent a significant advancement in building user interfaces, primarily by optimizing rendering time and improving overall performance. One of the key improvements is in how data is decoded for rendering; by processing components on the server, React reduces the amount of JavaScript that needs to be sent to the client. This leads to a smaller bundle size, which directly impacts load times. Server Components work seamlessly with traditional client-side components, allowing developers to gradually adopt them into existing projects without needing a complete overhaul. Another important aspect is the ability to stream component responses, enabling users to see parts of the UI load progressively rather than waiting for the entire page to render. This improves the perceived performance of web applications, making them more responsive and user-friendly. With simplified data fetching and rendering logic, developers can focus more on building features rather than tackling performance issues. Ultimately, React Server Components promise a more efficient, scalable, and enjoyable development experience while enhancing the end-user interaction with web applications.

item.title: 19.1.9 (July 21st, 2026)
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: React, Server Components, Performance, Decoding, Optimization

Summary: React Server Components provide a way to enhance performance by separating the server-side rendering and client-side operations. The architecture of Server Components allows the loading of the necessary data on the server, reducing the amount of JavaScript needed on the client side. This minimizes the bundle size, making applications load faster. Performance improvements are particularly evident during decoding, where the server handles heavy lifting, sending only the required HTML to the client. This reduces the time spent on parsing and executing scripts on the client’s side. Additionally, by utilizing streaming and suspense, React Server Components can prioritize what content is delivered first based on user interaction, further optimizing the user experience. Another significant benefit is reducing hydration costs since less JavaScript means that the client can become interactive more quickly. Overall, React Server Components lead to faster load times, improved interactivity, and a smoother experience for users, particularly on mobile devices or slower networks. This approach aligns with modern web development practices that prioritize performance and user-centric design. The shift towards using Server Components indicates a significant advancement in how React handles rendering and performance optimization.

item.title: v2.264.0
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Gateway, CloudWatch, Metrics, Glue, Alpha

Summary: The recent update introduces significant breaking changes in the `bedrockagentcore` and `glue-alpha` modules. In `bedrockagentcore`, gateway metric helpers now emit corrected CloudWatch dimensions for metrics using `{ Operation, Protocol, Resource }` instead of just `{ Resource }`. Likewise, RuntimeBase metric helpers have updated metrics dimensions to include `{ Operation, Name, Resource }` for individual metrics and `{ AggregateOperation }` for aggregated metrics, necessitating updates to existing alarms and dashboards. New features include updates to L1 CloudFormation resource definitions and support for alarm mute rules in CloudWatch. Bug fixes address the correct emission of gateway and runtime metrics, warning for CloudFront configurations missing certificates, and expanding EBS volume capacities. In the `glue-alpha` module, significant breaking changes involve the removal of `IDatabase.catalogArn` and `IDatabase.catalogId`, replaced with a type-safe `ICatalog`. New features include a new Catalog L2 and enhanced encryption for S3Table. Bug fixes enable key rotation for security configurations and simplify VPC interface referencing in `mediaconnect-alpha`. These changes are crucial for developers to adapt their implementations accordingly.

⚠ BREAKING CHANGES

  • bedrockagentcore: Gateway metric helpers now emit corrected CloudWatch dimensions per-gateway
    metrics use { Operation, Protocol, Resource } (was { Resource }). Alarms/dashboards built on the
    old dimensions must be updated.
  • bedrockagentcore: RuntimeBase metric helpers now emit corrected CloudWatch dimensions per-resource metrics use { Operation, Name, Resource } (was { Resource }) and aggregated metrics use { AggregateOperation } (was { Resource: 'All' }). Alarms/dashboards built on the old dimensions must be updated.

Features

  • update L1 CloudFormation resource definitions (#38526) (b5693cb)
  • cloudwatch: support alarm mute rules (#37504) (c3540bb), closes #37502

Bug Fixes

item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Turbopack, webp, GC, snapshots, error message

Summary: The server error inspector has received a core change where error message lines are no longer parsed as stack frames, improving clarity when dealing with server errors. In a significant update, Turbopack has removed the feature flag for webp support, now enabling it by default across builds to streamline the development process and enhance image optimization capabilities. Additionally, per-shard modified counts have been eliminated from snapshots, which should simplify snapshot management and reduce complexity. To further enhance performance, garbage collection (GC) has been enabled by default on the canary release, contributing to improved memory management. Furthermore, two specific paths related to GC have been fixed to prevent issues that could leave partial or incomplete dependency edges, ensuring better consistency and stability in the dependency management system. Finally, acknowledgments and thanks have been given to unnamed contributors who assisted in implementing these changes, underscoring the collaborative effort put into these updates.

Core Changes

  • Don't parse error message lines as stack frames in the server error inspector: #99888
  • Turbopack: Remove webp feature flag, always build with webp enabled: #99964

Misc Changes

  • [turbopack] Remove per-shard modified counts from snapshots: #99955
  • Enable GC by default on canary: #99596
  • [turbopack] Fix two GC paths that leave half-torn-down dependency edges: #99902

Byte Language Models: Scaling, Emergent Abstractions, and Information Allocation
item.content:encoded:
The paper challenges the assumption that language models need explicit tokenizers to be efficient demonstrating that standard flat Transformers can process raw byte sequences and actually outperform traditional subword models as parameter sizes scale. The prevailing thought in the field has been that processing raw bytes is computationally inefficient because the sequences are substantially longer. A typical subword contains around four bytes. The authors argue that this extra sequence length is actually a feature that provides useful additional computation under the same parameter budget. By implementing token-superposition training and hash embeddings, the byte models consistently hit lower optimal loss than subword models at matched parameter counts.

It's also interesting to see how the byte model handles the lack of explicit text abstractions. We usually rely on tokenizers to group characters into meaningful chunks, but it turns out that byte Transformers implicitly develop their own local abstractions without needing specialized hierarchical architectures. When tested on a copying task, the model attention concentrated heavily on a small set of specific segmentation positions rather than attending uniformly across the text. The researchers proved the strength of these internal structures by freezing up to a quarter of the intermediate layers and forcing them to process only these locally aggregated representations. The model maintained its downstream performance without any additional training, proving that the hierarchy of local abstraction and global reasoning emerges naturally within a standard Transformer.

Also, per-byte loss distribution showed massive variance compared to subword models. A huge number of byte positions have near-zero loss showing that the model is highly confident about most bytes in a word and only struggles near the boundaries of its learned local structures where the actual information density lies. This creates a massive opportunity for speculative decoding. Because so many bytes are predictable continuations, a small drafting model can accurately guess large chunks of the sequence. The authors found that a byte-level drafting model gets roughly 3.4 times more accepted tokens per target forward pass than a subword equivalent which easily offsets the sequential overhead of processing individual bytes.

In empirical tests, byte Transformers showed massive improvements in tasks requiring fine-grained perception. They achieved around a 40% relative improvement on CUTE word manipulation scores and a 20% boost on OCRBench compared to subword models. The implications for future language model design is that we might be nearing the end of rigid subword vocabularies. Sequence length, learned abstractions, and compute allocation are now closely connected dimensions for future architectures. Instead of building complex hierarchical networks to compress bytes, designers can use flat Transformers with sparse mixture of experts to reduce activated computation while letting the model allocate its compute dynamically to the hardest parts of a text. This could also drastically improve multimodal models because byte-level representations align much better with fine-grained visual features than arbitrary subword tokens do.

AWS Security Hub now exports findings to S3 in CSV or JSON format
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Security Hub, findings export, Amazon S3, CSV, OCSF

Summary: AWS Security Hub has announced a new feature enabling users to export findings directly to Amazon S3 in either CSV or JSON (Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework - OCSF) format. This functionality is designed for security teams that require access to findings outside the Security Hub console for tasks such as compliance reporting and audit evidence. Users can export findings from all sections of the Security Hub console, including Threats, Exposure, Vulnerabilities, Posture Management, Sensitive Data, and All Findings, without the need for developing their own data extraction pipelines. The export process can be initiated on demand from the findings page currently being viewed, allowing Security Hub to deliver results to an S3 bucket within the user's account. Choosing CSV format is suitable for reviewing or sharing findings in spreadsheet applications, while JSON format is more appropriate for integrating findings in OCSF. This new feature of findings export is accessible in all AWS Regions where AWS Security Hub operates. For further details, users are encouraged to visit the AWS Security Hub User Guide.

Today, AWS Security Hub announces support for exporting findings to Amazon S3 in CSV or JSON (OCSF) format. Security teams that need findings outside the console for use cases such as compliance reporting and audit evidence can now export findings from every findings page in the Security Hub console, including Threats, Exposure, Vulnerabilities, Posture Management, Sensitive Data, and All Findings, without building and maintaining their own extraction pipelines.

With this launch, you can start an export on demand from the findings page you are viewing and have Security Hub deliver the results to an S3 bucket in your account. You can choose CSV when you want to review or share findings in a spreadsheet or export in JSON if you need these findings in Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) format.

Findings export is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Security Hub is available. To learn more, visit the AWS Security Hub User Guide at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/securityhub-v2-findings-export.html.

item.title: Amazon EC2 R8gd instances are now available in additional regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon EC2, R8gd instances, Graviton4, bandwidth, EFA networking

Summary: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) R8gd instances are now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances are equipped with up to 11.4 TB of local NVMe-based SSD storage and operate on AWS Graviton4 processors, delivering up to 30% better performance compared to Graviton3-based instances. Built on the AWS Nitro System, R8gd instances are ideal for applications requiring high-speed, low-latency local storage. There are 12 different sizes of R8gd instances available, offering up to 50 Gbps of network bandwidth and up to 40 Gbps for Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS). Additionally, users can customize network and EBS bandwidth by 25% using the EC2 instance bandwidth weighting configuration, enhancing flexibility for workload optimization. Selected sizes, including 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl, support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking. This feature set positions R8gd instances as a powerful option for high-performance computing needs.

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) R8gd instances are available in AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances feature up to 11.4 TB of local NVMe-based SSD block-level storage and are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors, delivering up to 30% better performance over Graviton3-based instances. These instances are built on the AWS Nitro System and are a great fit for applications that need access to high-speed, low latency local storage. 
 
R8gd instances are available in 12 different sizes. They provide up to 50 Gbps of network bandwidth and up to 40 Gbps of bandwidth to the Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS). Additionally, customers can now adjust the network and Amazon EBS bandwidth on these instances by 25% using EC2 instance bandwidth weighting conﬁguration, providing greater ﬂexibility with the allocation of bandwidth resources to better optimize workloads. These instances offer Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) networking on 24xlarge, 48xlarge, metal-24xl, and metal-48xl sizes.

To learn more, see R8gd instances. To explore how to migrate your workloads to Graviton-based instances, see AWS Graviton Fast Start program. To get started, see the AWS Management Console.

item.title: Amazon EC2 R8g instances now available in additional regions
item.content:encoded:

Summary: Starting today, Amazon EC2 R8g instances are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors, offering up to 30% better performance compared to Graviton3-based instances. R8g instances are particularly suited for memory-intensive workloads like databases, in-memory caches, and real-time big data analytics. They utilize a specialized architecture that enhances performance and security by offloading CPU virtualization, storage, and networking functions to dedicated hardware and software. AWS Graviton4-based instances stand out for their performance and energy efficiency across various workloads. R8g instances feature larger sizes with up to 3x more vCPUs and memory than their Graviton3 counterparts, with up to 48xlarge configurations and 1.5TB of memory. They deliver significant performance gains, being 30% faster for web applications, 40% for databases, and 45% for large Java applications compared to R7g instances. Available in 12 sizes—including two bare metal—R8g instances provide enhanced networking bandwidth of up to 50 Gbps and 40 Gbps to Amazon EBS.

Starting today, Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) R8g instances are available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud (Germany) region. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton4 processors and deliver up to 30% better performance compared to AWS Graviton3-based instances. Amazon EC2 R8g instances are ideal for memory-intensive workloads such as databases, in-memory caches, and real-time big data analytics. item.title: Amazon Bedrock now supports reasoning summaries for OpenAI models
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Bedrock, reasoning.summary, OpenAI models, Responses API, human-readable summary

Summary: Amazon Bedrock has introduced the reasoning.summary parameter for OpenAI models through the Responses API. This new feature enables users to request a human-readable summary of how a model arrived at its response. It enhances understanding of complex tasks such as coding, analysis, and multi-step problem-solving. By providing insights into the model’s reasoning process, reasoning summaries offer developers greater context for evaluating responses and debugging their applications. This capability also assists in demonstrating to users how the model approached their requests. The reasoning summaries are included in the summary array of the reasoning output item, alongside the model’s answer. Importantly, this feature is available for all OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock and spans all AWS Regions where these models are accessible. This includes in-Region inference as well as geographic and global cross-Region inference. For more information, users can consult the OpenAI documentation and access guidance for getting started with OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock.

Amazon Bedrock now supports the reasoning.summary parameter for OpenAI models through the Responses API. This capability lets you request a human-readable summary of a model’s reasoning alongside its response, helping you understand its approach to complex tasks such as coding, analysis, and multi-step problem solving.

Reasoning summaries give developers additional context for evaluating responses, debugging applications, and showing users how a model approached a request. The summary is returned in the summary array of the reasoning output item, alongside the model’s answer.

This capability is available for all OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock in all AWS Regions where OpenAI GPT models are available, including in-Region inference, geographic (GEO) cross-Region inference, and global cross-Region inference.

To learn more, see the OpenAI documentation on reasoning summaries. To get started with OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock, see documentation here.

item.title: Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 are now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
item.content:encoded:

Summary: Two new Anthropic models are now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Claude Opus 5.5 is the most capable Opus model to date, improving on Opus 5 for long-running agentic coding. It intelligently adapts its effort per task, achieving roughly 40% fewer tool calls and about half the token usage compared to Opus 5 based on Kiro's internal benchmarks. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is the fastest Sonnet model, designed as an upgrade for teams using Sonnet 5. This model also offers a 1M context window, with a 1.3x credit multiplier. Users are encouraged to update their IDE or CLI to the latest version and restart it to access these new models through the model selector. For further details, users can consult the official resources or reach out to their AWS account team. More information about Kiro is also available online.

Two new Anthropic models are now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

item.title: Amazon Connect Customer now provides automated checks to improve performance evaluation forms
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Connect, performance evaluation, AI scoring, best practices, automated check

Summary: Amazon Connect has introduced a feature that enhances the accuracy of performance evaluation forms by using AI. Managers can now run an automated check on their evaluation forms with a single click to compare them against best practices. This feature identifies evaluation questions that lack context necessary for reliable AI scoring, providing managers with a list of these questions along with specific suggestions for improvement. For instance, a question like "Did the agent provide a sales disclosure?" may be flagged, prompting the manager to clarify what exact disclosures are required. This tool aids managers in creating more precise forms, ensuring fair and accurate evaluations of both human and AI agents. As a result, it helps reduce the time spent on refining evaluation forms, making the evaluation process more efficient. Additionally, this feature is available in several AWS Regions, including US, Canada, and various locations in Europe and Asia Pacific. For more information, users can visit the relevant Amazon Connect pages regarding the new features and pricing options.

Amazon Connect Customer now suggests changes to performance evaluation forms that improve the accuracy of evaluations automatically filled by AI. While setting up an evaluation form, managers can run an automated check that compares the form against best practices with a single click. Managers then receive a list of evaluation questions that are missing context for AI to score reliably, along with suggestions to make them more specific. For example, the check might flag "Did the agent provide a sales disclosure?" and prompt the manager to define exactly what the agent must disclose before a sale. This helps managers automatically score human and AI agents fairly and accurately, while spending less time refining their evaluation forms.

This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, please visit our documentation and our webpage. For information about Amazon Connect Customer pricing, please visit our pricing page.

item.title: Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon S3, Vectors, metadata, pre-filtering, AWS GovCloud

Summary: Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. This feature evaluates metadata filters before running similarity searches, enabling up to 5x more matching vectors, particularly when filters are selective. A new prefix match operator ($startsWith) has been introduced for filtering values like paths and URLs. These enhancements improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications by providing more relevant results. S3 Vectors ensures native storage and querying of vectors in Amazon S3, offering a cost-effective solution optimized for billion-vector scale. By default, new vector buckets in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions will use metadata pre-filtering, which requires no modification to vector writing through PutVectors or when executing filtered queries with QueryVectors. Existing indexes can utilize pre-filtering by updating them via the UpdateIndexMode API. Additionally, users can compare pre-filtering with current filtering on the same index per-query before updating. Metadata pre-filtering incurs no extra cost in all commercial AWS Regions with Amazon S3 Vectors and is also being deployed in AWS China Regions. Users can start utilizing this feature through the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console.

Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Pre-filtering evaluates metadata filters before running similarity search, returning up to 5x more of the matching vectors when your filter is selective. S3 Vectors also adds a prefix match operator ($startsWith) for filtering on values like paths and URLs. Together, these improvements give your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications more complete results when you filter, so your applications return more relevant answers.

S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in new vector buckets in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions use metadata pre-filtering by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use pre-filtering on an existing index, update it in place with the UpdateIndexMode API. You can also compare pre-filtering against your current filtering on the same index, using a per-query parameter on QueryVectors, before you update.

Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. We are in the process of deploying this change and plan to complete the deployment in the coming days. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation and the AWS News blog.

item.title: AWS Lambda supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Lambda, OAuth, Kafka, ESM, authentication

Summary: AWS Lambda has introduced OAuth authentication support for Event Streaming Management (ESM) with Kafka, including self-managed clusters and managed services like Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. This enhancement allows customers to authenticate Lambda Kafka consumers via their enterprise identity providers, meeting security and compliance requirements for Kafka applications. Use cases for event-driven Kafka workloads span payment processing, fraud detection, and real-time data pipelines, leveraging Lambda’s Kafka ESM to facilitate serverless consumers. Previously, Kafka ESM only supported authentication methods like SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mutual TLS (mTLS), which restricted access for customers in regulated industries requiring OAuth. Now, organizations can utilize their enterprise identity providers, such as Okta, to authenticate Kafka ESM, ensuring consistent identity governance and access policies across Kafka clusters and Lambda consumers. This new capability is available wherever self-managed Kafka ESM is supported. To implement OAuth authentication, users can create a new Kafka ESM with their authentication configuration through various AWS interfaces, including the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS SAM. For further information, customers are encouraged to refer to AWS documentation.

AWS Lambda now supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event source mappings (ESM), including Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. With this launch, customers can authenticate their Lambda Kafka consumers through their enterprise identity provider, helping them meet the security and compliance requirements for their Kafka applications.

Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as payment processing, fraud detection, and real-time data pipelines use Kafka ESM to build serverless Kafka consumers. Kafka ESM provides automatic scaling, error handling, batching, and event filtering. Previously, Kafka ESM supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mutual TLS (mTLS) as authentication methods, so customers in regulated industries that require OAuth could not use Kafka ESM with their clusters. With OAuth support, customers can use their enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta, to authenticate their Kafka ESM and apply the same identity governance and access policies across their Kafka clusters and Lambda consumers.

This capability is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To use OAuth authentication, create a new Kafka ESM with your authentication configuration through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS SAM. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda developer guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

item.title: Amazon Quick now supports brand templates for on-brand presentations and documents
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon Quick, brand templates, visual identity, brand managers, permissions

Summary: Starting today, Amazon Quick allows users to upload brand templates, enabling the creation of presentations and documents that align with approved visual identities. Brand managers can upload PowerPoint or Word templates, or utilize files from connected storage like SharePoint. Quick automatically extracts essential brand elements such as colors, fonts, logos, and layouts for review and editing by brand managers before publication organization-wide. The platform ensures adherence to brand rules during asset creation; if a request violates any rule, Quick will explain the issue and suggest compliant alternatives. For each new task, Quick intelligently selects the most appropriate template based on guidelines provided by brand managers, while users retain the option to choose different templates if desired. Administrators have control over which team members can create and publish brand templates, using customized permissions to ensure that only authorized individuals from brand, marketing, or other designated teams can define visual standards. Brand assets are currently accessible in the Amazon Quick desktop application, and users can start utilizing these features within minutes.

Starting today, you can upload brand templates in Amazon Quick, allowing you to create presentations and documents that match your approved visual identity. Brand managers set up a template once and everyone gets on-brand output, without hunting for the right file in each chat.

Brand managers upload PowerPoint or Word templates, or pull them from a connected file store such as SharePoint. Quick extracts the colors, fonts, logos, layouts and brand rules from each file. A brand manager reviews and edits what Quick found before publishing it to the whole organization.

Quick also follows a template's rules as it creates new assets. If a request breaks a rule, Quick explains why and suggests an on-brand alternative. For each task, Quick picks the best-fit template based on guidance the brand manager writes. Users can still choose a different template.

Administrators decide who can create and publish brand templates using custom permissions, ensuring that only the proper members of brand, marketing, or other approved teams can set visual standards. 

Brand assets are generally available today in the Amazon Quick desktop app. To learn more, see the Amazon Quick documentation, or create an account for free and start using Quick in minutes.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon SageMaker, Unified Studio, Tooling blueprints, CloudFormation, project environment

Summary: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio has introduced support for custom Tooling blueprints, enabling domain administrators to define project foundations through their own AWS CloudFormation templates. This allows for customization of project environments to align with organization-specific needs, including adhering to company naming standards for IAM role names and custom permissions boundaries rather than relying on AWS managed policies. Administrators begin by creating a CloudFormation template that outlines the desired project environment and then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service ensures the validity of the template during registration and checks for required resources at each project deployment, safeguarding against issues before team usage. The templates can feature any resource supported by CloudFormation, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and are designed to operate seamlessly across multiple AWS accounts and regions without the need for per-project modifications. During deployment, reserved template parameters, such as project ID and domain ID, are automatically populated, allowing administrators to set up their templates once and apply them universally across projects. This feature is accessible in all regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available.

Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints, giving domain administrators the ability to define the foundation of every project by using their own AWS CloudFormation templates. Administrators can tailor project environments to meet organization-specific requirements, such as IAM role names that comply with company naming standards or custom permissions boundaries instead of AWS managed policies.

Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio administrators start by authoring a CloudFormation template that describes the project environment they need, then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service validates the template at registration and again after each project deployment, confirming that the required resources exist before any team member uses the project. Templates can include any CloudFormation-supported resource, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and work across multiple AWS accounts and Regions without per-project edits. At deployment time, the service automatically populates reserved template parameters, such as the project ID and domain ID, so administrators define the template once and apply it everywhere.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, visit the Custom blueprints as Tooling documentation.

item.title: TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 model now available on Amazon Bedrock
item.content:encoded:
Amazon Bedrock now supports TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5, a video-to-text model that generates structured, time-coded metadata from video. Until now, finding a moment in a large video library meant knowing where to look before you could ask about it. Pegasus 1.5 reads an entire video and labels what happens and when, turning footage into data your applications can query.

You define what matters to your business, such as editorial segments, speaker changes, sports plays, or brand appearances, and Pegasus 1.5 finds those moments across the video and returns them with timestamps. It analyzes what it sees, hears, and reads on screen in a single pass, with no pre-indexing or ingestion pipeline to build first.

Pegasus 1.5 is accessible through the US and Global cross-Region inference profiles. To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock product page, access the model in the Amazon Bedrock console, or see the Amazon Bedrock documentation for supported Regions, APIs, features, and pricing.

item.title: Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection now detects data exfiltration and destruction in Aurora and RDS databases
item.content:encoded:
Amazon GuardDuty announces an expansion of RDS Protection that extends threat detection beyond login anomalies to identify data exfiltration and data destruction attacks targeting Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL databases. Available as RDS Protection for data activity, this new capability uses machine learning (ML)-based anomaly detection and integrated threat intelligence to continuously monitor database query patterns, helping you detect unusual data activity without requiring any agents, additional infrastructure, or database configuration changes.

As attackers increasingly target databases to exfiltrate or destroy critical data after obtaining valid credentials through phishing, social engineering, or misconfiguration, their malicious database activity can appear indistinguishable from legitimate application behavior.  RDS Protection for data activity establishes behavioral baselines for normal query patterns enabling GuardDuty to detect threats that traditional tools miss. 

You can enable GuardDuty RDS Protection for data activity as an add-on to RDS Protection for login activity. With a single click, they can enable it for their entire organization in the GuardDuty console, or programmatically via APIs, SDKs, CLI, or AWS CloudFormation. A 30-day free trial is available per account per Region.

This feature is available today in all AWS commercial Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, where Amazon GuardDuty RDS Protection is offered with support for Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. For supported versions visit GuardDuty RDS Protection documentation.  

To learn more and start your free trial, visit the Amazon GuardDuty product page.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.15: Read PSL block members from symbols instead of syntax nodes (#30674)
item.content:encoded:
Linked issue

n/a. First slice of the PSL mixins project; the project spec and plan
are in projects/psl-mixins/.

At a glance

export interface BlockSymbol {
  readonly kind: 'block';
  readonly name: string;
  readonly keyword: string;
  readonly node: GenericBlockDeclarationAst;
  readonly span: PslSpan;
  readonly entries: readonly KeyValuePairAst[];
  readonly attributes: readonly ResolvedAttribute<ModelAttributeAst>[];
}
- for (const entry of block.node.entries()) {
+ for (const entry of block.entries) {

Before this PR a generic block symbol (an enum, a policy_select, any
extension block) carried only its name, keyword and syntax node, and
every consumer read the block's entries and attributes from the node.

Summary

A consumer of the PSL symbol table now reads a declaration's members
from its symbol and never from the symbol's syntax node. This makes
buildSymbolTable the one place that decides which members a block has,
which the mixins work needs: a mixin's members will be added to a block
there, and every consumer has to see them. This PR changes no behaviour
and does not mention mixins in code.

Decision

  1. BlockSymbol gains entries and attributes, filled once by
    buildBlock in source order. entries is a list, not a record, because
    a map-mode block may repeat a key.
  2. All 23 production sites that read members through symbol.node read
    the symbol's records: the binder, the block-spec interpreter and the
    enum-member check in psl-parser; the SQL interpreter and attribute
    specs; the Prisma 7 and Prisma 6 interpreters; the language server's
    rename provider.

Reviewer notes

  • Two places paired lists by index and no longer do.
    bindAttributes in
    binder.ts
    and the model-attribute loop in the SQL
    interpreter.ts
    walked node.attributes() and the resolved attribute list side by side.
    Each now takes the syntax node from the resolved attribute's own node.
    The six if (node === undefined) continue; guards removed from the SQL
    interpreter were unreachable: model.attributes is built from
    node.attributes(), so the two lists always had the same length and
    order.
  • Node identity is preserved. The binder keys its tables by
    syntax-node identity. Red nodes are cached per parent slot, so
    block.entries[i] and attribute.node are the same objects a fresh
    traversal returns.
  • interpretExtensionBlockAttributes in
    block-spec/interpret.ts
    reads name, span and args from the resolved attribute. They are
    computed by the same expressions it used inline before.
  • Deliberately not changed: code that walks the syntax tree with no
    symbol in hand (completion, semantic tokens, the formatter), and
    fieldTakesMap in rename.ts finding a field's owner through
    field.node.syntax.parent.
  • Project artifacts. projects/psl-mixins/ is added in this PR: the
    project spec and plan, a brief used for the team's syntax discussion,
    and this slice's spec, plan and dispatch briefs. The folder is removed
    at project close-out.

Testing performed

  • pnpm --filter @internal/psl-parser test: 67 files, 1405 tests pass,
    including six new symbol-table tests (source order, repeated keys, enum
    members with @ attributes, block @@ attributes, a block inside a
    namespace, an empty block). No existing assertion was edited.
  • pnpm lint:deps, pnpm fixtures:check (no fixture changed), and
    lint for the four touched packages: pass.
  • pnpm typecheck: 170 of 171 tasks pass. prisma7-adoption#typecheck
    fails on my machine because Prisma 7 publishes no schema engine for the
    linux-nixos platform.
  • pnpm test:packages: 1735 of 1738 files pass (24824 tests). Three
    tarball-install tests (@prisma/orm-framework all-shells-tarball and
    module-identity, @prisma/orm-target-postgres cross-shell-tarball)
    fail locally with pnpm's ERR_PNPM_TRUST_DOWNGRADE for
    @vercel/detect-agent@1.2.5.
  • The four local failures reproduce with this PR's changes stashed. CI
    is the check for them.
  • rg "\.node\.(fields|members|attributes|entries)\(\)" packages -g '*.ts' --glob '!**/test/**' --glob '!**/dist/**' returns nothing.

Skill update

n/a — internal only.

Alternatives considered

  • Leave consumers reading the node and teach each one about mixins
    later.     That would put mixin knowledge into two family interpreters,
    two legacy-schema interpreters, the binder and the language server.
    Reading from the symbol keeps it in the symbol table.
  • entries as a record keyed by entry name. Rejected because
    map-mode blocks allow a repeated key, and order matters to consumers.

Checklist

  • All commits are signed off (git commit -s) per the
    DCO.
  • I read CONTRIBUTING.md and the change is
    scoped to one logical concern.
  • Tests are updated (or n/a if the change is doc-only / refactor
    with no behavioural delta).
  • The PR title is in TML-NNNN: <sentence-case title> form. No
    Linear ticket is used for this project.
  • The Skill update section above is filled in (or stated n/a — internal only).

🤖 Generated with Claude Code

Summary by CodeRabbit

  • Bug Fixes
  • Schema blocks and attributes are interpreted consistently across
    authoring tools, language services, and database integrations. Block
    entries retain source order and repeated keys, while attribute
    diagnostics continue to use accurate source locations.
  • Documentation
  • Clarified that symbols expose their declaration members, including
    block entries and attributes.

item.title: v8.0.0-rc.17-dev.11: The binder resolves entity names in type-constructor arguments (#30659)
item.content:encoded:
The PSL binder records a resolution for the entity name inside a
type-constructor argument, such as OrderStatus in status pg.enum(OrderStatus). Go-to-definition, hover, find references and
rename now work on such a name. Renaming a native_enum block renames
its pg.enum(...) usages, which #30633 left unchanged.

Changes

  • Binder
    (packages/1-framework/2-authoring/psl-parser/src/binder.ts): for a
    type whose name resolves to a constructor that declares entityRefArg,
    the positional argument at entityRefArg.index is bound through the
    path an entityRef attribute argument takes (writtenEntityReference,
    resolveEntity). It applies to fields of models, fields of composite
    types and named types. An unknown name is reported as
    PSL_UNRESOLVED_REFERENCE, Cannot find entity "X", on the argument.
    An argument that is not a name gets no resolution and no diagnostic. The
    binder does not read entityKind.
  • Tests: binder cases in binder-contributed-types.test.ts; two
    find-references cases for a constructor argument in the language
    server's references.test.ts. No language-server source change.

No interpreter is changed.

Known consequences

The SQL interpreter still resolves the constructor argument from its
written text. With the binder also binding it:

  • An unknown name in pg.enum(...) gets two diagnostics: the binder's
    PSL_UNRESOLVED_REFERENCE on the argument and the interpreter's
    existing PSL_UNKNOWN_ENTITY_REF on the type.
  • A top-level model that names, unqualified, a native_enum declared
    inside namespace public { } now gets Cannot find entity "X" from the
    binder: a name inside a namespace is not in scope outside it, as for
    models. public.X satisfies the binder, but the interpreter does not
    accept a qualified name, so such a schema has to declare the enum at top
    level or move the model into the namespace.

Verification

  • psl-parser tests (1399), typecheck and lint pass; language-server
    tests (1067), typecheck and lint pass.
  • SQL contract-psl tests (714) and the Postgres target's pg.enum
    column tests pass unchanged; pnpm fixtures:check passes.
  • A QA run drove the built CLI over stdio with the Postgres target:
    renaming native_enum OrderStatus from its declaration and from the
    pg.enum argument edits both and leaves no diagnostics. That run was
    made while the branch also contained an interpreter change, which has
    since been removed; it was not repeated.

item.title: AWS Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Dashboards now support Amazon Bedrock product attributes
item.content:encoded:
**Keywords:** AWS Cost Explorer, Amazon Bedrock, model attributes, cost management, AWS Budgets

Summary: AWS has enhanced its cost management tools to allow users to analyze Amazon Bedrock costs by new product attributes. This feature enables users in finance and platform teams to break down Bedrock spending by specific model types, such as Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5, as well as model providers like Anthropic and Cohere. The new dimensions include inference types (input tokens or output tokens) and features (on-demand inference or reranker). Users can group and filter costs based on these attributes in AWS Cost Explorer and Dashboards, making it easier to identify which models and workloads contribute to overall Bedrock expenditure. In AWS Budgets, similar filters allow for better budget monitoring. Users can also utilize cost allocation tags associated with inference profiles, projects, or workspaces, alongside IAM principal tags for user-specific spending insights. This allows for effective analysis of application costs tied to each model or user role. The Amazon Bedrock product attribute dimension is now available across all AWS Regions, except for AWS GovCloud and specific China Regions, at no extra charge. For further details, users can refer to the relevant user guides.

AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now let you analyze Amazon Bedrock costs by product attributes, a new dimension that breaks down Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature. In Cost Explorer and Dashboards, you can group and filter costs by these attributes. In Budgets, you can filter budgets by the same attributes.

With this launch, finance and platform teams get a direct view of which models and workloads drive their Bedrock spend, and can act on it in the billing tools they already use. The attributes include model (such as Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5), model provider (such as Anthropic or Cohere), inference type (such as input tokens or output tokens), and feature (such as on-demand inference or reranker). You can combine product attributes with cost allocation tags on application inference profiles, projects, or workspaces to see which applications drive spend on each model, and with IAM principal tags to see which users or roles drive it. Group a month of Bedrock spend by model in Cost Explorer to find your most expensive models, build a dashboard widget that tracks cost per provider, or set a budget that alerts on spend for a single model.

The Amazon Bedrock product attribute dimension is available today at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, excluding the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China (Beijing) and China (Ningxia) Regions. To learn more, see the user guides for Cost Explorer, Budgets, and Dashboards.

item.title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports minor version upgrade prechecks and a new RDS event to help reduce patching downtime
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: RDS for Oracle, minor version upgrade, precheck, maintenance, event notifications

Summary: RDS for Oracle has introduced a new feature that allows users to run minor version upgrade prechecks before initiating an upgrade or during a maintenance window. This new functionality, accessible via the `rdsadmin.rdsadmin_precheck_tasks.precheck_minor_upgrade` procedure, conducts checks for potential issues such as insufficient free storage and invalid Oracle-maintained objects. The precheck is read-only and does not impact workload, allowing users to identify and resolve issues prior to the scheduled upgrade. Additionally, during minor version upgrades or operating system updates, RDS for Oracle emits the RDS-EVENT-0596 event, indicating when the DB instance is ready to accept connections again. This allows applications to reconnect even while other maintenance tasks continue, resulting in reduced downtime. Users can subscribe to this event through Amazon RDS event notifications or Amazon EventBridge for automated reconnection processes. These enhancements are available across all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is offered, improving operational efficiency for database management. For further information, users are encouraged to refer to the Amazon RDS User Guide.

Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now lets you run a minor version upgrade precheck yourself, before you start an upgrade or before your scheduled maintenance window. RDS for Oracle now also emits a new event during patching that tells you when your DB instance is accepting connections again. With this event, you can bring your applications back while the remaining maintenance tasks are still in progress, which can reduce your application downtime during patching.

At the start of every minor version upgrade, RDS for Oracle checks for conditions that would prevent the upgrade from completing, such as insufficient free storage, invalid Oracle-maintained objects, or invalid triggers. If a check finds a problem, the upgrade stops, and you must fix the problem and schedule the upgrade again. Previously, these checks ran only as part of the upgrade itself. With the new rdsadmin.rdsadmin_precheck_tasks.precheck_minor_upgrade procedure, you can run the checks at any time. The precheck is read-only and doesn't affect your workload. It reports every issue it finds in a single log so you can fix them and run the precheck again until it passes before your maintenance window.

During a minor version upgrade or an operating system update, RDS for Oracle now emits RDS-EVENT-0596 as soon as your DB instance is accepting connections. Any remaining maintenance tasks then complete while your database is online. You can subscribe to this event through Amazon RDS event notifications or Amazon EventBridge to automate application reconnection or notify your teams that the database is back online.

These capabilities are available in all AWS commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more, see Running minor version upgrade prechecks in Amazon RDS for Oracle, Amazon RDS event categories and event messages, and Monitoring Amazon RDS events in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

item.title: AWS Network Firewall adds wildcard support for container attribute filters
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: AWS Network Firewall, wildcard matching, container attributes, Amazon EKS, security coverage

Summary: AWS Network Firewall has introduced wildcard matching in container attribute-based inspection filters for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) and Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS). This enhancement enables users to define attribute filters using wildcard patterns, allowing for the grouping of multiple container workloads under a single rule. For example, a pattern like app=payments-* can match all variations of an application such as payments-api, payments-worker, and payments-cron. This feature considerably streamlines firewall rule management within dynamic container environments where new application variants are frequently introduced. By reducing the need for individual container associations for each variant, it lowers operational overhead while ensuring consistent security across containerized workloads. Wildcard support is available in all AWS Regions that currently support container attribute-based inspection through AWS Network Firewall. Users looking to incorporate this feature or learn more about it can visit the AWS Network Firewall and service documentation for guidance.

AWS Network Firewall now supports wildcard matching in container attribute-based inspection filters for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). This enhancement allows you to define attribute filters using wildcard patterns to match multiple container workloads in a single rule, eliminating the need to create individual container associations for each variant.

With wildcard support, you can use patterns like app=payments-* to automatically cover all variants of an application, such as payments-api, payments-worker, and payments-cron. This simplifies firewall rule management for dynamic container environments where new application variants are frequently deployed, reducing operational overhead and ensuring consistent security coverage across your containerized workloads. 

Wildcard support for container attribute filters is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Network Firewall container attribute-based inspection is supported. For a full list of supported Regions, see the AWS Region Table.

To get started, visit AWS Network Firewall product page and service documentation.

item.title: Amazon GameLift Servers adds CPU burstability for container fleets
item.content:encoded:
Keywords: Amazon GameLift, CPU burstability, container fleets, game developers, performance headroom

Summary: Amazon GameLift Servers now offers CPU burstability for container fleets, enhancing flexibility in resource allocation for game developers. Previously, container fleets operated on a fixed CPU value that restricted both container packing density and imposed a strict runtime cap. This limitation forced developers to balance efficient resource use against the need for performance headroom. Game server workloads are inherently bursty, with CPU demands low during regular gameplay but spiking during critical tasks like physics calculations and AI processing. With the introduction of CPU burstability, developers can now optimize container packing based on average CPU needs while allowing processes to access additional idle CPU resources during peak demand. This opt-in feature is configurable for each container group and facilitates high-density deployments without compromising peak performance. Furthermore, CPU burstability is included at no extra cost as part of the standard pricing for container fleets. The feature is available in all AWS Regions that support container fleets, except for China Regions. For more detailed information about CPU burstability in Amazon GameLift Servers, users are encouraged to visit the relevant resources online.

Amazon GameLift Servers now supports CPU burstability for container fleets, giving game developers greater flexibility in how compute resources are allocated and consumed at runtime. Previously, container fleets relied on a fixed CPU value that simultaneously controlled both container packing density and imposed a hard runtime cap. This dual constraint forced developers to choose between efficient resource utilization and maintaining performance headroom for their game server workloads.

Game server workloads are inherently bursty, CPU demand stays low during most of a match but spikes sharply during physics calculations, AI processing, or collision detection. With CPU burstability, developers can now pack containers based on typical CPU needs while still allowing game server processes to burst into available idle instance CPU during peak demand moments. This opt-in feature is configured per container group definition, supports high-density deployments without sacrificing peak performance, and is included at no additional cost as part of standard container fleet pricing.

CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets is available in all AWS Regions where container fleets are supported, excluding China Regions.

To learn more about CPU burstability for Amazon GameLift Servers container fleets, visit the Amazon GameLift Servers Developer Guide or explore the Amazon GameLift Servers product page.
